The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges may be filed.

News.title: Britain to hold fresh talks with Mauritius next week as Burnham pushes ahead with Chagos deal
News.content:
ISLE TALK Britain to hold fresh talks with Mauritius next week as Burnham pushes ahead with Chagos deal

BRITAIN will hold fresh talks with Mauritius next week as Andy Burnham pushes ahead with Sir Keir Starmer’s controversial Chagos Islands deal.

Mauritian officials told The Sun they are due to meet the Foreign Office over the stalled agreement.



It comes after Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran defended the deal in the Commons yesterday and confirmed cash for the treaty remained budgeted for.

But Andy Burnham himself has yet to publicly set out his position on the agreement since entering No10.



Mauritius has now made clear it remains determined to push the deal over the line – with officials from the two countries having already met in July.

A spokesperson for the Mauritian Attorney General told The Sun: “Engagement between Mauritius and the United Kingdom on the Agreement is ongoing.



“Officials from both sides met in July, and a further meeting between the Mauritian team and the FCDO is scheduled for next week.

“Mauritius remains fully committed to the Agreement and to seeing it through to completion.”

The deal would hand sovereignty of the Indian Ocean archipelago to Mauritius while Britain pays to lease back Diego Garcia, home to a crucial joint UK-US military base.

But it has been stuck in limbo since February after President Trump withdrew his support and branded it a “great act of stupidity”.



It leaves Mr Burnham facing an early diplomatic headache over whether to press ahead with his predecessor’s agreement.

The PM risks a clash with Mauritius if Britain walks away but could put himself on a collision course with the White House if he pushes ahead.

The fresh talks also come just weeks before the UN General Assembly in New York, where Mauritius is expected to press Britain for progress.

Ms Kumaran told MPs yesterday that maintaining long-term operational control of Diego Garcia was a “top priority” and the “entire basis” of the agreement.

She also said Britain’s defence was best served by securing “legal certainty” over the islands.



The Tories have demanded Mr Burnham ditch the agreement, which they have branded a surrender of British territory.

Shadow Defence Secretary James Cartlidge said: “The Chagos surrender deal has damaged our global reputation and will put our security and that of our allies at risk. It belongs on the ash heap of history.

“Burnham should show some backbone and break with this terrible legacy of the Starmer years by ditching his crazy Chagos deal once and for all, and spending the savings on our armed forces.”

News.title: Europe’s loneliest school on ‘island within an island’ opens its gates… with just one pupil
News.content:
THE smallest school in Europe is set to open its doors this month, for just one pupil.

The young student will have the entire classroom to themselves when term starts on September 10.



Six-year old Aysha is set to become the only pupil at a new school opening in Ginostra on the Italian island of Stromboli, the Daily Mail reports.

This is a small village of around 40 residents on the island famous for its perpetually active volcano.



Residents in the tiny village once had its own school, but it closed due to the dwindling number of residents.

Local authorities agreed to reopen it after Aysha’s parents, Monica Abbate and Raffa Bazine, warned they would have to relocate in order to educate their daughter.

They also insist that she is happy as a sole pupil.

“We love this little paradise, the nature, the sea, even the volcano that looms over our homes. We don’t want to have to leave,’ Mr Bazine said.

“She hangs out with peers who stay here for months at a time, and she’s learned a few words of German from the neighbours’ children who go on vacation in Ginostra. She’s a happy child.”

The school will be located in a building owned by the local parish of the Catholic Church.



Ginostra is one of three villages on the island alongside San Bartolo and San Vincenzo.

It is so isolated that residents have dubbed it “the island within an island”.

The island and its active volcano have become iconic in popular culture, with J.R.R Tolkien claiming he based the fictional volcano, Mount Doom of Mordor on Stromboli.

Earlier this month, Britan’s smallest school in Wales closed its doors after its two remaining pupils headed off to secondary school.

Ysgol Y Garreg school, located in Penrhyndeudraeth, North Wales, shut at the end of August after 100 years.

News.title: Brit arrested after ‘stabbing wife, 34, to death with scissors in front of their son, 4, at luxury hotel’ in Albufeira
News.content:
HOTEL HORROR Brit arrested after ‘stabbing wife, 34, to death with scissors in front of their son, 4, at luxury hotel’ in Albufeira

A BRITISH man allegedly stabbed his wife to death with a pair of scissors in front of their son at a luxury hotel in Portugal.

The boy witnessed the horror on the eve of his fourth birthday, which he was due to celebrate on the family holiday today.



The 34-year-old mum bled to death at the scene after suffering multiple stab wounds in the Algarve resort of Albufeira at 6.45pm on Tuesday.

Emergency crews found the woman already beyond hope and her partner covered in blood at the four star Alfagar Alto Da Colina apart-hotel.



The traumatised child was found nearby and appeared to have suffered a leg injury in the deadly struggle.

A Portuguese source told The Sun: “She died after being stabbed with a pair of scissors in the corridor after running out of the room.”



The source added: “The couple began fighting inside a room on the second floor and the woman died of her wounds after running into the corridor.

“The child was with them and will have seen what happened and also seems to have been hurt.



“When police got there the woman was already dead and there was blood smeared all over the walls of the corridor outside their room.

“The crime scene was awful and the child has been taken into temporary care.”

Paramedics said the woman was already dead when they arrived at the scene and had suffered “multiple knife wounds” after being attacked in a hotel corridor.

Portuguese judicial police officers backed by forensic teams in protective clothing gear were seen taking photos of the scene at the four-star resort.

The victim’s partner remained in custody following the incident, being described by police as a “hotel homicide”.



Portugal’s national police force was also conducting inquiries but was not releasing the identities of either the victim or her partner.

The suspect remained in police custody this morning and is due to appear before a judge and is expected to be remanded in custody at a closed-court hearing.

The luxury resort is described online as having “striking sea views” and being within walking distance of the beach.

News.title: Radio hosts slammed for accusing shark attack victim of ‘lying’ after brave mum opened up about near-deadly ordeal
News.content:
THREE radio presenters are under fire for accusing a shark attack victim of lying about her traumatic story.

During an on-air discussion, a trio of Australian radio hosts questioned Leah Stewart’s account of the horrific shark attack she experienced on June 13.



Leah Stewart, a 35-year-old Australian mother, discussed on 60 Minutes how she was mauled by a great white shark on June 13 while swimming at Coogee Beach, Sydney.

She spent two weeks in a coma after being pulled out of the sea in “a pool of her own blood”.



In the emotional interview, Leah described the moment she went into “survival mode” to stay alive for her one-year-old daughter August.

Face-to-face with the shark she decided to punch it with her left arm, which she was more “willing to lose” because she is right-handed.



Melbourne FOXFM radio hosts Brendan Fevola, Nick Cody and Kate Langbroek discussed Leah’s interview on the Monday episode of the Fifi, Fev & Nick breakfast show.

Fevola cast doubt on whether Leah would have had ‘time to think’ during the attack.

Langbroek replied: “No, most people say you don’t even know what’s happening.”

Fevola added: “I was on the couch with my wife Alex going, “She’s lying! Too much time to think!’ You’re not thinking all that, are you?



“Come on, oh right or left? Like bro, you are amazing – you punched a shark in the face and survived – but you’re not thinking all that. That’s a lot of mayo.”

Fevola shockingly accused Leah of lying about choosing which limb she was willing to lose, given that she was right-handed.

However, the former AFL player admitted had he been in the same position, he “would have had a heart attack and would have been eaten.”



The trio then played videos of Leah recalling the terrifying attack and questioned how she remembered so many details.

Co-host Cody jumped to Leah’s defence saying: “You hear the phrase ‘Time stands still’. Is there a chance time stood still?”

Langbroek called it unusual and joked “the only other person I know who has punched a shark is Mick Fanning.”

She said: “He said at the time he didn’t even have a chance to think about what he was doing, it was like a reflex.”

Despite admiring Leah’s bravery, Fevola claimed she had embellished the story, putting “mayo” and “GST” on top of it.



“I’m so sorry for what happened to you and you’re an amazing woman because you have fought off a shark, but you’re not thinking all that,” Fevola continued.

Kate Langbroek was standing in for regular presenter Fifi Box.

The radio exchange immediately sparked outrage with listeners appalled by the lack of empathy and sensitivity from the hosts.



One listener wrote: “You had every opportunity to comment on what an incredible survival story it was instead you had to dampen it. Yet again the same old rhetoric of a man questioning the credibility of a woman’s story.”

Another called for the radio station to “Fire them pronto.”

Many have defended Leah’s recollection of the attack, including Andrew Fox, the son of a shark attack victim.

Speaking to the Daily Mail, he said his father’s recollection of his near-death experience is “just as detailed” as Leah’s.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Fox added: “The doubters are always jumping in with opinion but anybody that’s been through near-death experience will know an infinite number of possibilities are processed by your brain in microseconds.”



The Sun has contacted the radio station for comment.

News.title: Augsburg explosion: Casualties after blast rocks German train station
News.content:
Police warned members of the public to avoid the area 'widely' after an explosion rocked Augsburg's main train station at 5am

Two people have been injured in an explosion at a German railway station.

Police have confirmed the blast rocked Augsburg's main station at around 5am on Wednesday (September 2). Local news outlets reported an "unidentified object" exploded in a building passageway.

A statement from Schwaben North Police said at the time: "A major police operation is currently taking place in Augsburg on Bahnhofstr. Halderstrasse / Hübnerstrasse, Bahnhofstrase / Hübnerstrasse, and Viktoriastrasse / Bahnhofstrasse are closed. Public transport is disrupted."

The State Criminal Police Office (LKA) was on the scene with an explosive-disposal robot, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper said. The explosion caused window panes to shatter.

News.title: Tiger Woods avoids jail with last-minute plea deal over reckless driving charge that ended in horror crash
News.content:
Tiger Woods avoids jail with last-minute plea deal over reckless driving charge that ended in horror crash

Tiger Woods, the 15-time major winner, has lost his driving license for five years after appearing before a judge at Martin County Courthouse in Florida this afternoon

View 4 Images Tiger Woods was flanked by his girlfriend Vanessa Trump when he arrived at court (Image: Getty Images)

Tiger Woods avoided prison but had his driver's license suspended for five years after reaching a last-minute plea deal in his reckless driving case.

‌



He changed his plea to no contest today following a rollover crash in March near his home in Florida, where he initially was accused of driving under the influence. The golf great, told in April he could face jail time, appeared in a courtroom in Martin County where he agreed to the reduced charge. He heard a judge order that his driver's license be removed until 2031.

‌



Earlier this year, Woods was driving recklessly on a residential road on Jupiter Island, which had a 30-mph speed limit. His Land Rover clipped a truck, sending it onto its side. He walked away from the crash unhurt, escaping through the passenger side door.

‌



Today, the 50-year-old said little during the hearing and beforehand sat at the defence table, looking back at the courtroom gallery. He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump's former daughter-in-law.

View 4 Images Police body camera video showed the moment the sports legend was arrested (Image: AP)

Tiger Woods had perfect three-word response after being denied entry to The Open READ MORE :

Tiger Woods facing potential prison sentence following official charge in DUI case READ MORE :

Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters. He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing and was fined court costs, according to court documents.

‌



A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. The sport superstar was arrested after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road on Jupiter Island.

Police bodycam footage of Tiger Woods DUI arrest on Jupiter Island

A report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyzer test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test. He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge. Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials.

‌



But his Land Rover caused $5,000 (£3,700) damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck.

View 4 Images Woods stands by his overturned vehicle after it flipped over (Image: AP)

Woods is among the most influential figures in golf, but his career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.

‌



He has been involved in four crashes over the years. He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play.

View 4 Images Woods custody photo released by police in March (Image: Getty Images)

He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.

Article continues below

Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour's plans to revamp its schedule for 2028.

He remained as chairman of the tour's Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance.

News.title: Would a return to acting help improve Meghan Markle’s public image? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Would a return to acting help improve Meghan Markle’s public image? Take our poll and have your say

Rumours have swirled that the Duchess of Sussex is ‘in talks’ for a new acting role, eight years after stepping away from her career as an actress

View 4 Images Meghan, Harry and her children have relocated back to the UK (Image: GETTY)

Meghan Markle has moved back to the UK, along with her husband Prince Harry and their children Archie and Lilibet, as the family start a new chapter back in Britain for an ‘extended stay’. Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, are believed to be enrolled in UK schools to start the new year in the coming days, while the Duke of Sussex will focus more of his time on his charity projects based in his home country.

‌



The Duchess of Sussex will continue running her As Ever lifestyle brand, which is still based in California, but it is rumoured that she is ‘in talks’ for a new acting role.

‌



King Charles to host Emmanuel Macron at Bayeux Tapestry viewing after helping to secure its loan READ MORE :

View 4 Images Meghan Markle is said to be eyeing up a return to acting (Image: John Angelillo/UPI/Shutterstock)

‌



Meghan is believed to be ‘in talks’ for a role in the Netflix show The Gentlemen, which is filmed in the Cotswolds - where the Sussexes are rumoured to be living - and has been confirmed for a third season.

The Guy Ritchie crime show, which stars Theo James in the lead role, is about a British Duke who unexpectedly inherits his father’s country estate and discovers it is home to a cannabis empire run by notorious criminals.

Talks have been said to be at an early stage, with a role reportedly being written just for Meghan, meaning it is unclear how many episodes she would appear in.

‌



Before Meghan married into the Royal Family, she had a successful acting career, most notably starring in the legal drama series Suits as paralegal Rachel Zane for seven seasons. The Duchess starred on the show from 2011 before being written out of the show in 2018 before she tied the knot with Harry.

After the Duke and Duchess quit their royal roles in 2020 and moved to California, Meghan seemed to have no interest in returning to acting, as she told Variety in 2022: “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”

‌



However, a source close to Meghan told People magazine that she has been planning her potential return to acting for ‘quite some time’. Meghan has made a few on-screen appearances in recent years, from her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, as well as a cameo as herself in the film Close Personal Friends, which has yet to be released.

View 4 Images Meghan starred in the legal drama Suits for seven seasons (Image: USA NETWORK)

Meghan was spotted on the set of the film in November 2025, with a source telling People she appeared “very relaxed and happy”, as they added: “She introduced herself to everyone and was very sweet and down-to-earth.”

‌



Professor Jonathan Shalit, chairman of InterTalent Rights Group, believes Meghan can “do whatever she wants to do” following the move back to the UK, as he explained: “If she wants to return to acting, I have absolutely no doubt there would be interest in her.

“If Meghan decided tomorrow that she seriously wanted to act again, directors and producers would absolutely want to meet her and audition her. Would she automatically be handed every role she wanted? Of course not. Nobody is. But would the doors open? Absolutely.”

View 4 Images The Duchess was reportedly planning a return to acting for 'quite some time' (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The idea of the Duchess returning to acting has many royal watchers intrigued about her potential next move, as PR expert Mayah Riaz has encouraged the career change for Meghan, as she told the Mirror she has the chance to build a profile outside the Royal Family if she chooses the right project.

Mayah said: “A return to acting could actually be quite interesting for Meghan because it would take her back to an identity that existed before the Royal Family."

She added: "There can be something quite powerful about returning to an old profession rather than constantly trying to invent a new one. It could allow people to see Meghan as an actress again, rather than exclusively as the Duchess of Sussex.”

News.title: Newborn baby girl 'stabbed 15 times before body found in Sheffield outhouse' – five in court
News.content:
Newborn baby girl 'stabbed 15 times before body found in Sheffield outhouse' – five in court

Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath Jnr, 19, Peter Horvath Snr, 38, Nina Horvathova, 37, and a 15-year-old girl have appeared in court after a baby was found dead in Sheffield

View 2 Images Police were called to a house in the Wincobank area of Sheffield in the early hours of Sunday (Image: MEN Media)

Four people have appeared in court charged with murder after a newborn baby girl, named only as Baby S, was found dead with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.

‌



Prosecutors told a district judge at Sheffield Magistrates’ Court that the baby’s body was found in an outhouse at an address in the Wincobank area of Sheffield on Sunday.

‌



Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath Jnr, 19, Peter Horvath Snr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, appeared before the court on Wednesday morning charged with the murder of Baby S.

‌



They were remanded in custody and will appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday.

View 2 Images The baby’s body was found in an outhouse at an address in Wincobank, Sheffield, prosecutors said (Image: Rahmah Ghazali / Reach PLC)

Horvath Jnr, Horvath Snr and Horvathova, all of Holywell Heights, and Skopova, of Robey Street, Grimesthorpe, Sheffield, are also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime.

‌



All the defendants are Slovakian nationals, the court heard.

The four adults stood in court wearing identical grey t-shirts and flanked by four security guards.

A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named, appeared at the court later, in a separate hearing, charged with the same perverting the course of justice offence.

‌



The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail.

District Judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants.

Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson said the baby had suffered 33 wounds from 15 “separate stabbings”.

Article continues below

Two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail.

News.title: More than one million homeowners face £283 monthly increase in mortgage payments
News.content:
More than one million homeowners face £283 monthly increase in mortgage payments

1,095,905 homeowners who took out mortgages in 2024 are set to come off two-year fixed deals that had an average interest rate of 4.81%

View 2 Images It could pay to shop around for a cheaper mortgage (Image: fizkes via Getty Images)

More than a million homeowners face paying £283 extra in monthly mortgage payments as they come off cheaper fixes.

‌



New data from Compare the Market shows 1,095,905 homeowners who took out mortgages in 2024 are set to come off two-year fixed deals that had an average interest rate of 4.81%. In comparison, the latest Moneyfacts figures show the average standard variable rate (SVR) was 7.13% in July 2026. You normally roll on to your lender's SVR when your fixed deal ends - but this generally has the most expensive rates.

‌



The research shows any of these homeowners who move from a cheaper fix to their current lender’s SVR could see their monthly payment could jump from £1,149 to £1,432 – a £283 increase.

‌



View 2 Images SVR mortgages are generally the most expensive (Image: Bloomberg, Bloomberg via Getty Images)

This is based on an average mortgage debt of £200,250. Homeowners would pay £17,184 annually compared to £13,788 on their previous two-year fixed rate - an increase of more than £3,000 extra a year. However, households could avoid these higher repayments by shopping around for a new mortgage deal.

Switching from the current average SVR of 7.13% to a new two-year fixed rate mortgage with an average rate of 4.79% could result in up to £3,432 in savings per year.

‌



Laura Pomfret, Personal Finance Expert at Compare the Market, said: “A mortgage is likely to be the biggest outgoing in any household, so it’s worth paying attention to and looking for great savings for your budget.

“When a fixed mortgage deal is coming to an end, it’s a good opportunity to look at your finances as a whole. Understanding what your new repayments could be ahead of time means you can plan for any increase and consider where you might need to adjust your budget. “

How to save money on your mortgage

You can normally start looking for a new mortgage deal three to six months before your current one expires.

Article continues below

Start by using an online comparison tool, or by speaking to a mortgage broker, as they will often have access to deals that aren't available on the open market.

You should also speak to your current lender to see what rates it can offer you. This is known as a product transfers, which is where you get a new deal from the same lender.

When looking for a new deal, it is important to get all the relevant information about your existing deal - such as the rate you are on and your loan to value (LTV). This is the amount you are borrowing compared to the property's value.

News.title: Ebola vaccine trial at UK university is world first in fight against virus that has killed over 3,000
News.content:
Ebola vaccine trial at UK university is world first in fight against virus that has killed over 3,000

Conflict and attacks on health workers are hampering efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak which is spreading at an unprecedented pace across the Democratic Republic of Congo

View 4 Images The ebola outbreak is spreading as the World Health Organisation warns it could become the deadliest in history (Image: DIEUDONNE DIROLE/EPA/Shutterstock)

More than 3,000 people have now died in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as the country battles its deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.

‌



According to Congo’s Ministry of Health 6,186 confirmed cases and 3,007 deaths have been recorded since the outbreak was declared a global health emergency in May, making it the fastest-growing outbreak.

‌



The outbreak, which is being driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has spread across six provinces in DRC.L New cases have continued to emerge in recent weeks, including in two new health zones in North Kivu last week. where the fatality rate is much higher than in the rest of the affected provinces.

‌



It comes as Southampton University launches a world first trial of a vaccine for the Bondibugyo strain as it bids to recruit 50 volunteers to take part in a potential breakthrough against the virus

Ebola outbreak battle ramps up with first batch of 70,000 vaccines READ MORE :

Ebola deaths hit 2,000 in Congo as WHO warns virus could become most deadly outbreak on record READ MORE :

View 4 Images New cases of Ebola are emerging across the Democratic Republic of the Congo (Image: AP Photo/Samy Kamanga)

The rapid spread has been made harder to contain by conflict and insecurity in eastern DRC, where the outbreak is concentrated, as well as attacks on health workers and the movement of miners and other populations.

‌



Alongside the conflict the country's weak health infrastructure and gaps in contact tracing has further complicated the efforts to track infections and slow transmission rates. Health workers have also gone on strike multiple times over unpaid wages.

The scale of the outbreak has prompted warnings from the World Health Organisation that it could soon surpass the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record – the 2014-16 outbreak in West Africa, which killed around 11,000 people.

The current crisis passed 2,000 fatalities in around three months, though researchers believed the virus may have been circulating undetected since February.

‌



The Africa Centre for Disease Control and Prevention said the number of cases could be significantly higher than official figures suggest and could be possibly three times larger, as weak surveillance and contact tracing mean some infections may be going undetected.

View 4 Images The escalating outbreak is putting further pressure on an already fragile health system (Image: Getty Images)

The latest figures already make this the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC but efforts to contain the virus are being complicated by the lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain.

‌



Today the University Hospital Southampton (UHS) launched the world’s first clinical trial for a Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine. The trial will be delivered by the hospital through its NIHR Biomedical Research Centre.

The trial is set to recruit 50 healthy volunteers, where participants will receive either one or two doses of the vaccine or a placebo, and will attend regular appointments over a year.

View 4 Images Professor Chrissie Jones has said she is proud that Southampton University is playing a key role in the fight against Ebola (Image: University of Southampton)

‌



Professor Chrissie Jones, Principal Investigator for the study at University Hospital Southampton and the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Southampton, said: “The current Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak is a reminder that emerging infectious diseases remain a serious global threat.

"We're proud that Southampton will play a key role in this important international effort. By taking part, volunteers can make a real contribution to research that could help save lives around the world."

Authorities have meanwhile begun offering Ervebo vaccine to frontline health workers, with the first doses administered in Kisangani, in Tshopo province.

Article continues below

While Ervebo is licensed for protection against the Zaire strain of Ebola, rather than Bundibugyo virus. WHO said it may be able to offer some protection.

The escalating outbreak is putting further pressure on an already fragile health system as authorities and international agencies race to slow transmission and reach communities at risk.

News.title: A66 crash victim Michael Cahill 'linked to gang at centre of North East drug turf feud'
News.content:
A66 crash victim Michael Cahill 'linked to gang at centre of North East drug turf feud'

It is feared that the violence gripping Middlesbrough, which cost the lives of two police officers, stems from conflict between wider organised crime groups (OCGs) Michael Cahill one of the five young men who died in the A66 crash, had links with one group.

Debris left following memorial for man who died in A66 crash

One of the men who died in the A66 tragedy had links to an organised crime gang at the centre of a violent drug turf war.

‌



It is feared that the violence gripping Middlesbrough, which cost the lives of two police officers, stems from conflict between wider organised crime groups (OCGs). Michael Cahill was one of the five young men who died in the A66 wrong way crash.

‌



He had links to the Freeman organised crime gang, with a man closely linked to them posting messages from a vigil held for Cahill in Co Durham last week. Earlier this year, the High Court heard that the North East-based Freeman gang had a long running feud with another family, led by John Henry Sayers, who lived on Tyneside.

‌



Their rivalry was laid bare during an Old Bailey trial over a ramming and arson incident. In July, Sayers Snr and his son John Henry Sayers Jnr were cleared of causing grievous bodily harm after claiming self-defence during a violent confrontation with a member of the Freeman gang. Walter Patterson, used as a 'foot soldier' for the Freemans, was jailed for four years along with four other gang members.

View 5 Images Michael Cahill was one of five young men who died in the A66 crash. Investigators are now looking at the links between the accident and organised crime

John Freeman was jailed for three years in 2019 after setting up a fake drug deal and beating a rival in a gang turf war.

‌



"I am John Freeman, you have been selling drugs in my area," he warned the victim as he rained down "blow after blow" with two others before stealing half a kilogram of cocaine worth up to £22,000, Teesside crown court heard. Freeman added: "Do what you want in Sunderland and Washington but don't you come into Durham or Hetton again selling drugs."

A man closely linked to John Freeman attended the vigil for Mr Cahill in Haswell, Co Durham, where mobs of youths torched cars and let off flares and fireworks last week.

View 5 Images CCTV shows John Henry Sayers, 62, and his son John Henry Sayers Junior, 29, unleashing a furious attack on Walter Patterson, 38, in Newcastle last year

‌



The Mirror told how the A66 crash and drug turf feud was sparked by a 'fall out' between two rival gang members.

Police officers PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died after their marked police vehicle collided with a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 near Middlesbrough as it was driven the wrong way up a dual carriageway.

Cole Worthy, 17; Theo Rae, 17; Makai Saddington, 18; and 23-year-olds Cahill and Jacob Matusiak were in the Passat. They were pronounced dead at the scene in South Bank on the outskirts of Middlesbrough.

‌



Cole Worthy's father's home in Acklam, Middlesbrough, was ram-raided at 3am on August 22, just 40 minutes before the devastating A66 crash. One of the men said to have been in that vehicle was a rival of Cole Worthy.

It is believed Worthy and four friends then set off on a revenge mission to track down the Volvo XC60 used in the ram raid, ending in the collision that killed the two officers.

View 5 Images Tributes are left outside the Cleveland Police station near Wynyard where PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were based. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Police are investigating whether Cahill, Worthy and the other passengers killed in the Passat were being used by organised crime gangs in a drugs turf war in Grangetown, an area on the outskirts of Middlesbrough.

Natalie McDonald and her niece Valentina Foster died in a suspected arson attack there last week. A man has appeared in court charged with their murders. Cleveland Police say that the deaths are not believed to be linked to the A66 crash.

Previously, in a separate case, the Old Bailey heard that a 'number of individuals are known to be associated with the Freeman organised crime group'. Prosecutors explained that the OCG was led by John Freeman controlling the attacks on the Sayers.

‌



View 5 Images John Henry Sayers, 62, and his son John Henry Sayers Junior, 29, unleashing a furious attack on Walter Patterson, 38, in Newcastle last year. They were cleared by a jury who accepted they were acting in self defence.

In September 2022, masked men on an off-road bike set fire to a van owned by Sayers Jnr in Newcastle. It triggered a series of attacks on the Sayers' home in Newcastle and associated properties which went on for years, the High Court was told.

The jury heard that a "number of individuals are known to be associated with the Freeman organised crime group". Prosecutors said the group has a hierarchy with someone called John Freeman controlling the incidents against the Sayers family.

‌



The court was told police were aware from 2022 the organised crime group were behind a number of incidents aimed at the Sayers family.

View 5 Images Close friends Theo Ray (left) and Cole Worthy both died in the A66 crash (Image: Facebook)

On January 31 2025, Sayers junior's VW Golf was set on fire outside their home. The police also had information there was a rumour an organised crime group were recruiting someone to murder Sayers senior.

‌



Jurors were told "the police had information the same group responsible for (an earlier attack on Sayers) had been discussing finishing the job, with this potentially happening in the presence of his children".

Police told Sayers he was at risk of being killed. He was later issued with a further notice that he and his family were at risk.

It said: "Northumbria Police are in receipt of information that a member of the Sayers family is at risk of serious harm."

Article continues below

The court heard there was no evidence either defendant sought to respond to any of the attacks with violence.

News.title: Hunted star's extreme back-to-school advice after heartbreaking admission about own childhood
News.content:
Hunted star's extreme back-to-school advice after heartbreaking admission about own childhood

EXCLUSIVE: September is the peak for pupil absenteeism, figures show, but Hunted star Jordan Wylie - who suffered his own troubled childhood - believes there's a way for children and parents to get back on track

View 5 Images Jordan Wylie is on a mission to help combat the back to school nerves (Image: Jen Hilton Photography)

As millions of children head back to school this week, families and teachers are braced for the start of the autumn term - traditionally the peak period for pupil attendance problems.

‌



Department for Education data for 2025-26 shows that absences climbs in the autumn term, with a staggering 18.1% of pupils - equal to 1.29 million children - classed as persistently absent after missing at least 10pc of their classes, an increase of 10,000 from 2024-2025.

‌



Some 151,000 pupils were classed as severe absences, meaning they missed at least half of their term. Now, TV adventurer and Hunted star Jordan Wylie MBE warns that parental anxiety and screen addiction are compounding the crisis.

‌



Having grown up on a tough Blackpool council estate before joining the British Army and leading record-breaking expeditions, he understands the feelings of anxiety and isolation all too well . Calling himself a "little tearaway" from Grange Park - one of the biggest one of the biggest council estates in the country, he previously said: "I have seen, first hand, how coming from a challenging background you can easily end up on the wrong path because there are no other opportunities."

He spent his 15th birthday in a police cell and left school with no qualifications before joining the army. In 2015 he suffered a mental breakdown after leaving military service but used his "spirit of adventure" to recover. And he warns that screen addiction and overprotective parenting are leaving teenagers ill-equipped for real-world stress

Mum forced to teach autistic son at home after council denies specialist space READ MORE :

View 5 Images Jordan Wylie served in the military after leaving school without any GCSEs and now features on Hunted

‌



As a former military intelligence officer who has spent weeks off-grid in extreme environments including climbing kilimanjaro bare foot, defending ships from pirates and exploring the Antarctic, Jordan has found solace in the extreme environments away from the hubbub of everyday life.

"I've seen young people taking their own lives because of things that have happened on social media," Jordan told the Daily Mirror. "When I go out on an adventure into very remote places where there's often no signal or no connectivity, I can honestly say that my mental health is at its best than it ever has been.

"There's a real challenge in society with young boys' mental health and well-being. When I look at how teenage girls use social media, there's this constant comparison culture where young men and women are being made to feel not good enough because of what they see online. The challenges that young people have today are a lot more difficult and complex than certainly what I had 20 years ago."

‌



Instead of letting pre-term anxiety isolate children at home, Jordan urges parents and pupils to reframe obstacles into opportunities.

He is supporting Outward Bound - which has five centres across England, Scotland and Wales - as it launches its Big Shake-Up campaign to help support kids, parents and teachers with the major transition.

View 5 Images Jordan Wylie is part of the Outward Bound Big Shake Up campaign (Image: Supplied)

‌



"When you go back into the new school year, there are a lot of things that people are apprehensive about," Jordan said. "We're trying to encourage them to step into the unknown and get comfortable with being uncomfortable.

"When we're given challenges in life, they are our best opportunities to grow. Instead of seeing the stumbling blocks, let's look for the stepping stones that are going to help us, not cause us more stress."

Natalie Harling, Director of Business Development, The Outward Bound Trust, added: "We get more dropouts during the back-to-school period than at any other time of the year.

‌



"We believe young people grow when they step into the unfamiliar. Sometimes that happens on a mountain, a lake or a wild stretch of coastline - sometimes it starts with a different question in a classroom.

"Pupils notice something new, talk to someone different, share an idea, support a classmate or reflect on a small moment of courage. It can take five minutes in class, registration or assembly, but it might open-up a conversation that lasts a little longer.

Sixteen-year-old Lily, from Bristol, says applying that mindset changed her life. Suffering with anxiety, she had convinced herself to stay on at her school and study A-Levels there so she could stay with her friends.

‌



But after pushing herself through a two-week course in Cumbria - cliff jumping, rock climbing, and camping off-grid - meeting Jordan inspired her to break away from her comfort zone.

"Before I went, I was very stuck and a big people pleaser," Lily told the Daily Mirror. "I wasn't thinking about myself. But then I then spent time talking to Jordan and meeting new people and seeing what's out there.

"It completely changed everything. As soon as I got on the train to come home, I rang my mum and told her to apply for my place at Bath College for the paramedic course.

‌



"I spoke to Jordan, and he inspired me by talking about his past. He showed me I can now believe in myself to do something like that, and I'm just going to put myself out there."

Lily echoed Jordan's fears about screen addiction amongst her peers. "There is so much more than just what's on social media," she said. "I've seen so much of the world. There's a lot of people in my age range and below who are always on their phones and missing out on the things that are actually around them.

"They're very addicted to social media these days, and I think it's quite a heartbreaking thing."

‌



View 5 Images Lily said two weeks of outdoor activities pushed her out of her comfort zone and inspired her to take a new direction in life (Image: Supplied)

Jordan stresses that parental anxiety often filters down to children, as he warns mums and dads to watch how they talk about school at home. As someone that didn't enjoy school, or pass any GCSE exams, he tries not to speak negatively about education to his children.

"When you speak about school as a parent, speak about it positively. Remind them of the importance of kindness, especially when going into a new year."

‌



His top advice for families battling pre-term jitters this weekend is simple: turn off the tech and get outside.

"Put all your digital devices down, close the laptop, switch off the iPad, turn your phone off for a for a few hours and get in the outdoors," he urged.

"Pretty much everyone in the UK is within an hour of a national park or the coast. It allows us to reset as humans. Let's disconnect our technology to reconnect with our family."

‌



View 5 Images Lily believes that too many of her friends are addicted to social media (Image: Supplied)

And for kids terrified of the first day back? Jordan says it's all about reframing the feeling.

"Often when I speak to young children, they often talk about about nervous or being scared or fearful. When we're nervous, that's the exact same feeling as when we are excited," he told Daily Mirror.

Article continues below

"If I think of all the times I would say I'm nervous, whether I'm climbing one of the biggest mountains in the world, or about to go on stage in, I am nervous, but if I look at that differently, I'm actually really excited to go and do that thing.

"The Big Shake-Up for me is about being curious, it's about embracing discomfort, it's about working as a team, and it's about enjoying the journey and the way I do that is to incorporate that adventure mindset."

News.title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
News.content:
The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing â a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.

Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him.

These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.

Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away â leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.

In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.

And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.

Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.

Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.

While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.

Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.

As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

News.title: Farage tells BBC 'we live in a complainants' society' after questions over Reform funding
News.content:
Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's funding.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".

It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and Â£5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.

Farage said he expects it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed as part of the ongoing parliamentary investigation into whether he should have publicly declared the sum upon his election as an MP.

The Reform UK leader said he hoped the investigation, which was launched in May but paused during the by-election he triggered in his Clacton seat, would "move a bit faster" now he had been re-elected to Parliament.

Farage has faced weeks of headlines about funding, including Â£5m he received before entering Parliament from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based British cryptocurrency investor and major Reform donor.

Parliament's standards commissioner is investigating whether he should have declared that sum upon becoming an MP in his published register of financial interests.

Farage has said the Â£5m was a personal gift and did not therefore require registration under the rules.

He continued to insist he believes he had done "nothing wrong", but ultimately it would be a "matter of interpretation" for the investigation to resolve.

Asked about the funding questions that have dogged the party over the summer recess, he said: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society.

"If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."

He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do".

"There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat.

"There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing.

"So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."

Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour.

"People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything."

News.title: Four in court over murder of baby stabbed to death
News.content:
Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.

The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, having suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.

Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield, appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court alongside Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37, and Peter Horvath, 38, all of Holywell Heights.

They have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.

A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also appeared in the same court charged with perverting the course of justice.

All five Slovakian nationals were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday.

News.title: Lucy Letby 'boyfriend' doctor named as court order lifted
News.content:
Letby - who has always maintained her innocence - is serving 15 whole life prison terms. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is conducting a review of Letby's convictions.

At her criminal trial - the longest murder trial in UK history - Deakin gave evidence in relation to several babies. He was granted special measures as well as anonymity. These allowed him to give evidence from behind a screen so that Letby, the public gallery, and the media were prevented from seeing him.

Deakin's evidence provided detail of some of the emergency calls and resuscitations which he and Letby were jointly involved in. Their long nights of text messaging were laid bare and many of the messages shown to the jury.

When he was sworn in, on the first occasion he testified, Letby burst into tears, in what was the first display of emotion from her during the trial.

During her cross-examination, Letby was forced to deny that Deakin was her boyfriend, though she did accept that they had gone on a trip to London together.

The prosecuting barrister, Nick Johnson KC, said Letby "tried to get out the back of the dock" when the doctor first came to the witness box.

Letby said: "Yes, because I felt unwell."

Johnson said: "No, it's because you didn't like hearing your boyfriend giving evidence, did you?"

Letby said: "That's unfair."

Prosecutors also went through a WhatsApp message exchange between Letby and a friend who had teased her for being "flirty" with Deakin.

Johnson said: "She knew you were sweet on Mark, didn't she?"

Letby said: "What do you mean, sweet?"

Johnson said: "That you had a crush on him."

"No," said Letby.

"There was nothing between me and that Mark."

Johnson told the court that Letby told her friend she had received a "strange message" from the doctor.

Her colleague responded: "Did you? Saying what? Go Commando [laughing face emoji]."

While some media reports have described him as "a key witness", Deakin was one of many former colleagues of Letby's whose joint testimony helped to build the prosecution case against her, and none of the convictions rested solely on his evidence.

News.title: London mayor says conviction for untaxed car was due to a scam
News.content:
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan has been convicted and fined in a fast-track court system after being accused of not taxing a 24-year-old Nissan Micra in what his team has called a "scam".

The Labour politician, 55, was found guilty by a magistrate last month of keeping an unlicensed vehicle, in a criminal prosecution brought by the DVLA.

Court documents show that letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to Gordon Ramsay's east London restaurant and the car did not belong to the mayor.

An application has now been made to the magistrates' court to reopen the case and withdraw the prosecution.

A spokesperson for the mayor said: "This is a scam, which is a crime. It's not the first time the mayor has been victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle.

"Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware."

The mayor's adviser told BBC London the DVLA was "urgently" looking into reopening the case, with a view to withdrawing the prosecution.

The DVLA will also investigate the false registration, the adviser said.

The magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the Single Justice Procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a Â£220 fine, Â£85 in costs, and settle the Â£35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

After the mayor expanded the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) to cover the whole of London he faced a wave of protests, including from motorists who said they planned to register their car in his name - supposedly to make him liable for the Â£12.50 daily charge.

News.title: King Charles, Macron and Burnham to preview Bayeux Tapestry display
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla, Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, and Emmanuel Macron and Brigitte Macron will be shown key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.

School children from the UK and France will attend the event, with the King and the French president expected to make speeches marking the historic loan.

Sending the tapestry to the British Museum had been announced by Macron during the French state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.

There had been some worries that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said ahead of the royal preview: "The display conditions at the British Museum are ideal."

The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres, sewn more than 900 years ago.

It is believed that the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.

At a state banquet hosted by King Charles in Windsor, Macron had said the missing end of the tapestry was a symbol that "in the great mural of Franco-British history, the end is yet to be written - it is up to us to do it".

News.title: Tiger Woods gets five-year driving ban after reckless driving plea
News.content:
"I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case," Florida State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said at a press conference after the hearing.

He said he strove to treat Woods like any other defendant.

"Today I resolved case involving a man who drives a golf ball for a living," Bakkedahl said. "Tomorrow, I'll resolve a case in the same matter for a man who drives a nail for a living."

No one was injured in the crash, though Woods had to crawl out through the passenger door to free himself.

Police released body camera footage in April that captured the aftermath of the incident, showing the golfing legend after his vehicle clipped a truck and rolled over.

In the video, Woods appears calm, kneeling on one knee as he tells officers: "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom".

He passed a breathalyser test but declined to take a urinalysis screening for other drugs, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said at the time.

Woods told officers he had not consumed alcohol that day. When asked about any prescription medication, he responded, "I take a few", adding he had done so earlier that morning.

He then listed the medication, though that portion of the footage was redacted.

Officers told Woods they suspected his "normal faculties" were impaired by an "unknown substance".

Authorities later reported finding two white pills in his pocket, identified as hydrocodone, an opioid commonly prescribed to treat pain.

Woods wrote on social media following the incident, "I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in today.

"I am stepping away for a period of time to seek treatment and focus on my health. This is necessary in order for me to prioritise my wellbeing and work toward lasting recovery."

The incident marked Woods' second arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

News.title: Jurors return in Lindsay Clancy trial after judge asks them to break deadlock
News.content:
The jury in the US trial of Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Wednesday to try again to reach a verdict in the deaths of her three children.

The panel had told the judge a day earlier they had been unable to agree after days of deliberations and were instructed to keep trying. Clancy, who has pleaded not guilty, faces three counts of first-degree murder.

Prosecutors have alleged that she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill the children in their Massachusetts home in 2023.

Her lawyer does not dispute Clancy killed them but says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was unable to distinguish right from wrong - meaning she should not be held criminally responsible.

The jury began deliberating on Thursday after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses. The panel returned to the courtroom on Tuesday, after telling Judge William Sullivan they were deadlocked. The announcement drew audible gasps in the courtroom.

He instructed them to keep trying.

Clancy, a 36-year-old former nurse, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer. She was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window after the killings.

News.title: About 700 prisoners to be freed on 1 October under revised early release plans
News.content:
About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.

The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.

Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.

In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying".

"I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.

Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months.

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.

Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.

The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded.

The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:

From 10 November, 650 offenders serving up to three years and two months

From 8 December, 550 offenders serving up to four years and three months

From 12 January 2027, 600 offenders serving up to five years and nine months

From 9 February, 500 offenders serving up to seven years and six months

From 9 March, 200 offenders serving up to nine years

From 13 April, 200 offenders serving up to 10 years

From 11 May, 250 offenders serving up to 12 years

From 9 June, 250 offenders serving more than 12 years.

The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.

News.title: Family of murdered Stacy Hunter say new misogyny bill would not have protected her
News.content:
The family of Stacy Hunter has called for immediate action to protect victims of domestic abuse, after plans for a misogyny bill were announced by the Scottish government.

First Minister John Swinney announced plans to recognise misogyny as a "distinct form of prejudice and abuse" during his programme for government, external on Tuesday, alongside a public health campaign to target toxic male behaviour.

Stacy was murdered by her estranged husband, Jim Mair, at her home near Houston in Refrewshire in July. He was on bail for attacking her. His body was found nearby.

Her family is calling for tougher action on offenders.

Speaking on BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme, Stacy's brother said some aspects of the proposals were important but they are not "anywhere near good enough".

News.title: Nottingham attacks families not told 'stalker' had violent past
News.content:
Families of the Nottingham attacks victims said police did not tell them a man who had taken an interest in them had a history of violence when he attempted to visit them.

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023. He tried to kill three others.

Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, said he was told in 2025 that a man had visited his GP surgery in London. Emma Webber, Barnaby's mother, said he had also travelled to Somerset, but neither were informed of the man's history of mental ill health.

Nottinghamshire Police said it had received a complaint and referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The IOPC confirmed it had received a referral of a complaint from Nottinghamshire Police in relation to information the force allegedly withheld from the families of Calocane's victims about a potential witness who had tried to contact them.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The prime minister was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

News.title: Pub's 'beloved' manager stabbed to death in Germany
News.content:
A pub has paid tribute to its "beloved" manager after she was stabbed to death in Germany.

Rebecca Bullock, 31, was attacked at Rosenheim station shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00 BST) on Sunday. She was taken to hospital but later died.

Bavarian Police said a 27-year-old German man, of no fixed address, was arrested at the scene and later detained in a psychiatric hospital on suspicion of murder.

The White Swan, in Whitchurch, Buckinghamshire, said: "We are so deeply sorry to say that our beloved Becca passed away over the weekend whilst away on holiday."

"Becca was much-loved by all of the team at the White Swan and our amazing locals," its Facebook post read.

The pub closed from Monday after what it described as a "tough few days", but its landlords said it would reopen from 15:00.

They said: "We know this is what Becca would have wanted."

News.title: Missing British trekker's body found in Pakistan
News.content:
The body of a British trekker has been found in northern Pakistan, local officials have said.

Alexander Harris, who was originally from Birmingham, went missing on Saturday as he was descending from the summit of Musa Ka Musala, a mountain of just over 4,000m (13,000ft), in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

Khalid Iqbal, the area's deputy commissioner, said police and volunteers had been involved in a search for 30-year-old Harris and his body was found on a path in a forest, adding "most probably he slipped and fell".

He had been living in Pakistan's capital Islamabad where he worked for global advisory company Adam Smith International.

Harris, who also had Irish citizenship, had set off on the trek around 05:40 local time on Saturday with a hiking companion. They took some photos at the summit and then began to descend, before becoming separated.

"There was a difference in their speed," Iqbal said. "He [Harris] was moving faster, he got about 1-2km ahead. Then it started raining."

The deputy commissioner estimated that between 250-300 people were involved in the rescue operation including police and volunteers, searching on foot and with drones, although their use was limited by poor visibility.

A keen hiker and trail runner, Harris was a regular participant in long distance races in Pakistan.

Iqbal said the two trekkers had not told the authorities about the trip.

"The hotel had offered him a guide and police security," Iqbal says. "But he said that he knew the area and did not need any help."

News.title: Children as young as six going to A&E in mental health crisis
News.content:
There has been a sharp rise in children and young people - some as young as six - attending A&E units in England in a mental health crisis, NHS doctors are warning.

The number of six to 17-year-olds turning up in significant distress for things like self-harm and eating disorders, or in emotional crisis, rose by 36% between 2019 and 2025, according to the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health analysis.

Some faced waits of more than 12 hours once there. The college said A&Es were not the best place for them, but a lack of support in the community meant they often had nowhere else to turn.

The government said it was looking to improve services and would be setting out plans soon.

The analysis - based on figures provided under the Freedom of Information Act by NHS England - found there were 75,491 attendances at A&E by children and young people for a mental health concern in 2025.

That is up from 55,525 in 2019 with some of the biggest rises seen in very young children aged six to nine. The increases far outstrip the overall jump in attendances, which has risen by just over 8% over the period.

Doctors said the cases included children and young people brought in by families, carers and police - some of those in emotional crisis become aggressive or have challenging behaviour.

In total, more than 6,200, around 8%, waited over 12 hours in A&E.

Nicholas, a father-of-two, is someone who has seen the impact of this. His 10-year-old son has autism and suffers from mental health issues. It has caused a safety risk - he has attacked others and tried to jump out of windows.

He told BBC Your Voice: "There is no support when in crisis. GP won't prescribe anything. We are stuck on a children's mental health waiting list which is the only service who can provide interventions. The system is broken.

"When at A&E, half the time we don't see a doctor because you have to wait so long. Once my son calms down, it's best to go home rather than have him escalate again while waiting."

News.title: 'Heartless' scammer vowed to repay victims but still hasn't a year on
News.content:
Victims of a "heartless" fraudster, who faked her own wedding to con relatives and friends out of more than Â£12,000, are questioning why they have only received a fraction of what she was ordered to pay back.

Charlotte Blackwell, 32, from Bridgend, was handed a suspended prison sentence and ordered to pay Â£13,750 in compensation to the four victims by a judge in March 2025.

When she realised she would be avoiding jail Blackwell sobbed in relief and agreed to the judge's demand that she pay at a rate of Â£400 a month.

But her victims say she has only paid a total of Â£163.

The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said it could not give specific details on enforcement but added: "These were heartless crimes."

In October 2025, the victims had only received Â£25.45 each since the order was imposed seven months earlier.

Since that time Blackwell, a mother of two, has paid an additional Â£15.30 to each of the victims - with no payments made in the last four months.

When the victims asked for updates from the MoJ they said they were told: "It's being dealt with."

Helen Morse is owed almost Â£3,500.

"We've sort of given up because there's nowhere for us to turn. It feels like she's being protected rather than the victims."

Blackwell, who was previously spared jail for fraud against a children's cancer charity, made bogus wedding plans in a scheme to pay off her gambling debts.

Between 2022 and 2024 she took Â£12,682 from members of the supposed wedding party under the pretence it was for a planned ceremony in Turkey.

The four victims were her then-fiancÃ©'s mother Paula Thomas, who paid Â£3,296, and three of Thomas' friends - including Morse, who paid Â£3,311, Sue Chapman, who paid Â£3,272, and Tracey Roberts, who paid Â£2,803.

Blackwell was ordered to pay Â£3,500 in compensation each to Thomas, Chapman, and Morse, and Â£3,250 to Roberts to "reflect the additional aggravation and distress" she had caused them.

She was also handed a suspended 12-month jail term, 120 hours of unpaid work and five days of rehabilitation activity.

Her barrister Alice Sykes said her client would be able to pay the compensation, as she was working full-time as an estate agent on Â£1,700 a month, as well as receiving universal credit.

Blackwell was back in court in October 2025 after being fined for breaching her community service order.

Argentina’s president has issued a fresh warning to the UK over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, saying his country would defend its interests “with tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers”.

Javier Milei said he was preparing to make what he billed as a national announcement on Thursday night, saying the islands were “sacred” to his people and claimed his country’s national sovereignty had been “violated”.

On Tuesday, Downing Street said Britain’s commitment to the Falkland Islands was “unwavering” after Donald Trump suggested the US could review its position on the archipelago.

open image in gallery Javier Milei is to make a ‘national announcement’ on the Falkland Islands on Thursday ( Reuters )

In a statement on X, formerly Twitter, Argentina’s president wrote: “We announce a national broadcast for Thursday at 9:00 PM on a SACRED topic for Argentinians... a historic claim of the Argentine people that to this day continues to see its national sovereignty violated.”

He added: “What more important and strategic cause for the vital interests of the nation could there be more important than the Malvinas cause?... We will continue defending the interests of the Argentine nation with tooth and nail, no matter who it bothers. LONG LIVE FREEDOM, DAMMIT...!!!”

open image in gallery Downing Street said Britain’s commitment to the Falkland Islands was ‘unwavering’ ( PA )

James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, hit back at President Milei, saying the Falklands “are British and they will remain British”.

“British soldiers fought and died to defend our sovereignty and the freedom of the Falkland Islanders. That sacrifice will never be forgotten, and we will always stand by the people of the Falklands and their overwhelming desire to remain British,” he said.

The US’s stance is formally neutral, although Washington provided support for Britain’s campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

However, reports at the weekend suggested the US could revise its position if the UK government does not increase defence spending.

Asked about the reports on Monday, Mr Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That’s just one of many.”

The next day the PM’s official spokesperson said the UK’s position on the Falklands was “long-standing and unwavering”.

“Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount,” he said. “The UK’s position is clear. The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory.”

open image in gallery Donald Trump suggested the US could review its position on the archipelago ( AP )

Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory in a 2013 referendum, with 99.8 per cent voting in favour – and just three votes against.

But the issue hit the headlines this summer when Argentina’s football team controversially waved a banner in support of their country’s claim to the islands while celebrating their World Cup win against England.

Players held a banner after the semi-final match that read “Las Malvinas son Argentinas”, which translates as “The Falklands are Argentine”.

Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus, has made his first comments as the boss of perhaps the world’s most powerful company.

Mr Ternus took over control from Tim Cook on 1 September, following a long and carefully managed transition. But despite Mr Ternus’s key role at the company, and months of preparation, his personal life and professional views about Apple still remain largely mysterious.

In his first comments as head of the company, made in a memo sent to Apple staff, he largely maintained that mystery. But they hint further at what appears to be his priority in the top role: returning the focus of Apple to its products.

Numerous reports have suggested that the appointment of Mr Ternus – who most recently led Apple’s hardware team, taking responsibility for the design and production of the iPhone as well as its other physical products – is intended to focus the company on the devices that it makes and sells. Mr Cook will stay on as Apple’s executive chairman, and is expected to continue to take responsibility for the more controversial parts of its business, such as its relationships with politicians in US and China.

Mr Ternus’s statement appears to further confirm that direction. What few specific comments he made focused primarily on a “huge launch next week”, referencing the upcoming iPhone event, as well as “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together”.

Mr Ternus began his first memo by thanking “everyone for the warm wishes” and expressing “deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years”. He also pointed to the fact that Mr Cook had “led with his values and with such decency and humanity”.

But all of his comments about Apple focused on the products that the company has coming up.

“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” he told staff, in the widely reported memo. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal.

“Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible. I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. There’s no team in the world I’d rather build the future with.”

Around the same time, Mr Ternus launched an official account X, formerly Twitter. He posted a simple tweet that remains the only one on the newly created account.

Apple has sometimes had a contentious relationship with X, especially since it was bought by Elon Musk and renamed Twitter. Apple has pulled some advertising from the site after controversies around Mr Musk, for instance, and he has publicly criticised the company.

In recent times, however, Apple has more openly embraced the site, with both official marketing posts and statements from its executives. Mr Cook regularly used it to post ahead of Apple’s public events, for instance.
