Sports.title: Etienne chases first success at Bath
Sports.content:
We have a busy day’s racing on Wednesday with flat action from Bath and Newcastle, live on Sky Sports Racing...

2.00 Bath - Promising Etienne returns following Super Sprint fourth

Promising Etienne returns following Super Sprint fourth in the EBF Restricted Maiden Stakes.

Richard Spencer-trained Etienne was touched off by a short head on debut before improving further when finishing fourth in the Weatherbys Super Sprint.

He shaped best that day, conceding first run and running on to finish with the highest finishing speed of the front four.

The winner, Angel's Lane has since bolted up to win a good edition of the St Hugh's Stakes, and the level of form that Etienne brings to the race, looks a class apart from his rivals.

He contains Group One and Group Two entries this autumn, and the slight step up in trip should see him to best effect, and extremely tough to beat.

Tree Wizard and Anna Belardo contain one piece of form each which could see them run creditably against Etienne, but both need to bounce back to their best if they're to threaten Richard Spencer's runner.

5.02 Bath - Quebella headlines trappy fillies' handicap

Quebella headlines a trappy contest in the British EBF Fillies' Handicap.

Quebella has strung together two creditable third-placed finishes since moving to Owen Burrows.

She was very well backed last time out at Chester but a wide trip and drop in trip both did not see her to best effect. Back up a furlong and a half should suit, and she should go well.

Pierian looked promising when winning by nine lengths at Yarmouth in May, but has since disappointed. She was put into listed company before a handicap at Glorious Goodwood, so she is definitely thought better of, and she can prove competitive if progressing from her earlier season efforts.

The in-form duo, Mythical Bird and Aravalli both scored last time out, with the latter succeeding in four of her last five starts.

They should both go well in a wide-open fillies' handicap.

2.45 Newcastle - Intriguing 3yo Yordan bids to back up facile success

Intriguing three-yearold Yordan bids to back up facile success in the EBF Novice Stakes.

Yordan was purchased for 160,000gns as a yearling in October 2024, but had to wait until July 2026 to make his belated debut. He has made a promising start at three, finishing a close second on debut, before winning by nearly three lengths, going away when dropped to six furlongs last month at Southwell.

Harry Vigors has been booked to ride which offsets the winning penalty he shoulders, and with a clear class edge on paper, he could take all the beating when attempting to make it two wins from three.

Ennoble was previously trained by Joseph O'Brien and contains solid two-year-old form. However, Antony Brittain would need to revitalise this horse as it seems like he may not have trained on.

Brash has held a consistent level of form to date and can again run creditably; however, he is much more exposed and would need to make a miraculous improvement to even threaten Yordan.

Best of the rest

4.30 Bath - Course specialist, Blue Hero aims for 12th course win vs in-form Buckland Belle.

4.45 Newcastle - Let's Go Hugo bids for a hat-trick.

Eight-race Lyon-Parilly and Toulouse cards.

Sports.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
Sports.content:
Arsenal

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martineilli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

Key ins: Bruno Guimarães (Newcastle, £75m), Ezri Konsa (Aston Villa, £51m), Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)

Key outs: Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m), Gabriel Jesus (Barcelona, £8.6m), Fábio Vieira (Hamburg, £7.7m), Christian Nørgaard (Everton, £7m), Ethan Nwaneri (Borussia Dortmund, loan)

Aston Villa

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Ben Fisher

Key ins: Johan Manzambi (Freiburg, £51m), Nicolas Jackson (Chelsea, £47.5m), Ibrahim Mbaye (PSG, £47m), João Gomes (Wolves, £34m), Zion Suzuki (Parma, £30m), Taylor Harwood-Bellis (Southampton, £25m), Matteo Ruggeri (Atlético Madrid, £21.4m), Leon Goretzka (Bayern Munich, free), Aaron Wan-Bissaka (West Ham, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Chelsea, loan)

Key outs: Morgan Rogers (Chelsea, £117m), Ollie Watkins (Al-Hilal, £51m), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal, £51m), Youri Tielemans (Manchester United, £35m), Donyell Malen (Roma, £21.6m), Lewis Dobbin (Southampton, £9m), Lucas Digne (PSG, £8.5m), Emiliano Martínez (Chelsea, £7.5m), Evann Guessand (Crystal Palace, loan)

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Bournemouth

Perhaps Bournemouth’s best business was keeping hold of their coveted key players, chiefly Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan, Alex Scott and Tyler Adams. Bournemouth rejected bids from Chelsea for Scott and stayed true to their plan of resisting offers to give Marco Rose the best chance of succeeding, with the club attempting to juggle European competition and the league for the first time. The arrival of the Portugal centre-back António Silva, 22, from Benfica looks a typically smart replacement for Marcos Senesi, 29. Kroupi’s freak foot injury, which will probably keep him out until November, may have proved a blessing in disguise in terms of retaining the 20-year-old. BF

Key ins: António Silva (Benfica, £21.4m), Álvaro Rodríguez (Elche, £21.3m), Juanlu Sánchez (Sevilla, £11.1m), Michele Di Gregorio (Juventus, loan)

Key outs: Luis Sinisterra (Cruzeiro, £5.2m), Enes Unal (Getafe, free), Álex Jiménez (Fiorentina, loan), Marcos Senesi (Tottenham, free)

Brentford

Avoiding a repeat of last year’s upheaval was a major boost. Keith Andrews held on to his best players and made smart additions to a solid squad. Mamadou Sangaré has added quality in midfield since joining from Lens and looks the bargain of the summer. Callum Wilson has brought experience up front after signing on a free and Jaidon Anthony provides cover on the flanks after his £15m move from Burnley. El Hadji-Malick Diouf, signed from West Ham, offers potential at left-back. Jacob Steinberg

Key ins: Mamadou Sangaré (Lens, £39m), El Hadji Malick Diouf (West Ham, £35m), Jaidon Anthony (Burnley, £15m), Jannik Schuster (Red Bull Salzburg, £14m), Callum Wilson (West Ham, free)

Key outs: Ethan Pinnock (Coventry, £6m), Jordan Henderson (Chelsea, free)

View image in fullscreen Mamadou Sangare looks the bargain of the summer at £39m from Lens. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

Brighton

Deadline day deals to bring in the exciting Nigeria forward Femi Azeez from Millwall and the Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés from Stuttgart made it 12 signings in another summer of transition, Azeez’s arrival being announced almost 12 hours after the window shut. The departures of Jan Paul van Hecke, Carlos Baleba and Carl Rushworth brought in more than £140m as the Brighton model continues to deliver big profits, although losing last season’s top scorer, Danny Welbeck, to Chelsea for a mere £5m may be the biggest loss if the new striker Promise David cannot bring the goals. EA

Key ins: Luka Vuskovic (Tottenham, £46m), Zadok Yohanna (AIK, £21.5m), Chema Andrés (Stuttgart, £18.9m), Pascal Struijk (Leeds, £18m), Femi Azeez (Millwall, £15m), Jaouen Hadjam (Young Boys, £11.1m), Costinha (Olympiakos, £11m), Michael Svoboda (Venezia, £4.3m), Promise David (Union St-Gilloise, loan)

Key outs: Carlos Baleba (Manchester United, £70m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham, £52m), Carl Rushworth (Coventry, £22.5m), Diego Coppola (Paris FC, £15.3m), Danny Welbeck (Chelsea, £5m), Joël Veltman (West Ham, free), James Milner (retired), Solly March (released)

Chelsea

Xabi Alonso’s appointment as manager was the biggest signing of the summer. Chelsea have been sensible since turning to the Spaniard. Morgan Rogers has started well after joining for £117m. Maxence Lacroix adds power in defence, Marco Palestra versatility on the flanks. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson can raise standards in the dressing room. But there was the usual revolving door. Money was made on a host of outgoings. Marc Cucurella, one of the world’s best left-backs and sold to Real Madrid, looks a bigger loss than Enzo Fernández. However a worry is that Chelsea did not replace Fernández after selling him to Manchester City for £125m, their late £47m move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara collapsing at the last. JS

Key ins: Morgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £117m), Maxence Lacroix (Crystal Palace, £52m), Marco Palestra (Atalanta, £47m), Geovany Quenda (Sporting, £40m), Valentín Barco (Strasbourg, £34m), Emmanuel Emegha (Strasbourg, £21.6m), Pep Chavarría (Rayo Vallecano, £16.3m), Emiliano Martínez (Aston Villa, £7.5m), Danny Welbeck (Brighton, £5m), Jordan Henderson (Brentford, free)

Key outs: Enzo Fernández (Manchester City, £125m), Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid, £52m), Andrey Santos (Manchester United, £50m), Nicolas Jackson (Aston Villa, £47.5m), Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest, £45m), Trevoh Chalobah (Como 1907, £25.7m), Tyrique George (Everton, £18m), Marc Guiu (RB Leipzig, £14.5m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Tottenham, £7m), Axel Disasi (Crystal Palace, loan), Alejandro Garnacho (Aston Villa, loan), Benoît Badiashile (Napoli, loan), Robert Sánchez (Como, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Tottenham, loan)

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers has started well since his £117m signing from Aston Villa. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Coventry

It remains to be seen whether Coventry have struck the right balance in the market. Frank Lampard wanted to maintain momentum but add power and physicality. Coventry also sought to address their lack of Premier League experience with Taiwo Awoniyi and Ethan Pinnock. Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers last season but the step up means the pressure is on Awoniyi, never prolific for Nottingham Forest, Sidiki Cherif, a promising 19-year-old, and Ellis Simms to deliver before Haji Wright returns from injury. Stephen Mfuni, a teenage loanee from Manchester City and their 11th and final summer signing, increases their left-back options. BF

Key ins: Caleb Yirenkyi (Nordsjælland, £23m), Carl Rushworth (Brighton, £22.5m), Sidiki Cherif (Fenerbahce, £20.5m), Loum Tchaouna (Burnley, £20m), Aurèle Amenda (Eintracht Frankfurt, £15.4m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Nottingham Forest, £9m), Ethan Pinnock (Brentford, £6m), Gustavo Hamer (Sheffield United, £6m), Stephen Mfuni (Manchester City, loan), Frank Onyeka (Brentford, undisclosed), Dan Bentley (Wolves, undisclosed)

Key outs: None

Crystal Palace

The lost tug of war with Sunderland over Malick Fofana summed up another chaotic deadline day for Palace, who were still scrambling for signings in the final minutes and confirmed the arrivals of Ben Chilwell, Quinten Timber and Darío Osorio after the window shut. The new manager, Pierre Sage, will at least be pleased to have secured more defensive reinforcements after losing Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea, with the loanees Honest Ahanor and Axel Disasi adding much-needed depth. Palace also kept hold of Ismaïla Sarr – presuming he doesn’t join a club in Saudi Arabia before the Sunday deadline there – after rejecting an approach from Liverpool for the Senegal forward. EA

Key ins: Anan Khalaili (Union St-Gilloise, £21m), Quinten Timber (Marseille, £15m), Zavier Gozo (Real Salt Lake, £11m), Axel Disasi (Chelsea, loan), Evann Guessand (Aston Villa, loan), Honest Ahanor (Atalanta, loan), Darío Osorio (Midtjylland, loan), Dwight McNeil (Everton, swap), Takehiro Tomiyasu (Ajax, free), Óscar Mingueza (Celta Vigo, free), Ben Chilwell (Strasbourg, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea, £52m), Daniel Muñoz (Nottingham Forest, £22m), Brennan Johnson (Everton, swap), Borna Sosa (Cologne, loan)

Everton

It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. AH

Key ins: Tyrique George (Chelsea, £18m), Merlin Röhl (Freiburg, £17.3m), Hayden Hackney (Middlesbrough, £16.5m), Christian Nørgaard (Arsenal, £7m), Ainsley Maitland-Niles (Lyon, £4.2m), Brennan Johnson (Crystal Palace, swap), Jack Grealish (Manchester City, loan)

Key outs: Iliman Ndiaye (Manchester City, £60m), Beto (Fiorentina, £15.4m), Tim Iroegbunam (Hull, £13m), Dwight McNeil (Crystal Palace, swap), Idrissa Gueye (Al-Diriyah, free), Nathan Patterson (Torino, free), Séamus Coleman (released)

View image in fullscreen Jack Grealish is back at Everton on a second loan from Manchester City. Photograph: Dan Istitene/Getty Images

Fulham

It was a summer of change at Craven Cottage. Marco Silva departed after five successful years in charge and was replaced by the inexperienced Álvaro Arbeloa, who has focused on adding youth. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. Raúl Jiménez joined Wolves and Harry Wilson went to Leeds. Fulham looked to strengthen. They secured the midfielder Hugo Larsson and centre-back David Affengruber on deadline day but missed out on another target, the right-back Andrei Ratiu. JS

Key ins: Gonzalo García (Real Madrid, £34.3m), Shea Charles (Southampton, £30m), David Affengruber (Elche, £10.3m), César Palacios (Real Madrid, £8.6m), Jonah Kusi-Asare (Bayern Munich, £5.2m), Manuel Ángel (Real Madrid, £3.4m), Hugo Larsson (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan)

Key outs: Sasa Lukic (Ipswich, £9m), Issa Diop (Ipswich, £8.5m), Harry Wilson (Leeds, free), Raúl Jiménez (Wolves, free)

Hull

“Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

Key ins: Nobel Mendy (Rayo Vallecano, £20m), Konstantinos Tzolakis (Olympiakos, £20m), Lucas Herrington (Colorado Rapids, £17.1m), Ilyas Ansah (Union Berlin, £14.5m), Mohamed-Ali Cho (Nice, £13m), Brooke Norton-Cuffy (Genoa, £12m), Jens Hjerto-Dahl (Tromsø, £10m), Tim Iroegbunam (Everton, £13m), Christos Mouzakitis (Olympiakos, £12.9m), Sorba Thomas (Stoke, £7.5m), Joe Gelhardt (Leeds, £6.5m), Jack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m), Lucas Gourna-Douath (Red Bull Salzburg, £3.4m), Elliot Stroud (Mjällby, £3m), Robinio Vaz (Roma, loan), Hidemasa Morita (Sporting, free), Matt Targett (Newcastle, free), Óscar Zambrano (Maribor, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Ivor Pandur (Rangers, £6m), Cody Drameh (Genoa, £3.9m), Abu Kamara (Portsmouth, £2.5m), Kyle Joseph (Middlesbrough, undisclosed fee)

View image in fullscreen Nobel Mendy, the most expensive of Hull’s 18 signings, made a perfect start by scoring against Manchester United. Photograph: Mike Martin/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

Ipswich

The late addition of Burnley’s striker Zian Flemming brought Ipswich’s summer spend close to £200m. That appears to be the cost of giving yourselves a genuine shot at survival. Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. Gary O’Neil can call upon enviable depth in midfield and speed on the flanks, where Abdul Fatawu and Daizen Maida look sharp. But time will tell whether Ipswich strengthened their defence sufficiently for regular tests of the kind they failed at Old Trafford on Sunday. Nick Ames

Key ins: Julio Enciso (Strasbourg, £26m), Emersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Exequiel Palacios (Bayer Leverkusen, £23.5m), Zian Flemming (Burnley, £20m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Abdoul Ouattara (Strasbourg, £17m), Florentino Luís (Burnley, £16m), Daizen Maeda (Celtic, £10m), Sasa Lukic (Fulham, £9m), Kjell Scherpen (Union St-Gilloise, £8.6m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m), Kayne van Oevelen (Volendam, £3.4m), Cédric Kipré (Reims, £1.7m)

Key outs: George Hirst (Stoke, £6m), Arijanet Muric (Sassuolo, £6m), Harry Clarke (Preston, £3.5m)

Leeds

In an ideal world Daniel Farke might have wished for one more high-calibre attacking recruit but that should not detract from a very decent window, featuring seven extremely sensible signings. The importance of the acquisition of the England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City should not be underestimated. Trafford will almost certainly provide Leeds with a few more extra points – not to mention enhance their play courtesy of his stellar footwork. Just in front of him Tarik Muharemovic looks an outstanding defensive buy. Harry Wilson raises creativity levels and the attacking tone. LT

Key ins: James Trafford (Manchester City, £40.5m), Tarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Nico Elvedi (Borussia Mönchengladbach, £6.8m), Michael Zetterer (Eintracht Frankfurt, £4.3m), Jean-Mattéo Bahoya (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan), Melvin Bard (Nice, loan), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free)

Key outs: Pascal Struijk (Brighton, £18m), Joe Gelhardt (Hull, £6.5m), Lucas Perri (Torino, loan), Sebastiaan Bournauw (Hamburg, loan), Joël Piroe (West Ham, loan), Illan Meslier (Arsenal, free)

Liverpool

The final window of Richard Hughes’s spell as sporting director raised more questions over Liverpool’s direction under Fenway Sports Group, owners soon to be enriched by a £2bn investment from 1892 Holdings. The shift towards paying big money for big names continued with Bradley Barcola’s arrival from Paris Saint-Germain while Jérémy Jacquet and Victor Muñoz followed the older policy of developing young potential. Yet weaknesses remain at right back, defensive midfield and on the right wing, where Mohamed Salah’s exit was foreseen from December. Squad depth is lacking and a lot rests on the return to full fitness of Hugo Ekitiké, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni. AH

Key ins: Bradley Barcola (PSG, £123m), Jérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m), Ronald Araújo (Barcelona, loan)

Key outs: Curtis Jones (Inter, £25.7m), Harvey Elliott (Valencia, loan), Mohamed Salah (Trabzonspor, free), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)

View image in fullscreen Bradley Barcola’s signing was the latest example of Liverpool paying big for big names. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Manchester City

With Enzo Fernández’s deadline day signing for a British record-equalling £125m, Enzo Maresca can have zero complaints about a first window as Manchester City’s head coach. The No 8 follows two No 6s, in Elliot Anderson (£116m) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (£85m), and the wide players Allan Elias (£34m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£60m plus £5m) as major signings, the total spend on incomings about £457.5m. Factor in how City have generated about £281.8m in outgoings for a net spend of £175.7m, the divisions third-biggest of the window, and this sizable investment has to work - particularly the acquisition of Fernández. Jamie Jackson

Key ins: Enzo Fernández (Chelsea, £125m), Elliot Anderson (Nottingham Forest, £116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (Lille, £85.7m), Iliman Ndiaye (Everton, £60m), Allan (Palmeiras, £32m), Mathys Detourbet (Troyes, £21.6m), Gerónimo Rulli (Marseille, £1.7m)

Key outs: Sávio (Tottenham, £75m), Nico González (Newcastle, £52m), Tijjani Reijnders (Al-Qadsiah, £52m), Rodri (Barcelona, £51.3m), James Trafford (Leeds, £40.5m), Nathan Aké (Fenerbahce, £7m) Omar Marmoush (Tottenham, loan), Jack Grealish (Everton, loan), John Stones (Inter, free). Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free)

Manchester United

This was the window of the midfielder for Manchester United, with three recruited: Youri Tielemans (a No 8), Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba (No 6s). Yet missing was a left-back despite the targeting of Lewis Hall, and others, plus reinforcements for the rest of a creaking rearguard. The reason? A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. Will the specialist Luke Shaw, plus the stand-in options of Parick Dorgu (a wing-back/left forward), Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui (right-backs), Lizandro Martínez (centre-back) and Baleba prove adequate? JJ

Key ins: Carlos Baleba (Brighton, £70m), Andrey Santos (Chelsea, £50m), Youri Tielemans (Aston Villa, £35m)

Key outs: Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m), Casemiro (Inter Miami, free)

Newcastle

Newcastle describe their transfer window as “transformative” and, with reinvention the name of the game on Tyneside, it is easy to see why. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. The deadline day arrival of the exciting 21-year-old Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille is regarded as quite a coup. Have Newcastle choreographed a triumph from a window that, at one point, looked potentially disastrous? LT

Key ins: Nico González (Manchester City, £52m), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (Lille, £51m), Bazoumana Touré (Hoffenheim, £43m), Aladji Bamba (Monaco, £30m), Amar Dedic (Benfica, £29.5m), Lukas Hornicek (Braga, £25.7m), Ewen Jaouen (Reims, £21.6m), Sean Steur (Ajax, £20m)

Key outs: Sandro Tonali (Tottenham, £92.5m), Bruno Guimarães (Arsenal, £75m), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona, £69.3m), Nick Woltemade (Juventus, loan), Kieran Trippier (Wolves, free)

View image in fullscreen Matias Fernandez-Pardo’s signing from Lille is regarded as a coup. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

Nottingham Forest

Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Whether not sourcing a direct replacement for Anderson will hurt them remains to be seen but at least they did not panic, making it a measured window where they were able to trim the squad. Will Unwin

Key ins: Liam Delap (Chelsea, £45m), Ousmane Diomande (Sporting, £34.2m), Daniel Muñoz (Crystal Palace, £22m), Steven Benda (Fulham, free), Xaver Schlager (RB Leipzig, free)

Key outs: Elliot Anderson (Manchester City, £116m), Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry City, £9m), Omari Hutchinson (Milan, loan), Stefan Ortega (Olympiakos, free), Jota Silva (Olympiakos, loan), Morato (West Ham, loan)

Sunderland

After last summer’s 14 new faces this had been a bit of a conservative, almost slightly underwhelming, window. Or at least it was until Crystal Palace tried to hijack Sunderland’s agreement to sign the Lyon winger Malick Fofana and the two Premier League clubs engaged in an astonishing deadline day tug of war involving private jets from both sitting on the tarmac at Lyon airport and Fofana undergoing a medical in France unsure as to his destination until finally choosing Wearside. Arguably Sunderland’s biggest achievement was keeping last season’s star players. If persuading Granit Xhaka to stay rather than defect to Chelsea was vital, Régis Le Bris will be similarly delighted to have retained widely admired individuals of the calibre of Enzo Le Fée, Robin Roefs and Noah Sadiki. LT

Key ins: Malick Fofana (Lyon, £31m), Dayann Méthalie (Toulouse, £24m), Kevin Danso (Tottenham, loan), Thomas Meunier (Lille, free)

Key outs: Eliezer Mayenda (Rennes, £17.1m)

Tottenham

A comprehensive reboot, from back to front, featuring a club record outlay for a window and one of the most lavish by any club ever. In the first summer window since the departure of the longstanding chair Daniel Levy, the hierarchy have backed Roberto De Zerbi in an attempt to put the trauma of last season behind them. All the new signings have Premier League experience and – apart from Mateus Fernandes and Sávio – are aged 25 or over. In other words, they ought to be ready to hit the ground running. The opening two matches did not go to plan. It will get better. Won’t it? David Hytner

Key ins: Sandro Tonali (Newcastle, £92.5m), Mateus Fernandes (West Ham, £85m), Sávio (Manchester City, £75m), Jan Paul van Hecke (Brighton, £52m), Tosin Adarabioyo (Chelsea, £7m), Omar Marmoush (Manchester City, loan), Martin Dubravka (Burnley, loan), Mykhailo Mudryk (Chelsea, loan), Marcos Senesi (Bournemouth, free), Andy Robertson (Liverpool, free)

Key outs: Luka Vuskovic (Brighton, £46m), Cristian Romero (Atlético Madrid, £34.1m), Djed Spence (Inter, £25.6m), Radu Dragusin (Fiorentina, loan), Guglielmo Vicario (Juventus, loan), Pape Matar Sarr (Juventus, loan), Kevin Danso (Sunderland, loan)

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 12: Manchester United
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 7th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 4th

Prospects

It was all-change at Manchester United during pre-season, with the departure of their head coach Marc Skinner after five years followed swiftly by the appointment of Eva Olid as a new era begins. There have been significant outgoings from the playing group, including the senior squad members Melvine Malard, Gabby George, Millie Turner and Lisa Naalsund, as well as the end-of-contract exits of Leah Galton and Hannah Blundell, but the signings of the Spain youth international defender Andrea Medina, the former Germany youth international goalkeeper Janina Leitzig and the Sweden forward Monica Jusu Bah will give the squad a fresh feel.

Missing out on the Women’s Champions League places by nine points last season was disappointing and after a summer in which other clubs have spent big, it feels more likely United will be looking over their shoulder at challengers coming up from fifth and sixth than mounting a title challenge.

Tottenham’s and London City’s ambitious recruitment mean they could threaten United’s position but United have not turned into a bad team overnight. European quarter-finalists last season, their squad retains a strong level of quality international players, despite the sale of Malard to Chelsea in particular. The England internationals Maya Le Tissier and Ella Toone are the senior leaders in a squad that also retains a world-class goalkeeper in Phallon Tullis-Joyce, the dynamic England midfielder Jess Park and the talented Sweden wing-back Anna Sandberg. A top-half finish feels realistic and the club will hope for strong runs in the domestic cups. There is also understood to be a desire at the club to make the playing style more entertaining for supporters.

Off-field picture

As with the men’s club, the Glazer family own a majority stake and Ineos – led by Sir Jim Ratcliffe – has a minority stake but has control of football operations. The financial history of the women’s team divides opinion in the sport; some argue United are an example of how to run a professional women’s team sustainably, having recorded a profit of £397,000 in their most recent accounts and a profit of £1.34m since reforming their senior women’s team in 2018, while others lament a lack of investment from the ownership compared with the budgets of their rivals such as Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City.

The manager

Olid was appointed on 5 August on a two-year deal with the option of a further year. The Spanish coach, who turned 41 in late August, arrives after an impressive spell at Hearts, where she led the club to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title in May. That made her the SWPL’s manager of the season. It is understood she was chosen by United’s hierarchy because they feel her CV demonstrates a strong track record of developing and improving young players.

Star signing

Bah, who has 11 caps, looks to be an important signing for United from BK Häcken for a fee reportedly of about £400,000. The 23-year-old helped the Swedish club to win the inaugural Women’s Europa Cup – European club-level women’s second competition – last season and she said the opportunity to work with Olid was “perfect” because she wants to improve. She provided seven assists and scored 16 goals for her club last season and United will hope she can settle into the WSL quickly.

View image in fullscreen Monica Jusu Bah arrives in Manchester from the Swedish club BK Häcken. Photograph: Poppy Townson/Manchester United/Getty Images

Stat attack

United made a mockery of underlying data last season. Only Arsenal overachieved against their attacking expected goals by more and only City conceded fewer compared with their xG at the back. They were ranked fourth for expected goal metrics at both ends but the combined variance of +9.86 against those numbers makes them hard to predict this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Set for a breakthrough

Layla Drury, an academy graduate, became United’s youngest player and goalscorer when given her debut in the Women’s FA Cup in January at 16, and this summer the 17-year-old became the youngest player to sign a professional contract with the club. She has been added to England’s Under-20 squad for the World Cup in Poland in September and last Saturday scored for the Young Lionesses in their 11-0 warm-up victory against New Caledonia. The forward had previously played for Wales’s youth teams.

What they say

“I always say: ‘My life is football.’ I don’t have other things. I spend probably 24 hours every day on football. It’s my life, my lifestyle and I give everything for the team and for the players. They always have me. Doubts, questions, [it] doesn’t matter the time of the day, I’m going to be there for them. I want to make them better, and that is how I’m going to feel good as a coach, seeing the improvement, seeing that they are better, and of course, winning matches” – Olid to MUTV.

Where are they playing their home games?

United play at Leigh Sports Village, a 12,000-capacity venue which is also the home of the rugby league club Leigh Leopards and the United’s men’s under-21s. It has been their home ground since 2018. The stadium hosted a quarter-final at Euro 2022. United’s final home WSL fixture, against Arsenal in May, has been scheduled for Old Trafford, although that match may have to be rearranged if Arsenal reach the semi-finals of the Women’s Champions League because the second legs are that weekend.

Sports.title: Fernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester City
Sports.content:
Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea, who were left raging after their attempts to replace the Argentina midfielder were dashed by Monaco reneging on an agreement to sell Lamine Camara on Tuesday night.

On a day of twists and turns, City emerged in a strong position after they bolstered their attack by signing Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for up to £65m and secured one of Enzo Maresca’s biggest targets on a five-year deal. Chelsea held out for a huge fee for Fernández and it seemed they were going to find a replacement for him as the transfer window drew to a close.

The club moved to agree a £47m fee with Monaco for Camara, who was poised to sign a six-year contract with the option of an extra year. Chelsea swooped when Everton’s attempts to sign the USA striker Folarin Balogun ran into difficulties. It left Monaco needing to raise funds from elsewhere, prompting Chelsea to revive their move for Camara after having a £38.1m offer for the 22-year-old Senegal midfielder rejected earlier in the day.

Chelsea had a written agreement with Monaco but were stunned by the Ligue 1 club pulling out of the deal as the deadline approached. Sources called Monaco’s conduct “deeply unprofessional”. As an extraordinary situation developed it emerged that Everton, who have also loaned Jack Grealish from City, had refused to give up on Balogun, renegotiating the fee for the former Arsenal forward only for that deal to also fall down just after midnight.

The collapse of Camara’s move did not lead to Chelsea cancelling the sale of Fernández to City. The deal means City have spent £327m on midfielders this summer following the arrivals of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille for £86m.

“I could not be happier to be here, and I am ready for the challenge of helping City continue winning trophies. This is a club built for success,” said Fernández, who becomes this country’s most expensive player alongside Alexander Isak, who joined Liverpool from Newcastle for £125m a year ago.

“I pride myself on continually improving my game. Anyone who’s worked with me will know how hard I train every single day and how much I put into matches. I give absolutely everything and I can promise Manchester City that will continue now I’m here.”

View image in fullscreen Iliman Ndiaye also completed his move to Manchester City on a busy deadline day for the club’s sporting director, Hugo Viana. Photograph: Manchester City FC

Maresca has a good relationship with Fernández after coaching him at Chelsea and a reunion has been on the cards for a while. City opened talks with Chelsea on Monday night and will feel they have successfully rebuilt their midfield after selling Rodri to Barcelona and losing Bernardo Silva to Real Madrid, while also selling Nico González to Newcastle. They were also not put off even after Chelsea’s unofficial deadline for clubs to lodge bids of £120m for Fernández passed last month.

Fernández has been angling for a way out of Chelsea since March and his departure was announced in a short statement on the club’s website. The 25-year-old, who scored 31 goals after joining from Benfica for £106.7m in January 2023, initially had his sights set on joining Real Madrid. He grew disillusioned following Maresca’s acrimonious split with Chelsea this year. Fernández, the unofficial vice-captain, spoke out after Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by Paris Saint-Germain in March. Chelsea responded by banning him for two games.

Fernández reported back to training after the World Cup and was booed by Chelsea fans during a pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge. He featured in the club’s opening first game of the season, coming off the bench to help Xabi Alonso’s side to beat Fulham, but was left out of Chelsea’s next two fixtures.

Chelsea came round to the view that a sale was in their interests. There is a feeling within the club that Fernández, who won the Conference League and Club World Cup during his time in west London, had not shown himself to be vice-captain material.

Chelsea have made in the region of £500m in loans and sales this summer. They finished the window by selling Marc Guiu to RB Leipzig for £16m and loaning Dário Essugo to Strasbourg, Robert Sánchez to Como and Mykhailo Mudryk to Tottenham. Tosin Adarabioyo joined Spurs on a permanent deal.

Sports.title: Everton left with only one striker after Balogun deal collapses late on deadline day
Sports.content:
Everton’s £40m move for the USA international Folarin Balogun collapsed late on deadline day to leave the manager, David Moyes, with only one striker for the first half of the season.

Everton had agreed a £40m deal for Balogun only for issues with the striker’s medical to place the transfer in doubt after the Merseyside club had sold Beto to Fiorentina and Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City. Enquiries were made to Manchester United for Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa for Tammy Abraham but proposed loans for both forwards were rejected.

The structure of the deal was renegotiated late on – Monaco accepted a lower payment up front and more in appearance-related add-ons – and Everton submitted a deal sheet to complete the transfer in time. Balogun signed the squad sheet shortly before 11pm. But the 25-year-old, who is believed to have missed his scheduled morning flight to Merseyside and arrived later in the day, changed his mind over the move and walked away at the final moment.

The collapse of the deal leaves Thierno Barry as Everton’s one recognised striker and completed a shambolic end to the window by the club’s hierarchy, who were already under pressure having tried to sell Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest.

Everton also hit problems in their attempts to sign the right-back Kenny Tete from Fulham. A £9m deal had been agreed for the defender only for Fulham to fail to secure their preferred replacement, Andrei Ratiu of Rayo Vallecano. Everton finally concluded their long-running search for a right-back by signing the former Arsenal player Ainsley Maitland-Niles from Lyon for a fee of around £4.2m. The 29-year-old has agreed a three year contract.

Funds were raised by the sales of Ndiaye to City, for £60m plus £5m in add-ons, Beto to Fiorentina for £15.5m, Tim Iroegbunam to Hull for an initial £15m, and Nathan Patterson to Torino for an undisclosed fee.

Grealish returns to the Hill Dickinson Stadium on another season loan from City. The 30-year-old player enjoyed a productive spell on loan in 2025-26 before sustaining a fractured foot that ended his campaign in February.

Grealish, who will be out of contract at City when this latest deal ends next summer, could make his second Everton debut against Manchester United on Sunday. He said: “I’m so happy. I think I’m at my best at everything in life, not just football, when I feel loved. That’s what the manager has given me, what my teammates have given me and especially what the fans have given me. Every time I see an Everton fan, it’s just pure love.

“It means a lot to me and hopefully I’ve made a few Everton fans happy. I had a perfect time here for the first six months, then I stayed around after I got injured. I’ve been watching all the Everton games in pre-season and since the season started. Now I feel ready to go.”

Sports.title: Which footballer has had the most glittering club career? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Marquinhos won his 40th trophy in club football when Paris Saint-Germain beat Aston Villa in the Super Cup,” notes Paul Gage. “Has any player won more?”

The short answer is no: here’s Pete Tomlin with the breakdown. “I calculate that Marquinhos has actually won 41 trophies – one Copa Libertadores, 11 Ligue 1 titles, eight Coupes de France, six Coupes de la Ligue, 10 Trophées des Champions, two Champions Leagues, two Super Cups and one Intercontinental Cup.” Not a bad haul. “This puts him at No 1 in the list of club trophies won by a player. Just behind is Lionel Messi with 40 (10 La Ligas, 7 Copas Del Rey, 7 Supercopas de España, four Champions Leagues, three Super Cups, three Club World Cups, two Ligue 1 titles, one Trophées des Champions, one MLS Cup, one Supporters Shield and one Leagues Cup).

“Third on the list is the Egyptian midfielder Hossam Ashour with 39 (13 Egyptian League titles, four Egypt Cups, 10 Super Cups, six CAF Champions Leagues, one CAF Confederations Cup and five CAF Super Cups). Clear in fourth place is Dani Alves (one Copa do Nordeste, five Copas del Rey, five Supercopas de España, two Uefa Cups, four Super Cups, six La Liga titles, three Champions Leagues, three Club World Cups, one Serie A title, one Coppa Italia, two Ligue 1 titles, one Coupe de France, one Coupe de la Ligue, one Trophées des Champions and one Campeonato Paulista).”

Barcelona, Fifa and the Royal Spanish Football Federation credit Messi with winning the 2005 Supercopa de España, which would place him equal with Marquinhos, but he did not feature in the squad for either game so we’re not having that. If you have a player who can surpass that, drop us a line.

Oh brother(s)

“Three of Kevin Lisbie’s sons are playing professionally; in the Championship (Kyrell, Millwall), in League One (Kyreece, Reading) and League Two (Kaion, Colchester United),” wrote Stuart Willsher last week. “Have we ever had four brothers playing in all four top English divisions?”

Our thoughts immediately turned to the five Shankly brothers, Bill, Bob, Jimmy, Alec and John. All played professionally across Scotland and England but only including tiers one, three and four in England. Thankfully, Mike O’Dea and Michael Haughey were on hand with a better example. “As many will email in about, the five Clarke brothers of Willenhall – Frank, Allan, Derek, Kelvin and Wayne – all played league football but they were never spread across all four divisions,” Michael writes.

“Between 1975 and 1978 there were four Clarke brothers at league clubs. Kelvin in the third with Walsall, Derek in the second with Oxford and Orient, Frank in the second with Carlisle and Allan in the top flight with Leeds. Wayne made his First Division debut with Wolves in the final game of the 1977-78 season, so briefly there were five Clarke brothers playing in the league. That summer Frank and Kelvin retired, also Derek would play only one more game, while on loan at Carlisle. Allan joined Fourth Division Barnsley as player-manager. This was the only time one of the Clarke brothers played fourth-tier football. He promptly got Barnsley promoted at the first attempt.”

So the Clarke brothers played across the top four tiers in England if you allow for Allan covering tiers one and four, but they definitely didn’t cover all four in one season, missing out narrowly in 1978.

Caught in no-man’s land (part two)

It seems we have a new winner in regards to the question last month about the furthest up the field a keeper had been sent off, so kudos to Luke Levy, who got back in touch. “You mentioned Adrián’s incident in 2015 that got him red-carded outside the opponent’s box,” he writes, “but I can’t believe you’ve forgotten Oliver Kahn’s insane exploits in March 2001. With Bayern Munich trailing Hansa Rostock 3-2, Kahn went up for the corner and, using all his tenacity, explosiveness and wit, leapt above the rest to double-fist punch the ball into the opponent’s net. That was within the opponents’ six-yard box, with Kahn given a second yellow. I would like to see any other exploit in taking an early bath that beats that.”

“Midnite are the 26-27 shirt sponsors for three Championship sides; Middlesbrough, Sheffield United and Wolves,” Peter Skilton notes. “This means they will be the sponsors of at least one of the teams in 24% of Championship fixtures this season. Is this a record, and which brand has sponsored the most different teams in a single league?”

Dirk Maas comes in clutch with the answer here. “In 1987, Coca-Cola made a sponsorship deal with multiple Campeonato Brasileiro Série A teams. In 1990, 16 out of 20 teams were sponsored by Coca-Cola. Only Corinthians (Kalunga), Flamengo (Lubrax), Náutico (Banorte) and Portuguesa (Hudson) did not have Coca-Cola as shirt sponsor. Caixa almost matched Coca Cola’s feat in 2017: 14 out of 20 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A teams were sponsored by them.”

Knowledge archive

On 31 March 2012, towards the end of Stockport’s heroic 3-1 win at Kettering, a substitution took place with Daniel Lucas Rowe being replaced by Daniel Martin Rowe,” Alex Dixon wrote in 2012. “Both are known as Danny Rowe – is the first substitution involving two players with the same name?”

No, but luckily Henrik Hansen is on hand to elaborate and help us to flesh out this answer. “In the 1995-96 Danish Superliga season, FC Copenhagen had two players in their squad named Morten Nielsen,” he reveals. “One of them was usually referred to as Morten B Nielsen (short for Morten Bøhme Nielsen) to avoid confusion. On one occasion, an away game on 31 March at Vejle, the two players were substituted with Morten Nielsen replacing Morten B Nielsen after 73 minutes of play.”

Can you help?

“Slavia Prague and Fenerbahçe have played each other in the Conference League, Europa League and have been drawn to play each other in this season’s UCL league stage,” Önder Susam begins. “Has this happened before? Can it be bettered by teams who have also played each other in Intertoto Cup or Cup Winners’ Cup?”

“I read a few days ago that the Dutch outfit NEC Nijmegen have played six times in the Netherlands cup final and that they have lost all those (1972-73, 1982-83, 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2023-24, 2025-26),” Bogdan Kotarlic notes. “I have an impression that there must be an even worse team for losing cup finals, either in domestic or international cups. Am I right?”

“On Saturday, Clyde were winning 3-0 at The Spartans after an hour when Logan Dunachie was sent off. Twenty-eight minutes later, the score was 3-3. What is the biggest turnaround in a game following a red card/most quantitative blame that can be thrown at a player for getting sent off?” asks Jamie Wills.

“Chesterfield’s goalkeepers have saved the last five penalties they’ve faced (Zach Hemming with two and Ryan Boot with three.) Are they remotely close to a record?” wonders Stuart Basson.

Sports.title: Football connects communities but can pull them apart if governed carelessly | Cath Bishop
Sports.content:
The fight for the soul of football isn’t just happening in the offices of Uefa and Fifa, it’s taking place on pitches much closer to home. At the weekend games of football for 750 children aged five to six in Scotland were cancelled because of severe behavioural issues within the ironically named “Fun 4s” programme. Seventy-two red cards were handed out in the first week of the season. Accounts describe adults displaying aggression, intimidation and head-butting as if it’s the “wild west”.

This isn’t just a Scottish problem. Contacts I speak to in different roles around football confirm and almost accept that “youth football is atrocious”. This should be sounding major alarm bells, for the consequences go way beyond the pitch. The existing disciplinary systems and PR campaigns are not nearly enough to address and change the situation.

It’s incredibly selfish and socially corrosive for an adult to intervene and spoil the experience of kids playing football. There are no good outcomes. For the children, they learn to associate football, and potentially life more broadly, with violence and aggression. They are robbed of a space to be free, to play and develop and have fun alongside their friends. They see adults role-modelling a dog-eat-dog, win-at-all-costs mentality that is not laying the foundations for them to become good team players, school pupils or later civic-minded citizens. It also prevents young people from developing a love of being active and working positively in a team, perhaps one of the most powerful elements for a healthy life. It’s not a great way to develop parenting skills, either.

There is no shortage of evidence about how important it is – whether you are trying to develop skilful football players or healthy young people – that children need space to play, try stuff out and thrive. We also know that it’s what children want from sport. Research by Amanda Visek at the Milken Institute of Public Health at George Washington University, confirms that when it comes to organised sport, kids just want to have fun. What counts for girls and boys are things such as trying your best, working hard, playing well together as a team. When mapping 81 determinants of fun, “winning” ranked 40th in importance.

The Campaign for Children’s Rights in Football is an independent and impartial organisation. It’s preparing to launch and trying to create a greater platform for its work in the sport internationally. It’s needed more than ever.

The Centre for Young Lives set up the Raising the Nation Play Commission that published its report last year as part of a campaign for a national strategy to put play back into children’s lives. Last year the Scottish government published Scotland’s Play Vision Statement and Action Plan 2025-2030 to ensure that “every child is able to play across all stages and aspects of their life to support their social development, resilience, language and communication development, health, physical and mental wellbeing”. The Scottish FA had a “Let Them Play” campaign. But events playing out in Scotland show just how gaping the void is between government strategies, research and reality. This is going to take more than a communications campaign and a swathe of disciplinary proceedings. But investing in what is required for a deeper cultural change could create many positive ripples across our communities if the governing bodies get serious about making this their priority.

Creating thriving environments, ethics and focusing on the experience of those around you must become the first lesson in coaching training courses whether beginner or advanced. This needs to be the first part of training to be an official, or the conversation when your offer to volunteer is accepted by a local club. For any parents bringing their children to a club, clear standards, expectations and clarity on behaviours on and off the pitch should be integrated from the very first moment.

There is a bigger issue here. Sport is cited rightly as a great space to develop character, resilience, confidence. But that only happens in sports environments set up to develop those things. That wasn’t what was on offer on these Scottish youth football pitches. More sport may not help young people. Better experiences and environments will. That’s a crucial difference that has been missed when metrics have simply focused on growing participation and levels of activity.

Leadership is needed at the highest level. There’s a gap for our prime minister to call for sport to change itself in order to offer more to children and adults across the UK. When Andy Burnham called for “care to be at the heart of everything we do” that should include youth football and other sports experiences.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Elite football clubs have a responsibility, too, as key role models for how to play football. If there are things that happen in the Premier League that we wouldn’t want our children to emulate, we have to stop and ask why these things are happening at all. This question opens up a greater space for football to be a force for good. From their own talent-scouting interests, it’s also vital that future players are able to build on strong foundations of creativity, connection and strong intrinsic motivation – ie the love of the game, not just a love of winning.

Football and sport more widely have the power to unite a nation, to connect communities, to build positive solidarity. But we must also acknowledge, admit and understand that done poorly, without care, without strong leadership and clear cultural principles based on the experiences of all involved, it can pull apart the civic fabric we so desperately need to strengthen.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2 predictions: can Newcastle reach promotion and will Watford stay up?
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League 2 season, which gets under way on Friday when Watford host Burnley, comes with a tweaked format and the introduction of a new fixture. After the expansion of the WSL this summer, only the WSL2 champions are guaranteed promotion and the teams finishing second and third will contest a new, pre-qualifying match to determine who will face the WSL’s second-bottom side in the end-of-season promotion/relegation playoff decider. But which of the 12 sides have the best chances of going up. and who may occupy the relegation places?

Bristol City

Head coach Charlotte Healy. Last season 4th. Predicted finish 2nd.

The division’s top scorers last season, Bristol City’s inconsistency and a tendency to concede too often meant they finished five points off the top three. After a productive-looking transfer window, achieving at least a playoff place feels realistic. The club, owned by the Mercury13 group that also controls FC Como Women and FC Badalona Women in Spain, do not lack ambition. The re-signing of the defender Brooke Aspin from Chelsea is a boost to their backline and they will hope Lotta Lindström can help to replace the goals scored by Lexi Lloyd-Smith, who has left to join the top-flight side Crystal Palace.

Burnley

Manager Jackie Bachteler. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 8th.

Champions of tier three’s northern section after training full-time last term and completing an “invincible” season without a league defeat, Burnley have strengthened with an array of players with first- and second-tier experience, including the former England, Manchester United and Tottenham striker Rachel Williams, the former Chelsea, Reading and Newcastle defender Deanna Cooper and the former Birmingham captain Christie Harrison-Murray. Another, the Northern Ireland goalkeeper Jackie Burns, said: “We all know that it is very challenging [in WSL2] but we know we are capable of competing and actually putting our name out there as Burnley in this league.”

Durham

Head coach Willie Kirk. Last season 10th. Predicted finish 11th.

For a couple of anxious weeks in June, there was uncertainty as to whether Durham would reach the start line for this campaign. They issued a plea for investment, warned they would have to fold without an urgent cash injection and were saved by the local businessman Geoff Thompson. That was followed by the appointment of a new coach, Willie Kirk. Durham have been a continuous presence in WSL2 since its formation in 2014 and have frequently exceeded expectations, so underestimating them is dangerous, but for how long can this doggedly determined club defy the odds while the wealthier clubs around them spend significantly by comparison?

View image in fullscreen The Durham captain, Sarah Wilson, holds off Liverpool’s Alejandra Bernabé during a pre-season friendly in August. Photograph: Alan Edwards/Alamy

Ipswich Town

Manager David Wright. Last season 9th. Predicted finish 5th.

Ipswich did well in their debut WSL2 campaign last season to steer comfortably clear of relegation by winning their final three league games, and they have carried that momentum into the summer. They have raided the Scottish champions Hearts’ squad for three signings among more than a dozen in total, including Hearts’ top scorer from last season, Georgia Timms. No doubt their technical director, Sean Burt, previously Hearts’ head of recruitment, found his contacts book useful. With the former Spurs midfielder Kit Graham’s loan move made permanent too, the Suffolk club could be dark horses for a top-half push.

Leicester City

Manager Rick Passmoor. Last season Relegated from the WSL. Predicted finish 4th.

Winless since 14 December, Leicester endured a torrid campaign last term and were relegated in agonising fashion when they lost a penalty shootout against Charlton in the inaugural playoff. Inevitably, that prompted a vast number of senior players to depart, including good internationals such as Chantelle Swaby, Jutta Rantala and Hannah Cain. The relegation of the men’s team to League One cannot have helped the side’s resources. Nonetheless, any doom and gloom talk would feel hyperbolic: there remains a decent core of WSL-level players and they have done well to sign Sarah Mayling and Poppy Pritchard, as well as Tottenham’s Araya Dennis on loan.

Newcastle United

Manager Tanya Oxtoby. Last season 6th. Predicted finish 1st.

After drawing nearly half their games last season and not scoring enough, Newcastle have attempted to add quality to their forward line in a search for the goalscorers who can fire them to promotion. The arrivals of the former Manchester United forward Martha Thomas from Tottenham, the Republic of Ireland forward Leanne Kiernan from Liverpool and the Scotland striker Kathleen McGovern – who scored 51 times in 65 games for Hibs and has 10 goals in 14 matches for her country – should propel them to the promised land.

View image in fullscreen Martha Thomas brings a wealth of WSL experience to the Magpies. Photograph: Michelle Mercer/NUFC/Getty Images

Nottingham Forest

Head coach Tom Mallinson. Last season 7th. Predicted finish 6th.

Forest are one of three clubs – with Burnley and Durham – who have hired new coaches, with the appointment of their former men’s under-18s coach Tom Mallinson. The club have said they aim to “push towards the WSL”. They finished mid-table last season and are likely to continue building. The Forest goalkeeper Emily Batty said: “We want to get promoted, that’s the aim of the club. We know that isn’t a given, so it requires a lot of hard work. [It’s about] making sure we’re strong as a collective to get the best out of each other and hopefully help us get to that end-goal, come May.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sheffield United

Head coach Stephen Healy. Last season 11th. Predicted finish 9th.

Having struggled in the past two years – finishing bottom but getting a reprieve from relegation in 2025, then finishing four points above the drop zone – Sheffield United look likely to face another tricky campaign. Survival depends largely on whether the division’s third-top scorer from last season, Amy Andrews, is still at the club when the transfer window closes on Thursday. She scored nearly half of United’s measly total of 21 goals last season. But they have had a relatively stable, settled summer and have kept the core of their team, and one of their additions – Lucy Quinn – helped Birmingham to win this division last season.

Southampton

Head coach Simon Parker. Last season 5th. Predicted finish 7th.

With their budget understood to have been cut significantly, Southampton have endured a testing summer, and Sunderland signing Atlanta Primus, Tara Bourne and Fran Stenson will have been a blow after such an encouraging campaign last season and their run of five games without defeat at the end. Only Birmingham and Bristol City scored more WSL2 goals last season than Southampton. They have a good coach in Simon Parker, who has overcome adversity in this division before and defied a small budget at Blackburn, so his side should not be completely discounted.

Sunderland

Head coach Melanie Reay. Last season 8th. Predicted finish 3rd.

Sunderland have been taken over by the Bay Collective and have hired the former Tottenham and West Ham manager Rehanne Skinner as their technical director, so hopes are high that they can mount a challenge and become a force in the women’s game again. Melanie Reay is by far the division’s longest-serving head coach, having been in charge for more than nine years, and her team are finally getting true backing behind the scenes. Elise Hughes feels like a good signing from Palace and there is a feelgood mood that may make the difference.

Watford

Head coach Renée Hector. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 12th.

Promoted as southern section champions, Watford averaged nearly four goals a game. Their signings include the promising England youth international Vera Jones on loan from Chelsea. They look stronger than when last in the second tier in 2023-24 but staying up will be hugely challenging. Watford’s captain, Megan Chandler, who has been at the club since 2019, said: “The last time we were in this league, we were still part-time. Now we’ve transitioned to full time, that’s a huge step in the right direction. We’ve come on leaps and bounds. [We’d like to] establish ourselves in this league. People may think we’re a ‘yo-yo’ team because we have been previously, so I think this year is important for us to show people we’re not just here to survive, we’re here to compete as well.”

View image in fullscreen Flo Fyfe is one of 12 players to have signed a professional contract with the Hornets over the summer. Photograph: Tom Sandberg/PPAUK/Shutterstock

Wolves

Manager Dan McNamara. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 10th.

Another team who have transitioned to full time, professional status this summer are Wolves, who triumphed in the FAWNL promotion playoff against Plymouth Argyle in May after finishing second in the northern section, a point behind Burnley. Their revamped squad is a blend of new faces who have played at this level or higher and long-serving club stalwarts who will experience WSL2 for the first time. The step up will feel vast but they recruited well, aided by the arrival of their head of women’s and girls’ football, Russ Fraser, who has overseen recruitment at WSL clubs including Liverpool, Leicester, Reading and West Ham. The additions of Melissa Lawley, Yana Daniëls and Mel Filis, for example, should help them to stay up.

Sports.title: Sunderland pip Crystal Palace in battle of the private jets to land Malick Fofana
Sports.content:
Sunderland and Crystal Palace were involved in an extraordinary deadline-day tug of war that concluded with Malick Fofana agreeing to swap Lyon for the Stadium of Light in a club-record £31m move.

On Tuesday morning it had seemed that the 21-year-old Belgium winger was heading for Sunderland on a five-year contract, but then Pierre Sage led an attempt to hijack the deal. Palace’s manager coached Fofana at Lyon and forged a strong bond with a player he was keen to bring to Selhurst Park. After speaking to Sage on the phone, Fofana seemed to have changed his mind and decided he wanted to reunite with his old boss in south London. Sunderland, though, refused to surrender.

That meant Lyon had a bidding war on their hands and responded by agreeing improved deals with both clubs. Agents’ fees and Fofana’s personal terms were also understood to have risen accordingly. Meanwhile, two private jets, one dispatched by Sunderland and the other by Palace, sat on the tarmac at Lyon airport.

At one point Fofana was said to have been seen boarding the former aircraft before a flight to Newcastle airport but, in reality, he was headed to a private hospital in France for a medical commissioned jointly by Palace and Sunderland. With time running out, both clubs accepted this unusual arrangement was the only way a player targeted by Arsenal throughout much of the window would be heading to England.

In an attempt to remind Fofana, who scored 11 goals in 59 appearances for Lyon since arriving from Gent in 2024, why he had originally been so excited about playing for Régis Le Bris on Wearside, Kyril Louis-Dreyfus, Sunderland’s owner, flew to Lyon – presumably on a third jet – and spoke to him privately. It appears to have proved an inspired intervention as, shortly after 9pm, Fofana announced that he had made his choice and would be travelling to the Stadium of Light after all.

Although the initial fee agreed is £26m, add-ons dictate it should eventually rise to £31m. That leaves a forward capped five times by Belgium set to become Sunderland’s record signing, eclipsing the £30m paid to Strasbourg for midfielder Habib Diarra last summer. Sunderland have submitted a deal sheet and expect it to be concluded shortly.

Sports.title: Reiss Nelson lands new club days after Arsenal contract terminated
Sports.content:
Reiss Nelson is set to sign for Feyenoord less than a week after his Arsenal contract was terminated.

The 26-year-old winger officially left the Gunners after 18 years at the club on August 27, becoming a free agent.



2 Nelson had his Arsenal contract ripped up last week after 18 years at the club Credit: Getty

Nelson had been part of the Premier League champions' set-up since the age of eight, spending nine years in the first team squad.

But he struggled to ever break into the regular starting line-up over the years, being sent out on loan four times - most recently to Brentford - before his contract was ripped up a year early.

One of those loans was to Feyenoord in 2021/22, where he scored four goals and provided seven assists in 32 games.



And now the Dutch side, managed by ex-Arsenal player Giovanni van Bronckhorst, have returned to sign him again.

Nelson completes Feyenoord medical

Just days after he officially left the Emirates for good, Feyenoord have swooped in to bring Nelson back to the club.



Dutch outlet 1908.nl released images of Nelson arriving in Rotterdam, Netherlands to complete his free transfer.

He has agreed terms and completed a medical ahead of the move, which will see him play in the Eredivisie again.



Feyenoord are hoping to make the switch official by midnight on Wednesday to register the forward for the Champions League.

If they miss the deadline, Nelson would not be able to feature in any of their European fixtures this season.

The Dutch giants qualified for the Champions League last season after finishing second in the league behind PSV.

2 Nelson had some tough spells out on loan before leaving Arsenal permanently Credit: Getty



Nelson's next chapter

Nelson will hope to play more regular minutes this season after making the permanent move to Feyenoord.

He only played 14 times last term for Brentford on loan, in a campaign that was impacted by poor fitness.

The ex-England youth international featured 10 times in the Premier League for the Bees, not starting a single game.

Before that, he spent a year at Fulham on loan too, but a hamstring injury ruled him out for five months and he played just 11 games, scoring one goal and assisting another.



Nelson's first spell at Feyenoord came in 2021 and with 11 goal contributions during his spell, he impressed.

It was the same at his loan with German side Hoffenheim, where he scored seven goals in 29 matches.

He will hope to find some of that old form and consistent minutes now that he has officially left Arsenal.

For the Gunners, Nelson played 90 games across nine years, scoring just eight goals and providing nine assists.
