World.title: Mnangagwa Pledges Stronger Zambia-Zimbabwe Ties After Hichilema Re-Election
World.content:
Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has pledged to deepen cooperation with Zambia following President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration for a second term, saying the renewed mandate demonstrates the trust Zambians have placed in his leadership.

Speaking at National Heroes Stadium in Lusaka, Mr Mnangagwa described Zambia and Zimbabwe as longstanding brothers and pledged continued cooperation between the two countries in pursuit of shared development goals. He said the two nations enjoyed excellent relations strengthened by close historical, cultural and economic ties, and that their two peoples share close historical convictions built on the idea that political differences should never become national conflicts.

He commended Zambia for backing Zimbabwe’s successful bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for the 2027 to 2028 term, calling it evidence of the strength of regional solidarity. Mr Mnangagwa said he was confident that under the new mandate entrusted to Mr Hichilema by Zambians, the two countries would continue working together to broaden bilateral relations for the mutual benefit of their peoples.

Mr Mnangagwa urged African countries to take greater responsibility for their own development, modernisation and industrialisation rather than looking outward for solutions, arguing that the continent must build, modernise and industrialise its economies primarily through its own efforts. He said Africa must never apologise for being a proud, sovereign and independent continent, but must recognise that the responsibility to build and industrialise lies primarily with Africans themselves.

The Zimbabwean leader was among five African heads of state who attended the inauguration, alongside representatives from several other countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, Angola, eSwatini, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Rwanda and Mozambique, in what was widely seen as a strong regional endorsement of Zambia’s democratic transition.

He cited Zambia’s debt restructuring, exchange-rate stabilisation and declining inflation among the key achievements recorded under Mr Hichilema’s leadership during his first term, saying these reforms had positioned the country well for the growth phase now beginning.

Mr Mnangagwa said Zambia and Zimbabwe’s economic ties, including energy cooperation through the shared Kariba hydropower system, remained central to both nations’ development ambitions, and that the two countries would continue harnessing opportunities presented by the Southern African Development Community region and the wider African continent.

He said both nations remained mindful that the responsibility to build, develop, modernise and industrialise their respective countries lies with themselves, and pledged Zimbabwe’s continued partnership as Zambia embarks on the second phase of its Grow Zambia Agenda. His remarks drew warm applause from the crowd, many of whom had travelled from across the region to witness the ceremony, and were echoed by other visiting leaders who similarly framed Mr Hichilema’s re-election as a moment for renewed regional cooperation rather than continued rivalry.

World.title: Hichilema Unveils 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema used his second-term inauguration at National Heroes Stadium to launch a transformative economic blueprint he has named the Grow Zambia Agenda, telling thousands of supporters that the country’s focus now shifts from stabilisation to expansion.

Delivering his inaugural address shortly after being sworn in by Chief Justice Mumba Malila, the Head of State said the plan is coded 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1, targeting 10 million tonnes of maize, 10,000 megawatts of electricity, five million tourists, three million tonnes of copper, three million tonnes of soya, one million tonnes of wheat, one million tonnes of sugar and a billion US dollars in beef export earnings.

Mr Hichilema said the target for the next five years is to more than double the size of the economy, creating jobs, business opportunities and treasury revenue for further investment in social services that reach ordinary households rather than remaining locked in national statistics.

“Economic growth must mean something at the dinner table. It must mean education for our children, a job for a young graduate, a market for a farmer, capital for an entrepreneur, opportunity for a woman in business and a better future for every child,” he said, drawing sustained applause from the red-clad crowd that filled the 60,000-capacity stadium.

The President said his first term had been spent restructuring external debt, stabilising the Kwacha and rebuilding investor confidence, achievements he described as the foundation for the growth phase now beginning. He pointed to the successful conclusion of Zambia’s debt restructuring programme, improved international reserves and reduced inflation as evidence that the groundwork had been properly laid.

He acknowledged that stability had not yet translated into relief for every household, particularly amid continued pressure on the cost of living, telling the crowd directly that government had heard the concerns of families still struggling to make ends meet despite the improved macroeconomic picture. “We know that for many families, the cost of living has remained challenging, and that the benefits of our stabilisation have not yet been felt at every level. We hear you,” he said.

Mr Hichilema also announced that resources and responsibility would continue to be pushed down to local authorities through accelerated decentralisation, alongside deeper investment in education, skills development and healthcare, describing education as the greatest equaliser and the best inheritance the country could give its children.

Government would intensify the fight against corruption and protect public resources, he said, urging every public servant to place the national interest above personal gain and pledging that when all put national interests first, personal interests would in turn be taken care of.

The President said no province would be excluded and no district forgotten in the drive to expand the economy, and that development would continue to reach every corner of the republic regardless of political affiliation.

He linked the new agenda to a change of mindset he said the nation needed to embrace, moving away from what he termed the tantameni or handouts culture and toward growth, expansion, opportunity and prosperity built through production rather than dependency.

Economic analysts in Lusaka said the scale of the targets, particularly the tripling of copper output and the doubling of electricity generation capacity, would require sustained investment in infrastructure, power generation and irrigation over the coming five years, alongside continued reform of institutions that have historically slowed project delivery. Business groups welcomed the announcement but cautioned that translating the targets into results would depend heavily on how quickly government could unlock financing for the mining, energy and agricultural sectors central to the plan

World.title: Senegal: Senegal and IMF Strike $2.2bn Deal, Two Years After Debt Scandal Froze Funding
World.content:
Senegal and the International Monetary Fund have reached a staff-level agreement on a new $2.2 billion (€1.9 billion) lending programme, nearly two years after an earlier deal was suspended following the discovery of previously unreported public debt.

The 36-month arrangement, announced on Tuesday, is intended to support Senegal's economic and financial reform programme for 2026 to 2029.

However, it still requires approval from the IMF's executive board and depends on Senegal securing financing assurances from international partners.

The deal follows months of negotiations with President Bassirou Diomaye Faye's government, which came to power in 2024 after accusing the administration of former president Macky Sall of concealing the true scale of the country's debt and budget deficit.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Those revelations prompted the IMF to suspend a $1.8 billion (€1.55 billion) programme agreed in 2023 while it sought clarification over Senegal's public finances.

The Fund said the new agreement would require "decisive corrective measures" to address the earlier misreporting.

Finance Minister Cheikh Diba welcomed the breakthrough, saying Senegal and the IMF had reached a technical agreement that "paves the way for financing prospects".

'No blank cheque' for president or government says Senegal's Sonko

Debt burden remains high

Mercedes Vera Martin, a division chief in the IMF's African Department, said the Senegalese authorities had taken steps to improve transparency since the undeclared debt was uncovered.

Those efforts included audits and work to reconcile historical financial data.

Senegal's total public-sector debt was estimated at 132 percent of gross domestic product at the end of 2024, making it one of the most heavily indebted countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

There are, however, signs that the pressure is beginning to ease. The fiscal deficit fell from 13.4 percent of GDP in 2024 to 6.4 percent in 2025, largely as a result of tighter government spending, according to the IMF.

The economy also remained resilient, expanding by 6.7 percent in 2025 as Senegal benefited from its first full year of oil production. Growth outside the hydrocarbon sector was more modest, slowing to 2.2 percent.

Senegal began producing oil from its first offshore field in 2024, providing a new source of growth and revenue as the government works to stabilise the public finances.

The country has meanwhile continued to raise funds on regional markets, although borrowing there is generally more expensive than financing from international institutions and development banks.

Close 

IMF chief outlines plan to resume grants to Senegal

'Debt treatment'

The question of how Senegal should manage its debt has also become politically contentious.

Tensions between Faye and his former prime minister, Ousmane Sonko, intensified earlier this year over several issues, including relations with the IMF.

Faye dismissed Sonko in May, but Sonko later became speaker of the National Assembly, giving him an influential role as reforms linked to the IMF programme move through parliament.

Faye has favoured a more conciliatory approach towards the Fund, while Sonko has rejected conventional debt restructuring.

Asked whether the new programme involved restructuring, Vera Martin said it included "debt treatment", adding that Senegal had developed its own plan.

Diba stressed that the proposal was "not a restructuring in the traditional sense", but an approach designed around Senegal's specific circumstances.

Sonko, however, called for greater transparency in a Facebook post on Tuesday and demanded details of what "debt treatment" would involve.

He also said any commitments would ultimately be debated in the National Assembly, where his Pastef party holds a majority.

The agreement comes after Moody's last week downgraded Senegal's long-term foreign-currency debt rating from Caa1 to Caa2.

(with newswires)

World.title: Sudan: Air Attack Destroys Food Aid for Families in South Kordofan
World.content:
A map showing the location of Abyei and Southern Kordofan.

A massive supply of food destined for hungry families in South Kordofan state, Sudan, was destroyed in an aerial attack on two aid trucks over the weekend, the World Food Progamme (WFP) said on Wednesday.

The UN agency strongly condemned the attack which occurred on 30 August outside the city of Dilling.

The trucks carried 50 metric tonnes of WFP food including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil and salt--enough to provide lifesaving assistance to 5,800 people for one month.

They were heading to Kadugli, where WFP is supporting nearly 58,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or worse, and were clearly marked with its banners and flags.

End 'unacceptable' attacks

WFP said the attack was the latest example of the complex operating environment facing it and other humanitarian agencies in Sudan.

The UN has repeatedly called for an end to the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) which erupted in April 2023.

As a result of the conflict, some 30 million people required humanitarian assistance last year.

Since January, WFP has recorded eight aerial attacks that have damaged its premises and disrupted operations.

"Attacks on aid workers and humanitarian operations are unacceptable and must stop," WFP said, urging all sides to uphold international humanitarian law by protecting civilians, aid workers and humanitarian assets.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 2, 2026
World.content:
Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema Sworn In for Second Term

Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following an election overshadowed by opposition allegations of irregularities and the arrest of his main rival, Brian Mundubile, on treason charges. Hichilema was declared the winner of the 13 August election with 60% of the vote. Mundubile received 38% and claimed the results had been manipulated. Concerns were also raised after courts were sealed off on the final day available for a legal challenge. European Union observers pointed to weaknesses in the vote tallying and verification process. Despite the political tensions, Hichilema used his inauguration to call for unity and urged the opposition to work with his government. His second term comes after five years focused on stabilising Zambia's economy and restructuring its debt. The president is now pledging to shift his attention towards economic growth and prosperity.

Tunisia Faces Growing Crackdown on Civil Society



Tunisia is facing growing concern over what activists and human rights organisations describe as an intensifying crackdown on civil society and political dissent under President Kais Saied. Human Rights Watch said that the authorities have increasingly used arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and the suspension of organisations to silence independent voices and restrict the work of civil society groups. Activists have warned that the uncertainty surrounding possible arrests or prosecutions is creating a climate of fear, causing people to think twice before speaking publicly or working on sensitive issues. Saied, who has rejected accusations of authoritarianism, has defended his actions as necessary to tackle corruption and protect Tunisia's national interests. The crackdown comes amid renewed protests over worsening living conditions, water and electricity shortages and democratic backsliding. Surveys suggest a growing divide between younger Tunisians, who remain more sceptical of state institutions, and older citizens who are more supportive of the government.

DR Congo Schools Reopen Amid Ebola, Conflict and Strike Threat

Millions of students across the Democratic Republic of Congo have returned to school for the new academic year amid major challenges posed by an Ebola outbreak, continuing conflict in the east and a dispute between the government and teachers. The Ebola epidemic has affected six provinces, prompting authorities to introduce a three-tier system under which schools in high-risk areas will shift to limited remote learning. Those in lower-risk zones remain open under different health and safety measures. In territories controlled by the AFC/M23 armed group, schools are reopening under the movement's local authority even though teachers continue to receive their salaries from the government in Kinshasa. At the same time, the country's teachers are divided over whether to return to classrooms. One major union is maintaining a strike call and demanding higher salaries, payment for unpaid staff and improvements to pensions and health insurance. The new school year will therefore test the government's ability to keep children learning despite overlapping health, security and labour challenges.

FBI Confirms Tinubu Was Subject of 1990s Drug Probe

The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation has confirmed in a sworn declaration filed in a federal court that Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was the subject of a criminal investigation into drug-trafficking crimes in the early 1990s. The disclosure forms part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act case seeking the release of FBI records connected to a Chicago heroin-trafficking operation. A court had previously ruled that US agencies could no longer refuse to confirm whether such records existed. However, the FBI's acknowledgement does not establish that Tinubu committed a drug-trafficking offence or was convicted of any crime. Portions of the records remain withheld under exemptions protecting privacy, confidential sources and law-enforcement methods. Tinubu's government has dismissed renewed claims surrounding the records as politically motivated, accusing opposition figures and a Washington-based lobbying firm linked to former vice-president Atiku Abubakar of using decades-old documents to create controversy ahead of Nigeria's 2027 presidential election.

UNICEF Warns 162 Million Children at Risk From Looming El Niño Climate Shocks

UNICEF has warned that more than 162 million children across Eastern and Southern Africa could face severe risks as the strengthening 2026/2027 El Niño brings the threat of droughts, extreme heat and flooding to the region. The UN agency said the climate shocks could worsen food and water insecurity, disrupt healthcare and education. This could leave already vulnerable children exposed to malnutrition, disease, displacement and other dangers across 13 priority countries. Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan are among the countries facing particularly serious risks. Existing humanitarian and food crises are likely to be intensified by extreme weather. UNICEF has called for greater investment in anticipatory action, including strengthening nutrition, health and water services, protecting education and expanding social protection before the worst effects are felt. The agency is seeking US$173 million to provide life-saving assistance and warned that acting early could save lives and significantly reduce the costs of responding once a humanitarian crisis has already escalated.

Close 

Nigeria Anti-Corruption Agency Dismisses Over 40 Staff for Financial Misconduct

Nigeria's Economic and Financial Crimes Commission has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years. Several former staff members are already facing prosecution, and case files are being prepared against others. EFCC chairman Ola Olukoyede said the dismissals were part of efforts to strengthen accountability within an agency tasked with investigating corruption, fraud and money laundering. The commission has also introduced reforms, including renaming its Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of Ethics and Integrity and adopting a policy requiring officers to declare certain gifts and hospitality in an effort to prevent conflicts of interest. Olukoyede said the agency had also recorded significant results since he took office in October 2023, recovering 1.23 trillion naira and securing more than 10,000 convictions. However, the figures also show that the EFCC is increasingly dealing with cybercrime and fraud cases rather than focusing solely on corruption involving high-profile public officials.

World.title: Tunisia: Tunisia's Rights Defenders Decry Civil Society Crackdown
World.content:
Five years into the authoritarian rule of Tunisian President Kais Saied, Human Rights Watch and other activists warn that Tunisia's once vibrant civil society is in danger of being completely stifled.

"Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities."

Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues.

"What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention, the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report, published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely.

"It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights.

"The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW.

He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

Saied was elected president democratically in 2019. But in July 2021, he dissolved parliament and launched a power grab. Since then, he has dismantled most democratic bodies, repressed political dissent and arrested opposition figures.

For Anthony Dworkin, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations who focuses on human rights and democracy, Saied's goals remain unchanged. "They have been the same for the last five years, namely to consolidate power and remove potential checks on and critics of his rule," he told DW.

Saied has rejected accusations that he is an authoritarian ruler and argued that his measures are necessary to tackle corruption and uphold democracy. He has accused critics of receiving foreign funding to stir unrest and undermine Tunisia's national interests. DW reached out to the Tunisian presidency for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Growing discontent prompts calls for Saied's resignation

Despite the widespread crackdown on dissent, some people still dare criticize the government. On July 25, the fifth anniversary of the president's power grab, thousands took to the streets of the capital, Tunis, to protest worsening living conditions, democratic backsliding and the government's handling of basic services.

The demonstrations came amid widespread water and electricity outages, which Saied has described as "premeditated acts aimed at inflaming the situation by all means and spreading lies and rumors to sow confusion."

In late August, protesters once again called on the president to step down by chanting "The people want the fall of the regime," a popular slogan from the 2010-2011 Arab Spring uprising.

The demonstration was initiated by Nafas, a new citizen-led umbrella initiative that was launched in May. Mohamed Hawel, a university teacher and member of the Nafas collective, told the news agency AP that Nafas was created to unite people around basic necessities, including water, electricity and food.

Growing gap between older, younger Tunisians

Despite some unity at these protests, according to an Arab Barometer survey, there is an emerging generational divide in Tunisia. A report published in July on the basis of a survey conducted in the fall of 2025 found that older and less educated people had vastly different views on the country's economic and political conditions from younger, better educated people.

The survey showed that the older generation saw the current political and economic situation in the most positive light since the Arab Spring and had more trust in the government than over the past decade.

In comparison, younger Tunisians were more pessimistic about the country's economic and political development. They also remained more skeptical of state institutions while maintaining a high trust in civil society organizations: 49% of people between the ages of 18-39 expressed trust in these, compared with only 32% of those aged 40 and older.

Close 

"What really stands out in Tunisia is that the recent decline in trust in civil society is almost entirely a story about older Tunisians. Two years prior, there was almost no generational gap between citizens," Michael Robbins, the director of Arab Barometer, told DW. "Since then, trust in civil society among Tunisians 40 and older has fallen quite sharply, while it has not changed meaningfully among those who are aged 18-39."

Tunisia has a population of approximately 12 million people. People aged 18–39 account for roughly 30% of the population, while those aged 40 and older account for approximately 43%.

"I think the notion of a divided society is overstated," said Dworkin. "Moreover, the recent demonstrations are not large enough to pose a serious threat to Kais Saied," he added, while admitting that Saied had lost considerable public support over his failure to improve the country's economy. "But there are no attractive political alternatives and people are also tired of political upheaval."

In his view, many Tunisians are just trying to get by with daily life, while many others are looking to emigrate.

DW's Tarek Guizani in Tunis contributed to this report.

World.title: South Africa: Western Cape Braces for Hot Summer - South African News Briefs - September 2, 2026
World.content:
Western Cape Braces for Hotter, Drier Summer

Western Cape residents have been urged to prepare for a potentially hotter and drier summer, reports EWN. Experts are warning of increased wildfire risks and growing pressure on water resources. Local Government, Environmental Affairs and Development Planning MEC Anton Bredell said the province was taking the warnings seriously, particularly because extreme heat could pose greater risks in informal settlements. Authorities are securing firefighting aircraft, investing in equipment and training. They are urging residents and landowners to clear fire hazards and create firebreaks. Dam levels are already lower than last year. The province is also working to repair leaks, upgrade infrastructure and secure alternative water sources.

Ramaphosa's Phala Phala Bid Goes to Court

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

President Cyril Ramaphosa's application to set aside the Section 89 independent panel report on the Phala Phala saga is set to be heard in the Western Cape High Court, reports SABC News. The report found strong evidence that Ramaphosa may have violated his oath of office by stealing $580,000 in cash from his Limpopo farm. The National Assembly initially voted against the report. The Constitutional Court later invalidated that decision and ordered Parliament to establish an impeachment committee. The committee's proceedings were temporarily halted in July pending the outcome of Ramaphosa's application to review the report.

eThekwini Debt Tops R47 Billion

eThekwini Mayor Cyril Xaba has raised alarm over the municipality's growing debt, which has surpassed R47 billion, reports EWN. Households account for the largest share of the debt at R35 billion, followed by commercial clients owing R10 billion and government departments owing more than R2 billion. Xaba said the municipality could not function effectively with such a large and growing debt burden. He outlined plans to recover some of the money, including through disconnection campaigns and identifying residents who may qualify for indigent support.

World.title: Malawi: Chilima Plane Crash Inquiry Lays Bare Malawi's Aviation Safety Crisis
World.content:
The parliamentary inquiry into the June 10, 2024 plane crash that killed Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others has heard troubling testimony suggesting Malawi's aviation infrastructure suffers from long-standing structural deficiencies -- raising uncomfortable questions about institutional readiness that extend well beyond the immediate circumstances of the crash itself.

Fredrick Chisepeya, director of Aerodromes and Air Navigation Standards at the Civil Aviation Authority of Malawi (CAAM), told Parliament's Ad-hoc Committee investigating the disaster that the country risks failing next year's International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) audit unless significant investment is urgently directed towards safety and security infrastructure.

His testimony painted a picture of a system operating with minimal redundancy: Malawi possesses just one secondary flight surveillance radar, situated at Kamuzu International Airport in Lilongwe, whose effective coverage diminishes substantially for aircraft flying at lower altitudes.

It was this gap, Chisepeya confirmed, that meant the Malawi Defence Force aircraft was outside radar coverage entirely when it crashed in Viphya Plantation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The limitation is the radar coverage. When you are up, the range is wider and when you are down the range is narrower. So that makes the aircraft sometimes not to be seen," he told the committee -- an admission that speaks to a broader question of how a nation manages the tension between resource constraints and the non-negotiable demands of aviation safety.

The inquiry also heard that Mzuzu Airport, the aircraft's intended destination, fell well short of the protection standards required for medium-sized aircraft such as the Malawi Airlines Bombardier involved in the crash.

Using CAAM's own ten-point protection scale, Chisepeya estimated the airport's actual safety level at around three, against a required standard of six. He further noted deficiencies in fire response capacity and runway conditions, describing the surface as bumpy and substandard.

Perhaps most striking was the revelation that Mzuzu Airport was operating without a valid licence at the time of the crash, having only been licensed the following year, in 2025 -- and even then, with conditions attached.

Questions from committee chairperson Walter Nyamilandu drew a candid admission from Chisepeya that enforcement of aviation standards across Malawi's airports remains inconsistent.

The committee's scrutiny extended into the operational detail of the flight itself. Lilongwe Mude MP Mphatso Boti (Malawi Congress Party) probed whether formal aviation codes exist for reporting interference incidents, prompting Chisepeya to acknowledge that communication with aircraft becomes markedly more difficult once outside radar range.

Close 

Mwanza Central MP Felix Njawala (UTM Party) went further still, raising the possibility of frequency interference between the aircraft and ground officials -- noting that the pilot is understood to have made contact with Mzuzu Airport officer-in-charge Joseph Moyo only once throughout the flight.

Taken together, the testimony suggests the Chikangawa crash may prove less an isolated tragedy than a symptom of deeper, systemic underinvestment in the infrastructure meant to keep Malawi's skies safe.

World.title: Namibia: Drought Displaced Angolans Face Human Rights Abuses
World.content:
Angolan women and children displaced by drought into Namibia face serious human rights abuses arising from a lack of safe and legal migration pathways for people forced across borders by natural disasters, Amnesty International said in a new report.

The report, "The Drier it Gets, the Longer You Have to Walk: The Human Rights Impacts of Drought-Induced Displacement on Angolan Women and Children in Namibia, documents the devastating consequences of recurrent drought in southern Angola and the human rights impacts experienced by those displaced into Namibia, including persistent fear of arrest, detention and deportation, which in turn influences their daily decisions about whether to seek healthcare and other services.

"Namibian authorities must establish a rights-based approach to migration, ensuring that people displaced by drought and other natural disasters can access basic rights, including registration and documentation." Said Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa.

"The protection of already marginalized Angolans who are forced to move to Namibia in search of livelihoods is not just a humanitarian concern. This is a human rights crisis that demands international solidarity, including legal protection against refoulement," said Tigere Chagutah.



Namibian authorities must establish a rights-based approach to migration,ensuring that people displaced by drought and other natural disasters can access basic rights, including registration and documentation.Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International's Regional Director for East and Southern Africa

Between May 2024 and May 2026, Amnesty International interviewed at least 167 people, including displaced people, community leaders, government officials, representatives of civil society organizations (CSOs), academics, and members of the UN Country Team.

At the time of publication, Nambian government officials had not responded to Amnesty International's request for comment.

"The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig"

Southern Angola, particularly Cunene, Huíla and Namibe provinces, has been among the hardest hit by recurring droughts, which have been exacerbated by El Niño.

Together with long-standing structural vulnerabilities, these conditions have undermined traditional pastoral and farming systems, eroded people's resilience and forced them to migrate to Namibia in search of safety, food, water, work, and essential services.

The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig. Angolan Climate Activist

Women and children are disproportionately affected, often taking these journeys under great risk.

A young climate activist told Amnesty International that drought-induced displacement is not a simple story of people "running from drought", but a rational response to collapsing systems. "The drier it gets, the longer you have to walk, the deeper you have to dig," he said.

Namibian response to Angolan displacement

The report notes that Angolans displaced by drought have limited ways to regularize their stay in Namibia, as the current immigration and protection laws do not reflect the realities of climate-driven displacement. This has forced many people into irregular status as they cross the border in search of food, water, grazing land, healthcare, family support, and work following the droughts which destroys crops, livestock, and livelihoods.

In 2026, the Namibian Ministry of Home Affairs immigration control programme announced that more than 1,000 Angolan nationals had been returned to Angola after being found in the country without regular immigration status.

On 4 June 2025, Amnesty International witnessed Namibian authorities round up about 40 Angolan nationals, including women and children, at a community centre in Opuwo, and transport them the same day to the Ruacana border - over 100km away - for handover to Angolan authorities, without individualized screening, information about asylum or protection options, or assessment of the risks upon return. The absence of individual examination raises serious concerns under the prohibition of collective expulsion and the principle of non-refoulement.

The protection of already marginalized Angolans who are forced to move to Namibia in search of livelihoods is not just a humanitarian concern. This is a human rights crisis that demands international solidarity, including legal protection against refoulement.Tigere Chagutah

In other instances, Angolan children have also been subject to government-facilitated forcible returns without sufficient information being made publicly available to establish whether appropriate safeguards were applied.

The report highlights that Namibia's existing immigration framework does not adequately respond to the circumstances of people displaced across the border by drought. Although Angolan passport holders can enter Namibia visa-free through official border posts for limited periods, this does not provide a right to work, longer-term residence or a dedicated protection pathway.

Many people from drought-affected border communities also lack passports or other documentation and use informal crossing points. Once in Namibia without regular status, they have few accessible options to regularize their stay. This has left thousands of Angolans in fear of arrest, detention and deportation, a fear that shapes daily decisions about whether to seek healthcare and other services.

Amnesty International found that for those already living in northern Namibia, housing, water and sanitation conditions fell far short of international law and standards. Many families live in makeshift shelters, built from branches, plastic and cardboard, in severely overcrowded conditions or, in some cases, entirely without shelter.

The report details how undocumented Angolans were charged higher fees in hospitals than Namibian nationals, pushing them to delay treatment until illness became severe, and avoiding clinics altogether for fear that health facilities were linked to immigration enforcement.

"We only go when the pain is too much; otherwise, we just lie down and wait," one woman said.

Amnesty International calls on Namibian authorities to honour its international and regional legal obligations by ensuring that displaced Angolans can access legal protections, including registration and documentation needed to access rights. State authorities must conduct individual assessments before deportations and consider the human risk associated with return.

This reality underscores the need for the international community to recognize the injustice faced by these communities and respond with robust cooperation and support. It cannot wait.Tigere Chagutah

High-income, historically high-emitting states have heightened obligations in relation to climate action, while states that are able to do so must provide international cooperation and assistance, including adequate climate finance, according to their capacity, to support countries such as Angola and Namibia in adaptation, drought preparedness, resilience-building and addressing loss and damage.

"This reality underscores the need for the international community to recognize the injustice faced by these communities and respond with robust cooperation and support. It cannot wait," said Tigere Chagutah.

Angola's failure to invest in adaptation and preparedness

Angola's investment in climate adaptation, drought preparedness, and livelihood protection has remained uneven because of limited finance, weak institutional capacity, inadequate climate-monitoring infrastructure and continued dependence on donor-supported emergency and resilience programmes.

Close 

Angolan authorities must take urgent action to honour their legal obligations by putting in place safeguards to protect the drought affected through drought preparedness and climate adaptation mechanisms and protect communities at risk of displacement.Tigere Chagutah

The report shows how gaps in early warning systems, water infrastructure, veterinary support, and social protection mechanisms have contributed to the progressive erosion of pastoral and subsistence farming systems.

"Drought and the increasing risks posed by climate change cannot absolve the government from its legal obligation to protect people's rights to life, food, water, health, a healthy environment and an adequate standard of living," said Tigere Chagutah

"Angolan authorities must take urgent action to honour their legal obligations by putting in place safeguards to protect the drought affected through drought preparedness and climate adaptation mechanisms and protect communities at risk of displacement."

Background

Between January and July 2021, more than 7,000 Angolans, mainly women, including pregnant and lactating women, children and older persons, crossed into northern Namibia following consecutive years of severe drought and food insecurity in southern Angola. Drought and food insecurity have continued to contribute to cross-border movement in subsequent years, including during renewed severe drought conditions in 2023 and 2024. However, the true scale of drought-related displacement over this period is unknown due to the absence of comprehensive reception, registration, or data collection systems.

World.title: Nigeria: Over 1,000 Terrorists Killed, 777 Kidnap Victims Rescued in Two Months - Official
World.content:
Defence spokesperson, Samaila Uba, disclosed this on Tuesday during a security briefing at the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC).

The Defence Headquarters (DHQ) said troops killed 1,487 terrorists and insurgents, rescued 777 kidnap victims and arrested 354 suspects abductors during nationwide military operations conducted between July and August.

Defence spokesperson, Samaila Uba, disclosed this on Tuesday during a security briefing at the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC).

While presenting the military's operational assessment for the two-month period, Mr Uba said troops carried out 7,062 operations targeting terrorism, banditry, kidnapping, armed robbery and attacks on communities across the country.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The operations were conducted in Borno, Yobe, Taraba, Katsina, Kwara, Zamfara, Sokoto, Plateau, Benue, Niger, Oyo and Kaduna states, among others, he said.

According to him, the coordinated offensives combined land, air and maritime assets in clearance operations, intelligence-led raids, rescue missions and targeted arrests against terrorists, bandits, kidnappers, arms traffickers, oil thieves and other criminal elements.

"In total, 7,062 security operations were conducted. A total of 1,487 terrorists and insurgents were neutralised, 354 suspects were arrested, while 777 kidnapped victims were successfully rescued," he said.

The military spokesperson also reported that 93 security personnel and 249 civilians were killed during the period.

Troops recovered 991 firearms, 1,331 rounds of ammunition and several improvised explosive devices (IEDs), which were safely detonated.

The military spokesperson said one of its major achievements during the review period was the rescue of hundreds of kidnapped victims from terrorist enclaves.

It added that troops "neutralised" 309 Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters, arrested 354 suspects and recovered 44 IEDs during counter-terrorism operations.

The operations also led to the recovery of weapons, motorcycles and livestock, while several terrorist operational bases were dismantled.

Non-kinetic operations

Beyond combat operations, the military spokesperson said the military undertook nine dialogue and peace-building initiatives and held 15 stakeholder engagement meetings with traditional and religious leaders.

He added that 137 press statements were issued during the period, while 13 cases of misinformation were identified and countered.

Mr Uba said no major border or transnational security incidents, prison breaks or attacks on critical national infrastructure, including pipelines, railways and highways, were recorded during the review period.

The military spokesperson attributed the operational successes to joint military operations, inter-agency collaboration and community support, urging Nigerians to continue providing timely and actionable intelligence to security agencies.

Close 

He also thanked President Bola Tinubu for providing logistical support and strategic guidance to strengthen military operations, while urging the media to support ongoing security efforts through accurate, balanced and responsible reporting.

Since the Boko Haram uprising in 2009, Nigerian troops including the police have been actively engaged in operations against terrorists across the country.

The Boko Haram insurgency has spilled to other parts of the country including North-west and North-central where banditry, resource-based conflict and other security threats continue to destabilise the region.

The war which has now lingered for 17 years is now spreading to the South where jihadists kidnapped schoolchildren and their teachers.

World.title: NJ mom fatally stabbed in Times Square during first week back at Bank of America after maternity leave
World.content:

A Bank of America executive who had recently returned to work after maternity leave was fatally stabbed Monday in New York City’s Times Square, where a knife-wielding woman also wounded another person before police fatally shot the suspect.

World.title: Climber stranded on 6-inch ledge at 11,000 feet as 46 mph winds ground rescue helicopter
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A climber became stranded on a ledge just 6 inches wide about 11,000 feet up a California mountain, with strong winds preventing crews from reaching him by helicopter as the man fought to hold tight.

The climber ran into trouble Aug. 22 while attempting the Mendenhall Couloir on Laurel Mountain, according to a Facebook post from the Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue Team.

After mistakenly leaving the established climbing route, the man found himself in steep terrain where he could no longer safely move forward or retreat, the team said.

NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

The climber stopped on the narrow ledge and called for help using a satellite device.

Rescuers said the location was particularly dangerous because of the steep drop below — warning that a fall would "almost certainly be fatal."

A helicopter was requested — but winds gusting between about 35 and 46 mph at roughly 11,000 feet prevented crews from carrying out an aerial rescue, according to the post.

Technical rescue teams instead had to head up the mountain carrying about 1,200 feet of rope and other equipment needed to reach the climber.

CLICK HERE TO 

Once rescuers found him, they became concerned about how much longer he could safely remain in place.

The climber appeared to be repeatedly changing the leg he was standing on — which rescuers believed could indicate cramping.

Crews ultimately decided to begin a technical rescue that evening rather than leave him exposed on the ledge through the night.

Four rescuers used anchors and rope systems to reach the climber, secure him and guide him away from the steep gully.

The operation concluded at about 4:43 a.m. the following morning, according to the team.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"The team commends the subject for their incredible perseverance and determination, as well as for recognizing when help was needed and having the preparedness to call for it," the organization wrote.

Fourteen responders took part in the rescue, contributing nearly 172 volunteer hours, according to the post.

Fox News Digital previously reported on another climbing rescue in Georgia involving a man who became stranded on the side of Mount Yonah.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The climber called 911 after realizing he could no longer safely move up or down. Authorities used a drone to locate him on a roughly 20-by-20-inch ledge about 260 feet up the mountain.

White County firefighter Will Roper rappelled down the rock face, secured the climber in a harness and attached him to a rope before he was brought to the top of the mountain.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The rescue took about 42 minutes, and the climber later told Roper that he was familiar with Mount Yonah but had taken the wrong route and became stuck.

James Cirrone of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

World.title: Dolly Parton prayed in backyard church before recording comeback album, Ricky Skaggs says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ricky Skaggs is recalling how he and Dolly Parton prayed at the altar of a tiny church rebuilt in her backyard before recording the country comeback album that would help return her to the top of the charts.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 72-year-old bluegrass and country star remembered working on 1989's "White Limozeen" with the late music icon, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80.

Prior to making "White Limozeen," Skaggs told Fox News Digital that he visited Parton at her home in Nashville, where the two shared a private, faith-filled moment.

DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY

"She took me out in the backyard and showed me this little church that she used to go to when she was a kid up in East Tennessee. They had torn it down and they numbered all the slats and all the flooring and everything like that. They brought it down to her backyard and rebuilt it into a beautiful little church," Skaggs recalled.

"She wanted me to go in," he continued. "We went in there and they had a little piano in there and a little altar, just like the old Baptist churches in the mountains. So we got up by the altar and just started praying after talking in there for a while about our faith. And we asked God’s hand to be on this record, that he would bless it, bless the musicians, bless all the singers."

CARRIE UNDERWOOD HONORS DOLLY PARTON'S FAITH AND LEGACY DURING EMOTIONAL CONCERT TRIBUTE

"I just never have forgotten just the power of that day," Skaggs added. "That whole day was just wonderful. It showed me the kind of woman she was."

Skaggs recalled how he teamed up with Parton on "White Limozeen" after she invited him to produce the album following an appearance by the singer and his country band on her Los Angeles-based television show "Dolly."

WATCH: DOLLY PARTON PRAYED AT BACKYARD ALTAR BEFORE COMEBACK ALBUM, RICKY SKAGGS SAYS

DOLLY PARTON DEFIED COUNTRY MUSIC'S EXPECTATIONS FOR WOMEN AND BUILT A CAREER ON HER OWN TERMS: EXPERTS

"I came up and hugged her 'bye' and told her I really appreciate her having us on the show. And I said, ‘By the way, when are you going to do a real country album again?’" he remembered.

Skaggs continued, "She said, ‘Well, I’ve been thinking a lot about that. And I think I really want to do a country record. But I want you to produce it.’ I said, ‘What?'"

STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING

"I was shocked to the bone," he admitted. "That was one of the most mind-blowing, waking up smelling the roses kind of thing that I'd ever had happen at that time, musically for sure. But that was just being the right person in the right place at the right time around the right person."

"Only God could make those things happen."

DOLLY PARTON'S MOST ICONIC 'DOLLY-ISMS' ON BEAUTY, WIGS, BOTOX AND LIVING LIFE ON HER OWN TERMS

After rising to global fame as a country singer, Parton spent much of the late 1970s and 1980s broadening into pop-influenced material. Prior to "White Limozeen," she released her 1987 solo album "Rainbow," which was a critical and commercial disappointment. "Rainbow," which marked her most overtly pop-leaning solo album, struggled to find an audience, peaking at No. 18 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums and failing to produce a Top 40 country single.

With "White Limozeen," Skaggs brought Parton back to a more traditional country sound. The album became a hit, reaching No. 3 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums chart, yielding two No. 1 country hits, "Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That" and "Yellow Roses," and earning a Gold certification from the RIAA.

DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH

Although "White Limozeen" remained their only major recording collaboration, Skaggs said he and Parton shared a lasting bond rooted in their Appalachian backgrounds and Christian faith.

The Kentucky native said Parton lived out her beliefs through compassion and generosity, even though some were critical of her glamorous image.

BROADCAST BIAS: DOLLY PARTON TAUGHT THE WORLD THE WAY TO BE UNIVERSALLY BELOVED

"Some religious people would have really, and probably did, judge her for the way she wore her clothes, or the way that she did this and that and the other, but man, she reflected the love of Jesus everywhere she was," he said. "She did so much for the homeless, for the poor, for hurting people."

"She used what God had given her with her talent and her gifts, but she used that for His advantage, I mean, to show God's love to people that didn't feel loved by the world or by others, even other Christians," Skaggs continued. "And I just, I loved her for that. And I've really thought a lot about that since her passing."

BIG & RICH SAY DOLLY PARTON PUT FAME ASIDE TO HELP NEIGHBORS AFTER 2016 TENNESSEE WILDFIRES

Throughout her life, Parton was known for her philanthropy, which spanned literacy, disaster relief and medical research. In 1995, she launched the Imagination Library, a program that gifted hundreds of millions of free, age-appropriate books to children from birth to age 5 worldwide.

The 11-time Grammy Award winner also established the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires, providing eligible Sevier County families whose homes were destroyed with $1,000 a month for up to six months. In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 research.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Skaggs reflected on how the moment he shared with Parton in her backyard church had stayed with him and influenced his own band's pre-show ritual.

"Me and my band nowadays, we pray every time before we go out on stage and everything," he said. "We just say a prayer and thank God for our gifts and our talents and just ask that someone would be touched by the songs that we do."

"I just never have forgotten just the power of that day," he added. "That whole day was wonderful. It showed me the kind of woman that she was."

Skaggs also shared how he hoped that Parton would be remembered following her death.

"She was serious about music. She was serious about her life. She was serious about God," he said. "I'm telling you in her heart, I never met a person that had a more pure golden heart than Dolly."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"She was pure hearted," Skaggs added. "I never heard her judge anyone."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The "Country Boy" singer told Fox News Digital that he believed Parton's dedication to philanthropy would also be a major part of her lasting legacy.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We don’t even know what all that she’s done," he said. "Probably her family does, but she told them, ‘Look, don’t be out telling all the things I’m doing. I don’t want people to think I’m doing this for publicity. I don’t need it. I don’t want it. I want to do this because I love people and I want to help.’"

World.title: Dem megadonor among 400 Jewish Michiganders labeled AIPAC insiders for denouncing El-Sayed's leftist campaign
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

More than 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders are backing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and warning that they feel "threatened and alienated" by leftist candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his political allies.

Prominent Democratic donor Rob Orley, a senior advisor for O2 Investments, is among the signatories. He previously donated tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic campaigns, according to FEC campaign filings — but now he and other prominent Jewish leaders are ditching El-Sayed for Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

"Many of us have been fiercely supportive of Democratic candidates and principles," a letter signed by Orley and hundreds of others stated.

"If El-Sayed were to win the general election in this important swing state, we fear the far-left and anti-Jewish elements in the Democratic Party would become dominant, including in the imminent 2028 presidential race," the letter continues. "We cannot allow him to become the Democratic standard-bearer or Michigan’s senator."

Fox News Digital reached out to O2 Investments for comment.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS

The letter includes signatures from some of the most prominent members of Michigan's Jewish community, including Robert Gordon, the former president of Temple Israel, the state's largest Jewish congregation, which was the site of an antisemitic attack in March.

Shayna Levine, the daughter of the leading rabbi at Temple Israel; David Propis, cantor of Congregation Shaarey Zedek; Laurence Deitch, who served as a University of Michigan regent; and Hannan Lis, a Weight Watchers executive, have also signed the letter declaring that they feel "threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed."

But former Rep. Andy Levin, who is Jewish, is claiming that opposition to El-Sayed among Jewish Democrats is a minority view and that his old foe, the American Israel Political Action Committee, is really driving the letter. Levin lost his 2022 primary bid to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., after AIPAC spent more than $4 million in the primary race against him.

"It's not a surprise to me," Levin said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The people I know associated with it are all long-time AIPAC insiders and supporters." Levin added that AIPAC "represents a distinctly minority position about Israel and Palestine within the Jewish community."

Levin, who was first elected to Congress in 2018 to replace his late father Sander Levin, gave his endorsement to El-Sayed in November 2025.

"I am overwhelmed like literally every day except Shabbat — our sabbath on Saturday — with the incoming I get from Jewish people, young people, middle-aged people, older people, who are so mad about an effort like this and who want to do everything they can to make sure Abdul El-Sayed wins the election on November 3rd, that this U.S. Senate seat stays democratic, and that we do everything we can to save and expand our democracy," Levin continued.

However, attorney Daniel Cherrin, who signed the letter, told Fox News Digital that he has not attended an AIPAC event since college more than 30 years ago. Cherrin said he has tremendous respect for Levin, whom he has known for years, and previously worked with Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit and Wayne County. Although he considers El-Sayed a "good" person, Cherrin said he cannot overlook the movement backing his candidacy.

"I am very concerned about the movement that is behind Abdul, and for the safety of my community, I don't feel safe in that environment with the people that are standing in support of him," Cherrin told Fox News Digital.

DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN

"They don't understand the impact that their words and their actions is having on me and my children and my neighbors," Cherrin said. "And so, for that, I am very worried about should he be elected what that means for all those that are trying to advance his candidacy."

Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who has called Orthodox Jews inbreds and said America deserved 9/11, has been a top surrogate for El-Sayed's campaign. Over the past week, El-Sayed has attempted to distance himself from the social media influencer, suggesting that people focusing on his affiliation with Piker are "missing the boat."

Levin, who has condemned Piker's antisemitic falsehoods about the Oct. 7 attack, agreed with El-Sayed that too much focus is on Piker. He then argued that the Democratic National Committee received very little pushback for inviting Piker to stream during the 2024 Democratic National Convention, giving then-Vice President and Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris an opportunity to reach Piker's audience. Piker did not endorse Harris because of the Biden administration's policy in the Gaza war.

"So I'm not accepting Hasan Piker, but look in the mirror, sister," Levin said. "When it's a guy named Abdul with a guy named Hasan, you're blowing up about it and covering it massively. When it was not an Arab American or a Muslim who campaigned with him or did whatever Kamala Harris did, literally no one asked her a single question about it."

Last month, El-Sayed said he had "no plans" to continue campaigning with Piker.

Roslyn Schindler attends Congregation T'chiyah, which is a progressive Reform synagogue that touts its support for Black Lives Matter, and transgender rights, with Levin. A daughter of Holocaust survivors, Schindler has lived in the metro Detroit area for 50 years and taught Holocaust studies at Wayne State University. She shared with Fox News Digital that she has supported El-Sayed well before his primary victory, and that the Democratic Party is in need of a "major shake-up," citing El-Sayed's support for progressive policies like Medicare for All and getting money out of politics.

"I am certainly not an anti-Zionist, as many Jews who don't support Abdul think we are, but I am a committed Jew," Schindler told Fox News Digital. "I'm a committed Democrat. I believe that the Democratic Party should be a large tent, so to speak, that includes all members of that party, no matter what their perspective."

Fox News Digital asked Schindler for her thoughts on El-Sayed's affiliation with Piker and whether there is a place in the Democratic Party for people who follow his ideology.

EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER

"As a Jew, I certainly don't want anyone to be anti-Semitic. I don't want anyone to be anti-Muslim. I don't want anyone to be anti-LGBTQ, and the list goes on," Schindler said. "Is that realistic? Probably not. Do I want those people to be part of the Democratic Party? It's not really for me to want. It is what it is. They'll either be part of it or they won't."

"But I do believe there is enough traction within the Jewish community at large to counter anti-Semitism, and that's across the board," Schindler continued.

But Cherrin said the fact that his family has to pass security officers guarding synagogues and temples is evidence to him that the Jewish community at large can't tackle antisemitism by itself.

"It's not about AIPAC for me," Cherrin said. "It is about it is about how are we protecting the sanctity of the Jewish community in Michigan and frankly and across the country with all these other races that are out there."

"People within the Jewish community, who typically identify as Democrats, don't feel comfortable voting for the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate and are looking for a place to channel their frustration. That should not be discounted," Cherrin continued.

Cherrin pushed for both Rogers and El-Sayed to continue to reach out to Jewish community members outside of politics to get a "real pulse" on what Jewish voters are thinking.

"Abdul is grateful for the good conversations he’s had with Jewish leaders across Michigan, and he’ll continue to be actively engaged with communities to build the coalition that will defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate, and put a much-needed check on Trump’s reckless agenda," a spokesperson for El-Sayed's campaign said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Rogers, who previously served in Congress for 15 years, said he appreciates the growing support from the Jewish community — especially those crossing party lines to back his bid for U.S. Senate.

"As antisemitism rises and Jewish families worry for their safety, it’s critical that we have leaders who will confront hatred — not inflame it," Rogers said in a statement. "That’s where my opponent and I couldn’t be more different."

"Abdul El-Sayed fans the flames of antisemitism. We’re fighting to extinguish it," Rogers continued.

Although for progressive Jewish Democrats like Levin and Schindler, President Donald Trump and his MAGA allies like Rogers are the biggest threat to democracy.

"We have a chance to protect our Democracy by keeping this U.S. Senate seat democratic and expanding our democracy, by, for the first time, having, uh, electing a Muslim to the U.S. Senate," Levin said. "Most Jews that I know so believe in this democratic experiment, this Democratic project called America."

"And it's about damn time that Muslims had a senator and there's a brilliant person running here in Michigan who we can elect to be the first one. Will he do exactly what a Jewish person would do or something? No, but he will be someone we could talk to and who will be a great representative for all of Michigan and for the Arab American and Muslim communities in particular," Levin said.

World.title: Alaska finalizes Senate race: 3 Republicans, 2 Dan Sullivans and 1 Democrat
World.content:
The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election.

Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot.

Dan J. Sullivan and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska. AP; Getty Images

The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name.

Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns.

Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign.

The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary.

They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

Tom Begich, a Democrat who finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

World.title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
World.content:
Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates.

Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites.

The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it.

Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington.

Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote.

The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican.

Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote.

“The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press.

Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose.

Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years.

Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years.

“The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.”

Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.”

Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area.

“There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said.

A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources.

“I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

World.title: No plans for ICE to be at polls for midterms, DHS says
World.content:
ICE officers have not received guidance telling them they need to do anything in addition to their regular duties on the day of November’s midterm elections, a senior Homeland Security official told NBC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a news conference Tuesday in New York that ICE officers will be at a polling place only if “there is a threat to that polling place” or if officers are serving a warrant on someone “that we have been actively tracking down.”

“ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” Mullin said.

Asked whether ICE officers would enter polling places, Mullin said they would if they had warrants.

“If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be,” Mullin said.

President Donald Trump and Mullin have claimed without offering any evidence that there are over 250,000 noncitizens on voter rolls across several states. Mullin recently threatened state election officials with possible prison time if they didn’t comply with the administration’s methods to determine whether noncitizens were on their voter rolls. Several state officials have pushed back against sharing private state voter roll data that includes personal information, such as Social Security numbers.

World.title: Ariana Grande tearfully ends 41-show tour and steps back from public life
World.content:
LONDON — A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid a temporary farewell to her fans as her 41-show “Eternal Sunshine Tour” concluded in London on Tuesday night, kickstarting her planned withdrawal from public life.

Addressing the audience in London’s famed O2 arena, the pop singer said she was “grateful” to her fans for making her show “so special.”

“This has been one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life,” Grande said, dressed in black and perched on a stool on stage. “I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely.”

“I’ll cherish this experience always,” she added.

Grande, known for hits including “thank you, next” and “hate that i made you love me,” made global headlines in August when she said she would be taking a “step back from visibility” following “public scrutiny.”

The announcement came after the release of her latest music video, “petal,” which reignited a public debate about her health.

Representatives for Grande said last month that she was looking forward to finishing her tour “on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.”

Grande concluded her tour in knee-high boots rather than her signature heels after stating she was “bandaged up underneath” following a “deep cut” on her foot, which she called a “minor injury.”

Grande’s “Eternal Sunshine Tour,” which promoted the 2024 album of the same name, began in Oakland, California, in June. She previously labeled the shows “one last hurrah” and has expressed her desire to take on more acting roles.

Grande was nominated for an Oscar for her performance as Glinda in the hit musical movie “Wicked.”

She had been set to reunite with “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey in a revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” in London next summer, before she pulled out last month.

In a statement Tuesday on Instagram, Bailey said he has also decided to “step back” from the Sondheim show. He added that “Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering.”
