The Bank of Canada held its benchmark interest rate steady on Wednesday at 2.25 per cent, in a move widely expected by economists.

Canada’s central bank has been on hold since December 2025, with Wednesday’s announcement marking its seventh consecutive decision to leave its trend-setting policy rate unchanged.

In its decision, the bank said recent data confirms its prediction for a "broadening recovery" in the economy. However, policymakers also said the risks of higher inflation have increased — citing new U.S. tariffs and the escalating U.S.-led war with Iran.

"With the Middle East conflict still ongoing, and little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, upside risks to the bank’s inflation forecast have increased," bank officials said on Wednesday.

"The longer that high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist, the greater the risk of spillover to the prices of other goods and services."

U.S. benchmark oil prices have soared about 13 per cent since the bank’s last announcement in July. The U.S.-led war in Iran has intensified in recent weeks, resulting in slower tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime passageway for oil to reach global markets.

At the same time, the Canada-U.S. trade war has escalated significantly since the bank's prior meeting in July.

Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian products. Starting Sept. 8, Canada will match those levies with dollar-for-dollar tariffs on $27.6 billion of comparable U.S. goods.

Last week, the federal government rolled out a $7.5-billion expanded economic relief program for impacted workers and businesses. The new supports are on top of the nearly $25 billion in tariff support it implemented over the past 18 months.

'Uncertainties over trade'

CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said Wednesday’s hold was no surprise “amidst the fog of a trade war.”

“Newly heightened uncertainty over trade relations clouds that picture too much to be definitive about what lies ahead,” Shenfeld wrote in a research note published after the decision.

“The bank did judge that the direct impact of the latest tariff round would not be large, but cited the uncertainties over trade as being a further drag,” he added.

“It didn’t mention the downside implications of a failure to lower the existing tariffs on autos, metals and lumber that most economic projections were assuming would take place.”

A Reuters poll of economists taken on Aug. 22 found all 35 participants expected policymakers to leave the bank's key rate in place.

The Bank of Canada’s next rate announcement is scheduled for Oct. 28.

World.title: Teachers, students file new wave of lawsuits against OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lawyers representing victims and survivors of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting say they are filing 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI in U.S. federal court in California.

Edelson PC, a U.S. firm that specializes in class actions, says the new plaintiffs include educators, a principal and students, including siblings who were separated during the Feb. 10 attack in northern B.C.

The tragedy left eight victims dead, including six children, along with the 18-year-old shooter.

The lawsuits describe the horror they experienced that day and include new details of OpenAI's alleged negligence in preventing the shooting.

"The survivors — students, teachers, and parents alike — are living with physical and psychological injuries that will never fully heal," one lawsuit reads.

The new claims have been filed in California, where OpenAI is headquartered, and where seven other cases against the company have been filed by families of the shooting victims.

Edelson says OpenAI's safety team repeatedly asked to notify authorities about Jesse Van Rootselaar's activity on ChatGPT eight months before the tragedy, which allegedly included planning violent scenarios.

But the lawsuits allege those appeals were overruled by Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s head of global affairs.

They claim OpenAI's leadership "ignored its own safety staff and refused to alert police," yet acted to safeguard its own offices after learning of threats to employees three months before the Tumbler Ridge shooting.

The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of "choosing profit over the lives of the children of Tumbler Ridge" as it prepares to become a publicly-traded company.

Demolition of the former Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in August. (Tom Summer/CBC)

Jason Kwon, chief strategy officer at OpenAI, said in a response posted on X that he thinks of the tragedy at Tumbler Ridge daily.

He said the company has teams that "work hard to define standards and processes for when to report cases to law enforcement and to apply those standards to really difficult and complex situations."

"They work continuously to identify potential warning signals of serious violence, while also protecting the privacy and security of the vast majority of the more than one billion users who use our tools responsibly."

Kwon said it was frustrating to see what he said were false claims made in the suits about his teams and individuals not involved in the process. Kwon said it is "absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision, or that our investigators report to him in any way."

"It's also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are 'political' or 'public relations' factors at play."

The company previously acknowledged that it banned Van Rootselaar's account in June 2025, but said the activity did not meet the "higher threshold required" to refer it to police at the time.

CEO Sam Altman has apologized to the Tumbler Ridge community and says the company has updated its protocols.

WATCH | Lawyer calls Altman's Tumbler Ridge apology 'crocodile tears': Altman apology just 'crocodile tears,' lawsuit needed to hold OpenAI accountable: lawyer | Duration 6:19





The B.C. government is also planning legal action against OpenAI, and has since demolished the site of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The first set of lawsuits filed against the tech giant included the family of Maya Gebala, a 12-year-old student who was shot in the head and survived the shooting.

In a Facebook post Monday, Cia Edmonds shared a video of her daughter that showed her relearning to speak, saying "mom" into the camera before cracking a smile.

"Tears of awe as I watch her crawl out of the rubble that her mind lives in," Edmonds wrote. "One step at a time. She shows me, more and more what miracles look like."

John Rice of Rice Parsons Leoni & Elliott, Canadian co-counsel for the latest complainants, said in a news release that victims and families are looking for answers and justice.

He said they want to have the chat-log material between Van Rootselaar and ChatGPT released, as well as internal OpenAI documents showing why Canadian authorities weren't alerted about Van Rootselaar's plans.

The families are also seeking historic compensatory and punitive damages to penalize OpenAI, if the allegations are proven true, and "to express society's condemnation and outrage over such egregious corporate malfeasance."

Rice said they hope to prevent another AI-facilitated mass shooting by reforming major platform safety, including with mandatory law enforcement reporting for "all foreseeable and imminent acts of violence."

Subscribe to CBC’s Fort St. John Weekly for a roundup of the best news and stories from B.C.’s Peace and Northern Rockies.

World.title: The battle that made Canada bleed: Operation Medusa, 20 years later
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Canadian troops crossed the Arghandab River, the first indication to former corporal Bruce Moncur that something was amiss came with the sight of a green pen flare shooting across the sky.

"I remember looking at it thinking, well, that's weird," said Moncur, who realized that since NATO troops in Afghanistan fired red flares, green must have belonged to the Taliban.

"That was an indication that we had walked far enough into the trap."

The Taliban had waited until he and his section of troops had dismounted from the protection of their armoured vehicles before springing their three-sided ambush.

Moncur recalls every detail of that day 20 years ago with a stark, blinding clarity.

It was the opening phase of Operation Medusa, a savage, close-quarters battle in the vineyards and dusty villages of Kandahar.

WATCH | Moncur describes the start of Operation Medusa: 'I'll never forget': Canadian veteran recalls opening phases of Operation Medusa | Duration 1:14 Former corporal Bruce Moncur describes the opening phases of Operation Medusa when his unit crossed the Arghandab River in Kandahar, Afghanistan, in September 2006 and was ambushed by Taliban fighters ahead of a 'five-hour firefight.'

The battle began on Sept. 2, 2006, with an artillery and air bombardment.

A day later, Moncur's unit set off to cross the river.

The Canadians ran into a deeply entrenched enemy that was firing machine guns, rocket-propelled grenades and small arms.

The battle was different in the sense the Taliban force had chosen, unusually, to stand and fight.

More than 2,000 NATO troops, including over 1,000 Canadians, took part, alongside Afghan forces and American, British, Dutch and Danish elements.

It would be the biggest battle Canadians had fought since Korea and their largest conventional operation of the Afghan war.

WATCH | From 2021: The legacy of the Afghan war: Canadian veterans on the legacy of Afghanistan war | Duration 4:40 Two Canadian veterans reflect on their experiences fighting in Afghanistan, how it changed them and what it’s like to see the Taliban regain control.

Moncur's unit, Charles Company, 1st Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment (1RCR), had been drawn into the insurgent ambush after crossing the river as they were pushing toward their objective, a little white school house the Taliban had occupied.

The firefight lasted five hours. Four Canadian soldiers were killed: Warrant Officer Frank Mellish, Warrant Officer Richard Nolan, Sgt. Shane Stachnik and Pte. William Cushley. An additional 16 troops were wounded before the order was given to retreat.

"In that firefight, I was all over the battlefield. Some vehicles were stuck and left behind, and we had to try to salvage them," Moncur said. "One soldier was left behind. We obviously don't leave anyone behind. So, we had to go and rescue his body."

In an interview given to reporters at the time, the commander of Bravo Company 1 RCR said the depth and strength of the Taliban force, which were later estimated at a total of 1,000 insurgents, was not something the Canadians expected.

"Truthfully, I was surprised by the resistance they put up," the commander, Maj. Geoff Abthorpe, said. "We came at them with what I perceived to be a pretty heavy fist."

"I think closer to about 400 Taliban fighters and men that had fought all their lives versus 80 Canadians that had … this is their first time at combat, first time in a real firefight," said Moncur.

In the late summer of 2006 prior to the battle, hundreds of insurgents had massed in the Panjwai and Zhari districts, roughly 30 kilometres west of Kandahar city, the provincial capital.

They had dug trenches, fortified compounds, planted mines and improvised explosive devices and established defensive positions around the nearby village of Pashmul.

The timing was deliberate. NATO had only recently taken responsibility for southern Afghanistan from the U.S.-led coalition, and the Taliban appeared determined to test whether the alliance had the stomach for a serious fight.

Bruce Moncur was severely injured in a friendly fire incident during Operation Medusa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Sean Maloney, a historian at the Royal Military College of Canada, said all throughout the spring and summer of 2006 Canadian troops had been fighting running battles with the Taliban.

The ones that decided to fight in Pashmul were different. They were better trained, more co-ordinated and better equipped.

There has been a long running debate in Canadian and U.S. military circles about whether Pakistan's notorious intelligence service had contributed — in some way — to the sophistication of the insurgents who fought NATO forces.

"They're definitely a major factor in this," said Maloney.

A U.S. military study of insurgent tactics, written long after the battle in 2018, also pointed to potential Pakistani involvement, including the redirection of foreign fighters to bolster the ranks of local Taliban.

The report noted how the insurgents mounted planned ambushes and counterattacks and, when NATO firepower became overwhelming, conducted what the study calls a "disciplined retreat."

Several weeks after the operation, Pakistani journalist and noted Taliban expert Ahmed Rashid wrote a piece quoting NATO commanders, who believed the battle had exposed the Taliban’s support structure in Pakistan to an "extraordinary degree."

Friendly fire

After the failed river crossing on the second day of the battle, disaster struck Moncur's unit again.

An American A-10 mistakenly strafed Canadian positions, killing Pte. Mark Graham and wounding more than 30 others, including Moncur, who suffered a major head injury.

"I'm sitting there eating, and my fire team partner comes to sit next to me,' said Moncur, who compared the sensation of being strafed to being electrocuted. "I just remember being tossed in the air like a rag doll…. I remember feeling like my body was being, like I touched a socket or something."

He tumbled down a rocky slope before losing consciousness. When Moncur came to, he knew his head was bleeding.

"If you've ever washed your face in a basin and just filled up and splashed yourself with water, that's how much blood ended up filling in my hands," Moncur said.

He crawled to a nearby medic, who was also wounded, before passing out again.

"I basically made peace with this. That was going to be the final moments of my life," Moncur said.

But it wasn't.

He was rushed to the military hospital at Kandahar Airfield before being evacuated to a U.S. military trauma centre in Germany, where he faced a long, painful road to recovery.

Following the friendly fire attack, Charles Company was effectively removed from the battle.

WATCH | Moncur describes friendly fire incident: Canadian Afghan war veteran describes being wounded by friendly fire | Duration 2:13 Former corporal Bruce Moncur recalls the moment he was wounded by friendly fire in Kandahar, Afghanistan, after his unit was strafed by an American A-10 warplane during Operation Medusa in September 2006. 'I'm thinking, this is it,' Moncur said. 'I'm probably going to die here in the middle of nowhere.'

The commanders — Brig.-Gen. David Fraser and Lt.-Col. Omer Lavoie — shifted the axis of the main attack to the north.

The battered remnants of Charles Company remained in the south, helping convince the Taliban another river assault was coming, while Canadian forces pushed down from Highway 1.

The operation lasted another two weeks and ended with hundreds of insurgents killed.

Maloney said it was a pivotal moment in the war. The intention of the Taliban, at the time, was to eventually push into Kandahar city.

The decisive defeat forced them to switch back to hit-and-run tactics of improvised explosives and ambushes.

It was also an important political moment.

"That's when the Afghans realized, yeah, we're going to fight," Maloney said. "And as one of them walked up to our people and said — in shock — you're willing to bleed for us."

World.title: Plane spotter or Chinese spy? Ontario university student suspected of espionage at airports
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Ontario university student is suspected of espionage after the FBI said he admitted to accessing airport facilities in Toronto and Chicago to take photos on behalf of a shadowy figure from China.

Weiheng Zeng, himself a Chinese citizen, was arrested in Michigan on Aug. 23 after crossing the Ambassador Bridge from Windsor, Ont. He was charged with one count of making false statements.

Zeng appeared in a federal court in Detroit on Tuesday and agreed to remain in custody as he awaits his trial.

A University of Waterloo undergraduate student born in 2004, Zeng first raised U.S. authorities' suspicions in April, after an incident captured on security video at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, according to a criminal complaint reviewed by CBC News.

FedEx security cameras at O'Hare airport captured images of a man taking photos, the FBI said in a criminal complaint. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

At the time, FedEx employees spotted a man taking photos, climbing a forklift and attempting to open a locked delivery truck and a shipping container in the company's parking lot at the Chicago airport, the criminal complaint said.

According to the complaint, Zeng acknowledged he had climbed the forklift at O'Hare 'to get a better angle to take pictures.'

Investigators later linked Zeng to a dark blue Chrysler Town & Country minivan with Ontario licence plates seen on nearby CCTV.

When he attempted to re-enter the U.S. last month while driving the same vehicle, Zeng told U.S. Customs and Border Protection he was headed to Chicago for a one-day trip. Instead, border officers interviewed him three times.

And according to the criminal complaint, his story kept changing.

At first, when border agents found numerous photos of military aircraft on his phone, Zeng purportedly said they were for a flight radar website. He said taking pictures of planes was his hobby.

"Zeng's phone was also found to contain pictures of him and other individuals in tactical clothing and in tactical formations, holding rifle-styled firearms," FBI special agent Robert Holbrook wrote in the complaint. Zeng purportedly said the weapon was an airsoft gun.

He denied having any military service or training.

According to an FBI criminal complaint, Zeng acknowledged he had climbed a forklift in a FedEx parking lot at O'Hare airport 'to get a better angle to take pictures.' (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

According to the criminal complaint, Zeng eventually said he was being paid by someone — identified in the U.S. court records only as "Chinese contact" — to photograph specific planes and their tail numbers.

Zeng believed his contact worked for a Chinese security service and that it was "cool," according to documents filed in U.S. District Court in Detroit. Zeng said they had met on a Chinese forum for aviation enthusiasts in 2024.

Chinese SIM cards, Huawei phone

Zeng, who lives in Cambridge, Ont., also outlined to investigators a convoluted system he purportedly used to communicate with the unnamed individual, who paid him via bank transfer in Chinese yuan.

The "Chinese contact" would mail Zeng a new SIM card every four to five months, which he was directed to use in his Huawei cell phone, according to the criminal complaint.

"Zeng, at the direction of 'Chinese Contact,' would subsequently destroy the SIM cards, delete the conversations, and delete the photos he took," wrote Holbrook, the FBI agent.

A Chrysler Town & Country minivan with Ontario licence plates was seen in a FedEx parking lot at Chicago's O'Hare airport on April 21, according to an FBI criminal complaint. Zeng purportedly tried to re-enter the U.S. in August in the same vehicle. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

"The SIM card, which was from China Telecom, allowed Zeng to by-pass Canadian cellular network and connect directly with the Chinese provider network to send text messages to 'Chinese Contact.' "

In a separate interview last month with the FBI, Zeng purportedly said his contact had directed him in October 2025 to take photos inside a FedEx facility at Toronto Pearson International Airport.

He said he was confronted by a FedEx employee and only managed to take pictures outside the building. Still, he said he sent the photos to his contact and received the equivalent of $200 US.

Zeng a flight risk, prosecutor says

At Zeng's first court appearance in Detroit last week, a federal prosecutor said he posed a flight risk and urged that Zeng be held in custody.

"He is a foreign resident and a foreign citizen," assistant U.S. attorney Alyse Wu told the court.

"According to what is alleged in the complaint, his only known tie to this district appears to be using it as a crossing point to enter our country for what appears to be espionage-type activities."

At another hearing on Tuesday, a court-appointed federal defender said Zeng consented to remain in custody. Speaking through a Mandarin-language interpreter, Zeng confirmed his name and his understanding that he would remain behind bars.

A man believed to be Zeng was captured on security video at O'Hare airport on April 21, trying to open the door of a locked FedEx delivery truck, according to an FBI criminal complaint. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

The allegations against him have not been proven in court.

It's unclear what undergraduate program Zeng was enrolled in, or when he first came to Canada.

University of Waterloo spokesperson Pamela Smyth told CBC News in an email, "we don't normally comment on ongoing criminal matters."

Waterloo police said they weren't involved in the investigation.

The Chinese embassies in Ottawa and Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Edmonton woman says she was ‘unpersoned’ by church after Orthodox clergyman charged with sexual assault
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A member of the clergy with an Orthodox church in Edmonton has been accused of sexually assaulting a woman more than two decades ago, and the complainant in the case says she was ostracized from the church after reporting the alleged crime.

Jesse Isaac, 43, was charged by the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) in July in connection with an alleged sexual assault in October 2004. The allegations have not been proven in court.

According to the website for St. Olga of Alaska Orthodox Church, Isaac serves as a protodeacon at the south Edmonton church. The church is part of the Orthodox Church in America (OCA), which includes hundreds of parishes across Canada, the United States and Mexico.

At the time of the alleged assault, Isaac was serving at the St. Herman of Alaska Orthodox Church, which also belongs to the OCA.

As of Tuesday afternoon, I saac remained listed on the OCA’s Archdiocese of Canada website as an active member of its clergy, more than six weeks after the charge of sexual assault was laid against him.

Protodeacon is a senior rank bestowed on married deacons for dedicated service and they serve the church by assisting a bishop or priest during services, as well as leading congregations in prayer .

'So broken'

The woman who alleges Isaac assaulted her has been granted a court-ordered publication ban, but shared her story with CBC News, along with emails and messages that document her attempts to have her claims investigated by the church.

She said she felt compelled to report what happened to police, years later, in May 2025 out of a desire for justice and healing.

She said Isaac has remained in his position long after church leaders became aware of her allegation, making her feel like a criminal investigation was her only remaining recourse.

“I was so broken,” she said. “I was seeking accountability.”

In response to a request for comment, CBC News received a statement from a lawyer representing the OCA.

“The church takes allegations of criminal wrongdoing very seriously in every instance and fully co-operated with the Edmonton police,” wrote Mark Hamilton of Eckert Seamans Cherin & Mellott, LLC.

“Yet other than to offer prayers for the welfare and healing of all those involved, the church does not comment on ongoing police investigations or criminal proceedings.”

Church officials declined to answer CBC News’ questions about the internal investigation or Isaac’s future with its congregations, citing the ongoing court case.

Jesse Isaac, 43, was charged by the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) in July in connection with an alleged sexual assault on Oct. 1, 2004. (Submitted)

Isaac has not responded directly to requests for comment. In a statement to CBC News, his criminal defence lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing court proceedings.

According to his profile on the church website, Isaac was ordained as a deacon in 2011 and elevated to the rank of protodeacon in 2015. He spent many years serving at the St. Herman of Alaska Orthodox Church in Edmonton but was transferred in 2025 to St. Olga’s Mission, a newer mission church established by St. Herman's.

EPS has declined to provide specific details about its investigation, the evidence gathered against Isaac or the relationship between the accused and the complainant.

Court records show Isaac was arrested on July 18, 2026, and has since been released on bail with conditions.

The case will be prosecuted by indictment, a process reserved for more serious offences, which means a conviction could result in a sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

The case remains in its early stages and is set to return to provincial court on Sept. 2.

Documents, including emails and text messages the complainant shared with CBC News, show it has been more than 17 months since she formally shared her allegation of sexual assault with church officials.

The complainant was a young woman at the time of the alleged assault. She told CBC News she had just moved to Edmonton and joined an OCA congregation after converting to the Orthodox faith.

She said that by spring of 2025, the memory of what happened to her had become an unbearable burden, leading her to confide in a few close friends within the congregation.

She said word of her allegations soon spread and reached church officials, in what she characterized as a betrayal of her trust that resulted in her being ostracized.

“I was robbed of the chance to heal quietly,” she said.

Internal investigation

Documents she shared with CBC News show that after being questioned by church officials, she later detailed her allegations to OCA leadership in March 2025, and her complaint was referred to the Office for Review of Sexual Misconduct Allegations (ORSMA).

ORSMA is a dedicated body within the church responsible for tracking and assisting with investigations into allegations of sexual misconduct.

Correspondence shared with CBC News shows that ORSMA was formally informed of the allegations on April 3, 2025, after local church leaders became aware of the alleged sexual assault and filed a formal report.

Documents show Isaac served a 10-day suspension from his role with the church, from April 3 to April 13, 2025. The church announced the suspension on its website but did not provide a reason to its parishioners.

'Like losing a family'

Correspondence shared with CBC News indicates ORSMA later determined the allegation fell outside its purview because the alleged assault occurred before Isaac was ordained as a deacon.

The complainant said she repeatedly called for further investigation and repercussions, but felt her demands went unheard. Documents she shared with CBC News show she messaged and emailed church leaders repeatedly and sent parish-wide emails sharing her concerns .

After weeks of sharing her complaints, she said she was told to leave the congregation outright.

In late April 2025, according to an email she shared with CBC News, she was informed that she no longer had the “blessing” of church leaders to attend services or receive sacraments at St. Herman’s or St. Olga’s.

In the email, church officials told her she was no longer welcome, that due to her allegations against church leadership, they could no longer give her the spiritual guidance she needed.

The email also stated the ORSMA investigation had concluded after determining the “incident, if true,” occurred prior to Isaac’s ordination.

The complainant said there is no clear mechanism for victims to seek accountability within their church communities. She said the parish she attended for 20 years no longer feels like a safe place to practise her faith.

“It’s like losing a family,” she said. “They unpersoned me.

“I still have faith … but it killed my spirit.”

She said she feels punished for attempting to seek spiritual support for what happened to her.

In a statement provided to CBC News, EPS officials wrote that historical sexual assault investigations can be complex but delayed reporting of such crimes does not prevent a thorough investigation.

“Police recognize that victims of sexual violence may take months, years or even decades before feeling ready to disclose what happened to them,” EPS said.

World.title: Telus accused of misleading B.C. consumer watchdog in probe sparked by mistaken $1,400 cancellation fee
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C.'s consumer watchdog is locked in a court battle with Telus after accusing the telecommunications giant of stonewalling an inspector trying to determine if a mistaken $1,435.65 cancellation fee was part of a systemic issue.

According to documents obtained by CBC News, Consumer Protection B.C. (CPBC) claimed Telus provided misleading information in response to a request for copies of complaints Telus first insisted did not exist — only to later admit the files were too numerous to sift through.

Last month, Telus appealed to B.C. Supreme Court for a judicial review of an order demanding more than $40,000 in fines and legal fees along with an improvement in how the company responds to regulatory requests and identifies records.

The penalty followed more than a year of back-and-forth between CPBC and both internal and external lawyers for Telus; they accused an agency inspector of overstepping his mandate by issuing what the company considered "illegal" orders for a "fishing expedition."

CBC News obtained records of the investigation through a freedom of information request to the provincial regulator. The documents detail an underlying conflict over the extent of the regulator's right to demand corporate accountability on behalf of frustrated citizens.

"Telecommunications is comprehensively regulated by the federal government," Telus lawyer Julia Won wrote in an email to inspector Jason McColl.

"It is not a good use of public or private resources to engage in investigations of matters already addressed in detail by an industry-specific regulatory regime that also includes investigation and enforcement powers."

'Can you please provide an explanation?'

The case highlights a complaint-resolution landscape that can be confusing for customers of telecommunication companies.

The federal Commission for Complaints for Telecom-Television Services resolves service complaints, but CPBC's mandate includes investigations into alleged violations of B.C.'s Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act (BPCPA) — including contract breaches.

Telus was fined by Consumer Protection B.C. in relation to a probe into a cancelled contract. The decision is in limbo pending an application for judicial review. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Under those terms, McColl claimed CPBC had a right to initiate an investigation into Telus in January 2025 after receiving a complaint from a customer who claimed she had cancelled a sales contract "but that it was not cancelled."

"It is our understanding that Telus is headquartered in British Columbia, as evidenced in Telus contracts," McColl wrote.

"If this is correct, it means that all Telus contracts (not only the ones with British Columbia based customers) must be in compliance with the BCPCA, notwithstanding that a consumer to a contract may be situated outside of British Columbia."

The records obtained by CBC News do not include a copy of the complaint itself, but at one point McColl asked about a timeframe that saw the woman receive a cancellation notice on Christmas Eve of 2024 along with a "fee of $1,435.65 for said cancellation."

"Can you please provide an explanation for why this fee occurred?" McColl asked.

'We do not have records'

Telus responded to McColl's initial query within weeks, insisting the issue was an isolated incident, cancelling the fee and blaming "human error or misunderstanding by an agent" who continued charging for a service they had been asked to cancel.

But instead of wrapping up his probe, McColl used the complaint as a springboard to open a new inspection.

Telus has filed a B.C. Supreme Court petition seeking a judicial review of a decision by Consumer Protection B.C. which accused the telecommunications giant of providing misleading information during an investigation. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"We noticed some potential issues of non-compliance with contract provisions under the Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act," he told Won.

"We appreciate your position that there is no systemic issue and our inspection will look to confirm this."

As part of the new investigation, McColl issued an order requiring Telus to disclose copies of all records relating to consumer requests to cancel contracts because they did not meet the terms of the consumer protection legislation.

He also asked for records of "penalty payments demanded and/or collected ... from a consumer seeking to cancel a contract."

Won insisted that Telus did not capture data or make records based on a consumer's request to cancel a contract because it didn't meet the terms of the BCPCA or because goods or services were not supplied within a specific time period.

"We do not have records that respond to your request," Won wrote.

"To be clear, we do not impose 'penalties' on consumers. [ Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission] regulations do not allow penalties, but do permit an 'early cancellation fee' under specific circumstances."

'There are thousands of complaint files'

According to the email exchanges, McColl later tested those claims by providing Telus details of a complaint from a customer in Coquitlam, B.C., which he claimed fit the exact parameters of the inspection order.

He then demanded to know why the complaint wasn't located through the company's own searches.

Telus has its corporate headquarters in downtown Vancouver. As such, Consumer Protection B.C. maintains that all Telus contracts must comply with provincial legislation. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

In an email, Won accused McColl of testing Telus and said the company had "deep concerns about the nature of these inquiries."

"Nothing in the Act contemplates that an inspector may run tests of this nature," she wrote.

"We reiterate our request that we focus on actual consumer issues and complaints. If consumers are bringing complaints to your office, we want to know about them ... However opaque general fishing expeditions do not allow for those discussions."

In the aftermath of that exchange, an external lawyer for Telus wrote an email to McColl blaming technical issues relating to "the capacity and scope of electronic searches" for the lack of records.

"As you can appreciate, in a company with millions of customers, there are a vast number of customer communications. TELUS applied certain filters to identify the files most likely to contain responsive communications," the email reads.

"There are thousands of complaint files over the time period referred to in your demand for information. [There are] far too many records to review manually to assess whether customers have made specific allegations about compliance with the BPCPA."

'Demonstrably false or misleading'

Telus offered to manually search 200 customer files and provide records responding to the request, but said even that effort would "require multiple employees to be fully dedicated to the review for several weeks."

McColl's final report to the director of Consumer Protection B.C. claimed the lawyer's email directly contradicted the company's "earlier categorical representations that no such responsive records existed."

"If potentially thousands of consumer files may contain potentially responsive material, then [Telus's] absolute statements of non-existence are inconsistent with any reasonable or diligent search," the report says.

"Difficulty retrieving records is not the same as the absence of records. By repeatedly stating that its searches revealed zero responsive items and asserting that no such records existed, [Telus] supplied information that was demonstrably false or misleading."

Consumer Protection B.C. issued a decision in June finding Telus had supplied misleading information and had failed to produce records.

The ruling came with a demand for $19,000 in fines and $22,000 to cover the costs of McColl's inspection.

The company was also ordered to "develop, revise and implement written policies and procedures governing its response to inspection orders and inquiries" from the regulator.

The fines and order for compliance are in limbo pending the outcome of the Supreme Court challenge in which Telus accuses Consumer Protection B.C. of making unlawful and unreasonably broad demands for information.In a statement, Telus said the company "fundamentally disagrees with the findings of Consumer Protection B.C., and we look forward to presenting our arguments in court."

Consumer Protection B.C. told CBC News the agency would not comment while the case is before the courts.

World.title: Iran attacks U.S. bases across Gulf after reports of deadly strike on wedding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Iran and its Arab neighbours were plunged back into war on Wednesday by the biggest exchange of fire between Tehran and Washington since July, with U.S. forces striking Iran's southern coast and Iran firing at American bases across the region.

The United States threatened more devastating strikes. Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing five people and wounding dozens.

Asian and European stocks fell after the renewed U.S. airstrikes, which pushed oil prices back up to levels unseen since July, compounding the economic impact of a global sell-off in bonds as disrupted energy supplies fuel inflation worldwide.

The U.S. military's Central Command said it struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday. Iranian media reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway where Tehran has threatened tankers attempting to pass without its permission.

"Last night was like the end of the world," Mahmoud, 38, a municipal worker in Sirik County along the strait, told Reuters by telephone, describing the attacks on the area which includes the city where the wedding was reported to have been hit.

Iran responded by striking what it said were U.S. assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was now to drive U.S. forces out of the vast network of military bases they have maintained for decades across the Middle East.

"American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences," Iran's military command said.

WATCH | Hostilities flare: U.S., Iran trade new strikes, warnings as hostilities flare | Duration 3:08 The U.S. launched a fresh round of airstrikes against Iran on Tuesday, following a weekend exchange of fire that broke a month of relative calm in the conflict. Tehran said it responded with missiles and drones on U.S. targets in the region while warning that U.S. attacks would 'tighten the lock' on the Strait of Hormuz.

Jordan's military said it dealt with 13 missiles, 10 of which were intercepted and three which fell in remote areas. The IRGC said it killed a large number of U.S. forces in Jordan, but U.S. officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.

In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the vast U.S. Ali Al Salem Air Base and targeted the accommodation of a U.S. commander. Kuwait’s fire service said crews put out a blaze at a residential complex early on Wednesday that was struck by an Iranian drone causing damage but no casualties.

Qatar, home of the largest U.S. airbase in the Gulf, said it holds Iran "fully legally responsible for these attacks and their repercussions and consequences." Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the U.S. navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.

Iran also said two tankers were struck by mines while being steered through the Strait of Hormuz by U.S. personnel.

Washington says that despite Iranian attacks it is guiding ships through the strait. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said more than 17 million barrels of oil exited on Monday.

Saudi Arabia's national shipping company reported on Wednesday that two Filipino crew had been killed aboard an oil tanker in the strait two days earlier.

5 killed during wedding in Iran

Iranians who endured U.S. strikes for much of the past six months were fearful that the war could restart at full throttle.

“It’s very difficult to live like this. We don’t know when America will strike. My family and I are constantly worried about where will it strike,” Mahpari, 28, a woman in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, told Reuters by phone.

Iran reported at least 12 deaths from the night of U.S. strikes, with five people including a four-year-old said to have been killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik, a town along the coast of the strait.

Blood stains are seen next to a pair of sandals on a carpet inside a building that Iranian media said was damaged in a U.S. strike in Kuhestak, southern Iran, early Wednesday. (Morteza Akhoondi/Tasnim News Agency/The Associated Press)

Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of several injured children in hospital. Iranian officials compared the incident to a strike on a girls' school that killed 160 people on the war's first night.

Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident and U.S. officials did not comment on it. Video filmed by Iran's West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard of a home. A pair of strappy women's dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.

"I am just glad the casualties weren't even worse," said Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride.

Worst exchange of fire since July

The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.

Iran's war-battered economy and degraded conventional forces have left it stretched thin, while Washington has used up much of its stocks of air defense munitions and burned through its precision long-range missiles.

Still, Trump, who has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching "Operation Epic Fury" in February — to end Iran's nuclear program, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbours and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers — repeated his declarations that victory was at hand.

"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," he said on Tuesday.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington was looking at targeting airlines, the maritime industry and digital assets as part of a campaign to increase economic pressure on Tehran.

Sources have told Reuters Trump aides were trying to keep the war quiet for now to avert a rout in congressional elections in November. Polls show Americans oppose the war by more than a two-to-one margin.

Iran, for its part, is determined to emerge from the war stronger than before, with sanctions lifted, blocked funds released, and a newfound grip over the strait letting it collect fees from ships that normally carry a fifth of global oil.

World.title: Colby Cosh: The U.S. president breaks his own laws in waging the trade war
World.content:
Article content

Last month, two Georgetown trade lawyers offered a different array of potential challenges to Trump’s use of Section 338 — angles they say are likely to encourage the courts to circumscribe his trade war, though perhaps not negate it altogether. The section gives the president authority to “offset” the effects of other countries’ discriminatory trade policies up to the 50 per cent limit. But Trump isn’t doing anything of the kind. His claim is that Canada’s discriminating against the U.S. when it comes to automobiles, booze and dairy products; that makes his included tariffs on other products like Canadian hockey sticks and cement (and orchids and statuettes and pliers) prima facie illegal. And even when it comes to the directly relevant sectors, the math doesn’t add up: his tariffs on motor vehicles alone will massively outweigh the White House’s own estimate of the costs of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. auto industry.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
