World.title: Slovenian parliament lifts former PM Golob’s immunity in police-meddling probe
World.content:
Robert Golob at the last televised political debate in Ljubljana on March 20, 2026. | Jure Makovec/AFP via Getty Images

Former interior minister alleges ex-PM asked her to interfere in police staffing.

Slovenia’s parliament on Wednesday allowed prosecutors to pursue a criminal case against former Prime Minister Robert Golob over allegations that he improperly meddled in police staffing after taking office in 2022.

All 75 lawmakers present — including Golob himself — voted against granting him parliamentary immunity, allowing proceedings to move forward. The decision was taken without debate or explanations of the voting.

Golob had already told parliament he would not invoke immunity and wanted the case resolved as quickly as possible.

World.title: TikTok ban divides European Commission
World.content:
“We follow the evolution of the platform, in particular the status of developments regarding data protection and cybersecurity concerns,” the Commission said.

There is little sign the Commission’s policy is about to change. Dana Spinant, the Commission’s director-general for communications, opposes creating an official account, according to another official familiar with the discussions. Spinant did not respond to a request for comment.

A third official said there was frustration in some commissioners’ cabinets that Brussels was absent from a platform where young Europeans increasingly derive their news and views. A second official argued that Russia has no such qualms about using social media platforms to influence European public opinion and that the Commission could not afford to cede ground.

The debate comes as President Ursula von der Leyen and her commissioners are seeking to reach more Europeans using social media. Von der Leyen will invite influencers, including some who share content on TikTok, to her State of the Union speech this month. The third official called it ironic that the Commission is encouraging influencers to communicate its message on a platform while refusing to establish a presence there itself.

The Commission is instead increasingly turning to YouTube, a U.S.-based platform where it has more than 500,000 subscribers, according to two of the officials.

World.title: EU’s Kallas labels Leipzig drone attack ‘state-sponsored terrorism’
World.content:
Other ministers struck an equally hard line. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called the attack part of a “long-running attempt by the Kremlin to destabilize the European Union, its democratic processes” and weaken support for Ukraine.

“We will not let an act of such gravity go without consequences,” Barrot said, adding that France would support Germany’s sanctions proposals and propose measures against additional Russian vessels.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said Europe had moved beyond talking simply about “hybrid threats.”

“We’re talking about significant activity,” she said, accusing Moscow of a “very, very clear attempt” to divide EU governments and “put fear into citizens.”

Berlin formally blamed Moscow on Tuesday for the Aug. 4 incident, in which three explosive-laden drones were detected around Leipzig-Halle Airport. Germany announced retaliatory diplomatic measures and plans to seek fresh EU sanctions. Russia denies any involvement.

Kallas added that another 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex were already “in the pipeline.”

No decision will be made at Wednesday’s meeting. But, she said, Germany has the political backing of its EU partners. “This is the unified response that we need.”

World.title: Is Burnham living in a economic dreamland?
World.content:
As Andy Burnham prepares for his first Prime Minister’s Questions, he faces a gathering economic storm.

With markets driving up government borrowing costs and the prospect of another interest rate rise, Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine what the turmoil could mean for mortgage holders, public spending and the government plans going forward.

Could the chancellor be left with almost no room for manoeuvre ahead of October’s budget?

The duo also look ahead to the looming Holborn and St Pancras by-election and whether the Green Party leader – Zac Polanski – will consider standing?

Plus, as Emmanuel Macron arrives in Britain, why are the French taking such a keen interest in the new PM.

World.title: Conservative and far-right MEPs rally against Spain’s government over Ceuta crisis
World.content:
Around 500 people gathered in front of the European Parliament in Brussels on Wednesday to protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis in Ceuta, where several thousand of more than 70,000 migrants who arrived in the exclave on 30 July remain.

 

MEPs and staffers from the centre-right European People’s Party and far-right Patriots for Europe gathered in the area in front of Parliament, waving the flags of Ceuta and Spain, and accusing Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of failing to defend Spain’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

Two separate demonstrations were launched by Spain’s Popular Party and Vox in Brussels on Ceuta Day. Despite being organised separately, both gatherings took place at the same time and in the same location, with EPP and PfE lawmakers standing side by side.

“Sánchez has handed over responsibility for the security of Ceuta to a third country,” EPP vice-president Dolors Montserrat told reporters, claiming the Spanish Prime Minister “is bowing” to Morocco.

Online newspaper El Español reported on Wednesday that Spain's National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) had concluded the incident "was guided by Moroccan security forces", contradicting Sánchez’s stance that there is no proof of any involvement by the authorities in Rabat.

Madrid has so far avoided publicly blaming Rabat for the incident. It generally considers Morocco a cooperative partner in migration management.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska asked police chief Francisco Pardo to verify the information, which CENIF reportedly sent to a judge gathering information on the incident, according to ministry sources.

Vox, the leading Spanish far-right party, claims Sánchez has “betrayed” his own country and is pushing to activate Article 102 of the Spanish Constitution, which would trigger a criminal trial against the prime minister and his cabinet.

“The situation is untenable. This government cannot continue to lead Spain,” Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé Villalba told reporters, claiming this is the “hardest hour” for the country since the Catalan attempted secession in 2017.

Vox’s MEPs also sent a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Home Affairs Commissioner Magnus Brunner.

They call for condemning and sanctioning Morocco, declaring the massive entry “an act of hybrid warfare” and immediately suspending all international agreements between the EU and Morocco, as well as the granting of visas to Moroccan citizens.

The European Commission told Euronews it will not comment on leaks and considers the ongoing investigation into Morocco’s involvement “a matter for the national authorities.”

World.title: Trump becomes first sitting US president to appear on a coin as Mint releases $1 piece
World.content:
American money now carries the current US president's face.

 

The US Mint confirmed on Thursday that the "golden dollar" featuring the likeness of US President Donald Trump has been released, urging people to check their pocket change while collectors can buy it in rolls and bags sold exclusively through its own channels.

The products are priced at $61 for a 25-coin roll and $154.50 for a 100-coin bag.

In practice, finding one in everyday change may take patience, since dollar coins have caught on widely with American shoppers and circulate far more sparsely than notes.

Collectors also have another detail to chase as the US Mint struck 250,000 of the coins on 4 July carrying a special "July 4th" privy mark, dispersed through the rolls and bags.

Despite its colour, the coin contains no gold, being 88.5% copper with smaller quantities of zinc, manganese and nickel.

The coin was struck in Philadelphia and carries no mint mark.

Chief Engraver Joseph Menna designed the obverse from an official White House photograph, showing Trump facing almost directly forward beneath the inscriptions "LIBERTY", "IN GOD WE TRUST" and the dual date 1776 to 2026.

The reverse carries the Presidential Seal, originally sculpted by former chief engraver Frank Gasparro, with the numeral 250 added to the eagle's shield to mark the country's 250th anniversary.

There is one precedent for this initiative, though an imperfect one.

Calvin Coolidge appeared alongside George Washington on a 1926 half dollar marking 150 years of independence, making him the first living president on American coinage.

However, that was a commemorative issue rather than a coin intended for daily use. The legal basis for placing a Trump coin in circulation has been contested.

US law generally bars portraits of living people from coins, and the administration has relied on the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020, signed by Trump during his first term, which permits $1 coins bearing designs emblematic of the anniversary throughout 2026.

The design process also drew criticism.

The US Commission of Fine Arts had recommended a profile portrait and a different eagle design, neither of which was adopted, while the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, which normally reviews Mint designs, declined to consider it.

World.title: Venice Film Festival: Clooney, conflicts and competition dominate as ceremonies begin
World.content:
George Clooney is the undoubted star of the show as the Venice Film Festival opens for its 83rd edition.

 

In the nearly 30 years since he first stepped onto the Lido Out of Sight, he’s become something of a staple fixture. It’s a city where he’s enjoyed many significant moments, from his wedding at the Aman Venice to the debut of Good Night, and Good Luck, which earned him his first Oscar nomination for best director.

Now, the actor, director and producer is due to receive a lifetime achievement award but when facing the press, he didn't appear to want to talk much about the journey that's led him to be the centre of the spotlight at the world's oldest celebration of cinema.

Ahead of the prize-giving ceremony on Wednesday, the 65-year-old wanted to discuss anything and everything it seemed but his life on or behind the camera.

Whether it was talk of artificial intelligence,climate change, power brokers in Hollywood and beyond and the state of journalism today, Clooney had two cents and more to spend on a range of topics.

"There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people,” he said. “I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now. But we’ll get through it.”

On artificial intelligence, Clooney said that his industry is going to have to find ways to survive, and that he would “like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead.”

He also criticised the fact that some of the world's richest men own The Washington Post and X and said that the proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. was “a complicated thing because I don’t know how this works out, I don’t know how it goes through."

The state we are in

Clooney was by no means alone is decrying the state of current affairs. Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal also made her feelings clear on a variety of subjects including, sexism, politics and conflicts.

“Look, we could say how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency,” Gyllenhaal said. “To me the answer has something to do with empathy.”

Venice Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal poses for photographers at the jury photo call during the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival, 3 September 2026 AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt/Invision

She also addressed the dearth of female directors in the competition lineup, with only one film directed by a woman. Perhaps in response to critics, just last week, NAZA - a documentary about Gaza co-directed by a woman - was added to the lineup.

“I guess it’s just finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal joked, before speaking about the systemic issues facing female directors, like financing and preconceived notions about high art.

Over the course of 11 days, many stars and celebrities from Hollywood and beyond are expected on the red carpet, from Robert Pattinson to Noel and Liam Gallagher of Oasis.

The sprawling lineup also includes documentaries about , Elon Musk (Musk) and independent Russian journalists covering the war in Ukraine (My Undesirable Friends — Part II: Exile) as well as Palestinian films and a short about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minneapolis.

The festival will open with Danny Boyle's Ink a competition title featuring Guy Pearce as media baron Rupert Murdoch and Jack O'Connell as tabloid newspaper editor Larry Lamb. The movie dramatises Murdoch's acquisition of The Sun newspaper in 1969 and how Lamb reversed its fortunes from a failing venture into Britain's bestselling daily.

The Venice Film Festival runs until Saturday 12 September.

World.title: EU readies fresh cash for Ukraine’s air defence as Patriot stocks run low
World.content:
Brussels is assessing a new payment request from Kyiv worth several billion euros to bolster Ukraine’s air defences, as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks and Ukraine seeks more US-made Patriot interceptors.

 

“We have received a new payment request. It is worth several billion euros and would cover Ukraine’s air defences, including the highly advanced PAC-3 Patriot air defence systems,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at a joint press conference with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

EU countries now need to approve a derogation from the conditions of the Ukraine Support Loan, which limits non-European sourcing to 35% of the value of a defence product unless no European alternative is available.

The Commission president did not disclose the exact amount requested, as doing so could have put pressure on member states to approve the full sum sought by Kyiv, a Commission official who asked not to be named told Euronews.

Part of the payment could also come from NATO, although discussions were still ongoing, the official added. No other derogations were requested under this payment apart from the one covering the Patriots.

Russia has intensified its aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, at times launching as many as 30 ballistic missiles in a single night and further straining Kyiv’s already depleted stocks of interceptors.

Patriots are among the most advanced systems available for intercepting ballistic missiles. They take considerable time to manufacture, while stocks have been depleted by more than four years of war in Ukraine and by the US-Iran conflict earlier this year, which forced Gulf states to use large numbers of their own interceptors.

At an informal meeting of EU defence ministers in Ireland earlier this week, EU officials lobbied member states with significant remaining stockpiles to share them with Kyiv. So far, however, the pressure has failed to produce the hoped-for results.

“Member states are currently looking at Ukraine’s request, but I can say it’s going in the right direction,” von der Leyen said.

According to Ukrainian media reports, Kyiv has asked the European Commission to allow it to spend around €2 billion on Patriot interceptor missiles. The number of missiles that sum could purchase would depend primarily on the terms of the deal.

For Kyiv, however, the main challenge is not funding but availability.

In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would need at least 140 Patriot interceptors to defend against a single Russian attack involving around 70 ballistic missiles.

Ukraine has already secured a derogation for US-made Patriots under the €90 billion loan, alongside another allowing the procurement of Chinese drone components, even as France ramps up pressure to phase out non-European suppliers.

National representatives are due to discuss the request on Monday, with a view to approving it as early as next week. The Commission would then need signed procurement contracts before it could disburse the payment.

Von der Leyen also pointed to Freya, a pan-European anti-ballistic missile defence project led by Ukraine’s Fire Point and involving several European companies, as a potential way to help close a critical gap in Europe’s air-defence capabilities.

“Since June, we have issued €8.5 billion for drones and missiles for Ukraine from this loan. And this money would also buy fighter jets from European industry,” she said.

World.title: Matthew Perry three-part documentary coming to Netflix next month
World.content:
A new three-part documentary series about Friends star Matthew Perry has been announced and will be released on Netflix next month.

 

Titled The One With Matthew Perry, the documentary will explore the actor’s life and struggles as told by the people who were closest to him.

Netflix’s Press release reads: “Anchored by never-before-heard testimonies from Perry’s sister Mia Perry Bowick and his lifelong best friends, the three-part series, which features unreleased photos and videos from the Perry family’s private archive, traces his journey from rising comedic star to the man the world still loves as their favourite Friend. First-hand memories from his creative collaborators and friends who adored and supported him are woven with candid new details on his private struggles.”

It is not yet known whether any of the Friends cast will appear in the docuseries.

“It’s taken time for me to feel ready to share these memories and what it was like to love Matthew through all the complexity of his life - to see him as a whole person, not just as Chandler, and not just as someone who struggled with addiction,” Perry Bowick said in a statement.

“As his sister, he shaped who I am today, the person I strive to be and the work to which I’ve devoted my life. Matthew had a beautiful heart and a generous spirit, and even in his darkest moments, he could still make you laugh and feel loved. I hope this series gives everyone who loved him, whether personally or from afar, a deeper appreciation for who he truly was, and the legacy he leaves behind.”

Matthew Perry AP Photo

The actor, known worldwide for playing Chandler Bing on the celebrated 90s sitcom, was found unresponsive in a hot tub in his Los Angeles home on 28 October 2023. He was later pronounced dead, at the age of 54.

He died from “acute effects of ketamine” according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office. The autopsy report also cited drowning, coronary artery disease and the effects of buprenorphine, a drug used to treat opioid use disorder, as contributing to his death.

In May, Perry’s assistant was jailed for three years and five months fo his role in the actor’s death, while infamous drug dealer Jasveen Sangha was sentenced to 15 years for supplying him drugs.

The One With Matthew Perry is due to debut on Netflix on 27 October.

World.title: Ukraine formally warns airlines that Russian airspace is unsafe
World.content:
Ukraine has formally informed the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) that Russia's airspace is unsafe for civilian traffic, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Wednesday.

 

“Ukraine has officially notified ICAO that the Russian airspace is not safe for civilian aviation because of increased military activity. We urge everyone to avoid it,” Sybiha said on X.

He said Russia had been “deliberately ignoring the existing threats” created by its all-out war against Ukraine, arguing that the risks had already resulted in several aviation incidents in recent years.

“This is our responsible decision to notify ICAO and all airlines, and governments to take caution — even if Russia refuses to fulfill its responsibility to inform them. We want to prevent unintended incidents,” Sybiha said.

The formal notification came a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines, insurers and businesses using Russian main airports that the country’s airspace is now becoming increasingly dangerous as Kyiv expands its long-range drone operations.

“Today we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.

Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation, Zelenskyy insisted, while warning that the growing scale of Ukrainian drone operations inside Russia meant the risks could no longer be ignored.

He said Russian airspace would “effectively be closing” as the consequences of Moscow’s war increasingly returned to Russian territory.

Few hours after Zelenskyy’s statement, a few flights between Turkey and Moscow were disrupted overnight.

Turkish low-cost carrier Pegasus Airlines cancelled 12 flights to and from Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport overnight on Wednesday, according to airport data.

A Pegasus flight from Antalya to Moscow was also diverted because of security concerns in Russian airspace, according to Turkish media reports.

Turkish Airlines, the country's flagship carrier, mostly kept its Moscow services running, although it cancelled two departures and two arrivals from and to Istanbul.

Ukraine’s airspace has been closed to civilian aviation since 24 February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

Russian civilian aviation, by contrast, has continued operating throughout the war, despite increasingly frequent disruptions and temporary airport closures during Ukrainian drone attacks.

Despite the risks, Russian airspace still carries significant international passenger traffic.

European and US carriers stopped flying over Russia following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Major airlines including Emirates, Turkish Airlines, Air India, Etihad and Qatar Airways, as well as several Chinese carriers, continue to fly to or through the country.

World.title: 'Climate policy must survive, because we want to survive in Europe,' EU Commission says
World.content:
The European Union's worsening exposure to extreme weather and imported fossil fuels makes decarbonisation as much a matter of economic and security policy as climate policy, a senior European Commission official said.

 

Russia’s war against Ukraine and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have raised successive warnings about Europe’s dependence on imported oil and gas, Jan Dusik, director general at the Commission's climate department, said on the sidelines of the think tank Bruegel Annual Meetings on Wednesday.

“Climate policy must survive, because we want to survive in Europe,” Dusik said, arguing that abandoning or weakening the agenda would ignore its links to energy security, resilience and affordability.

The EU's premise is faster electrification of its economy and the development of domestic energy sources to reduce its vulnerability to volatile fossil-fuel markets, Dusik said, which have raised energy bills and are threatening the bloc's industrial competitiveness.

At a time when climate policy is being contested as too onerous for industry competitiveness vis-a-vis China and the United States, the Commission is rolling out its next climate measures in stages, with the end goal of reaching net-neutrality by 2050, even if many critics argue the climate targets are becoming unrealistic and can become counterproductive if the market stops believing in it.

Pierre Wunsh, the governor of the National Bank of Belgium, did not mince his words when discussing Europe’s credibility test over its 2050 net-zero target.

"Most people will tell you we're not going to be in net zero in 2050. That's what I hear. And so it creates some cognitive dissonance, because by pretending we are going there, but having a lot of people believing we're not going there, you lose the credibility of the instruments,” Wunsh told the Bruegel audience on Wednesday.

But the EU executive remains focused on pursuing climate neutrality. The first step came in July with the proposed review of the EU carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS).

Next month, the Commission plans to present a climate resilience framework to help Europe better cope with heatwaves, floods and other climate impacts. By the end of 2026, it plans to unveil the rest of its post-2030 climate package, setting out how the EU intends to deliver its 2040 emissions-cutting target.

ETS: defending the credibility of the 2040 pathway

On the ETS, Dusik rejected suggestions that the EU executive is effectively “playing with numbers” by allowing flexibilities, existing carbon allowances and future carbon removals while simultaneously targeting a 90% reduction in net greenhouse-gas emissions by 2040.

The Czech EU politician said the ETS and the wider post-2030 climate package were designed as a single system and will ultimately have to add up to the EU’s overall carbon budget.

"There are moments where we look at how the legislation is implemented, and we are doing adjustments as we have done for the market stability reserve, as we are doing for the benchmarks in the ETS, which does not jeopardise that total carbon budget that we should have in 2040 or 2050. It needs to add up and this is designed to add up," Dusik said.

The key mechanism, Dusík suggested, will increasingly be price rather than simply the quantity of carbon allowances. As the number of allowances declines through the 2030s, prices are expected to rise, creating a stronger financial incentive for companies to invest in cutting emissions rather than continue paying for carbon.

The Commission is also preparing to introduce additional flexibility through carbon removals and international carbon credits.

But the official stressed that these should complement, rather than replace, European investment.

International credits could help lower the overall cost of meeting targets, but Brussels does not want a system in which European companies simply buy reductions abroad instead of investing in clean technologies at home.

"This needs to be done in a very smart way, knowing what the amount of credit is available, how it complements rather than replaces domestic investments. Because after all, we are also interested in investing in Europe, rather than purchasing investments abroad. So it needs to be the right mix," the Commission official said.

Climate adaptation is becoming unavoidable

The official also acknowledged that the EU is increasingly having to deal with climate impacts that cannot be prevented by mitigation alone.

Following a summer marked by extreme weather, the Commission plans to put forward a climate resilience framework, arguing that Europe needs to prepare for a world in which climate impacts become increasingly severe.

Even if the world fails to stay within the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal, the official argued, every fraction of additional warming still matters because it translates into higher economic and social costs.

Related Brussels pivots from climate mitigation to adaptation as heatwaves expose vulnerabilities

“This doesn't mean that we will give up on the Paris targets. It means that we have to recognise that the challenge is going beyond being able to stay under the one and half degree target," Dusik said.

"At the same time, we know that every fraction of a degree is a massive impact, a massive cost for the whole society, and the longer and the further we get into the overshoot, the more of the problem it will be.”

ETS revenues: Brussels wants more money going back into industry

One of the sharper criticisms focused on how governments use the revenues generated by the ETS. The Commission's analysis, according to the EU official, found that only around 5% of ETS revenues are actually being returned to industry for decarbonisation.

Since its inception in 2005, the ETS was not supposed to function simply as a source of government revenue. With a growing climate finance gap, Brussels wants more of the money generated by carbon pricing to finance the transition itself, including hydrogen, batteries, carbon capture and storage and other industrial technologies.

The proposed 'ETS investment booster', the industrial decarbonisation bank and the Innovation Fund are intended to turn carbon pricing into an investment mechanism rather than simply another cost for companies, the EU official said.

World.title: Back or elbow pain? You might be gaming too much on your phone
World.content:
Mobile gaming may be taking a physical toll on young people, according to new research that links problematic gaming behaviour with significantly higher rates of pain in the neck, upper back, elbows and wrists.

 

As gaming becomes an increasingly routine part of young people’s digital lives, a few more breaks — and perhaps a little less time hunched over a phone — could matter for physical health as well as digital wellbeing, researchers say.

The study surveyed 364 medical students at universities in Jordan and examined whether mobile gaming addiction was associated with musculoskeletal problems.

About 9% of the students — 34 people — met the study’s criteria for mobile gaming addiction.

The differences in reported pain were particularly striking in parts of the upper body commonly involved in prolonged handheld-device use.

Among students classified as addicted, 85.3% reported neck pain, compared with 65% of those who were not classified as addicted. Upper-back pain was reported by 64.7% of addicted students, compared with 55% of their peers. The gap was even wider for elbow pain: 41.2% of addicted students reported it, compared with 12.5% of those who were not addicted. Addicted students also reported more wrist and hand pain — 41.2% compared to 34%.

The study found that students with gaming addiction were also more likely to report that musculoskeletal problems interfered with everyday activities, including studying and hobbies. Some were more likely to have sought medical attention for pain affecting their wrists and hands, hips and knees.

Prolonged mobile gaming can also create an ergonomic problem: holding a phone for extended periods can involve sustained gripping, fixed arm and neck positions and repetitive movements.

The authors argue that gaming should therefore not be viewed solely as a question of screen time or psychological wellbeing.

The researchers call for greater awareness of digital health, ergonomic education, posture training and behavioural changes among students. Universities could incorporate guidance on breaks, device positioning and healthy gaming habits into student health programmes, particularly for groups spending long periods studying or working on screens.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: US sanctions halt TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran, disrupting study plans
World.content:
Students in Iran can no longer take TOEFL and GRE exams after a US sanctions exemption was suspended. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.

Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations.

"My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW. She said she had spent months preparing applications for a PhD program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges.

ETS, the US-based organization that administers both exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran.

"Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice.

ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing.

TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE, also administered by the same US organization, is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada.

Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy.

No timeline for testing to resume

An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes.

The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume.

That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing documents, contacting professors and paying application-related costs.

The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams.

Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same.

Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising costs for applicants

Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable.

"European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW.

"But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Travelling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza.

Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee.

For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant.

Many Iranian students pursue post-graduate education abroad Image: Sigrid Gombert/Image Source/IMAGO

Students launch petition

Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams.

The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates.

"Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states.

Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities.

"I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition."

Experiences of international PhD students navigating Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The organizers are calling on OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible.

They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy.

When sanctions impact education

Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran.

For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad.

Bahar, who is applying for PhD programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United Statesbecause obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult.

"American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for PhD programs more readily than European universities," she told DW.

Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle.

Missing a required exam can add months, or even a year, of waiting for affected applicants Image: Rainer Unkel/Imago Images

"There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said.

For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more.

While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad.

World.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy warns airlines to avoid Russian airspace
World.content:
09/02/2026 September 2, 2026 Ukraine says Russian airspace 'not safe' amid drone surge

Kyiv says it has formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) that Russian airspace is "not safe" as a result of increasing Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian territory.

Ukraine has also asked the UN agency to prohibit member countries from using Russian airspace, according to a government letter to the ICAO cited by Reuters.

It came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines to stay away.

"We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said.

"Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," he added. "The sky over Russia is currently for drones ... as long as the war continues."

Last week, Zelenskyy threatened to deploy up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

The ICAO has not commented on the request from Ukraine.

Russia's aviation watchdog regularly closes airports in response to the Ukrainian drones. Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the war started in 2022.

While European ​and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the conflict, the airspace is used by other airlines from China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries.

Russia has stepped up its strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks. Ukraine has responded with long-range drone strikes on Russian energy and military infrastructure.

World.title: Guinea-Bissau referendum tests democratic future
World.content:
Following voter approval of a constitutional change that expands presidential powers, Guinea-Bissau faces renewed debate over legitimacy, civilian rule and democratic safeguards.

Guinea-Bissau is facing a new political test after voters approved a referendum on a proposed charter that will give the president the power to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers, while reducing the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65..

Sunday's referendum came less than 10 months after a coup in which the military seized power and three months ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled to take place on December 6.

The transitional authorities say the constitutional reform is intended to bring stability to the impoverished West African country and prepare it for a return to civilian rule.

Victory claimed, legitimacy disputed

On Monday, the National Transitional Council claimed victory for the "Yes" camp. "The majority of those who went to vote voted yes. In conclusion, the victory of yes is guaranteed," council spokesman Alberto Pinto Pereira said.

On Tuesday, the National Electoral Commission (NEC) confirmed victory for the "Yes" side, saying it had received 70% of the vote, compared with 30% for the "No" camp, and that voter turnout exceeded 50%.

NEC chairperson Carmen Izaura Lobo described the Guinea-Bissau referendum as a success, due to the "organizational capacity, professionalism and dedication" of teams on the ground, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.

Lobo praised the "transparency" and "credibility" of the process.

The army took power in Guinea-Bissau in November 2025 just days after a presidential election Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

The opposition, however, says the referendum has no legal basis because it was organized by institutions created after the military coup. It had called on voters to boycott the vote.

Domingos Simoes Pereira, leader of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), who was detained after the military coup and later released into house arrest, rejected the referendum as legally invalid.

Speaking to DW from Portugal, he said the institutions established by the military have no democratic mandate to rewrite Guinea-Bissau's constitution.

The PAIGC and other opposition groups maintain that the vote is a continuation of the November coup.

Fernando Dias Costa, the main challenger to then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo in the November 2025 presidential election that was annulled by the military, disputed the official turnout figures.

"Very few citizens took part in this referendum," he said, noting that the people have sent an important message that must not be ignored.

"They are not prepared to simply accept political changes that are clearly unconstitutional and have not been publicly debated."

More power for the president

The proposed constitution would move Guinea-Bissau toward a much stronger presidential system. The president would appoint and dismiss the prime minister and government ministers and would have the power to dissolve parliament.

Supporters argue that the existing political system has repeatedly led to conflicts between the president, government and parliament. They say stronger presidential authority would create greater stability.

Bubacar Ture, head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, told DW that the draft constitution would lead to "an excessive concentration of power in the person of the president."

He argues that the proposed system could make parliamentary elections less meaningful because the president would have much greater control over the government regardless of the parliamentary balance.

Ture also criticizes the way the constitution was drafted. "No one was consulted," he said. "Neither the parties nor civil-society organizations, nor traditional or religious authorities. Everything was produced in secret."

He is particularly concerned that provisions concerning constitutional oversight have been removed. In his view, this would weaken the rule of law.

Supporters and critics view the referendum through the lens of the political crisis that began in November 2025, when both former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias claimed victory in a disputed presidential election.

Before the results could be officially announced, the military seized power.

Embalo was briefly detained and subsequently left the country. His current whereabouts are unclear, and speculation continues over whether he retains influence over the military leadership or could seek a political comeback.

The referendum in Guinea-Bissau also reflects a broader trend across parts of Africa, where constitutional reforms have sparked debate over the concentration of presidential power.

In recent years, countries including Togo, Chad, Uganda, Zimbabwe and Guinea have seen leaders pursue constitutional changes that critics say strengthen executive authority.

What comes next in Guinea-Bissau?

Despite the "Yes" vote, opposition and civil society groups continue to challenge the legitimacy of the process. The referendum also takes place against a backdrop of longstanding political instability.

Guinea-Bissau has experienced repeated coups and attempted coups since independence, contributing to recurring periods of political instability.

The December elections are intended to mark the return to civilian rule. But opposition criticism of Sunday's referendum has raised further questions about how difficult that transition may be.

A key point of contention is whether the new constitutional order will strengthen democratic institutions or concentrate more power in the presidency.

World.title: India rejects Hague ruling on Indus waters: What's next?
World.content:
By rejecting an international arbitration panel's ruling, New Delhi has cast fresh doubt on the future of the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.

The Indus Waters Treaty is facing a fresh dispute after India rejected a Hague-based Court of Arbitration ruling that the 1960 agreement remains in force.

Pakistan has welcomed the decision and says India remains bound by the treaty.

India's Ministry of External Affairs described the tribunal as a "so-called Court of Arbitration" that was "illegally constituted."

It said the body had been established by the World Bank in breach of the treaty and that India "categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body."

"The Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India's sovereign decisions," the ministry said.

What to know about the treaty

The Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, governs the use of water from six rivers flowing through India and Pakistan.

The agreement largely gives India rights over three eastern rivers while Pakistan has rights over the western Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India is allowed to use the western rivers for specified purposes including certain hydroelectric projects.

India, Pakistan could be ready to talk 1 year after standoff To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The treaty had endured wars and prolonged periods of intense hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.

But India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025 as part of a package of diplomatic and economic measures announced after a deadly attack in India-administered Kashmir killed 26 people, mostly tourists.

New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack. Pakistan denied the charges.

High stakes for Pakistan

Millions of people in Pakistan depend on the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers for drinking water, farming and daily life.

The rivers are particularly important to Punjab and Sindh provinces, whose agriculture is central to the country's food supply and rural economy.

After India's move to suspend the treaty, Pakistan approached the court in The Hague over the status of the accord.

Pakistani officials have repeatedly warned that any attempt to deny the country its share of the waters of rivers flowing across the border would be treated as an act of war.

Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said India had challenged the treaty on both political and legal grounds.

"Politically, abeyance hands India a new point of leverage, one more lever to press Pakistan into changing its behavior on cross-border terrorism," Bisaria told DW.

He also pointed to India's earlier requests to renegotiate the treaty, citing climate change, new dam-building technology and the deterioration of relations between the two countries.

India chose to put the treaty in abeyance rather than formally abrogate it. Bisaria said the Hague ruling would not change that course.

"The tribunal will not alter this trajectory," he said. "India's course on the Indus Waters Treaty is set. The treaty will not be revived in its present form."

A 'frozen conflict': India-Pakistan tensions persist To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Legal battle over water

Pakistan has taken the opposite view.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the ruling "decisively rejects" India's attempt to place the treaty in abeyance and reaffirmed that it remains "fully in force and binding on both parties."

"The Award vindicates Pakistan's consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside," Dar said in a post on X.

He added that India must comply with its obligations under the treaty and with binding decisions arising from its dispute settlement mechanisms.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and defense analyst, said the ruling may be difficult to implement if India refuses to accept it.

"The arbitration court's ruling may not be implementable because the court doesn't have the force to do so," Siddiqa told DW.

But she said the decision gave Pakistan an advantage as a lower riparian state.

"It does give Pakistan a moral edge," said Siddiqa, a senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King's College London.

She also questioned what India's rejection of the ruling could mean for its international position, particularly given that India has accepted international legal decisions in other disputes.

"This is not just an issue of pure military power but an international standing where India will not be able to justify its position to the world any longer," she said.

Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, a South Asia analyst and founder of the Mantraya think tank, said the ruling did not materially change India's position.

"The Permanent Court of Arbitration is an administrative body, not a conventional sovereign court with enforcement capabilities," D'Souza told DW.

"In this particular case, India chose not to participate in the proceedings. This allows it not to recognize the tribunal's rulings. Therefore, it has no enforceable constraint on India and nothing changes materially for New Delhi," she said.

A dispute over the rules

India and Pakistan have disagreed for years over the interpretation of the treaty, particularly over Indian hydropower projects on rivers allocated primarily to Pakistan.

Uttam Kumar Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies in New Delhi and author of "Trial by Water," said India is now no longer merely contesting the interpretation of the treaty, but rather "contesting the authority of the treaty's dispute-settlement mechanism itself."

New Delhi maintains that the tribunal was improperly constituted and that its decisions have no legal effect on India.

Sinha describes the emerging contest as "lawfare," with Pakistan likely to use the ruling in international forums and frame the dispute around treaty obligations and international law.

India threatens to dry out Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The limits of India's leverage

The practical implications will also depend on what India does with its infrastructure on the western rivers.

D'Souza said the treaty's abeyance gave India more political and psychological leverage than an immediate ability to alter the flow of the rivers.

"To effectively stop or significantly alter the flows of the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab rivers, substantial infrastructure like dams, canals and large storage systems would be required, and such structures do not currently exist," said D'Souza.

"Furthermore, geographical and technical constraints limit India's capacity to block these rivers."

Sinha echoed this view.

"India cannot simply 'turn off' the western rivers," he said.

Large storage and diversion projects would take years or decades, require substantial investment and involve difficult construction in the mountainous Himalayan region, as well as environmental and domestic approvals.

"There is a significant gap between India's potential strategic freedom on the western rivers and its actual physical capacity to change water flows," Sinha said.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Police exhume body of former Czechoslovak foreign minister Jan Masaryk
World.content:
The top diplomat was found dead on March 10, 1948, in the courtyard beneath his bathroom window, supposedly after a fall. Police said their probe aims to settle questions that have surrounded the death ever since.

Czech police said Wednesday they had begun exhuming the remains of former Czechoslovak Foreign Minister Jan Masaryk in an attempt to clear up speculation surrounding his death nearly 80 years ago.

In a statement posted to X, police said they planned to examine the remains, buried at Prague's Olsany Cemetery, "using the most modern forensic methods."

"We believe that today's actions will bring us closer to clarifying the circumstances leading to the death of Jan Masaryk," the statement said.

What happened to the former top diplomat?

Masaryk was found dead on March 10, 1948, dressed only in his pajamas, in the courtyard at the Foreign Ministry beneath his bathroom window.

The mysterious circumstances surrounding his death, at the height of the Cold War, have fueled speculation for decades.

At the time, the Interior Ministry claimed that he had committed suicide. Others believed his fall may have been an accident, or that he was murdered by Soviet agents.

Jan Masaryk was found in the courtyard of the Foreign Ministy, housed in Prague's Czernin Palace Image: UPI/dpa/picture-alliance

Who was Jan Masaryk?

Born in Prague on September 14, 1886, Masaryk was the son of the first Czechoslovak president, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk.

He served as the country's top diplomat from 1940 to 1948, first for the government-in-exile during World War II and then for the post-war coalition government.

Following the Czechoslovak communist coup of February 1948, he stayed on as foreign minister, refusing to step down.

The case of his death has been reviewed several times since the collapse of communism in the 1989 Velvet Revolution. The country later split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

Jan Masaryk served as foreign minister during World War II and in the post-war government [File photo: 12 July, 1947] Image: Josef Mucha/CTK/picture alliance

World.title: Armed men abduct Kenyan editor, employer suspects government
World.content:
A newspaper editor in Kenya was kidnapped from a car late on Tuesday and then located near a dam far away a few hours later. The Standard paper said it suspected state involvement in an attempt to intimidate reporters.

An associate editor for one of Kenya's largest news outlets, The Standard, was abducted by armed men overnight and then released near a dam far from the scene around nine hours later, his employer said on Wednesday.

Alex Kiprotich was taken from a car at around 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday on a road near the city of Nakuru.

"The circumstances of Mr Kiprotich's abduction remain deeply troubling, and we will continue to press for full accountability," the government-critical outlet said in a press release after his discovery.

Late on Tuesday the Standard Group's CEO Chaacha Mwita had also said that the "abduction bears all the hallmarks of a targeted attack on a journalist for doing his job."

Kiprotich (left in picture) and CEO Mwita appeared at a Nairobi press confernce on Wednesday Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

What do we know about the apparent abduction?

The newspaper released a video overnight of what appeared to be dashcam footage from the car Kiprotich was traveling in when he was abducted.

A white vehicle without any markings apparent in the footage came to a stop in front of the car in an area where temporary barriers created a single-lane bottleneck on the Gilgil-Nakuru highway, and put on its hazard lights.

Four men in civilian clothes and obscuring their faces — some holding firearms and others carrying what appeared to be baseball bats — emerged and converged on the car, soon taking a man back to their vehicle and driving off.

On Wednesday, Standard Group said that Kiprotich had been located near a dam more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) southeast the scene of the abduction roughly nine hours earlier.

"Mr Kiprotich was located by a Standard Group team led by the Group CEO Chaacha Mwita at around 6:30 a.m. near Masinga Dam, after being dumped by his captors in the early hours of the morning," it said.

Kiprotic was "safe, though understandably shaken by his ordeal," his employer said. Kiprotich works for newspaper The Standard, a flagship of the wider media group known for its critical coverage of President William Ruto's government.

Rights groups say activists still being abducted in Kenya To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Right groups call for investigation, warn of pattern of abductions and intimidation

Police and the government in Kenya did not immediately comment on the incident.

Dozens of government critics and activists have been abducted in Kenya this year alone, according to a report released this week, with the practice becoming more common since widespread anti-government protests in 2024.

Human rights groups have accused state agencies of being responsible, with Standard Group voicing similar suspicions in this case.

Kiprotich had said in June that he narrowly escaped a previous attempt to kidnap him, which came three days after Ruto called out the Standard Group on social media.

Kenya's editors' guild said it was "shocked, outraged and deeply perturbed" by Tuesday's abduction, describing it as "a disturbing escalation in the intimidation and targeting of journalists in Kenya."

Amnesty International Kenya called for an independent investigation, saying the incident raised "serious concerns for media freedom."

World.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
World.content:
The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the attempted attack had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." She said the EU was summoning a Russian envoy, with France announcing a similar step.

The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.

Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'

"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.

The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."

France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.

"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest," Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.

Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks.

Germany's Wadephul says 'pressure on Russia is being stepped up'

German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks."

"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Urkaine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.

The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences."

He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict."

What did Germany say about its investigations?

Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.

Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.

Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

World.title: What really helps Europe deal with drought
World.content:
Fix leaks, or ban pools? As European countries prepare for hotter, drier years to come, here's what the data says about how to really save water

Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier , the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.

"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade," says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.

"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."

For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.

The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.

German municipalities impose water restrictions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.

Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."

So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.

Which European countries use the most water?

Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.

Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.

In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2,000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.

Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1,000 and 2,000 liters per capita daily in total.

Where Europe can save the most water

"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."

And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.

For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.

Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue

So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.

Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.

Better irrigation can help in agriculture

In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.

Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water

In EU countries, around one-in-four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination, according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.

In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.

Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.

Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.

"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."

What Europe can learn

Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.

This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," says Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.

What one of the world's driest cities teaches us about water To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.

"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she adds.

Public and politics are paying more attention to water use

Both Elsner and Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.

"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022," Psomas tells DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."

What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.

"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone. I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."

Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün
