A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. The improvement has come after a series of measures by the Polish authorities to improve road safety, which was previously among the worst in Europe https://t.co/kXhpXSOwH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Vinohrady’s Americká Street Block Party Returns on September 12
World.content:
Americká and Záhřebská streets in Prague’s Vinohrady will turn into a pedestrian festival zone on Saturday, September 12, for the 15th edition of Zažít Americkou jinak.

From 10:30 AM to 9:30 PM, the streets will host a full-day programme of live music, dance, workshops, design, food and activities for children. The festival is free to attend.

A major part of this year’s programme will focus on Mexico and Latin American culture, including a celebration of Mexican Independence Day.



The main programme will take place on the La Calle Mexicana Stage, hosted by DJs Roxana Velasco and José. Visitors can look forward to performances by Studio Anyo, traditional Mexican music, a piñata, a dance workshop and appearances by Mexican musicians Razcarmelo and Andrea Viruega.

One of the highlights will be El Grito, the traditional ceremony marking Mexico’s Independence Day. The event has become an annual gathering point for the Mexican community in Czechia and festival visitors.

The programme will also feature Mariachi Azteca de Praga, described as the first authentic mariachi band based in the Czech Republic.

The evening will continue with international acts including Faustina Calavera, a ten-member band from Wrocław combining Latin American cumbia, Balkan brass and ska, followed by ONIXIA, an Argentine singer, dancer and songwriter based in Berlin who blends electronic music with Latin American rhythms.

More Space to Relax

This year’s festival will also feature an expanded chill-out zone at the intersection of Americká and Jana Masaryka streets, with seating, workshops and space to meet friends and neighbours.

Music will also be played at two additional locations. The Burza #4 Stage will return by the fountain at the corner of Americká and Záhřebská streets, while another stage on Záhřebská Street will focus on world and house music.

MINT Market, Food and Local Businesses

The festival will once again include MINT Market, bringing together dozens of Czech designers, independent makers and creators from Latin America. Visitors can browse fashion, jewellery, illustrations, ceramics, natural cosmetics and other handmade products.

Food will be another major part of the day, with Mexican, Latin American and international cuisine, street food and special offers from cafés, restaurants and other local businesses.

During the festival, Americká and Záhřebská streets will be closed to traffic and parking.

World.title: New Pharmacy Partnership Makes Prescription Drugs Easier for Foreigners in Czechia
World.content:
Foreigners from outside the EU insured with Maxima pojišťovna can now collect prescription medicines at selected pharmacies without paying upfront.

The Czech insurer has expanded its network of partner pharmacies through a new agreement with LÉKÁRNA U MUZEA in Prague 1.

Under the arrangement, the pharmacy and insurer handle the reimbursement directly, bringing the process closer to the system used by patients covered by Czech public health insurance.



The change is aimed at simplifying access to medicines for foreigners, who can face difficulties navigating the Czech healthcare system and understanding the costs associated with medical treatment.

According to figures cited by the insurer, nearly 900,000 people from non-EU countries have been living in the Czech Republic on a long-term basis. They account for about 8.2 percent of the country’s population.

How the new system works

Previously, foreign clients with commercial health insurance could be required to pay for prescribed medicines at the pharmacy and then submit the receipts to their insurer for reimbursement.

Under the new arrangement, this step is eliminated. Eligible Maxima clients can collect their prescribed medicines through the partner pharmacy, while the financial settlement takes place directly between the pharmacy and the insurance company.

The model has already been operating for more than a year at the pharmacy operated by Maxima’s healthcare partner Innova Healthcare at the Hůrka Polyclinic in Prague.

The data also highlights some of the most common medical needs among patients visiting the participating clinics. More than 63 percent of patients seen by general practitioners, pediatricians and gynecologists were prescribed antibiotics.

More than 37 percent required treatment for sideropenic anemia, or iron deficiency, while 20 percent received prescriptions for blood-thinning medication following injuries.

The pharmacy in Prague 1 will also stock medical equipment and rehabilitation aids. Its range includes orthoses, crutches, wheelchairs and products for convalescence, rehabilitation and everyday healthcare.

Maxima says it intends to expand the direct-settlement model to additional partner pharmacies in the future.

World.title: Dozens of Hot Air Balloons to Fill Czech Skies During September Festival
World.content:
Dozens of hot air balloons are expected to take to the skies over eastern Bohemia this week as the Balonové Nebe festival returns to Hradec Králové, Jaroměř and nearby areas.

The five-day event will run from Wednesday, September 2, through Sunday, September 6, with a program combining competitive balloon flights, mass launches and evening shows. All public events are free to attend.

Weather will play a major role in the festival schedule. Balloon flights can only take place under suitable conditions, meaning launch sites and departure times may change at short notice.



Organizers say the exact location of each flight will depend mainly on wind direction and other weather conditions. Planned flights may also be postponed or cancelled if conditions are unsuitable.

The festival has established itself as one of the country’s major hot air balloon gatherings. Last year’s event set a Czech record when 81 balloons flew into the sky at the same time.

The 2026 edition will once again feature morning competitions, during which pilots will complete a series of tasks while large groups of balloons rise over the region.

Evening programs will offer a different spectacle, with balloon shows planned for spectators. The precise locations of these events will be announced according to the weather forecast and flying conditions.

Visitors planning to attend are advised to check the festival’s official website before setting out. The organizers will publish the latest information about launch locations, times and any changes to the schedule there.

World.title: VIDEO: Golden STARLUX Lands in Prague for the First Time
World.content:
A golden Airbus A350-1000 operated by Taiwan’s STARLUX Airlines landed at Václav Havel Airport Prague for the first time on Tuesday, September 1.

The aircraft, registered as B-58554, carries the special AIRSORAYAMA Gold livery created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama.

Prague is one of only three destinations where STARLUX plans to operate the specially designed aircraft on a regular basis, alongside Tokyo and Phoenix.



The arrival marks another step in the expansion of STARLUX’s new direct connection between Prague and Taipei.

The airline launched the route on August 1, initially using the smaller Airbus A350-900. From September, the carrier has switched to the larger A350-1000, which can carry up to 350 passengers in four travel classes.

STARLUX, Airbus and paint manufacturer Mankiewicz developed a multilayer coating using mica particles to create the metallic effect while meeting aviation safety requirements.

Increasing capacity on Prague route

STARLUX launched Prague as its first European destination on August 1, connecting the Czech capital directly with Taipei three times a week. The service currently operates on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Flight JX101 leaves Taipei at 12:10 a.m. and arrives in Prague at 8:35 a.m. The return flight, JX102, departs Prague at 10:35 a.m. and arrives in Taipei at 7:55 a.m. the following day.

The switch to the A350-1000 increases the available capacity on the route. The aircraft has four travel classes, including First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy and Economy.

An additional Monday flight is scheduled to operate from October through November, bringing the route to four flights per week during that period.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.

On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: BREAKING: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again – Here’s what Budapest wants
World.content:
Hungary has blocked Ukraine’s EU accession process for a third time, with the government saying it will only lift its objection if Kyiv makes progress on the rights of the country’s Hungarian minority.

The latest dispute emerged at the European Council’s Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession (COELA), which held its first meeting after the summer recess on Tuesday, 1 September.

According to Ukrainska Pravda citing European Pravda’s sources in Brussels, Hungary refused to approve the screening results for Ukraine’s second and third negotiating clusters. Without unanimous support from all 27 EU member states, the Council cannot move forward with formally opening the clusters.

Budapest links its position to minority rights

The Hungarian government has said that it will not support further progress in Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv takes what Budapest considers necessary steps to fulfil its commitments concerning national minority rights.

The issue is particularly sensitive because Ukraine is home to a sizeable ethnic Hungarian community in the Transcarpathia region, near Hungary’s eastern border.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has previously taken a somewhat different approach to Ukraine from his predecessor, Viktor Orbán. In June, Magyar and Ukraine reached what the Hungarian leader described as a “historic agreement” aimed at guaranteeing the educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia.

Despite that agreement, Budapest has maintained objections to several stages of Ukraine’s EU accession process.

What are the two clusters Hungary is blocking?

The latest Hungarian objection concerns Cluster 2, covering the EU internal market, and Cluster 3, which deals with competitiveness and inclusive growth. Hungary had previously blocked technical preparations for Ukraine’s Clusters 2–6. It subsequently lifted its objection to Cluster 6, which covers foreign and security policy, trade policy and relations with third countries.

In July, Hungary also supported advancing Cluster 3 for Moldova. However, most EU member states, led by Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, opposed separating Moldova’s and Ukraine’s accession tracks. As a result, neither country made progress on the matter at the time.

The next COELA meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, 2 September, although Ukraine and Moldova are reportedly not on the agenda, Kyiv Post writes.

Ukraine’s accession talks remain complicated

Ukraine formally began its EU accession negotiations in 2024, but opening individual negotiating clusters requires the unanimous agreement of the bloc’s member states. That gives Hungary significant leverage over the process.

The latest blockage comes after EU governments formally opened the first negotiating cluster — “Fundamentals” — for Ukraine and Moldova on 15 June.

Under the previous government, Viktor Orbán repeatedly opposed Ukraine’s EU membership and used concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as one of the reasons for his position. His government had also held up the opening of the first cluster for years.

The change in Budapest’s approach under Magyar has therefore been notable, although it has not removed Hungary’s objections to Ukraine’s accession process.

Budapest says it does not want all clusters opened at once

Magyar has previously argued that Ukraine’s accession negotiations should proceed gradually rather than seeing all six clusters opened simultaneously.

“There are six clusters in total, and we don’t think opening them all at once is a good idea,” he said in June, arguing that the process should also take into account the Western Balkan countries that have spent years working towards EU membership.

For Kyiv, however, every delay is significant as it seeks to advance through the lengthy accession process and bring the country closer to EU membership.

World.title: School canteen employees were stealing food meant for children in Hungary, mayor caught them red-handed — Video
World.content:
Four kitchen employees at a primary school in Gyömrő, Hungary were reportedly caught with large quantities of food intended for pupils, after the town’s mayor stopped them in the school car park. Mayor Szabolcs Kisberk called the police, and an investigation has been launched into the case.

Kisberk, the mayor of Gyömrő, reported the incident on social media and also published video footage of what happened. According to his account, the incident took place on the first day of the new school year, when the four kitchen employees were allegedly preparing to leave the school premises around an hour before the end of their official working hours.

They were reportedly leaving with bags full of food

According to the mayor’s account, he stopped the four employees in the school car park and asked them to show him what they were carrying in their bags. An inspection reportedly revealed significant quantities of food used for school catering.

One particularly striking detail was that, according to the account, the food had been divided equally among the four employees. The mayor said this was not simply leftover food that kitchen staff might normally be allowed to take home, but ingredients intended to be served to pupils, reports 444.hu.

Only 900 grams of six kilograms of grated cheese allegedly left for pupils

One of the largest quantities involved was reportedly grated cheese. According to the account published by the mayor, the kitchen had six kilograms available, of which 5.1 kilograms had allegedly been put into the employees’ bags. That would have left just 900 grams for several hundred pupils.

The same amount of sliced ham was reportedly available. Of the six kilograms, the employees allegedly took 3.5 kilograms, leaving 2.5 kilograms for the children. According to the report, the six kilograms of margarine were also divided equally between the employees and the school kitchen’s supplies for the pupils.

Vegetables, fruit and prepared meals also found

The food allegedly taken was not limited to sandwich ingredients. According to the mayor’s account, nearly three kilograms of green peppers and five kilograms of peaches were also among the items found.

The list also included soup pearls, several prepared sandwiches, portions of cooked food and a diet meal. The mayor further reported that several kilograms of cooked side dishes had been hidden in one of the refrigerators.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Police called to the scene

Following the incident, Kisberk contacted the police. Officers from the Monor Police Department reportedly arrived at the scene and took action. According to the published account, all four employees admitted to the alleged offence during the police intervention. Pest County Police have confirmed that an investigation is indeed under way in connection with the case.

However, as the criminal proceedings are still ongoing, the four people involved cannot legally be considered convicted offenders at this stage. Their criminal responsibility will ultimately be determined through the relevant legal proceedings.

According to the mayor’s statement, the employment of all four kitchen workers was terminated following the incident. He said they were dismissed with immediate effect as part of disciplinary proceedings. The case has attracted particular attention because the food used in school catering is intended specifically to provide meals for pupils, while parents also contribute towards the cost of the school meals.

Parents and residents outraged

The incident has reportedly caused considerable outrage among parents and local residents in Gyömrő. According to the accounts published following the incident, some parents have questioned whether similar losses may have occurred previously and whether such practices could have affected the portions served to children.

However, there is currently no verified evidence in the available sources that similar incidents took place in previous years. The current case alone cannot establish that this was a long-standing practice.

In case you missed it: Police claims five men beaten and kept as modern-day slaves in Hungary for years

Tighter checks planned

Following the incident, the mayor said the local authority would introduce stricter controls in the kitchens of municipal institutions. The planned measures reportedly include closer monitoring of food stocks and stricter accounting for ingredients used in school catering.

The police investigation is ongoing, and the precise legal circumstances and responsibility of those involved will depend on the outcome of the proceedings.

World.title: PM Magyar signals Tisza’s next EU move after meeting with Manfred Weber
World.content:
Péter Magyar says Hungary’s governing Tisza Party will be ready to join the European People’s Party (EPP) once the EU’s Article 7 procedure against Hungary has been closed.

Magyar, who became Hungary’s prime minister after Tisza’s election victory in April, made the announcement after meeting Manfred Weber, the president of the European People’s Party, in Budapest on Wednesday.

The two politicians discussed how Hungary has changed since the election, with Magyar highlighting what he described as the end of publicly funded “hate campaigns” in the country.

According to Magyar, Weber said that supporting Hungary had always been important to him as a Bavarian politician and that he had personally found the previous government’s attacks on him difficult to experience.

Tisza eyes full EPP membership

One of the most politically significant points of the meeting was Magyar’s announcement that Tisza intends to join the European People’s Party itself.

Tisza has already been part of the EPP’s European Parliament political group since 2024, but membership of the wider European party family would represent a further step towards closer cooperation with Europe’s largest centre-right political family.

Magyar said Tisza would “gladly join” the EPP once EU institutions have closed the Article 7 procedure launched against Hungary.

The procedure was initiated by the European Parliament in 2018 over concerns relating to the rule of law and other fundamental EU values. It has remained unresolved for years.

The question of ending the procedure has gained renewed attention since Tisza came to power. Weber said as early as April that the European Parliament should take steps towards ending the process.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Weber offers help over EUR 1 million daily fine

The meeting also focused on Hungary’s long-running dispute with the EU over its asylum and migration policies.

Magyar said Weber had offered to help find a solution that would allow Hungary to stop paying the EUR 1 million daily fine imposed over its failure to comply with EU asylum rules concerning the protection of the bloc’s external borders.

The Hungarian prime minister said he made clear that the country would continue to protect its borders. He also said the new government would seek to have the fines already imposed on Hungary credited during negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget.

The dispute dates back to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found Hungary had failed to fulfil its obligations under EU asylum law.

If you missed it: Extraditing Hungarian MOL’s head to Croatia? Péter Magyar gives cryptic answer at Bled forum

‘No blank cheque’ for Brussels

Magyar also stressed that closer cooperation with the EU would not mean giving up Hungary’s interests. He said the Tisza government’s priority would remain representing the interests of Hungarian people and businesses, adding that the government would not give anyone a “blank cheque” in EU decision-making.

The comments come as Budapest prepares for negotiations over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, one of the major issues facing the new Hungarian government.

António Costa next on Magyar’s Budapest agenda

Magyar’s meeting with Weber is part of a busy week of high-level European diplomacy. The Hungarian prime minister said he would also meet António Costa, president of the European Council, in Budapest after Wednesday’s government meeting.

According to Magyar, talks with Costa will focus on the EU’s new seven-year budget and the challenges facing Europe.

World.title: What’s happening? Forint plunges to its weakest level since Hungary’s election
World.content:
Hungary’s forint has suffered a sharp sell-off, briefly falling beyond the psychologically important level of HUF 370 to the euro on Wednesday morning. The currency has not been this weak since the days immediately preceding April’s parliamentary election.

The forint had been trading at around HUF 365 to the euro on Tuesday morning, but lost further ground over the following day. By Wednesday morning, the EUR/HUF exchange rate briefly climbed above 370 before settling just below that level.

This move is a significant reversal for the Hungarian currency, which had enjoyed several relatively strong months. Just a week earlier, on 25 August, the euro was trading at around HUF 360.

USD/HUF up 10 forints in a few days

The weakening has not been limited to the euro. The dollar-forint exchange rate has followed a similar trajectory, rising from around HUF 309 a week ago to approximately HUF 319 on Wednesday morning.

According to ERSTE market analysts cited by Forbes, a combination of international developments and rising energy prices is putting pressure on the Hungarian currency.

One of the key factors is the strengthening US dollar and rising American bond yields. Higher US yields can make dollar-denominated assets more attractive to investors, reducing demand for riskier emerging-market currencies such as the forint.

The US 10-year Treasury yield has risen towards 4.79%, while expectations of higher interest rates and increased demand for safe-haven assets have also supported the dollar.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Oil prices add to the pressure

Rising oil prices are another concern for Hungary, which relies heavily on energy imports.

Brent crude has climbed by almost 5% and moved above USD 95 a barrel amid renewed tensions in the Middle East. For an energy-importing country, more expensive oil can worsen both external-balance and inflation prospects, creating additional pressure on the national currency.

The combination of higher oil prices, a stronger dollar and rising US yields has therefore created an unfavourable environment for emerging-market currencies.

If you missed it: Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%

A sharp reversal after months of stability

The speed of the forint’s decline is particularly notable. The currency was trading near HUF 360 to the euro as recently as last week, meaning that the euro has become roughly HUF 10 more expensive in just a few days.

This move takes the forint back to levels not seen since before the April election, which shows how quickly international market developments can affect Hungary’s currency. Whether the forint can regain lost ground will depend in part on developments in energy markets, the Middle East and US interest-rate expectations in the coming days.

World.title: New battery industry plant could be coming to Debrecen despite earlier government denial
World.content:
A CATL subsidiary is seeking approval for a new battery repackaging and reassembly facility in Debrecen, months after Péter Szijjártó insisted that no new battery industry investment was planned for the city.

CATL subsidiary behind planned Debrecen facility

According to local news portal Debreciner, a new battery-related industrial facility could be built in Debrecen by GreenPower Energy Debrecen Kft., a Hungarian subsidiary of Chinese battery giant CATL, according to documents published by the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office.

An environmental impact assessment procedure for the project has been underway since 23 June, although the public was only informed about the procedure through a notice published on 31 August. A public hearing will also be held, with its date and details to be announced at a later stage.

The planned facility would be located in a 44,000-square-metre industrial hall built by state-owned Inpark in Debrecen’s southern economic zone. Inpark began constructing the hall last year but had previously declined to say what kind of industrial activity would take place there.

The facility would be the latest addition to Debrecen’s rapidly expanding battery industry, which already includes CATL’s major battery manufacturing project and a separate battery module assembly operation.

Former Foreign Minister Szijjártó previously denied another battery investment

The plans are particularly notable because they appear to contradict a categorical statement made earlier this year by then-Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó. At a press conference in Berettyóújfalu on 17 February, Szijjártó rejected claims that another previously unannounced battery-related investment was coming to Debrecen or elsewhere in Hajdú-Bihar County.

He had also accused Debreciner of spreading false information over reports about further battery industry developments in the area.

At the time, however, Inpark was already constructing the new industrial hall. When asked about its intended use in January, the state-owned company said only that it would provide modern industrial infrastructure for international companies and support economic growth in the region. It did not publicly disclose that the building could be used for battery-related activities.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

No cell manufacturing, but up to 85 tonnes of hazardous waste

The planned operation would not manufacture battery cells. According to the environmental documentation, GreenPower Energy would modify the packaging of battery cells, modules and packs, carry out module- and pack-level assembly operations, and manufacture and repair tools and equipment used on production lines.

The documentation stresses that the electrochemical operation of the batteries would not be altered at the facility. There would be no electrode manufacturing, electrolyte handling or battery cell production.

Nevertheless, the plant would generate substantial amounts of waste.

The facility is expected to produce around 2,000–2,200 tonnes of non-hazardous waste every year, largely consisting of paper, cardboard, plastic and wooden packaging materials, as well as metal waste and defective or rejected batteries.

It is also expected to generate 80–85 tonnes of hazardous waste annually. This would mainly include adhesive waste, packaging contaminated with hazardous substances, contaminated components and other technological residues. Battery waste would be handled by specialised waste management companies before being sent for final treatment.

If you missed it: Cause of poisoning at Debrecen battery plant revealed — but there is good news too

More than 100 lorries a day

The environmental documentation also estimates that the facility would generate significant additional traffic. The calculations take into account an expected daily increase of 124 articulated lorries, 52 cars and light commercial vehicles, and 12 buses.

While the increase would reportedly be moderate compared with existing traffic on major roads such as the M35 motorway and Routes 47 and 481, the impact would be considerably greater on roads directly serving the industrial site.

According to the assessment, heavy goods vehicle traffic on the Inpark access road and Hermann Konseder Street could roughly double. The project will now go through the environmental assessment process, including a public hearing, before the authorities make the relevant decisions.

World.title: Major shake-up in Budapest: Government bill would hand key city-centre spaces to the capital for free
World.content:
A new government bill submitted to Hungary’s Parliament on Tuesday would place several prominent public spaces in central Budapest, as well as a number of properties along the Danube in District 22, under the asset management of the Municipality of Budapest. The proposal would also re-establish the Budapest Public Development Council and set out a new framework for the future of the Planetarium.

The bill, submitted by Minister for Transport and Investment Dávid Vitézy, proposes amendments to legislation concerning the development and management of Budapest properties, as well as road transport. The full proposal is available on the Hungarian Parliament’s website.

Central Budapest squares could come under city management

Under the proposal, Vörösmarty Square, Podmaniczky Square, Széchenyi Square and József Attila Street in District 5 would be transferred free of charge to the asset management of the Municipality of Budapest for 99 years from 1 October.

The measure is justified on the grounds that it would allow the capital to carry out its public duties related to urban development more effectively.

The bill would also repeal a provision that previously entrusted the operation of Erzsébet Square in central Budapest to the District 5 municipality. Under the existing arrangement, contracts for the development and maintenance of green spaces and public areas could be concluded by the Hungarian National Asset Management Company (MNV) on behalf of the state.

According to Vitézy’s proposal, there is no longer a justification for maintaining the restriction concerning the conclusion of such contracts.

Have you heard? Cash refund for recycling bottles could soon disappear in Budapest

Danube-side properties also included

Several properties in District 22, located along the Danube, would likewise be placed under the asset management of the Municipality of Budapest. The government argues that this is justified because the capital is responsible for the urban planning regulations governing the city’s riverfront areas.

The bill would also transfer the asset management rights for the Planetarium property from the Society for the Dissemination of Scientific Knowledge to the Hungarian Museum of Science, Technology and Transport. The stated aim is to facilitate the future use and renovation of the Planetarium.

Changes would affect the City Park and Buda Castle district

The proposed amendments would also affect Budapest’s City Park (Városliget), where maintenance and investment responsibilities would be separated.

The minister responsible for state investments — currently Dávid Vitézy — would be authorised to decide by declaration who acts as the developer for a particular project. Depending on the decision, the developer could be the minister himself, a company wholly owned by the Hungarian state, or a budgetary body.

Hungary’s Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy. Photo: Facebook/Vitézy Dávid

The minister responsible for state investments would also be authorised to designate a state-owned company or budgetary body as the developer of ongoing projects in the Buda Castle district in order to ensure their completion.

Meanwhile, the bill would keep the House of Fates complex and its neighbouring plots within the state asset portfolio. The properties had previously been earmarked for free transfer to MTK Budapest as part of the planned Alfred Brüll House – Hungarian Jewish Heritage Park project.

If you missed it: Hungary’s new 2026 budget reveals a massive multi-billion-euro hole

Budapest Public Development Council to return

One of the most significant elements of the proposal is the re-establishment of the Budapest Public Development Council, which would serve as the coordinating and advisory body for development policy in the capital.

The council would have 10 members: five representing the government and five representing the Municipality of Budapest. Decisions would have to be made unanimously. The prime minister would serve as chairman, while the mayor of Budapest would be the co-chair. If the prime minister were unable to attend, a minister designated by him could act in his place.

Vitézy announced on Monday that the Budapest Public Development Council would be re-established. He argued that cooperation between the government and the capital was indispensable, adding that the new body would provide this cooperation with a new professional and political framework.

World.title: Hungary has plenty of people working. So why is its business environment lagging?
World.content:
Hungary has one of the highest employment rates in Europe, matching Germany at 81.1%, but its relatively weak performance in innovation and digitalisation has dragged it down to 22nd place overall in a new business environment ranking.

The 2026 Doing Business in Europe study by Leadfeeder ranks 29 European countries based on nine indicators covering labour productivity, employment, investment, innovation, knowledge-intensive employment and the adoption of technologies such as cloud computing, artificial intelligence and e-commerce.

Hungary ranks 22nd overall, despite recording the joint sixth-highest employment rate among the countries included in the study. Its 81.1% employment rate for people aged 20–64 puts it level with Germany and ahead of Austria, Ireland and Denmark.

The figures suggest that Hungary’s challenge is not primarily getting people into work, but making the economy more productive, innovative and digitally advanced.

Hungary’s strong employment rate

The Netherlands records the highest employment rate in the ranking, at 83.4%, followed by Czechia at 82.9%, Sweden at 81.8%, Estonia at 81.7% and Cyprus at 81.3%. Hungary and Germany share sixth place, both recording an employment rate of 81.1%. At the other end of the table, Türkiye has the lowest employment rate at 58.1%, followed by Bosnia and Herzegovina at 59.5%.

Leadfeeder’s analysis points to a clear distinction between employment and productivity. A large proportion of the working-age population may be employed without the economy necessarily generating correspondingly high output from that labour.

Norway, for example, has the highest labour productivity in the ranking, with a score of 123.0, but finishes sixth overall. Its employment rate is therefore not the only factor behind its strong performance.

If you missed it: Would you work in Hungary for this median salary? Half of the Hungarians earn even less

Investment offers little relief

Hungary performs somewhat better on gross fixed capital formation, ranking joint 16th, alongside Finland, with investment equivalent to 21.9% of GDP. However, the country’s weaker results in several other areas prevent this from translating into a strong overall ranking.

Hungary ranks 24th for innovation, while enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence stands at just 10.4%, placing the country 22nd. Its share of e-commerce orders is 21.3%, corresponding to 21st place.

Knowledge-intensive employment also remains relatively modest. Hungary and Slovenia are joint 14th, with 36.5% of employment classified as knowledge-intensive. Together, these figures point to a gap between the number of people working and the sophistication of the activities they perform.

Digitalisation closely linked to overall performance

The Leadfeeder study also found a strong relationship between digitalisation and countries’ overall positions in the ranking. Digitalisation rank has a correlation of 0.89 with the overall ranking, while investment rank has a much weaker correlation of just 0.14.

This suggests that simply investing more is not necessarily enough to create a stronger business environment. The ability of companies and economies to turn investment into productivity, innovation and digital capabilities appears to matter considerably more.

The contrast is visible elsewhere in the rankings. Germany, Europe’s largest economy, ranks fifth overall and records the highest number of patents per million people. Norway has the most productive workforce but finishes sixth, while Türkiye has the highest investment relative to GDP but ranks only 19th overall.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Sweden tops Europe’s business environment ranking

Sweden takes first place in Leadfeeder’s 2026 ranking, with an overall score of 74.8. Denmark comes second with 69.2, followed by the Netherlands with 64.6. Germany ranks fifth despite being the largest economy covered by the study.

According to Leadfeeder, Sweden’s success comes not from dominating the individual indicators but from maintaining consistently strong performance across them. It leads only one of the nine metrics, yet has the largest gap between itself and the next country in the top nine.

The study covers 29 European countries with complete data across all nine indicators. Eleven other countries — including Switzerland, Iceland, Luxembourg, Malta, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Ukraine and Kosovo — were excluded from the overall ranking because of missing data for one or more indicators.

Leadfeeder says differences of less than 0.1 points in the overall score should not be interpreted as meaningful separations. Several individual indicators also contain exact ties, including Hungary’s joint sixth-place position with Germany for employment and its joint 16th-place position with Finland for investment.

The full Doing Business in Europe: Where the Action Is in 2026 study is available from Leadfeeder.

World.title: Croatian restaurant sends Hungarian tourists away for ordering only pancakes
World.content:
A holiday dining experience on Croatia’s Krk Island has sparked a heated online debate after four Hungarian visitors were reportedly asked to leave a busy restaurant because they wanted to order only pancakes during dinner time.

Hungarian tourists ordered pancakes in Croatia, then they were told to leave

According to an account shared by the mother of one of the young men, the four friends waited around 10–15 minutes for a table at a popular, crowded restaurant. When the waiter arrived, each ordered a portion of pancakes costing EUR 7, meaning the group would have spent EUR 28 in total.

The waiter reportedly reacted angrily, questioning why they wanted only dessert during the dinner rush. With other customers waiting outside, he allegedly asked the group to give up their table and leave. The story quickly divided social media users.

Was the restaurant right to refuse them?

Some commenters condemned the waiter’s behaviour, arguing that EUR 28 for four portions of pancakes was hardly an insignificant amount and that customers should be free to decide what they want to order. Others defended the restaurant, pointing to the economics of a busy dinner service. A table for four occupied during peak hours could potentially generate considerably more revenue if the guests ordered full meals rather than dessert.

Several commenters also noted that similar situations can occur in other popular tourist destinations, including Hungary, Italy and Spain, where restaurants may discourage customers from occupying larger tables during peak periods if they intend to order only drinks, coffee or dessert. But does a restaurant in Croatia have the legal right to require customers to spend a minimum amount?

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

No general minimum-spending rule in Croatia

To clarify the legal position, the Hungarian representation of the Croatian National Tourist Board was contacted about the incident. Mira Horváth, a senior member of the organisation, explained that there is no general Croatian rule or code requiring every restaurant customer to spend a minimum amount, writes Blikk.

Restaurants must, however, clearly display their prices and terms of sale and comply with them. The Croatian National Tourist Board also stressed that it is primarily responsible for promoting and developing tourism rather than investigating individual complaints.

Customers who believe a restaurant has breached the rules can contact the Croatian State Inspectorate, which supervises hospitality and other establishments. They can also submit a complaint directly to the service provider, which is required to respond within the legally prescribed timeframe. The organisation expressed regret that the Hungarian visitors had such an experience and said it hoped the incident was an isolated case.

In case you missed it: Budapest taxi fares rise from today – airport pickups also become more expensive

Wider complaints about Croatian dining

The Krk incident comes amid wider online discussions among tourists about prices, food quality and service on Croatia’s Adriatic coast. Some travellers have complained about high-season prices in destinations such as Split, Dubrovnik and Hvar, while others have criticised inconsistent food quality and service.

Such individual experiences should not, however, be taken as representative of Croatian hospitality as a whole. Croatian tourism authorities have stressed their efforts to improve service standards, while the country has seen a growing number of Michelin-recognised restaurants.

For the four Hungarian visitors on Krk, the immediate issue was considerably simpler: they wanted four portions of pancakes during a busy dinner service. While the restaurant may have had commercial reasons for preferring customers ordering full meals, Croatian law does not impose a general minimum-spending requirement on restaurant guests.

Whether the restaurant handled the situation appropriately remains a matter of opinion — and one that has clearly divided diners online.
