World.title: Initiated by First VP Mehriban Aliyeva, wage reforms contribute to healthcare dev't - MP
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 2. The increase in salaries for doctors of various specialties, introduced on September 1 at the initiative of First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva and upon the instruction of President Ilham Aliyev, is another important step toward improving the compulsory health insurance system, which has been developing steadily for years, and enhancing the social welfare of healthcare workers, member of the Azerbaijani Parliament’s Health Committee, MP Soltan Mammadov told Trend.

According to Mammadov, the increases will contribute to the development of the compulsory health insurance system and help address a number of existing challenges in the sector by strengthening outpatient and primary healthcare services and emergency medical care, as well as introducing incentives to tackle the shortage of medical professionals in the regions.

The MP welcomed the comprehensive nature of the wage reform, which will cover 72,212 healthcare workers.

“The reforms cover a range of areas, including selected medical specialties, the quality of work performed, improvements to certain healthcare services and working conditions for doctors in the regions, as well as measures to attract qualified doctors to the regions. In line with the reforms, the annual payroll budget across the TABIB system has been increased by 189 million manat (around $111 million),” Mammadov said.

“Salary increases of 60, 70 and even up to 100% for certain doctors, particularly pediatric anesthesiologists and intensivists, neonatologists and hemodialysis specialists working in the regions, will help improve the quality of these services and provide additional incentives for doctors. At the same time, in regions facing shortages of doctors, excluding Baku, Absheron, Sumgayit and Ganja, a 1.3 coefficient will be applied to additional performance-based payments for surgical care, inpatient therapeutic care, physiotherapy and rehabilitation, anesthesia and interventional radiology services. This will help improve access to healthcare services,” the MP said.

Furthermore, Mammadov noted that the reforms will include corresponding salary increases for doctors working in emergency medical services. For example, doctors at the Republican Center for Emergency and Urgent Medical Care and emergency departments of medical centers are expected to receive a 61% salary increase.

The MP emphasized that the reforms also cover primary care physicians working in outpatient services, as well as head nurses and other mid-level and junior medical staff at several healthcare facilities. Monthly salaries for 36,041 mid-level healthcare workers will increase by 17%, while salaries for 20,367 junior healthcare workers will rise by 18%.

Mammadov added that the initiatives and decisions of President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva provide significant support for the development of the healthcare sector and complement the healthcare policies pursued by TABIB and the Ministry of Health, as well as the targeted reforms being implemented in the sector.

World.title: Dutch Embassy thanks Azerbaijan for rescuing injured national in Sheki
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 2. The Embassy of the Netherlands in Azerbaijan has thanked the Azerbaijani authorities for rescuing a Dutch national who was injured in Sheki.

This was reflected in a post published by the embassy on its X account.

“We express our gratitude to the relevant Azerbaijani authorities for the rescue and provision of emergency medical assistance to the Dutch national who was injured on August 29 while hiking in the mountainous area of Sheki.

In particular, we thank the State Border Service of the Republic of Azerbaijan for the emergency rescue operation carried out in challenging mountainous terrain and in darkness, the prompt evacuation by helicopter, and the provision of initial medical assistance at the scene,” the post said.

The embassy also expressed its appreciation for the medical assistance, professional approach and prompt intervention provided by Sheki District Central Hospital and Yeni Klinika in Baku.

“The swift and coordinated response of the relevant authorities during this incident made an important contribution to ensuring the safety of the Dutch national,” the embassy said.

On August 29, a Dutch national who sustained serious injuries after being attacked by dogs in a mountainous area near Bash Zayzid village in Azerbaijan’s Sheki district was rescued by State Border Service personnel. The injured person received initial medical assistance at the scene and was evacuated by helicopter to Sheki District Central Hospital, where they underwent emergency surgery.

The rescue operation was carried out at an altitude of 2,000 meters above sea level, in darkness and difficult mountainous terrain.

World.title: Robert Cekuta urges thorough, hard-headed review of UN programs and agencies
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 2. A thorough, hard-headed look at UN programs and agencies is needed, former U.S. ambassador to Azerbaijan Robert Cekuta told Trend.

The former ambassador emphasized that there is a strong sense around the world that the UN needs reform and needs it now.

“The problem is a lack of agreement on what exactly to tackle and how to do so. The United Nations has severe budgetary problems. Some countries want changes to the Security Council. There is also the reality that the UN is really subject to the will of its member countries, not the other way around. And there is the reality that countries enjoying certain roles and prerogatives today do not want to give them up,” he explained.

According to Cekuta, widespread recognition of the problems facing the UN and the multilateral system today, and the election of a new secretary-general, means there might be a chance for meaningful, concrete reforms/changes.

“But we have to be realistic in terms of what to expect and to what we can try to tackle.

With those thoughts in mind, I would suggest a thorough, hard-headed look at UN programs and agencies. Most, if not all, were created because members wanted them; but numerous experts complain there are often a number of agencies doing the same thing, that some are more efficient/effective than others, and that some may have outlived their usefulness. Secretaries-general themselves have said this. So, tackle this situation first,” he added.

The former U.S. ambassador believes it is necessary to show member countries measurable progress.

“Putting the UN’s financial situation in order could create the conditions for more extensive and far-reaching—and, most importantly, absolutely necessary—structural reforms,” he concluded.

During the “SCO Plus” meeting held on September 2 in Bishkek, the capital of the Kyrgyz Republic, the necessity of reforming the UN was widely discussed.

Speaking at the event, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev emphasized that the development of appropriate mechanisms is required for the swift implementation of UN Security Council resolutions.

“A little over a year ago, Azerbaijan and Armenia initialed the text of the peace agreement, putting an end to a 30-year conflict. Thus, the South Caucasus region, which was a long-standing conflict zone, is becoming a zone of peace.

Four resolutions adopted by the UN Security Council in 1993 were implemented three years ago, 30 years later. Azerbaijan is already supplying petroleum products to Armenia and providing transit for third-country cargo. Together with Armenia, we are working to increase the volume of mutual trade, expand the range of goods, and create new overland transport links. However, unfortunately, the UN played no role in the implementation of these resolutions. Azerbaijan entirely restored its sovereignty and territorial integrity on its own. The development of appropriate mechanisms is required for the swift implementation of UN Security Council resolutions. If implemented, this would serve to enhance the UN's prestige and the organization's role in conflict resolution,” the head of state said.

In addition, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov stated that existing shortcomings in the work of the United Nations should not serve as a pretext for weakening its role or bypassing the organization. According to him, on the contrary, they underscore the need to work together to strengthen the UN, enhance its effectiveness, and improve its mechanisms in line with contemporary realities.

“Kyrgyzstan supports the reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council. Such reform must be carried out through broad consensus,” Japarov said.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also emphasized the need to strengthen the organization and enhance its effectiveness, noting that the UN must remain the core of the international system, and its Charter—the universal foundation of international law. According to him, amid acute geopolitical tensions, it is particularly important to preserve and strengthen the UN’s central coordinating role.

Russian President Vladimir Putin also stated the need to improve the UN’s effectiveness, expand representation in its bodies—including the Security Council, to include countries from the Global South and East, and adapt the organization to fundamental changes in global politics and the economy.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was even more unequivocal: “Today, the UN is in dire need of reform. It must become more accountable and more responsive.”

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, for his part, has repeatedly spoken of the need for international institutions to adapt to modern realities.

"Our relationships are changing, but multilateral organizations still largely reflect the realities of 1945. We must reform our multilateral institutions, including the United Nations and the Bretton Woods system, so that they reflect today’s realities and increase the representation and influence of developing countries in order to build a just world order,” he said.

World.title: Iran accuses US of a 'war crime' after strikes kill people at wedding party
World.content:
Iranian authorities are accusing the United States of committing a "war crime" after people at a wedding party were killed by missile strikes.

Footage of ruined decorations, abandoned shoes and debris strewn on the ground circulated widely in Iran on Wednesday, local time, following a celebration that was turned "into a funeral" by strikes in the coastal town of Kuhestak along the Strait of Hormuz in southern Iran.

Iranian officials have since compared the incident to a strike on a girls' school that killed 160 people on the war's first night.

The strike hit on Tuesday night, local time, according to the Iranian Red Crescent, after the United States announced attacks against targets belonging to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

Authorities say this piece of a projectile was found at the site of the strike in Kuhestak, southern Iran. (Masoud Mohammadi/Tasnim News Agency via AP)

Iranian authorities said the strike killed at least four people, including a child, and wounded 68 others at the wedding.

Iranian Foreign Minister Esmaeil Baquaei described the attack on X as a "war crime" and vowed that: "Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness."

"Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished," Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, added on X.

Shortly after the strike, footage began circulating online showing debris and rubble at the wedding site, with people heard screaming as rescuers rushed to provide assistance.

US launches fresh strikes on Iran The US has launched a barrage of air strikes on Iranian targets, prompting Iranian retaliation and a warning it would "tighten the lock" on the Strait of Hormuz.

Another video showed colourful decorations on the ground and shoes apparently left behind in the chaos, with the man holding the camera picking up a white sandal with glittering straps and remarking sarcastically: "Another pair of military boots in this military base."

"You wicked people have attacked people's homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral," said the man in the video carried by Fars news agency.

In other footage, a state television reporter holds up a charred piece of metal he said was a fragment from "the American missile... that turned a wedding celebration into a tragedy".

The United States did not specify what it targeted in Kuhestak.

In a post on X, US Central Command said it was carrying out strikes against targets of Iran's Revolutionary Guards following their "recent attempted attacks … against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region".

A CENTCOM spokesman, when asked about reports of civilian casualties, insisted "the US military never targets civilians".

Iran has been at war since February 28, when the United States and Israel launched a surprise bombing campaign that killed its supreme leader.

An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment, but sporadic exchanges of fire have continued, particularly in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has virtually blocked since the start of the war.

The renewed exchanges have punctured a pause in hostilities between the US and Iran. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP)

'Still shaking'

Authorities in the southern province of Hormozgan said several "telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged" in the latest strikes, causing disruptions to communication networks in the area.

In Kuhestak, state television showed footage of a collapsed communications tower, with twisted metal debris spread across a street.

Some Iranian media outlets estimated the tower to be around 140 metres from the wedding site.

On Wednesday morning, the Red Crescent shared a video apparently filmed from above after daybreak, showing a hole in the roof of a house at the wedding site, with wreckage and rubble strewn across nearby alleyways.

In a separate video carried by state media, the father of the bride, Ali Mallahi, called it "a very saddening incident".

"I really don't know what to say. Thank God the casualties were not higher."

Loading...

Other footage carried by Iranian media showed wounded children lying in hospital beds.

One man, apparently suffering from a head injury and lying in a hospital bed, said he had been on his way to the wedding when he heard fighter jets overhead.

"As we arrived there, an explosion happened. It was really powerful, so powerful that even before I arrived there, pieces and debris from the building smashed into my head and face and I passed out," the unnamed man said in a video carried by local media.

"Lots of children and women were horribly injured. All the people were ordinary people," he added.

On Instagram, a woman with her hands covered in henna and wearing purple posted a video following the strike, saying: "My hands and feet are still shaking."

"May god have mercy," she said, adding in another post that the bride, the groom and all their immediate family were "safe".

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Armed gang raids security cars of gold in one of PNG's biggest robberies
World.content:
Police in Papua New Guinea are investigating what could be one of the biggest robberies in the country's history, after armed men held up a security convoy in Port Moresby and made off with 25 gold bars and $315,000 in cash.

Police Commissioner David Manning confirmed a major investigation was underway into the early morning hold-up on Wednesday, in which two private security vehicles were intercepted while transporting the bullion and cash through a city street.

"It is reported that at around 4:30 this morning two private security vehicles were intercepted by unknown vehicles in Port Moresby," Commissioner Manning said.

" Ten armed assailants held the security crews at gunpoint and proceeded to steal a quantity of gold and cash, as well as firearms. "

It is understood the stolen haul included 20 gold bars from the Porgera Gold Mine in Enga province, operated by mining company New Porgera Limited, along with five gold bars from Lae-based gold buying and exporting firm Golden Valley Enterprise Limited.

Also taken was a million kina ($315,000) in cash, along with a pump-action shotgun and a carbine belonging to the security crew.

A major investigation is underway into the hold-up in Port Moresby. (Supplied)

It is unclear how heavy the gold bars were, or how pure the gold was, but a standard retail gold bar weighing 1 kilogram usually sells for about $200,000.

A larger brick, like the gold held in central bank reserves, weighs about 12.4kg and is worth more than $2 million.

While the estimated value and weight of the 25 stolen gold bars are yet to be confirmed, a senior police source has described this week's theft as one of the biggest robberies in the country's history in terms of the value of gold stolen and is likely worth millions.

Convoy ambushed in staged road block

According to a timeline of events provided to police, the two cash-in-transit vehicles pulled out from their security base shortly after 4:30am and headed for Papua New Guinea's International Airport via the Poreporena Freeway.

As the vehicles approached a roundabout, they encountered what appeared to be a staged roadblock.

The driver of the lead vehicle opened the door to ask to pass, but was held at gunpoint before three more vehicles pulled up behind the convoy, blocking their exit.

Close to 10 armed men, some allegedly carrying military-style rifles, are reported to have forced the security crews from both vehicles at gunpoint before making off with the gold, cash and firearms.

No shots were fired and no injuries were reported.

Police Commissioner David Manning says a major investigation is underway. (Facebook: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary)

Commissioner Manning said early indications suggested shortcomings in how the transport had been handled.

"Police had not been alerted to the movement prior to it taking place," he said.

"There are a number of witnesses that are being interviewed, including the private security crews, as well as management and workers from the firm.

" This is a very serious incident. Early indications are that the movement of these valuables by the security company leave a lot to be desired in terms of how the private operation was conducted. "

Police sources said there were further concerns about the security arrangements around the transport, including how alarm and response procedures were handled.

It is understood at least four people are currently being questioned by an investigative team, as police work to identify those involved and recover the stolen gold and cash.

Echoes of the Kapris era

Kapris killed PNG's most notorious criminal, William Kapris, killed in a shoot-out with PNG police.

Police Deputy Commissioner of Specialist Operations Donald Yamasombi, who is overseeing the investigation, said the robbery was one of the biggest since the days of notorious criminal figure William Kapris.

Kapris was linked to a 2007 armed robbery in which thieves stole K78,000 ($25,000) in cash and gold bars worth more than K2 million ($630,00) from a Port Moresby refining operation.

He was later shot and killed by police in 2013, after spending months on the run following his escape from Bomana maximum-security prison.

World.title: Queensland Police receive safety notices over watch house conditions
World.content:
Queensland's work safety watchdog has issued multiple regulatory notices to the state's police service after undertaking a compliance blitz on watch houses, the ABC can reveal.

The Queensland Police Union (QPU) lodged a formal complaint with Workplace Health and Safety (WPHS) in March, citing severe overcrowding and unsafe staffing levels inside watch houses.

A police source told the ABC that inspections were undertaken at Brisbane and regional watch houses, including those in Caloundra and Caboolture.

The QPU has also confirmed that site visits were conducted at Ipswich, Cleveland, Southport and Beenleigh.

QPU president Shane Prior said he had been advised that several notices had been issued for the Brisbane watch house regarding chemical storage and building maintenance deficiencies.

Shane Prior says officers in watch houses are facing "disgusting" conditions. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Caloundra and Caboolture each received five improvement notices, according to Mr Prior.

In Caboolture, one of the notices related to there being no sexual harassment prevention plan, according to Mr Prior.

The notices are not fines but written directions requiring the Queensland Police Service (QPS) to fix a workplace health and safety problem.

In its complaint to WPHS, the union also reported extended detention of adults for 21 days and young people for up to 30 days, and hygiene failures at aging and underfunded facilities.

Other reported concerns by the union included unreliable CCTV, poor ventilation, mould, and insufficient personal protective equipment.

The union told the regulator that despite multiple reviews into Queensland watch houses, key risks remained unaddressed.

Do you know more? Contact regional Queensland investigations reporter Eden Gillespie at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au

at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au If your information is sensitive, you can also reach her at eden.gillespie96@proton.me

Mr Prior told the ABC a few months ago that overcrowding in regional watch houses was of particular concern, with prisoners sleeping on floors, in exercise yards, or in makeshift overflow areas.

"Frankly, the working conditions that our people turn up to every day to do their job are disgusting," he said at the time.

Mr Prior described conditions as a "ticking time bomb".

"I fear more police will be seriously hurt or a person in custody may lose their life," he said.

The police union is concerned overcrowded watch houses pose a risk to officers and prisoners. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

WPHS did not answer questions about how many watch houses were inspected or how many notices were issued due to legal restrictions.

A spokesperson from WPHS told the ABC they had "recently undertaken a program of site visits to QPS watch houses throughout the state".

"As a result of this compliance program, a number of regulatory notices have been issued; however, no fines were issued," the spokesperson said.

"WPHS continues to monitor compliance with these notices and undertake ongoing regulatory oversight of the relevant workplaces."

The QPS did not directly answer questions about the notices issued by WPHS.

The police union says watch houses have been so crowded that prisoners have been forced to sleep on mattresses on the floor. (Supplied: Queensland Police Union)

A QPS spokesperson said the service remained "focused on delivering custody operations that support community safety and is committed to the training, safety and wellbeing of members performing duties in watch houses across the state".

"The QPS continues to progress all 34 recommendations arising from the QPS Watchhouse Review, with a focus on delivering sustainable improvements across all watch houses."

The ABC has contacted the police minister for comment.

World.title: Albanese bristles at pre-COP questions as UN delivers sobering report
World.content:
The prime minister has defended the number of leaders attending a high-profile climate meeting in the Pacific Islands, as a United Nations report warns the world will breach the 1.5C global warming benchmark within the next five years.

The federal government had initially wanted world leaders to attend pre-COP next month, ahead of the main climate talks in Türkiye in November.

Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting the lead-up event as part of a compromise, after Australia's failed bid to host COP31, the world's largest annual climate summit.

There had been reports Australia was struggling to convince leaders outside the Pacific to attend a special meeting in Tuvalu, before Fiji's foreign minister, Sakiasi Ditoka, gave the first public account of those going.

He said Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, Thailand, Maldives and Timor-Leste had so far agreed to send leaders to the event, and Germany, Mexico and South Korea will send ministers.

Anthony Albanese speaks at a presser at the 2026 Pacific Island Forum today. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

When questioned about attendance at the pre-COP while speaking to media at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, Anthony Albanese said the government had always anticipated that a pre-COP event would not attract the same level of patronage as COP itself.

"The fact that the pre-COP is being held in Fiji with a side trip to Tuvalu as well is something that is really welcomed because what it will do is provide a focus on what is happening in the Pacific.

" The entry fee for credibility at the Pacific Islands Forum and for bilateral engagement in the Pacific is taking climate change seriously. "

The prime minister also voiced his displeasure with the line of questioning.

"You are being so disrespectful to the Pacific leaders who are here," he said.

"We need to actually have some respect for the process and respect for our Pacific leaders, and Australia has an absolute interest in engaging with the Pacific."

The government pitched pre-COP as an opportunity to show leaders the perils that climate change poses to low-lying island nations in the Pacific, and to drive greater global action on climate change.

An ocean sand barrier on the reef island of Nanumanga, only 3 square kilometres in size, with a population of less than 400. (ABC)

However, the nations sending leaders are hardly major polluters, nor do they need reminding of the risks climate change poses to vulnerable countries.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said pre-COP was a "key opportunity" for the Pacific.

"The Pacific said to us, 'We thought it would be good to invite some leaders.' We've done that," he said.

"There's a very small component in Tuvalu, which is a small country, with limited capacity to host people.

"But that will be important in terms of not only prime ministers, heads of multilateral development banks, cabinet ministers who often don't attend pre-COP either but are coming to this one."

'Every fraction of a degree counts'

The growing climate risks confronting Pacific nations have been underscored by a landmark UN report, which has warned the world will likely pass 1.5C global warming in 2030.

It found that a temperature rise peak of 1.8C above pre-industrial levels was now the best-case scenario and highlights what can be done to return to 1.5C after the overshoot.

Climate change demonstrators hold placards during a march in London. (Reuters: Simon Dawson)

Countries have been trying to keep global temperatures to well below 2C as part of the Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty on climate change.

That includes an agreement to "pursue efforts" to limit warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial times.

That target was chosen because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) indicates that crossing that threshold risks unleashing far more severe climate change impacts.

Climate Change Authority chair Matt Kean said urgent climate action remained necessary, despite the likelihood that the 1.5C target would be exceeded.

"Every fraction of a degree that we can limit global warming will reduce the danger and reduce the cost," he said.

"There is a huge reason for Australia and indeed the rest of the world to limit global warming; the economic consequences will be dire if we don't, and the danger to lives and livelihoods will be severe if we don't.

"So the message is very clear: we need to speed up the pace at which we're reducing our emissions."

Matt Kean currently serves as the chair of the Climate Change Authority. (ABC News: Harriet Tatham)

Malte Meinshausen, professor of Climate Science at the University of Melbourne, said the energy transition means some of the worst scenarios that were possible a few years ago are no longer likely.

Climate scientist caught up in Europe's 'dystopian' summer Stefan Rahmstorf was holidaying in southern France when he came face to face with the climate future he has tried to fight.

But he added that failure to reduce global emissions quickly meant the ideal scenario of limiting warming to just above 1.5C was no longer available.

"Compared with our options five years ago, the new paths are more costly, come with more floods, fires and droughts and the need to draw, at some point, carbon emissions out of the atmosphere that we are currently emitting," Professor Meinshausen said.

" Acting now is still the cheaper option than not acting now, as we can still achieve 1.5C in the longer term. "

Calls for Australia to do more

Speaking at the Pacific Islands Forum, Vanuatu's Climate Change Adaptation and Energy Minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said Australia was not doing enough to curb carbon emissions.

"Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels; we all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis," he said.

"The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that. You need to stop expansion, and you need to start transitioning away."

Vanuatu's climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, has criticised Australia's continued fossil fuel exploration. (Supplied)

The comments come a day after Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King helped open a project that will feed gas fracked from the Beetaloo Basin into the Northern Territory's power grid.

Mr Albanese defended Australia's approach to the energy transition, saying the country was "highly regarded" when it comes to climate change.

"The Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we've taken, and they also understand […] because they're dealing with it as well, that the transition can't happen overnight.

"It requires strategies and policies to be put in place, and one of the things that renewables require is firming capacity, and gas has a role to play in firming capacity."

World.title: Ciraldo calls out NRL over delayed rule-change communication
World.content:
Cameron Ciraldo wants rule changes for 2027 to be communicated to clubs well in advance of the season's start date as Canterbury prepares to become the latest crash-test dummies in trials for the NRL's kick-off experiment.

With the Bulldogs and Thursday's opponents Brisbane both out of finals contention, the NRL has again opted to stress-test changes to the kick-off rules, where teams conceding a try can opt to kick or receive from the restart.

The concept was widely panned by players in Melbourne's win over Brisbane, and Ciraldo claimed on Wednesday he only learned his team would be guinea pigs in their regular-season game via email.

Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story It's been a long time since Damien Cook was known merely as a beach sprint champion, but ahead of the champion hooker's final NRL game, all the old stories are being told one last time.

Ciraldo would have a right to feel aggrieved by the NRL's constant tinkering, given his side were firmly entrenched in the top four last year.

The Dogs slipped back in the pack when the NRL changed the six-again threshold from the 40-metre line to the 20-metre mark weeks out from the season starting.

Canterbury has righted the ship since officials have eased off on calling six-agains.

And while Ciraldo won't solely attribute his club's early-season form slump to the changes, he would prefer clearer communication so clubs can plan their conditioning and roster management accordingly.

"If you look at our form at the start of the year you can blame that, but I think there's a lot of factors that went into our results at the start of the year," Ciraldo said.

"We'll look to address those over the next few weeks.

The Bulldogs have corrected their form of late after referees eased off on the six-again calls. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

"As the rules came back to what they were last year, we sort of found our rhythm a little bit more, and were able to get back to our style of footy.

"I think it coincides with a number of other things as well.

"I think everyone would like to know what the rule changes are to start the pre-season and not find out about them during the trial period."

Ciraldo said Canterbury had little time to put the trialled kick-off interpretations into practice this week.

"I don't check my emails that often, so someone had to tell me," Ciraldo said.

Canterbury's clash with Brisbane will be the last for Bronson Xerri (Melbourne) and Josh Curran (Perth) before they move on to new clubs in 2027.

Ciraldo paid tribute to the pair for being key parts of the Dogs' revival, and confirmed Sean O'Sullivan had agreed to a contract at Belmore for 2027, despite interest from the Super League.

World.title: Boy, 14, charged over alleged rock attack that left man unconscious
World.content:
A 14-year-old boy has been charged with assault after a man was seriously injured and left convulsing on the ground in an alleged rock throwing attack in a fast food restaurant car park.

WARNING: This story contains a video and images some people may find distressing.

Police say an altercation took place on Monday afternoon between a group of juveniles and a 25-year-old man outside a Hungry Jacks in the Mandurah suburb of Falcon, south of Perth.

During the incident, the man allegedly had rocks thrown at him, before the 14-year-old allegedly threw a rock that caused him to fall face first on the bitumen, leaving him unconscious.

Police said the man and the group of children did not know each other.

Loading...

The incident was filmed and posted on social media, with at least six juveniles seen crowding around the man in a car park with some filming on their phones.

The ABC has blurred the identities of the people in the video for legal reasons.

Man stepped in to help: police

Mandurah acting senior sergeant Jamie Raper said the footage was very confronting.

"It's very horrific ... and obviously we can understand why the community is quite upset about that," Sgt Raper said.

"We believe there might have been an altercation earlier in the restaurant where the juveniles were potentially harassing the workers there and we believe this male has stepped in to protect those workers.

"We don't encourage people to step into these incidents … we don't want members of the community hurt, we'd prefer if they do step back and call Triple Zero."

The man had a seizure after being knocked unconscious. (Supplied)

The 25-year-old man was taken to Peel Health Campus with severe facial injuries and has since been released.

Sgt Raper said he will require ongoing medical treatment with a long road to recovery ahead.

Police have since arrested and charged a 14-year-old boy with assault occasioning bodily harm and he will appear in court later this month.

Sgt Raper said police knew the identities of others in the group, and were investigating further.

World.title: Darwin hospital opens new ward with hopes of easing capacity pressures
World.content:
A new multi-purpose ward at the Royal Darwin Hospital (RDH) has received its first patients this week, with hopes the additional beds will ease months — if not years — of intense staffing and capacity pressures.

Construction of Ward 1C was announced by the former Territory Labor government in 2023, with the $23.95 million investment designed to address the high patient demand and overcrowding that has persisted at the ageing hospital.

NT Health Minister Steve Edgington said 13 patients were now receiving care at the new ward, and the government expected all of its 32 beds would be available to staff and patients by the end of this month.

The new ward means an additional 32 beds are now available for patients at RDH. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

"Very soon we'll be opening up the 24-bed mental health facility as well, so, with 24 beds at the mental health [ward], 32 beds here, we are expecting that to ease the overall pressure throughout the hospital," he said.

In a statement, an NT government spokesperson said the new facility had been designed as a "multi-purpose ward to care for bariatric, renal and general medical patients".

They said the ward's "flexible" design would allow for "cardiac monitoring, additional isolation capacity, bariatric accommodation, and additional space for patients experiencing cognitive impairment".

Patients started receiving care in the new RDH ward this week. (Supplied: NT government)

The opening of the new ward comes after six code yellows — when extraordinary levels of patient demand lead to emergency procedures being put in place — have been called at the Darwin and Palmerston hospitals since January.

NT Health issues urgent call-out for more hospital staff NT Health has issued an urgent call-out for qualified health workers to take up short-term roles at the Darwin and Palmerston hospitals.

The most recent lasted for weeks in July through to August, and was described by the NT's nursing and midwifery union as "the worst one we've ever had".

The emergency prompted NT Health's acting chief executive Susan Bowden to issue a call-out for almost 60 qualified non-frontline workers to return to the hospital floor to relieve exhausted staff.

Today, Ms Bowden said she was "really happy" to share that more than 30 staff had taken up the call.

"We were listening to particularly the nurse's federation, that there was pressure on the staff," she said.

"We wanted to make sure that they had the opportunity to have a break during that very busy time, so [we're] very appreciative of those who put their hand up."

Federal funding to be used as 'efficiently as possible'

In July this year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a Commonwealth investment of $10 million to improve facilities at RDH's maternity ward.

Hopes of new NT hospital dashed Anthony Albanese has dashed hopes of federal funding for a new hospital in Darwin.

He said the federally funded upgrades would include refurbishment of the ward's birthing suites and installation of a nursery, a lactation room and a new bereavement room.

"We are planning and ensuring that we're ready to go and ready to commence the works as soon as possible after we receive that money," Mr Edgington said.

With the NT government's original request for $35 million federal funding knocked back, Mr Edgington said the $10 million would be used as "efficiently as possible" but that some of the upgrades needed to RDH maternity services may be jettisoned.

"We want to get as much coverage as possible; there may be some things that can't be covered, but we'll look at how we manage those moving forward," he said.

"That scope of works is being looked at at the moment, being prepared so that we can go to tender ASAP."

The NT government says the new multi-purpose facility will help ease capacity pressures at RDH. (ABC News: Oliver Chaseling)

The minister also addressed the findings of a recent scathing parliamentary report into the Acacia patient record system, which examined the project's ever-growing cost to taxpayers and claims of a "toxic" workplace culture within the NT Department of Corporate and Digital Development and made 11 recommendations.

"Bullying is totally unacceptable. We want to ensure that there's a safe place for every employee in NT Health, and we'll consider all of those recommendations further," he said.

World.title: Victorian man defrauds women of more than $45,000 after meeting them online
World.content:
An unemployed Gippsland man who pretended to have been injured at a job he did not have will be sentenced next month after defrauding four women and taking money from three of them.

Stephen James Cross met the women online and began relationships with them under the alias Jimmy Smith between September 2021 and November 2023.

The 43-year-old pretended to be a landscaper and made up stories about injuries, his mother being unwell and his bank accounts being hacked.

He also lied about owning properties in Inverloch and Warragul, in Victoria's east, even taking a woman to an open house and saying he hoped they would live there with their children.

Cross previously pleaded guilty in the Latrobe Valley Magistrates' Court to multiple charges relating to obtaining property by deception and attempting to obtain property by deception.

The court heard Cross met the women through the online dating apps Zoosk and Hinge.

Stephen Cross used online dating apps like Zoosk to meet women. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

'He did not tell me the truth'

In her victim impact statement, one woman told the court she felt sick thinking about their time together and recalled watching the show The Tinder Swindler with Cross one night.

"One memory that continues to haunt me is when we sat together watching The Tinder Swindler," she said.

"I remember us talking about how disgusting the behaviour of that man was, how someone could manipulate people, gain their trust and take advantage of their kindness, generosity and love.

"I remember sitting behind him on the couch listening to him condemn that behaviour and agreeing with him.

"That night I went to sleep beside him completely unaware that I was sharing my life with someone who was capable of deceiving me in similar ways."

She was in a relationship with him for 22 months.

Stephen Cross sat in the front row of Latrobe Valley Magistrates' Court to listen to the impact statements of his victims. (ABC News: Rachael Lucas)

At one point, Cross stopped contacting the woman for three months, the court heard.

She was fearful something had happened to him.

Instead, he was in prison related to other, similar matters.

"I spent a great deal of time trying to understand what had happened and why I heard nothing from him," she said.

"When he eventually returned, he did not tell me the truth.

"Instead, he told me he'd been staying on a friend's farm in western Victoria."

The woman had allowed Cross to move into her house, and was in a relationship with him between January 2022 and November 2023.

Between January 2021 and November 2023, Cross was also in a relationship with another woman, from whom he took $45,000.

At one point, Cross asked her for $16,000, saying he was in hospital with appendix issues, the court heard.

She refinanced her mortgage to give him the money.

On another occasion, he asked for $3,000 and met her in Warragul to collect the cash.

"At this time, [the victim] observed the accused wearing a moon boot," prosecutor First Constable Lisa Gray told the court.

"The accused told her that he had dropped a concrete sleeper on his foot at work."

In September 2023, he told her he had been in a car accident and needed $54,000, but she did not give it to him.

Stephen Cross appeared in the Latrobe Valley Magistrates' Court. (ABC News: Nicole Chvastek)

Beachside bluff

Cross's third victim began dating him on the app, Hinge.

In January 2023, he took her to a house in Inverloch worth $1.6 million and told her he hoped they could move in together, with their children.

First Constable Gray told the court he did so to make himself look rich.

"At this time the accused did not have the financial means to purchase this property and used this as a tactic to portray a false financial status to [the victim]," First Constable Gray said.

Cross also asked her for money for fabricated situations.

"Each time he told me one of these stories, I felt genuine fear, worry and responsibility," she said in her victim impact statement.

"And I tried to help him because I believed he was experiencing real emergencies."

The victim chose to move house, fearing he would return.

"I trusted the image he created, and because of that trust I allowed him into my home and into my children's lives," she said.

"Learning later that this information was not true deeply affected me and my relationship with my children.

"The offender became part of our daily lives, and I believed he was someone safe to have around my family."

While his fourth victim did not loan or give him money, Cross communicated with her under a false identity and told her he had a beach house at Inverloch, the court heard.

He regularly told her he needed money for different scenarios, sending her messages and then pretending they were for someone else.

She found out about his real identity after a post about him on social media and reported her dealings with him to police.

Cross's defence lawyer John Brancarto told the court his client accepted he would be imprisoned and wished to begin pre-sentence detention.

"It's accepted that what's aggravating, particularly with regard to that, not only is it the same or similar prior, but this offending occurs really either side of that term of imprisonment as well," he told the court.

"Something that occurs prior to going into custody and then he serves three months and shortly after being released from custody falls into it and does exactly the same thing against these four vulnerable victims."

Cross was remanded in custody and will face court again in October.

World.title: Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTiger Woods Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case Daniel Kozin Updated September 3, 2026 — 1:00am ,first published 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge and his driver’s licence was suspended for five years on Wednesday following a rollover crash in March in Florida, where he initially was accused of driving under the influence (DUI). Before the hearing in Marin County began, Woods, 50, sat at the defence table looking back at the mostly empty courtroom gallery. He said little as he agreed to the reduced charge. Tiger Woods arrives at court in Florida with girlfriend Vanessa Trump. AP Photo/Lynne Sladky He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, US President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law, and she sat behind him during the proceedings. Woods, still one of golf’s most influential figures and as recognisable as any athlete in the world, has had a remarkable fall since winning the 2019 Masters for his 15th major. His career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.



Woods in court on Wednesday. Crystal Vander Weit/Treasure Coast Newspapers via AP He was arrested in March after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road near his home on Jupiter Island. A sheriff’s report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyser test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test. He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge. Tiger Woods strapped into a patrol car after his arrest. AP The prosecutor in the case said two toxicologists found there was insufficient proof of his impairment and determined Woods had built up a “pharmacological” tolerance.



Thomas Bakkedahl, a state attorney, defended his decision to accept the plea, saying, “I did what I think is right.” Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters. He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing after the crash and was fined $US1500 ($2092), according to court documents. “If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would immediately go back to jail,” Judge Darren Steele told Woods. Woods’ overturned vehicle on Jupiter Island, Florida. AP Woods’ attorney did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.



A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. Related Article Updated

Tiger Woods Tiger Woods arrested on suspicion of DUI after crash Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials. But his Land Rover caused $US5000 ($7000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck. Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years. He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play. He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.



Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour’s plans to revamp its schedule for 2028. Woods remained as chairman of the tour’s Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance. World.title: Spag bol vs the state
World.content:
“Jonty Grinter comments that it was difficult to get 3¢ change for spaghetti bolognaise at the Rocks Push (C8),” notes Karin Viles of Annandale. “The price was deliberate as most people opted to leave it as a tip to the person serving. Bruce Viles would later be taken to court at the time as the spaghetti, according to the licensing police, was not a “proper meal”. A prominent barrister defended the case pro-bono, the case was won and there were long queues from then on for this cheap meal.”

With all these missives regarding hospitality governance making things difficult for the punter, it’s gratifying to see a bit of country town goodwill, like that experienced by John Brown of Kianga: “In 1987 we stayed at the Black Stump Hotel Trunkey Creek. Four of us, including a non-drinker, drank them out of red wine (two bottles). Asking for port, the reply was ‘do you want 5s or 7s (ounces)?’ followed by ‘Could you scrape your plates into the dog’s bowl?’ We had a great stay – memorable – including an invitation to the 21st birthday party in the hall across the road. Very fond memories.”

Jim Dewar of Davistown reports that “No records were ratified at the World Humanoid Robot Games (C8) because of the suspicion that all times were wand assisted.”

“After watching much of the often incredulous testimony during the ICAC live stream (C8), I decided an appropriate description for the contagion brought into the witness stand is Dumbentia,” advises Lionel Latoszek of Long Jetty.

“If we were to open up a museum for idiot ideas that came from simple fools, would Pauline’s recent net zero coffin displace Scotty from Marketing’s lump of coal as the best exhibit?” enquires Toby Waters of Emerald Beach.

World.title: PNG halt Hudson pursuit after NRL’s decisive call on $3.3m offer
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 PNG halt Hudson pursuit after NRL’s decisive call on $3.3m offer Dan Walsh September 2, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The PNG Chiefs have paused their pursuit of Raiders and NSW Origin star Hudson Young based on concerns that matching Canberra’s record $1.1 million-a-year offer and the NRL’s market valuation would warp their salary cap. Young has become the unwitting poster boy for recent angst among rival clubs around the Chiefs’ market power when he left the Raiders three-year, $3.3 million offer – the largest per annum in club history – on the table last month to explore interest from PNG. Loading Looking to bring the situation to a head, Canberra CEO Don Furner granted Young permission to negotiate with PNG before he comes off contract on November 1 and also tour the incoming club’s Port Moresby facilities later this month. Furner also followed up this masthead’s reporting with the NRL salary cap auditor that PNG must register any contract at what head office deems to be the player’s market value. That notion was reiterated by ARL Commission chair Peter V’landys in a fortnightly CEOs hook-up on Wednesday, without referencing Young specifically.



Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the delicate nature of negotiations have said that Canberra’s $1.1 million-a-year offer could prove insurmountable for the Chiefs, given they have budgeted to carry at most, a salary of $950,000 for Young. The club has been told that figure is unlikely to be registered by the NRL’s salary cap auditor. Hudson Young’s PNG talks are on ice. Getty Images While Young is undoubtedly among the top few back-rowers in the NRL, clubs are yet to be provided with a new benchmarking document, which is used to help clubs ascertain player values based on market values. The last available document from 2025 calculated the average wage of the top five highest paid second-rowers to be $887,635. Manly’s Haumole Olakau’atu and North Queensland’s Jeremiah Nanai featured in that quintet, as did David Fifita, who took a hefty pay cut when he moved from the Titans to South Sydney late last year.



PNG’s tax-free wages and lucrative third-party earning opportunities offer a significant advantage in the market, prompting concerns across the game, particularly compared to the signing struggles of the Perth Bears, who begin their first pre-season in less than two months. PNG has a rookie coach and general manager of football in Willie Peters and Michael Chammas, a former reporter at this masthead, shaping their roster, alongside recruitment chief and ex-player manager Liam Ayoub, and Chiefs officials are mindful of the club being used to drive player prices up, be it by player agents or rival clubs. The Raiders have tabled Hudson Young the richest deal in the club’s history. Getty Images PNG splashed out $1.2 million on inaugural signing Jarome Luai, and have since added Alex Johnston, Zac Lomax, Joey Manu, Brian To’o, Connor Watson and Matty Lees to their 2028 roster. While the salary cap for that season is predicted to rise to around $15 million, PNG have negotiated each of their seven contracts so far without the ratchet deals that are widespread across the NRL. Young’s three-year offer from Canberra did not include a ratchet clause, either.



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL considers introducing AFL-style wildcard finals weekend The NSW back-rower had been due to visit PNG next month, and Chiefs officials had been quietly confident of landing their key forward target given every player who has toured the country has subsequently signed. As it stands from the Chiefs perspective, all talks will be paused until November 1, when Young enters regular free agency. Speaking at the Blues awards night on Monday, the 28-year-old said ”I have no interest in playing for another NRL club, and [coach] Ricky [Stuart] and I have spoken about that. “It’s more just the opportunity, with the PNG thing, and he’s been open and I’ve been transparent with him on how I feel and what I want to do”.

World.title: CCTV captures second possible mistaken identity killing in Sydney in as many days
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime CCTV captures second possible mistaken identity killing in Sydney in as many days Riley Walter and Jack Gramenz Updated September 2, 2026 — 8:14pm ,first published 4:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has been shot dead in the doorway of a western Sydney home with two children inside in what police are treating as the second mistaken-identity shooting in the city in as many days. The man, believed to have been aged in his 40s, was killed at the duplex in Merrylands West a day after university student Marco Tapia was shot dead inside his family’s home in what detectives believe was a botched targeted assassination. CCTV footage appears to show the sedan stopping outside the house before shots are fired from the back passenger window. SCN WorldStar Wednesday’s brazen shooting, believed to be linked to organised crime, marks the most significant escalation in Sydney’s ongoing gangland conflicts in several years and has alarmed senior police. “It’s very early on in the investigation, however, tragically, that is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders,” Detective Superintendent Simon Glasser said.



Police are reviewing CCTV footage of a grey Audi sedan in the area at the time of the shooting. Video posted by social media channel SCN Worldstar on Wednesday night appears to show the sedan stopping outside the house before shots are fired from the back passenger window. The footage seems to have been captured by a security camera at the front yard of the property where the man was shot. Officers at the scene of a deadly shooting in Sydney’s west. Wolter Peeters Glasser said the owners of the home in Bruce Street were known to police and linked to organised crime. The victim did not live at the property, but had arrived there with a resident and two children moments before he was shot about 3.15pm. “The victim has no links to organised crime that we are aware of; however, he is associated with people that reside at this address,” Glasser said.

World.title: Where are all the music teachers? Industry warned of soft skills crisis
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAustralian music Where are all the music teachers? Industry warned of soft skills crisis Nick Dent September 2, 2026 — 8:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Music educator Ricky Kradolfer recalls ending a primary school lesson and strumming his guitar while the next class of students filed into the room. A young boy from the new group looked like he wanted to sing along, so Kradolfer gave him the microphone and kept playing. “He started kind of rapping, but I could tell the words weren’t fully formed, but he was trying to find melody and flow. And then the principal came in and started crying and then she was getting out her iPhone and filming,” Kradolfer said. Amplify co-founder Natalie Kradolfer with Sasha McLeod (Sycco), Ian Haug (Powderfinger) and Sam Cromack (Ball Park Music). Simone Gorman Clark “And then we finished and all the kids were super excited and I was like, ‘what was all that about?’ And the principal said, ‘that student’s non-verbal.’” Kradolfer’s story illustrates some of the less quantifiable but invaluable impacts of music in classrooms.



He is the co-founder of Amplify Music Education, a provider of arts education software currently used in more than 1000 Australian schools that helps non-music teachers deliver quality music lessons. Amplify is one of the sponsorship partners of Brisbane’s annual music industry conference Bigsound, helping launch its education stream. Sessions bring together researchers, consultants and curriculum experts as well as Australian music stars such as Sam Cromack (Ball Park Music), Ian Haug (Powderfinger) and Sasha McLeod (Sycco). Bigsound is both a festival and a conference, and celebrates its 25th anniversary in 2026. Morgan Roberts The main topic of conversation was the same as Amplify’s reason for existing: the shortage of classroom music teachers.



Sydney-based Kradolfer and his wife Natalie started the business when he was facing burnout while teaching at five different schools a week. Making the hard decision to drop one, he asked the school what it would do to replace him, and was told: “Nothing. We won’t be able to find another teacher”. University of Melbourne professor of education futures, Glenn Savage, says he sees this happening at schools across the country. “At a school I visited very recently in Western Australia, they had a fantastic music program, a fantastic music teacher, a fantastic choir. And 18 months ago, that teacher left. They have no music program now, it’s just stopped.” Jane Polley, who heads the arts curriculums at the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (ACARA), said the Australian curriculum explicitly states students need to be experiencing the arts, but it can be difficult to deliver in practice. “Where it breaks down is in systems: rural and regional areas find it very difficult to run arts programs. One person might leave, it takes a lot of expertise and training to be done really well, or it can happen that arts education is done poorly and that has real ramifications down the line.”



The conversation is taking place as Queensland’s system for scaling subjects comes under scrutiny, with educators warning the current system is accelerating a decline in enrolments for creative arts subjects. Related Article University ‘ATARmaxxing’: The school trend experts say is quashing the creative sector Savage said the lack of value placed on music is at odds with a world rapidly being reshaped by AI. “The OECD traditionally has said schools are primarily for making young people job-ready, and it’s why we have things like NAPLAN,” he said. “They are now admitting their own logic is flawed, and they’ve come up with a very bold idea: we need to refocus the purpose of schooling around the idea of ‘human flourishing’.”



The OECD’s Education for Human Flourishing plan emphasises teaching ethical competence, adaptive problem-solving, understanding the world, appreciating the world, and social and emotional skills. “What can we create in schools that can build this, that can deliver on this vision? I would say build music, build the arts,” Savage said. Education consultant Kathleen Jenkins, who has both primary school teaching and music industry experience, said schools are good at measuring numeracy and literacy but are less good at measuring ‘soft’ skills like collaboration, creativity and expression. Stand Atlantic performing at Bigsound in 2024. Morgan Roberts “If we take away an arts curriculum, we’re not taking away things that [just] look pretty in the world,” she said. “For the child, we’re taking away developing those core muscles.”



Bigsound, which has been running for 25 years, is a showcase for the music industry, with more than 100 performers across three nights in Fortitude Valley. Kat Gibbs, head of people and culture at Unified Music Group, said school music education had a role to play in preparing young people for that industry. “Building those capabilities through music education … is so, so important, because it can put them on a path. If we don’t provide that opportunity at a young age, we’re taking away the voices that will ultimately shape our culture of music. “It’s not just about musicians, there’s a whole ecosystem of roles that create the industry. I think there’s so much opportunity.” Former Powderfinger guitarist Ian Haug, who now plays with The Church, spoke affectionately of his early primary school teacher, Mr Fildes, as one of the people who put him on that path.



“We’d go into the classroom and he’d be sitting in the front with a guitar, and the song I remember him playing a lot was Walk Right In, by Dr Hook. He made everyone join in,” he said. “He wasn’t specifically a music teacher, but the way he got everyone to participate set a mood of joy through the day. “It’s just so good for your soul and for mental health to do music.” Bigsound runs from September 1-3. World.title: Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTiger Woods Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case Daniel Kozin Updated September 3, 2026 — 1:00am ,first published 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge and his driver’s licence was suspended for five years on Wednesday following a rollover crash in March in Florida, where he initially was accused of driving under the influence (DUI). Before the hearing in Marin County began, Woods, 50, sat at the defence table looking back at the mostly empty courtroom gallery. He said little as he agreed to the reduced charge. Tiger Woods arrives at court in Florida with girlfriend Vanessa Trump. AP Photo/Lynne Sladky He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, US President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law, and she sat behind him during the proceedings. Woods, still one of golf’s most influential figures and as recognisable as any athlete in the world, has had a remarkable fall since winning the 2019 Masters for his 15th major. His career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.



Woods in court on Wednesday. Crystal Vander Weit/Treasure Coast Newspapers via AP He was arrested in March after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road near his home on Jupiter Island. A sheriff’s report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyser test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test. He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge. Tiger Woods strapped into a patrol car after his arrest. AP The prosecutor in the case said two toxicologists found there was insufficient proof of his impairment and determined Woods had built up a “pharmacological” tolerance.



Thomas Bakkedahl, a state attorney, defended his decision to accept the plea, saying, “I did what I think is right.” Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters. He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing after the crash and was fined $US1500 ($2092), according to court documents. “If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would immediately go back to jail,” Judge Darren Steele told Woods. Woods’ overturned vehicle on Jupiter Island, Florida. AP Woods’ attorney did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.



A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. Related Article Updated

Tiger Woods Tiger Woods arrested on suspicion of DUI after crash Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials. But his Land Rover caused $US5000 ($7000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck. Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years. He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play. He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.



Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour’s plans to revamp its schedule for 2028. Woods remained as chairman of the tour’s Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance. World.title: Spag bol vs the state
World.content:
“Jonty Grinter comments that it was difficult to get 3¢ change for spaghetti bolognaise at the Rocks Push (C8),” notes Karin Viles of Annandale. “The price was deliberate as most people opted to leave it as a tip to the person serving. Bruce Viles would later be taken to court at the time as the spaghetti, according to the licensing police, was not a “proper meal”. A prominent barrister defended the case pro-bono, the case was won and there were long queues from then on for this cheap meal.”

With all these missives regarding hospitality governance making things difficult for the punter, it’s gratifying to see a bit of country town goodwill, like that experienced by John Brown of Kianga: “In 1987 we stayed at the Black Stump Hotel Trunkey Creek. Four of us, including a non-drinker, drank them out of red wine (two bottles). Asking for port, the reply was ‘do you want 5s or 7s (ounces)?’ followed by ‘Could you scrape your plates into the dog’s bowl?’ We had a great stay – memorable – including an invitation to the 21st birthday party in the hall across the road. Very fond memories.”

Jim Dewar of Davistown reports that “No records were ratified at the World Humanoid Robot Games (C8) because of the suspicion that all times were wand assisted.”

“After watching much of the often incredulous testimony during the ICAC live stream (C8), I decided an appropriate description for the contagion brought into the witness stand is Dumbentia,” advises Lionel Latoszek of Long Jetty.

“If we were to open up a museum for idiot ideas that came from simple fools, would Pauline’s recent net zero coffin displace Scotty from Marketing’s lump of coal as the best exhibit?” enquires Toby Waters of Emerald Beach.

World.title: PNG halt Hudson pursuit after NRL’s decisive call on $3.3m offer
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 PNG halt Hudson pursuit after NRL’s decisive call on $3.3m offer Dan Walsh September 2, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The PNG Chiefs have paused their pursuit of Raiders and NSW Origin star Hudson Young based on concerns that matching Canberra’s record $1.1 million-a-year offer and the NRL’s market valuation would warp their salary cap. Young has become the unwitting poster boy for recent angst among rival clubs around the Chiefs’ market power when he left the Raiders three-year, $3.3 million offer – the largest per annum in club history – on the table last month to explore interest from PNG. Loading Looking to bring the situation to a head, Canberra CEO Don Furner granted Young permission to negotiate with PNG before he comes off contract on November 1 and also tour the incoming club’s Port Moresby facilities later this month. Furner also followed up this masthead’s reporting with the NRL salary cap auditor that PNG must register any contract at what head office deems to be the player’s market value. That notion was reiterated by ARL Commission chair Peter V’landys in a fortnightly CEOs hook-up on Wednesday, without referencing Young specifically.



Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the delicate nature of negotiations have said that Canberra’s $1.1 million-a-year offer could prove insurmountable for the Chiefs, given they have budgeted to carry at most, a salary of $950,000 for Young. The club has been told that figure is unlikely to be registered by the NRL’s salary cap auditor. Hudson Young’s PNG talks are on ice. Getty Images While Young is undoubtedly among the top few back-rowers in the NRL, clubs are yet to be provided with a new benchmarking document, which is used to help clubs ascertain player values based on market values. The last available document from 2025 calculated the average wage of the top five highest paid second-rowers to be $887,635. Manly’s Haumole Olakau’atu and North Queensland’s Jeremiah Nanai featured in that quintet, as did David Fifita, who took a hefty pay cut when he moved from the Titans to South Sydney late last year.



PNG’s tax-free wages and lucrative third-party earning opportunities offer a significant advantage in the market, prompting concerns across the game, particularly compared to the signing struggles of the Perth Bears, who begin their first pre-season in less than two months. PNG has a rookie coach and general manager of football in Willie Peters and Michael Chammas, a former reporter at this masthead, shaping their roster, alongside recruitment chief and ex-player manager Liam Ayoub, and Chiefs officials are mindful of the club being used to drive player prices up, be it by player agents or rival clubs. The Raiders have tabled Hudson Young the richest deal in the club’s history. Getty Images PNG splashed out $1.2 million on inaugural signing Jarome Luai, and have since added Alex Johnston, Zac Lomax, Joey Manu, Brian To’o, Connor Watson and Matty Lees to their 2028 roster. While the salary cap for that season is predicted to rise to around $15 million, PNG have negotiated each of their seven contracts so far without the ratchet deals that are widespread across the NRL. Young’s three-year offer from Canberra did not include a ratchet clause, either.



Related Article NRL 2026 NRL considers introducing AFL-style wildcard finals weekend The NSW back-rower had been due to visit PNG next month, and Chiefs officials had been quietly confident of landing their key forward target given every player who has toured the country has subsequently signed. As it stands from the Chiefs perspective, all talks will be paused until November 1, when Young enters regular free agency. Speaking at the Blues awards night on Monday, the 28-year-old said ”I have no interest in playing for another NRL club, and [coach] Ricky [Stuart] and I have spoken about that. “It’s more just the opportunity, with the PNG thing, and he’s been open and I’ve been transparent with him on how I feel and what I want to do”.

World.title: Fewer Kiwis contracting sexually transmitted diseases
World.content:
The number of New Zealanders contracting sexually transmitted diseases has fallen, a newly released report shows.

Syphilis rates have had the biggest drop - about a quarter - and have fallen everywhere except the South Island.

PHF Science analysis on the country's sexually transmitted disease rates in 2025 shows there were drops across all of the three reported diseases - gonorrhoea, chlamydia and syphilis.

Health authorities had been worried about syphilis when it spiked in 2023 but it was now on the decline.

There were 605 cases of infectious syphilis notified last year, a 27 percent drop the previous year, and the lowest rate since 2022, the report said.

The South Island did not improve on the previous year, however its rate of 11 cases per 100,000 was the same as most of the country.

The Northern region - Auckland and Northland, had 13 cases per 100,000.

For gonorrhea, the rate of cases fell by 17 percent last year, with 6306 cases reported.

The Northern region had the highest rate at 1.7 cases per 1000, with the South Island on the lowest at 0.6 per 1000.

Chlamydia rates were down by 13 percent.

The Northern region had the highest rate of five cases per 1000, and the South Island had the lowest at 3.8 per 1000.

PHF's report said the decrease in STIs was likely due to better prevention, testing and management of contacts.

Some at risk people were sometimes prescribed preventative antibiotics.

The report showed New Zealand had had its first recorded case of a super drug resistant strain of gonorrhoea known as XDR neisseria.

The case was linked to overseas and there had been no transmission in New Zealand but it showed the country needed to keep up good surveillance, the report said.

The number of gonorrhoea cases that were antibiotic-resistant to a lesser degree was growing.

World.title: Earthquakes hit near Milford Sound
World.content:
A series of earthquakes struck near Milford Sound on Wednesday evening, the first hitting soon after 6pm.

They began with a 5.5 magnitude quake at 6.13pm, followed by a 5.6 at 6.57pm.

Those two were followed by weaker quakes - 4.8 at 7.12pm, 4.6 at 7.39pm and 3.8 at 8.05pm.

The first quake hit 40km northeast of Milford Sound. The first two were listed on Geonet as moderate in intensity, while the third and fourth were light and the fifth, weak.

All five were relatively shallow, at five kilometres deep.

Within 10 minutes of the first earthquake, 6000 people had reported feeling it on GeoNet.

Some people on social media described it as a "decent shake", with one person in Invercargill saying they felt a jerk and swaying.

One person in Alexandra described it as "quite scary".

"Loud boom here before the shake arrived."

Another said it was "short and sharp compared to the one a couple of months ago".

"Loud rumble, cracking noise and windows rattled. Something in the pantry fell to the floor."

Historic bridge closed for inspection

Queenstown Lakes District Council said it would close Edith Cavell Bridge overnight

"As this bridge is a historical asset with heritage status, an inspection is required following earthquakes like the one we just experienced," it posted on social media.

Traffic from Arthurs Point will need to detour via Malaghans Road in Dalefield, the council said.

"Engineers will inspect the bridge at first light tomorrow morning and we'll provide a further update when we know more.

"Please also take care around our alpine passes like Crown Range Road as debris caused by the recent earthquake could be possible."

The area has experienced a few light shakes in recent days, of up to magnitude 3.3.

World.title: Reserve Bank hikes official cash rate to 2.75%
World.content:
RBNZ raises official cash rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent

The rate rise followed a similar-sized rise in July and was widely expected

The monetary committee says inflation has likely peaked and a economic recovery is likely to gain pace

A recovering economy does not need same stimulation of low cash rate

At least one more rate rise is expected this year - future rises will be guided by numbers and global events

Further rate rises are expected next year

The Reserve Bank has raised the official cash rate (OCR) for a second meeting in a row to tackle inflation pressures, and has signalled more increases could be coming this year.

The Monetary Policy Committee raised the benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 2.75, percent following a similar sized rise in July.

The move upwards was widely predicted by economists.

The committee said inflation had surged because of the Middle East war, but discounting the spike in fuel prices was on the way down.

"Excluding vehicle fuels, annual CPI inflation decreased to 2.9 percent in the June quarter. Most measures of core inflation are within the 1 to 3 percent target band."

It said higher fuel prices would drop out of the annual inflation calculation, and along with the slack in the economy and gradual rises in the OCR then inflation would hit the desired 2 percent rate by the end of 2027.

It said the economy has shown signs of recovery after being knocked off track by the US-Iran conflict.

"After lacklustre growth in the June quarter, New Zealand's economic recovery has most likely resumed, but remains uneven."

It said strong exports were boosting incomes and investment in parts of the economy and in the regions, which was being offset by weak income growth, job insecurity and flat house prices which were weighing on household spending.

The committee said global events posed risks to recovery and tackling inflation and would be a factor in setting rates.

But it signalled further rate rises to come.

"The committee judges that gradually removing monetary stimulus is appropriate to return inflation to the 2 percent target mid-point while supporting growth and employment.

"Future policy decisions will depend on the committee's judgement of the balance of risks to medium-term inflation."

Reserve Bank hikes official cash rate Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

The committee has two further meetings this year, in October just before the election and December.

Interest rate guidance in the statement suggested at least one more 25 basis point rise to 3 percent by year end, and possibly two more rises by the middle of next year.

'Positive news for New Zealanders'
