Epilogue’s also teamed up with the developers of Delta Emulator so you can plug real carts into your phone, and even built its own Flashback app if you want to turn your phone into a Game Boy Camera.

The Operator’s 3D trapezoidal prism shape doesn’t exactly lend itself to portability, but I stuck a magnet ring to it just right.

With all these amazing features, I just think Epilogue should be a little bit more upfront on its product pages about the compromises you need to make.

You should know the limitations: the Operators don’t work with multi-game flashcarts, they don’t work with the Super Game Boy, and their heavily marketed “Counterfeit cartridge detection” has been very hit or miss in my tests, to the point I wouldn’t really trust it. The company advertises that it can turn your Game Boy Camera into a webcam, but it’s more of an OBS screen recording hack than I would have guessed.

The GB Operator.

And if you, like me, have original Game Boy cartridges with original batteries, it may be too late to save some of your saves by now. It’s far too late to pull Pokémon off second-gen games like Pokémon Gold, Silver and even Crystal, whose real-time clocks drained their backup batteries and might not have lasted more than a decade.

As for first-gen Game Boy games, I pulled a Charmander off an original Pokémon Red cart last year, but even those carts are reaching their battery’s end of life. I have a 30-year-old copy of The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening whose battery was working last month. Last week, I found its save, too, was gone. Thankfully, the GB Operator backed up my progress a few months ago.

Now I just need to install a new battery, flash my save, and I’ll be back in business.

Tech.title: The robot butler dream doesn’t have legs
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The idea of humanoid robots running our homes has been the stuff of science fiction for years. But unlike hoverboards and self-tying sneakers, a robot housekeeper has never felt close to rolling into our homes. Until now.

This has been the year of the humanoid robot. At CES, there were dozens of human-shaped bots on the show floor, a handful designed for homes. US-based robotics company 1X has already put its $20,000 Neo robot into homes to do housework (with a lot of remote assistance); and this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin, around half a dozen humanoids, mostly from China, will take to a catwalk to show off the alarming (?) acceleration of their skills as they plan to backflip into our lives.

Robots on the Runway takes place on Saturday, Sept. 5th at IFA in Berlin, and will include robots from Primebot Robots, Agibot, Unitree, Ollobot, and Astrall Dynamics. Image: IFA

But do we really need mechanical, multimodal robots that do our housework, or is there a smarter path that doesn’t involve 170-pound hunks of metal that could accidentally kill your dog with one misstep?

During my time with these robots, two things have become clear.

A fully humanoid robot housekeeper just isn’t practical

First, despite my tech-reviewer fascination with humanoid robots, a fully humanoid robot housekeeper isn’t practical. Unlike factories, where humanoids have seen some success, homes are messy, unpredictable environments. Also, most people have stairs. Solving that problem requires a robot that can either fly or have a pair of legs that can exert substantial force — neither of which is a good fit for a home. (Just ask Ring where its much-touted Always Home flying camera is).

Second, tech history has proven that precious few gadgets do multiple things well. We don’t need an expensive jack of all trades and master of none. At CES, I walked around the Las Vegas show floor with a bottle of laundry detergent, challenging every humanoid robot I met to open it. Not a single one could. I was repeatedly told it had to learn how to do it first.

Switchbot is another smart home company developing a robot housekeeper. Its Onero home robot will be at IFA this week, showing its skills. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

What I think is more practical is a robot brain: an AI-powered smart home controller that can orchestrate the autonomous devices we already own based on the needs of the house and its occupants. Instead of one expensive machine trying to do everything, imagine a smart home that can proactively manage itself and adjust to the occupants: send the robot vacuum out when the dog spills his kibble, start the washing machine when energy is cheap, or dispatch the lawnmower when the edges need trimming.

Today, smart homes are mostly command-and-control or based on routines you create that require triggers. A robot brain could run your home autonomously and use reasoning to adapt when the home’s unpredictabilities arise. This appeared to be the idea behind Samsung’s Ballie robot (which never launched), and LG’s CLOiD humanoid (which looks more promising). It’s also the long-term vision of Amazon’s Alexa Plus and Google’s Gemini for Home smart assistants. No one is close.

Doova is a robot companion designed for seniors living alone. Image: Tuya

At IFA this week, Tuya, a global AI cloud platform service provider, will launch a similar concept but with a tighter focus. Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors living alone. It is a short, round robot on wheels with no arms, but it does have “dynamic facial expressions.”

Tuya says Doova can track its owner in the house and be ready to assist in an emergency. It can open a live video call with family if they don’t respond. It will also provide “conversational companionship” and work as a smart home hub to control lights, curtains, and kitchen and bathroom appliances. The company hasn’t announced a price or release date, but says it will come to market.

The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything

Doova doesn’t need to fold laundry or load a dishwasher to be useful; it can understand what’s happening in the home, connect people to the home, and control machines already there. It does, however, present the other huge challenge for robots in our homes: They need cameras to navigate and interact, and cameras in our homes raise major privacy concerns.

CLOiD loading (plastic) dishes into a dishwasher. Hands could make home robots much more useful, but they are very hard to perfect. Image: LG

Still, there is appeal in the idea of a robot brain that can do some manual chores — pick up clutter, load and unload a washing machine and dishwasher, and other tasks that require hands. I tested a robot vacuum with an arm that was supposed to pick up shoes and socks, and it mostly failed, but the idea is solid.

The middle ground between an imposing full-sized humanoid with legs and an armless robot companion is a wheeled bot with arms. That’s the direction LG took with CLOiD, a wheeled bot/smart home controller with arms boasting 7 degrees of freedom and five individually actuated fingers per hand.

I saw a live demo of CLOiD at CES this year using these appendages to perform simple tasks like folding clothes, taking items out of the fridge, and loading a washing machine, but not unscrewing a detergent bottle (I guess it uses pods?). Along with (very slow) physical actions, it also connected to and controlled smart appliances, including a washer, dryer, and oven.

This week, LG announced it is training hundreds of CLOiDs at a new data factory in Seoul, where they will practice a range of cleaning tasks in a home environment. By the end of this year, the company says this training data will feed roughly 100,000 hours of training data — equivalent to 12 years — into its own robot foundation model, built using Nvidia Cosmos open-world models.

It’s clear home robots are coming. But I don’t believe we need a robot butler that caters to our every need — very few people could afford one anyway. The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything, but a team of robotic machines, coordinated by a robot brain. And if that brain happens to come with a pair of hands that can open my laundry detergent, even better.

Tech.title: Is this the future of America?
Tech.content:
InIn 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizerâs earlier career as a radio DJ didnât exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a âreal jobâ and stumbled into a role at Loudounâs economic development authority.

This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the countyâs revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the countyâs tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst â those of the dot-com era.

The county had been home to the headquarters of AOL, which by 2000 was the USâs largest internet provider. Combined with its proximity to the nationâs capital and access to resources including water and electricity, Loudoun quickly emerged as the physical manifestation of the internet, the place responsible for how the majority of Americans got online. Estimates suggest that as much as 70 percent of the planetâs internet traffic passed through Loudoun County.

But after the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2000, followed by AOLâs disastrous merger with Time Warner, much of that industry dried up, and Loudoun was left with hulking, empty buildings and miles of fiber optic cable already laid in the ground. Where some people saw abandoned infrastructure, Buddy Rizer saw opportunity: âAnd so I thought if we can fill those, that would be a good start,â he says. Rizer soon realized that the same factors that made Loudoun County attractive to AOL could once again make it a hot spot for technology. It still had an internet exchange point, lots of land, a government eager for investment, and a capable local electricity utility. âAnd so we came up with this plan to attract data centers.â

Buddy Rizer, executive director for economic development in Loudoun County, has become known as the âGodfather of Data Centersâ for courting the massive data center buildout to the area.

Today, Loudoun County has another moniker: Data Center Alley. Over just a small portion of its roughly 515 square miles, itâs home to about 250 data centers, the densest concentration in the world. For a long time, residents there recall only a passing understanding of this, if they realized it at all. The development of data centers in Loudoun was just something going on in the background of many residentsâ lives. They noticed construction along main roads, paid an increasingly lower property tax rate, and sent their kids to coveted public schools.

The countyâs data center boom arrived as tech companies expanded into the cloud, a sanitized name for the blocky buildings that house rows and rows of servers. And with that business came prosperity: 22 new schools built in just the last 15 years, tax revenue from data centers alone that exceeded the countyâs operational budget by $35 million in 2024, and a decline in real property tax rate for residents from about $1.29 to 80 cents per $100 in assessed value since 2008.

Some longtime residents never heard of their countyâs nickname until recently, when the effects of data centers on the community started to become impossible to ignore. What had been a relatively quiet boon locally was starting to foment a national backlash elsewhere, and starting to disturb daily life in Loudoun, too.

The current, massive US data center buildout has been accelerating thanks to the widespread adoption of generative AI, which has created a growing need for the physical infrastructure to run tremendous amounts of âcomputeâ â the industry term for processing power. There are already 3,000 data centers in operation around the US, according to an April analysis by the Pew Research Center, with 1,500 more in development. When Rizer began recruiting companies to build data centers in Loudoun, he sat on conference panels for secondary markets. Now when he attends data center conferences, Loudoun is the biggest market there, and âthereâs more economic developers than there are data center companies, because everybody sees the opportunity.â

Loudoun County residents are also starting to take notice. Within the past few years, data centers have been elevated from an unremarkable part of daily life in Loudoun to something that many residents now think about every day. For some, itâs the constant hum they hear from their decks; for others, itâs the transmission towers that loom over their favorite green space, or the surprise call from their energy utility that one of those towers could go up in their own backyard. While residents recognize that data centers have brought a lot of prosperity to the county, theyâre beginning to wonder how much more they can take.

As communities around the country begin recognizing the potential opportunities of building data centers, the efforts have also faced immense pushback. Opposition to this development is shaping strange alliances across the political spectrum and has become a central issue in this yearâs midterm elections. New York and Texas have begun pumping the brakes on new data center buildouts, worried about how their energy grids could support them without leaving residents stuck holding the bag if major tech players change plans. Local stories from around the country show that residents are coming out to community meetings in droves to oppose data centers. In at least one case, a violent attack on a local Indianapolis official appeared motivated by his support for data centers. And national polls show that many Americans do not want to live near them.

With its long history hosting data centers, Loudoun residents have more recently taken to calling it something new: the canary in the coal mine of data center development. Want to know what the countryâs future looks like? Loudoun Countyâs past gives a strong glimpse of it.

Even in Loudoun, where the existence of data centers has been a fact of life for nearly two decades, Rizer says that in the last few years, community opposition has become more vocal. âBefore then, people understood what we were doing,â he says. These days, residents seem more aware of the inconveniences.

Rizer is no stranger to this kind of response to his projects, but the tone of the pushback is different. Residents have always had myriad worries: economic, environmental, and aesthetic. That part isnât new. âIâve done $70 billion of deals here, and the only thing in common is that somebodyâs been against every single one of them,â Rizer says. âI have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.â Asked to put his radio DJ hat on to choose a soundtrack for this moment, he chuckles and says the first one that jumps into his head is Taylor Swiftâs âYou Need to Calm Down.â

As Rizer and other officials in Loudoun field their own residentsâ concerns about data centers, theyâre also being flooded with calls from local officials across the country looking for their advice. Rizer is the first to admit that hosting a data center, let alone hundreds, is not the right choice for every community. He stands by the work heâs done to bring them to Loudoun, and still believes theyâve benefited the county on the whole. But data center expansion in Loudoun has recently taken on a life of its own, to the point that even Rizer no longer spends his time courting new facilities. âWe donât want more data centers here, but we want those that are here to be successful and continue to contribute to our community,â he says, diplomatically.

But new facilities are coming anyway, and even Rizer, the âgodfather of data centers,â is powerless to stop them. Over a series of visits to Loudoun County, I wanted to see for myself what itâs like to cross through communities surrounded by the cloud. Is the data center future that so many across the country seem to fear all itâs been built up to be?

âI have never seen, in my entire career, the vitriol, the hate that is associated with this.â

Long before it became Data Center Alley, Loudoun County was already solidifying its role as the hometown of the modern internet. In 1996, AOL decided to move its headquarters from neighboring Fairfax County to Loudoun, eventually employing more than 5,000 workers in Ashburn at its peak in 2004. Soon, the first internet exchange point, MAE-East, would make a similar move to Ashburn, making Loudoun the physical location where much of the worldâs internet traffic flowed. It was further solidified as a tech juggernaut when telecom company MCI WorldCom also opened a large office in the area, which became its headquarters in 2003.

The companies brought more than just jobs and a new workforce to the area. They also laid fiber underground across the county, attracting other tech firms to the area because of the convenient promise of low latency and proximity to the nationâs capital. The attention earned Loudoun nicknames like âthe Silicon Valley of the Eastâ and âDulles Technology Corridor,â after the nearby airport.

For a while, AOL and MCIâs presence made Loudoun an unlikely but bustling tech hub. Between 1990 and 2000, the county population doubled to 170,000. Early AOL employees have recounted lavish parties thrown by the company in its heyday, including âgo-go-style dancersâ and a sushi conveyor belt around an airplane at the nearby annex of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

During this time, data centers were already starting to pop up in Loudoun County, but with little fanfare. The first one arrived in 1997, and after that there was a slow drip of new data centers permitted in the area. In 2000, the local zoning administrator made a decision that would have lasting consequences later on, but made little noise at the time. Because data centers looked similar to offices, they became designated as âoffice parks,â meaning that they could be built on any land zoned for office space âby rightâ â bypassing more time-intensive regulatory review. That meant that unlike other commercial facilities like heavy machinery plants, which face more restrictions being built near populated residential areas, data centers could be built wherever offices had been allowed.

Data center construction like at this location in Sterling, Virginia, is a common sight all around Loudoun County.

Then the dot-com bubble burst. In early 2000, AOL announced a blockbuster merger with Time Warner for more than $160 billion. But as the first wave of internet companies suffered sharp declines, AOLâs ad revenue tanked, and the countryâs largest provider of dial-up internet was soon undercut further by the rise of faster cable broadband. MCI filed for bankruptcy in 2002 after a major accounting scandal. By 2006, it was acquired by Verizon, and a year later, a much diminished AOL announced it would move its headquarters to New York. Soon after came the financial downturn that became the Great Recession. Looking for unique ways to pitch the county, Rizer, then a newly minted business development manager, saw an opportunity in the recently emptied buildings and miles of fiber still lacing Loudounâs roads. From 2002 to 2005, no new data centers had been permitted. In the years after Rizer began courting them, only a few were permitted per year, county data shows, but growth was slow and steady. Then, in 2014, the number of data centers permitted jumped to seven. Rizer recalls feeling like the county could finally start relying less on its taxes from residents and more on commercial revenue. âWe were catching up on schools and catching up on salaries for our workforce,â he says. He recalls no pushback out of the ordinary on any development project, and says that for 15 years, âeverybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our community.â In 2018, data center permits tripled to 21 in a year, and they reached a new peak in 2022 at 25. The remains of the first AOL data center in the area are in the process of being demolished to make way for a new data center. Only those who were really paying attention seemed to notice that Loudoun was quickly becoming the data center capital of the world. Many longtime residents I spoke to sheepishly admit they hardly recognized Loudounâs global reputation for data centers, though they perhaps passively noticed the new, blocky buildings that popped up along main roads or the tall transmission towers near their favorite running trail. Over the past 20 years, though, Loudoun residents have seen a direct impact of data centers on their lives, whether they knew it or not. Real property tax rates declined dramatically, while property values have gone up in some communities as much as 182 percent in the last decade, even at residences close to data centers, according to county officials. The county has paved smooth roads and built sprawling athletic fields, a recreation center with an Olympic-size pool, and an average of nearly one and a half state-of-the-art public school buildings every year for the past 15 years, all thanks largely to the revenue generated by the county taxes data center companies have to pay anytime they get new equipment. And while data centers have gotten a reputation for creating relatively few jobs once theyâre constructed, the county says that for every job inside those buildings, three and a half non-construction jobs are âsupportedâ throughout the rest of the state economy. Those include ongoing maintenance at data centers, like electricians or HVAC technicians, and employment at other tech companies that move to Loudoun to be near where the data lives. While the data centers take advantage of a long-standing tax exemption from the state, Rizer emphasizes that the county has never spent a dime to attract them to the area. âA majority of the people that live here now only know prosperity, only know the strongest local economy in the country, only know great services and great schools,â Rizer says. âAnd so they donât necessarily connect to that. They donât see that common thread between the fact that the data centers are here and they have a great quality of life.â

Soccer fields at Hal and Berni Hanson Regional Park have been made possible through data center tax revenue.

My most recent visit to Loudoun is on a July day when wildfire smoke thatâs wafted down from Canada has sent air quality into a Code Purple. The ashy filter makes the grayish buildings all around look especially drab, though when I visit a local bike trail lined with trees and transmission towers, I still see plenty of cyclists braving the AQI that exceeds 200 in some spots. Julie Bolthouse, a longtime Loudoun resident who grew up across northern Virginia, drives me by the old AOL campus and points out a building with a playground on the other side of the street. âThat used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here,â she says. âNow itâs just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.â Loudoun County officials say that tax revenue generated from data centers benefits public schools like Independence High School. The lot where the old AOL campus sat is now filled with construction equipment and several-story buildings. The old headquarters has been demolished to make way for â you guessed it â more data centers. Throughout Loudoun, Bolthouse remembers land that now houses data centers being home to business centers and dentistâs offices. She returned to the area after college, enjoying that it made an easy trip to both DC and Virginiaâs Shenandoah National Park, and feeling comfortable in an area thatâs generally not prone to major weather events like hurricanes. In 2017, the organization she joined, Piedmont Environmental Council (PEC), began tracking the impact of data centers on the local environment. A year later, Loudounâs Board of Supervisors had one of its most contentious votes ever, narrowly approving a 750,000-square-foot data center spanning over 100 wooded acres near Goose Creek. Groups like PEC loudly objected to the development over environmental concerns, while those in favor of the proposal argued development would happen there regardless; it was just a matter of what would get built.

Data centers have become a regular sight and part of daily life in Ashburn, Virginia.

âEverybody loved the data centers because of the difference it made in our communityâ

Today, Bolthouse is the director of land use at PEC and helps lead a coalition of Virginia groups that advocate for stronger protections, tracking, and transparency around data center development. Bolthouse isnât dispositionally anti-data center, nor does she want to see existing ones in the area torn down or shut off. But she does advocate for a pause on new development. âThis industry is kind of creating a narrative that theyâre up against communities, and that thereâs a community backlash, and we just need to explain to the communities the benefits of data centers,â she says. âBut what theyâre really up against is physics. Theyâre up against the reality of what it takes to build out gigawatts of power, and the impact of building out gigawatts of power has direct impacts on people.â

Recently, sheâs found, more of her neighbors are paying attention. She recalls 2025 as a turning point, where PEC no longer had to do the legwork to get people invested, but instead was triaging which press requests would make the most impact given its limited capacity. And for residents, data centers were becoming more than just eyesores. They were beginning to disrupt life in Loudoun.

Vicky Hu lives in a red brick home on a cul-de-sac beside a peaceful, tree-lined stream. Her backyard stretches far along the water, where a white gazebo gives shade to sit and watch the deer she says regularly cross her yard. Including her mother and daughter, three generations of Huâs family have lived in this house. Having grown up in the city of Taipei, Hu marveled at the nature that surrounded her new home: deer as well as turtles and cranes. âTo me, this is like a dream. My dream home,â she tells me.

Madison Taggart says she doesnât want to think about what her childhood backyard would be like if forced to adopt a transmission tower.

Until last year, when Hu got a call that pierced that dream. She got a voicemail from a Dominion Energy representative and first wondered if there was an issue with her energy bill payment. Instead, she was told that a new transmission line connecting two substations would cut directly through her backyard. âAre you out of your fucking mind?â she yelled at the rep.

On the day I visit, the gazebo is filled with poster boards of blown-up maps of the community â and new development plans that threaten to overtake it. The trees along the stream are tagged with bright pink ribbons tied around their trunks. They mark the land Huâs family says would be cleared should Dominion Energyâs plan to string 185-foot transmission towers through their backyard go through as planned. âItâs like the sort of thing you only think youâd see in a dystopian nightmare,â Huâs daughter, 23-year-old Madison Taggart, tells me as she shows me around her childhood home.

Growing up, Taggart says that home always felt âlike a timeless place that no one else could touch.â Hu bought it shortly after her daughter was born, having seen the community built from the ground up. She worked for a developer and recalls watching workers bury power and communication lines beneath the community from her trailer across the road. By 2003, sheâd nearly finished selling the community, except for one lot that was reserved for a VP at her company. As Huâs aging mother struggled with the stairs in her townhome, she kept thinking about that lot on the cul-de-sac next to the water. She asked her colleague if she could buy it, and two years later, she moved in.

Now, Hu is engaged in a yearlong fight to redirect the transmission line to another route â one that, so far, sheâs on the losing end of, pending an appeal to the Supreme Court of Virginia. After that first phone call, Hu said she ran around the neighborhood âlike a crazy woman,â ringing doorbells and asking if anyone had heard of the proposal. She said they hadnât. By the time I visit, a sign in her backyard shows a diagram of the proposed 185-foot transmission tower next to a comparatively stout Statue of Liberty (if you exclude the base she stands on).

âThat used to be a major daycare center here in the heart of Data Center Alley, because there were so many people who worked here. Now itâs just these big, giant computer energy-guzzling, water-guzzling warehouses.â

Dominion insists that building the transmission line is necessary to power not only data centers, but also homes, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The local school district has been dragged into the fight over the route as well, though, with one proposal cutting close to two nearby schools. Huâs homeowners association donated a portion of land that would be cut through to the school district, preventing it from being seized by eminent domain.

Both the school district and residents in Huâs community have been fighting the planned routes, and worry that the expansion could signal even more encroachment on key facets of the community down the road. âThereâs also a deep concern for having this be a precedent that it could normalize easing the planning by just putting them on school property,â says April Chandler, Loudoun County School Board chair. Her concerns are with the kids and faculty of her community. âAs a school board member, itâs not my job necessarily to consider whatâs best for Dominion Energy or for data centers.â

Dominion Energyâs proposed transmission tower would loom taller than the Statue of Liberty.

Despite working or living in Loudoun since 2000, Hu had never heard the nickname âData Center Alleyâ until last year, when a Swiss reporter came to interview her about life in the data center capital of the world. Now, she canât unhear it. She notices transmission towers everywhere she goes. And she worries nowhere is truly safe from the ever-expanding buildout. âThis is just the first power line coming through a neighborhood. Where do you think the rest of the power lines [are] going to go through?â she asks. She predicts that in the next five to 10 years, âwhen you look at the sky in Ashburn â¦ youâre going to see a power line running everywhere, like a spiderweb.â

Should she lose the fight to preserve her backyard, Hu says sheâd have no choice but to leave. âDo I want to stay here sitting on my deck watching the power pole? â¦ Or should I stay here for a couple years to see if Iâm going to get cancer or a brain tumor?â She has lost sleep and hair fretting over how to save her home this past year. âItâs just very sad,â she says. âYouâre thinking, âYou work your whole life, you own something.â But you actually donât own it, because a power company can say, âI like your house. I want to take it.ââ

As I get out of the car a couple blocks down from the Vantage VA2 data center, I can already hear the whirring. Because I visited on a day with such poor air quality, what Iâm told are usually invisible emissions plumes make a faint outline in the smoggy air. Theyâre emitted, Bolthouse tells me, by the diesel generators powering the facility. She compares the noise to that of a lawn mower. (I later find out that the generators are never supposed to run on day with such poor air quality, but an emergency circuit issue required them to kick in temporarily.)

It doesnât always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise, nearby residents like Lindsay Shaw tell me. We meet while sheâs out for a walk with her dog, and she describes the way the sound permeates into her home. Constant light from the data center shines right into her bedroom at night unless the bathroom door is fully closed. Her fiancÃ© has taken to wearing an eye mask.

Piedmont Environmental Council land use director Julie Bolthouse worries about how Loudoun will keep up with the energy demands imposed by data center expansion.

Nobody wanted it this way. In an ideal world, Vantage would have done what hundreds of other data centers in the area have done and connected to the Dominion energy grid by the time the site went online last year. But after Vantage had already signed agreements with customers leasing space in the new data center, Dominion informed Vantage it didnât have enough capacity to get the 800,000-square-foot data center on the grid. Rather than let the building sit dormant until Dominion built up capacity, Vantage decided to create its own energy source using gas turbines. This is becoming more and more common in other parts of the country, as the new AI-motivated data centers require vastly more energy than the old cloud servers.

Residents and local politicians acknowledge that the Vantage site is an outlier because of its unusual reliance on on-site generated power from natural gas â albeit a very annoying one. Before it was built, Shaw tells me she thought a data center would be among the best options that could come to the lot across the street, in part because it wouldnât be something that would drive a lot of traffic near what she says is an already dangerous intersection. But now she says the data center has caused plenty of other problems and feels the operators have not been proactive enough in engaging neighbors. Vantageâs senior vice president of global public policy, John Stephenson, says he âwould respectfully disagreeâ that they havenât proactively engaged nearby residents. He notes that they held a community meeting at a nearby brewery to field questions early on, but admits that âin retrospect, we probably could have done more.â The company has taken different approaches to mitigate the noise, including installing insulation and repositioning the turbines to lower their tone.

But residents who live near other data centers throughout Loudoun â even those that donât have to generate their own power on-site â also complain of noise. Jason Mello says he hears a constant âlow-frequency droneâ he attributes to the HVAC systems of nearby data centers from his Ashburn home. Living near Dulles Airport, many Ashburn residents are used to the sound of planes overhead, âbut planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.â

Mello shows me videos of the noise from his deck outside a town hall meeting where we meet. He says heâs already spent $2,600 getting two new window inserts, with three more to go in his bedroom. He was quoted at least $15,000 for new siding that would further mitigate the noise. âAs a homeowner, if I want to live in peace at night, that addresses the inside,â he says, âbut if Iâm sitting on my deck, I can constantly hear that humming. And I think thatâs why you got to fix the problem also at the source.â

âYouâre thinking, âYou work your whole life, you own something.â But you actually donât own it, because a power company can say, âI like your house. I want to take it.ââ

Data centers have become next-door neighbors for many Loudoun County residents.

Several residents tell me that the boom in infrastructure needed to support the data centers has impacted their ability to enjoy the natural resources of Loudoun that once attracted them. âYou can barely hear the birds anymore,â says Jessica Medeiros, another resident who lives across the street from the Vantage data center. Even when she tries to retreat from the noise near her home, sheâs regularly reminded of the data centersâ presence. As a regular runner on the famed Washington and Old Dominion trail for the past 20 years, Medeiros says the âconstant construction,â towering power lines, and reduced shade because of cleared trees âruins the experience with nature.â She often says that when she dies, âI want my ashes scattered along the trail. But I think that trailâs going to look a lot different in another 10 years.â

âThe greenery is gone. The sense of community is gone. It feels very stale,â says Jenny Marza, another Loudoun County resident. âThereâs no more trees left and every inch is taken up by greed.â

While fighting new development near her own home, Marza has already felt pressure from the data center explosion on her small export logistics business. For years sheâs been looking at buying office and warehouse space in the area to be near the airport, but prices have been so astronomical that sheâs been forced to continue leasing. Now, even her current office rent has skyrocketed â she suspects because every landlord knows that data centers are willing to pay an average of $3.76 million per acre.

It doesnât always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise.

Marza says âIâm kicking myselfâ over a warehouse she came close to buying last year for around $5 million, but held off because it was more space than she needed at the time. âAnd then we put a pause on the search for two years and when we returned, it was like, âHoly crap, thereâs nothing left.ââ Anything that was selling at $5 million was now $10 million. To Marza, the residential property tax savings and increased home values mean little when compared to the quality-of-life concerns she has and the ability to help her small business survive. âI feel like itâs a drop in the ocean of what theyâre getting in return,â she says. âI feel like nobody protected our interests as a community.â

âDone the right way, you can be good neighbors,â Shaw says, reflecting on the Vantage site near her home. âBut this one was done like that shady neighbor next door that has people coming in and out all hours of the night. And then the FBI raids them and youâre like, âWell, I knew something shady was going on.ââ

When I arrive at the Loudoun government building on a July evening shortly before 6:30PM, Iâm handed a red flyer outside by a group advocating for local government control of utilities used to power data centers. Inside, the nearly full room is prominently speckled with light blue shirts that read âI support data centers.â The shirts list the reasons: âBecause I like: lower taxes, excellent schools, better job opportunities.â They also include caveats: âWhen they are: in the right location, well-designed, quiet, environmentally sensitive.â The slogan doesnât exactly roll off the tongue.

I comfortably score a seat, but later hear complaints from some attendees who say they arrived shortly after me and were relegated to the overflow room. Though itâs a first-come-first-served event, those critical of data centers grumble that industry supporters seem suspiciously well organized in their early arrivals.

Still, it doesnât have the kind of fireworks or soundbites that have made community meetings about data centers around the country into national news. While some residents voice strong frustration, the two-and-a-half-hour forum is cordial and respectful of Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randallâs request of no cheering nor jeering.

âPlanes come and go. The data center hum never stops.â

Tippettâs Hill Cemetery, one of the oldest African American cemeteries in the area, is surrounded by data centers.

Randall is in a tough spot. As head of the elected nine-member panel tasked with adopting local ordinances, appropriating funds, and rezoning land, Randall has just enough power for her constituents to lay responsibility for their criticism at her feet, yet not enough to change some of the things she says she wishes she could. At the meeting, she listens to residentsâ concerns, promising to follow up with phone calls for some while repeatedly acknowledging and lamenting the quality-of-life frustrations many of her neighbors have about living near data centers. But she also declines to give ground on topics she said are unfounded or detached from political reality.

Randall walks residents through the history of data centers in Loudoun, including what they are and how they came to be zoned the same way as office parks. Before getting to the audience participation portion, she clicks to a slide that says â4 Things That Are Unpopular But Trueâ with a grimace emoji. The first: At one point in time, residents actually preferred data centers over new housing developments. She references opposition to a 2021 proposal to build up to 779 residential housing units in Ashburn, called Hyde Park. Across about 125 comments, residents reportedly worried about increased traffic and infrastructure strain. Nearly two years after submitting the application, the developer withdrew and decided to establish a by-right data center there instead. âOne of my worst days was January 5th, 2023, when the applicant called me and said, âForget it. Iâm going to go build a data center,ââ Randall says. âAnd I pretty much begged them not to.â

âSo do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?â

The second unpopular truth: Itâs not legal for Loudoun to enact a moratorium on development without the stateâs permission.

Third: Both the Biden and Trump administrations have indicated AI infrastructure buildout will be a national priority, so thatâs unlikely to change anytime soon.

And fourth: Despite resident backlash to certain data center land use exceptions the board has granted, the alternative would have been that those data centers could take the land by right anyway, with much less in return. The lesson being, if data centers can break ground whether government officials want them to or not, the county might as well get something out of it.

Residents who speak at the hearing do not dispute her account of the countyâs history. Many express frustration about the buildings encroaching on greenery or creating annoying and near-constant noise issues. But many others, including several in the blue shirts, argue in support of data centers as stewards of the community they are proud to be known for. One Ashburn resident describes a peaceful experience living across from a data center. âWhen the weather is good, Iâll open my bedroom windows, from which I can see it directly. It is silent, it is clean. It is a good neighbor,â he says. Another resident, who leads the nonprofit Northern Virginia Science Center Foundation, credits data centers with generating revenue that can help fund such endeavors to a greater degree than it sees in nearby Fairfax. The organization lists Loudoun County, Dominion Energy, and data center company QTS among its partners.

Randall affirms residentsâ data center complaints, but also fact-checks several claims about supposed data center projects she says never existed in the first place. One Ashburn resident, for example, bemoans what he calls the âAshburn Commons proposalâ that would create a blight next to existing housing, greenery, and other community institutions. Randall asks him to clarify if he is thinking about a proposal near the Harris Teeter grocery store.

âYes!â he answers.

âThatâs not real,â Randall says. Her colleague adds the would-be developer hasnât even submitted a formal application for it, and the government had denied an initial request.

âWell,â the resident cries out, âpraise the Lord on that!â

âI donât want to be the example of what not to do.â

For all the gripes, Iâve still yet to meet anyone in Loudoun County who actually says they oppose data centers entirely. Whether theyâre currently living next to gas turbines or their backyard could potentially be seized to build a transmission tower, Loudoun residents still recognize that data centers help power the technology we use every day. After all, they need to go somewhere. Why not there?

But even if Loudoun residents have accepted the economic benefits as a tradeoff for the loud eyesores near their homes, it doesnât mean theyâre open to an expansion of that deal.

âItâs not about trying to get rid of the existing data centers. These data centers are here. Theyâre running. I donât want them to go anywhere,â Bolthouse says. âThe question isnât, âDo we need data centers?â The question is, âIs it worth threatening our air quality, threatening our water supply, and throwing our communities into chaos, and taking peopleâs private land for transmission lines to get it?ââ

I spoke with over half a dozen Loudoun residents, and universally, this is what they want communities considering data centers to understand: Know what youâre getting into. That means making sure existing laws and ordinances will apply to data centers, that local utilities have a plan to ensure enough capacity for the expected buildout, and that neither data centers nor the infrastructure needed to power them can be built too close to homes or schools.

Even Rizer says the buildout in Loudoun has, in some places, gone beyond what heâd have hoped. âThereâs no data centers here that arenât where theyâre allowed to be, but I think sometimes thereâs a difference between what youâre allowed to do and what is probably best for the community,â he says. âAnd thatâs what weâve had to clean up a little bit.â At the town hall, Randall showed aerial images of several residential communities that were directly bordered by data centers. Those arrangements are not what any Loudoun official or resident considers ideal â but even so, she said, property values in those communities have only gone up.

There are limits. Loudoun hasnât had a strategic focus on bringing in more data centers since 2019, Rizer says. More recently, the local government is pursuing a plan to pump the brakes further â doing away with the ability for data centers to use office-zoned land by right, and considering pausing new permit reviews while contemplating zoning changes that could better address community impacts.

When peers around the country contact him about whether they should invite data centers into their communities, Rizer says, âItâs not right for every place. So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?â

For Loudoun, unlike many yet-to-be-developed areas in the US, there is a definitive end in sight. The county has an ever-diminishing amount of space left to develop data centers, after which point it will continue to collect tax revenue when the companies update equipment within their walls.

Loudoun residents hope that by the time it gets to that point, the things that they love about the area are still there. For many, itâs the convenience of living near DC, but still close to nature. Itâs also often about the quality public schools, funded in part with the revenue raised by the colossal energy-guzzling slabs in their backyards.

HVAC units on top of data centers can contribute to the loud noise many residents complain about.

AOLâs roots helped make Loudoun the first major data center capital, and that came with both advantages and challenges. For communities starting to consider their first data center today, Bolthouse says theyâre in a much better position than Loudoun was because the industry isnât yet âembeddedâ in layers of government. She still thinks their story could become a beacon of hope for others, rather than a warning â but itâs an uphill battle to get there.

âI donât want to be the example of what not to do,â she says. âI want to be the example of what to do. I want to bring journalists out to see how we fixed problems, how we are doing much better, and how communities are happy with these facilities because theyâve done something better.â Hearing Bolthouseâs frustration with the ever-expanding energy demands imposed by data centers, itâs surprising to hear her embrace the ones that are already here. But for all the friction theyâve caused in her community recently, itâs also clear from my visits and conversations that data centers have played a central role in supporting many positive aspects of life in Loudoun. The question, now, is whether Loudoun can manage its existing demand and successfully serve community needs as the data center footprint continues to grow.

If Bolthouse sounds optimistic, she is certain that something has to give. In the past, Loudounâs data center buildout was quiet and steady. Todayâs is anything but. âI donât see how that happens with the scale and speed to market that the industry is pursuing.â

Tech.title: Adobe acquires Indian market intelligence startup Rilo
Tech.content:
Adobe has acquired India-based marketing intelligence startup Rilo in a deal involving licensing and team acquisition, TechCrunch learned and the company confirmed. This is Adobe’s second acquisition from India after it bought video platform Rephrase.ai in 2023. The companies didn’t disclose the deal’s terms.

Beyond confirming the deal, Adobe declined to comment.

The acquisition gives Adobe a small team and technology focused on automating marketing workflows, which have been changing as companies use AI to build tools to automate the creation, deployment, and tracking of campaigns, get action items from meetings or calls to complete tasks, and increase brand visibility on platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. Rilo’s technology could bolster Adobe’s existing products as the company targets its larger customers.

Founded by IIT batchmates Georgi Boby and Dhruv Jaglan in 2025, Rilo raised $1 million from investors including PeakXV, DeVC, and Day Zero Ventures at a $10 million valuation. A source told TechCrunch that investors will get an exit from this deal, and Adobe will integrate some of Rilo’s IP along with the six-member team.

The company worked on letting go-to-market teams create custom workflows, including competitor intelligence, content repurposing and distribution, and sales call analysis. It also allowed teams to set up custom workflows comparable to tools like Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Work.

Post-acquisition, Rilo will shut down and won’t be available to its customers.

Rilo co-founders Dhruv Jaglan and Georgi Boby. Image Credits: Rilo Image Credits:Rilo

“We’re very excited that Rilo has been acquired by Adobe in such a short span of time,” Rahul Gupta, Managing Partner, Day Zero Ventures told TechCrunch over email. “Their workflow builder product was way ahead of the curve and shall be extremely valuable to a giant like Adobe in enhancing customer experience and productivity.”

Adobe made a marquee marketing acquisition last year by buying SEO optimization company Semrush for $1.9 billion.

DeVC’s Rahul Mathur told TechCrunch that Rilo could fit into Adobe’s CX and marketing suite to handle complex workflows and give customers visibility into actions they take on the creative company’s platform.

Rivals like Canva have also bolstered their marketing portfolio with acquisitions and new launches. Meanwhile, Amazon, Google, and Meta have built their own AI-powered marketing rails.

Tech.title: Norway considers ban on camera-enabled wearable ‘pervert glasses’
Tech.content:
In Brief

Norway is considering a ban on smart glasses and other camera-enabled wearable headsets as it seeks to regulate the controversial technology amid privacy concerns.

The country’s digital minister Karianne Tung, as quoted by the AFP news agency, said that the government is looking to regulate the use of camera-enabled wearables, such as those made by Meta and Snap. These wearables feature cameras, are internet-connected, and may soon include facial recognition, drawing ire from civil liberties advocates, who say the devices intrude on people’s privacy. Some call the devices “pervert glasses,” prompting considerable consumer backlash.

Norway’s Tung said there is a “clear trend toward combining artificial intelligence with cameras and microphones built into glasses, headphones, hats and other objects we use in everyday life.”

“We must prevent this equipment from being used to monitor other people in public places,” said Tung, who added that this may include banning the use of facial recognition of other people in public places.

Tung plans to set up a group of experts to advise the government on better protecting people’s privacy rights.

Tech.title: Adobe is making its tools available in Slack
Tech.content:
Customers can now use Adobe’s apps like Firefly, Adobe Express, Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, InDesign, Illustrator, Stock, Lightroom, and others directly with Slack’s AI chatbot, Slackbot, Adobe announced on Monday. In addition, more than 70 Adobe tools will become available in Slack through the Adobe for Slack MCP app.

With the Slackbot integration, users will be able to describe what they want to do, and the bot will call the right Adobe tool to complete the task. Adobe said that while calling its tools, Slackbot also takes in the context of the conversations. For instance, users can get information from conversations or Canvas and turn it into PDFs, images, and videos. They can also bring in assets from previous campaigns or the Creative Cloud asset library into a chat and edit them.

At launch, this integration will be available to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ teams.

While productivity and creative companies have been busy adding AI features into their tools, most people still work in conversational boxes. This pushes the tool providers to make their features available through services like ChatGPT, Claude, and Slack.

Last month, Adobe introduced a similar integration for ChatGPT and is planning to launch a Gemini integration soon. Deepti Pradeep, Senior Director for Agentic AI at Adobe, told TechCrunch over email that people are using the company’s tool in other apps for repeatable workflows like batch-editing images or resizing creatives without leaving the app.

“In focus groups, people talked about the value they get from this experience very clearly: saving time, getting to the outcome they want faster without having to micromanage every step, being able to access Adobe wherever they’re already working. That’s been interesting for us because it’s pushed us to think less about individual edits and more about the larger outcome someone is trying to get to,” Pradeep said.

Other creative tools like Canva and Figma are also making their capabilities available in chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. On the other hand, companies like Anthropic are releasing tighter integrations in Slack, because team context is often captured through those conversations.

Pradeep said that consumers having choices between tools is a good thing, but Adobe has the advantage of providing both creative and productive tools across different modalities.

Tech.title: Uber is laying off 10% of staff, or 3,300 people
Tech.content:
In Brief

Uber is laying off about 3,300 people, or about 10% of its global headcount, in a bid to cut management layers and invest more in its ride-sharing, delivery and robotaxi divisions. The company announced the changes in an internal email sent by CEO Dara Khosrowshahi and published online Wednesday.

According to the email, the layoffs are part of a restructuring exercise that would shrink the number of managers by 20%, and some personnel in these roles would work as individual contributors going forward.

Bloomberg first reported news of the layoffs.

The ride-sharing giant is reducing the number of teams with one or two members by 50%, and letting go staff who are “more than seven layers down from the CEO,” per Bloomberg. Khosrowshahi’s email said the company is combining its engineering, science and delivery divisions. The company is also bringing together its delivery operations across restaurants, retail and direct divisions.

Remote jobs at the company are going away, too, with Uber only allowing less than 1% of its staff to work remotely.

“We’ve built new products, expanded into new businesses, reached more consumers and supported more earners, and become a much larger and stronger company. But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale,” Khosrowshahi reportedly wrote in the email.

Tech.title: OpenAI faces 30 more lawsuits tied to Tumbler Ridge shooting
Tech.content:
Edelson PC, the law firm that filed seven lawsuits against OpenAI in April on behalf of victims and families connected to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, is filing 30 additional complaints this week. The new plaintiffs include teachers, a principal, and students who were in the building during the attack but not physically shot.

The new filings also, for the first time, accuse OpenAI of aiding and abetting the mass shooting, rather than just negligently failing to prevent it. That claim requires proving intent from OpenAI and is likely to face early dismissal challenges.

The complaints come as OpenAI continues to deal with the fallout of another high-profile safety incident after one of the company’s AI models escaped its sandbox during cybersecurity evaluations and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face’, a company that hosts open-source AI models and datasets. OpenAI has also faced several lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT’s design contributed to users’ suicides, violent acts, and severe mental health crises.

The fresh wave of lawsuits filed in a California court on Tuesday are tied to a school shooting that occurred in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada on February 10. That day, teenager Jesse Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother at home, then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed six more people and injured dozens of others before dying by suicide.

The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI staff had been alarmed by VanRootselaar’s use of ChatGPT, including conversations around gun violence and advice for how to plan an attack. OpenAI employees reportedly urged leaders to alert Canadian law enforcement about Van Rootselaar’s potential for real-world violence, but leaders decided not to contact the authorities. Instead the company deactivated Van Rootselaar’s account, but she was able to make another one shortly after.

OpenAI has justified its actions, claiming Van Rootselaar’s activity didn’t meet the company’s internal bar for an “imminent and credible risk” of serious physical harm to others required to engage with law enforcement.

“That judgment is not infallible, but it is always rooted in looking out for this balance for people,” Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer who oversees the team of human reviewers and the company’s legal department, said in a statement shared with TechCrunch.

The new set of complaints specifically name OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane as the person who told staff to stand down and not contact the authorities, though the complaints offer no direct evidence that he was personally involved, and OpenAI has denied his involvement.

Lehane is a well-known political operator and PR spin master with particular expertise in damage control, having worked in that capacity on behalf of the Clinton administration, at Airbnb, and now at OpenAI. The plaintiffs allege that his background contributes to a culture at OpenAI that prioritizes public relations and damage control over safety.

“The Intelligence and Investigations Team—the only team inside OpenAI responsible for identifying ChatGPT users who pose a threat of real-world violence—was placed under [Lehane’s] control,” reads one of the complaints, shared with TechCrunch. “As a result, the decision whether to alert law enforcement to a user planning a mass attack was not made by the trained threat-assessment professionals who urged OpenAI to contact the [Canadian police]. It was made, on information and belief, by Lehane himself, or by someone in his chain of command, and ratified by Sam Altman.”

“On information and belief” is a legal term meaning the plaintiffs believe a claim to be true based on secondhand information, even though they can’t yet prove it directly. TechCrunch was unable to confirm whether Lehane indeed has the authority to override recommendations from the intelligence and investigations team, or whether he was involved in this specific case at all. Notably, Lehane is not listed as a defendant in the complaints, though, as in the previous seven complaints, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is.

“We are not laying out all of our evidence at this point,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer on the cases, told TechCrunch, noting that Lehane and Altman will be “critical witnesses” alongside the safety team. “We can tell you that we are basing this in part on the org chart, but also our broader investigation, which includes what we have learned about how Lehane operates within the company.”

“It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision, or that our investigators report to him in any way,” Kwon said. “It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”

The fresh complaints also seek to rebut OpenAI’s previous defense that it did not alert Canadian authorities to Van Rootselaar’s conversations with ChatGPT due to “imminence” and “privacy” justifications. The complaints point to an incident in November 2025, during which OpenAI locked down its San Francisco offices following an alleged threat from an activist.

“Although OpenAI acknowledged there was ‘no indication of active threat activity’—and thus no indication of an ‘imminent’ attack—the company… immediately locked down its offices, warned employees, distributed the suspect’s name and photograph, and notified the San Francisco Police Department,” a complaint reads.

“When its own people were at risk, no ‘privacy’ interest stopped OpenAI from notifying the police or circulating the man’s name and photograph to thousands of employees. Nor did it wait for the attack to become imminent because it recognized that waiting would jeopardize employee safety.”

Tech.title: Larry Page’s flying car company Pivotal loses its CEO
Tech.content:
The CEO of a flying car company backed by Larry Page has left the company.

Ken Karklin, who was Pivotal’s CEO for more than four years, left the role this week, according to a press release. Pivotal said Karklin is “pursuing new endeavors” but didn’t offer any other information about the executive’s departure from the electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) firm.

“Leading Pivotal has been the privilege of my career. Together, we’ve moved beyond the promise of light eVTOL and proved it out in practice,” Karklin said in a statement. “This industry has moved past prototypes and press releases; it’s now operating in the real world, under real constraints, with real consequences for the future of Advanced Air Mobility. As I turn to new endeavors, I do so knowing the foundation we built here will help carry this industry forward.”

Karklin will be replaced on an interim basis by Mike Ross, an aviation executive who joined Pivotal’s board of directors in November 2025. Karklin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Karklin’s departure comes two years after Pivotal started sales of Helix, its first lightweight electric personal aircraft. The single-seat aircraft doesn’t require a pilot’s license to fly and starts at around $200,000.

“Ken’s leadership over the past four years has been instrumental in bringing Pivotal to where it is today. Our team, our priorities, and our roadmap remain steady through this transition,” Ross said in a statement. “I’ve had the honor of working closely with Ken as a Board member and watching Pivotal’s disciplined approach to safety, engineering, and accessibility deliver on the vision of electric VTOL flight. I look forward to working with the team and guiding the company forward as we bring our fourth-generation Helix aircraft to market.”

Pivotal has also spent years developing an aircraft called BlackFly that is aimed at defense and first-responder use cases. Last month, BlackFly was used to respond to an emergency in North Carolina for the first time ever. The company says it beat an ambulance responding in parallel to the call by 20 minutes. BlackFly has flown more than 10,000 times, according to Pivotal.

Pivotal is one of a number of companies in the space that was selected for the Federal Aviation Administration’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, which was created to increase testing of these types of aircraft around the country.

Tech.title: Reliance’s JioHotstar takes its streaming empire global — without sports
Tech.content:
JioHotstar, the streaming platform controlled by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries, is taking its brand outside India for the first time and will replace Hotstar in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore as it begins a wider global push.

The streaming service will launch with more than 160,000 hours of entertainment content but without the live sports that have helped drive its massive audience in India, including the Indian Premier League (IPL), Women’s Premier League (WPL), and Indian national cricket matches. JioStar said it is not offering sports at launch because of existing content deals but did not rule out adding them in the future.

The absence of sports at its global debut marks a significant difference from JioHotstar’s offering in India, where the company says it has more than 500 million monthly active users and sports is a major audience draw. The service streams some of India’s biggest cricket events alongside the English Premier League; tennis tournaments, including Wimbledon and the U.S. Open; and domestic leagues for sports such as kabaddi and hockey.

JioStar confirmed to TechCrunch that starting September 2, Hotstar will “cease to exist” in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, with JioHotstar replacing it. Hotstar users in the three markets will no longer be able to access the service through the Hotstar app, though their existing login credentials will work on JioHotstar, the company said. The JioHotstar app will be available in all three markets through the App Store and Google Play Store on mobile devices, as well as on connected TVs.

For years, Hotstar has operated internationally, including in the U.K. and Canada. It also previously had a stand-alone service in the U.S. before shutting it down in 2021. However, JioHotstar is not launching in the U.S. as part of this initial international rollout. The company plans to expand into additional overseas markets over time.

JioHotstar will launch with a trove of Indian films, TV originals, and reality shows like “Bigg Boss,” along with live TV channels under the Star banner such as Star Plus, Colors, Star Vijay, Asianet, Star Jalsha, and Star Pravah. The company said its content is available in 12 languages, including English, Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Kannada, and Marathi, with dubs and translations also available.

In 2024, Reliance merged its media assets with Disney to form an $8.5 billion joint venture. As part of the deal, streaming services Hotstar and JioCinema merged to create JioHotstar for Indian consumers. At the time, the two services accounted for 85% of the streaming audience in India.

Data from India’s Ministry of External Affairs suggests that across the three countries where JioHotstar is launching, the service could have a target audience of more than 4 million people. Some of its content could also appeal to the broader South Asian diaspora.

“South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations, and households. At the same time, audiences globally are increasingly seeking stories and cultures beyond their own. We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience — not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets,” JioStar’s Head of International Business, Amit Malhotra, said.

JioStar has priced JioHotstar at £19.99 (about $27) quarterly and £69.99 (around $95) annually in the U.K. In Canada, subscriptions cost CA$19.99 (about $14) quarterly and CA$49.99 (around $36) annually, while in Singapore they cost SG$29.98 (about $24) and SG$69.98 (around $55), respectively. The prices are similar to what Hotstar charges, but JioHotstar will offer only entertainment content at launch. Customers who want sports may have to pay extra for another service.

By comparison, JioHotstar subscriptions in India start at ₹79 (about $0.80) a month for viewing on a single mobile device and go up to ₹2,199 (around $23) a year for its top-tier plan.

Tech.title: Apple follows Google in adopting Trump’s ‘Lake America’ name
Tech.content:
Apple has followed Google’s lead and officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on its Apple Maps service less than a week after President Trump ordered the change.

Apple Maps users in the United States will begin to see Lake America, not Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes in North America — when using the website or mobile app. The change will only be shown to users in the United States. Apple Maps users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, while those outside the two countries will see both names.

The change is in response to an executive order signed by Trump on August 27 that gave the Interior Department 30 days to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service and other federal databases.

“In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America,” the order reads.

Trump’s directive — and Apple’s and Google’s compliance — has escalated an already strained relationship with Canada after trade talks between the two countries broke down.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment. Google Maps explained its reasoning for the change, noting in its announcement last week that it updates names to reflect changes in official government sources such as the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

However, not every map service has adopted that same policy. MapQuest said that it would not change the name of Lake Ontario on its maps, choosing to continue using the name that people are familiar with. (It also did not change the name of Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America last year.)

Apple’s and Google’s actions over the name of this lake have driven a significant boost in users to MapQuest. Downloads of the so-called OG of mapping services have skyrocketed, pushing the iOS app to the No. 1 position in the U.S. App Store’s Top charts. That even put MapQuest ahead of perennial chart-topper ChatGPT as of September 1.

MapQuest also reached the No. 6 position overall in Google’s Play Store across both apps and games. And the company doesn’t appear to be budging. It posted on X a GIF of an apple, with the line “Them Too.” In another post showing a screenshot of MapQuest as the No. 1 downloaded app, the company wrote. “The people have spoken. We are working.”

There is precedent to Apple’s and Google’s deference to Trump. Last year, both of these tech companies changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America after that name-changing order by Trump.

Tech.title: The Cybercab Is Almost Here. Now Comes the Hard Part
Tech.content:
Matte gold, sloped, and steering-wheel-free, the Tesla Cybercab seems designed to catch the eyes of looky-loos. Now rubberneckers may have more opportunities: Tesla is set to host an event on Thursday at its Austin, Texas, headquarters to debut the Cybercab.

Tesla first rolled out a prototype Cybercab at a flashy event on the Warner Bros. lot in 2024. This week’s unveiling will likely mark the vehicle’s official introduction to the electric-auto maker’s small ride-hail service. It has operated a pilot program in Austin since last summer, and has since expanded to a handful of other cities in Texas and Florida, with permits to launch in Arizona and Nevada. (A “robotaxi” service in the San Francisco Bay Area is not legally permitted to operate without drivers behind the wheel.) Before the event, Tesla added 51 Cybercabs to its fleet of vehicles registered to operate in Texas (263 Model Ys are also registered).

“The streets won't be the same anymore,” Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, posted last month on X. When an X user asked whether the Cybercabs would “flood Austin,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk, with his characteristic moth-to-the-flame tendencies toward hyperbole, responded with a simple “Yes.”

Details on the event are still scant, and the basic business model for the Cybercab is in question—are the vehicles just for ride-hail operations, or meant to be sold to individual drivers? States regulate autonomous vehicles, and some tightly control permits and data collection. However, Musk still insisted this year that Tesla will sell Cybercabs directly to consumers before the end of 2026.

Either way, the physical Cybercab slated to be shown off in Austin on Thursday may be the easiest lift in Tesla’s deeply ambitious plan to shift from a company that builds cars to one entirely focused on autonomous vehicles and robotics. Manufacturing a car isn’t easy. But neither is running a functional autonomous vehicle service, nor building the software to power it. Tesla hasn’t yet proven that it can do either at scale.

“Longer term, the software is the most important piece,” says Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst for Morningstar who follows Tesla. “This is a very important step, to put the Cybercab in production, but ultimately, it only matters if the software can allow a car to navigate safely.”

Musk has promised for nearly a decade that the Teslas sold to everyday consumers are just a software update away from driverless capabilities, but that has yet to come true. (Musk admitted earlier this year that some vehicles will need a hardware upgrade to get the capability.) The company’s critical thesis is that a car can drive on complicated, chaotic public roads with only inexpensive cameras, which could allow it to deploy self-driving robots much more cheaply than the competition. Waymo, the US industry leader, took a direct swipe at Tesla last month, writing in a blog post that “cameras are incredible, but they aren’t enough.” Waymo’s more expensive setup uses lidar and radar along with cameras.

Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) product, available to drivers for a $99 monthly fee, currently does many driving tasks, including changing lanes and stopping at red lights. But the company warns in its manuals that drivers must pay attention and be ready to intervene at all times. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the US’s top auto safety regulator, opened an investigation into crashes involving FSD in 2024 following concerns that the system falters in situations with poor visibility. That probe is ongoing.
