Tech.title: Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
Tech.content:
Pangram is an AI startup with 24 employees, headquartered above a Popeyes in Brooklyn. It has raised $13 million to date—about 0.0072 percent of what OpenAI has—and was virtually unknown until earlier this year. But if Pangram is to be believed, it’s the one force standing in the way of a full machine takeover of the written word.

Pangram promises to detect how much AI was involved in the generation of any given text, and it does so as a best-guess percentage (using AI, of course). In January, speculation swirled on Reddit and YouTube that the author Mia Ballard may have used AI to write Shy Girl, a self-published novel picked up for traditional publication by Hachette. Although Ballard denied it, Pangram’s CEO posted on X that the book was 78 percent AI-generated. Hachette later canceled the release.

A barrage of similar accusations followed. The New York Times was called out for running an AI-generated installment of its Modern Love column. Pangram score: 100 percent. Then came a winner of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize (100 percent), the novel Daggermouth (60 percent), and a thriller titled Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body that had sold for $2.4 million (97 percent). In late July, Substack announced it was integrating Pangram into its platform so readers could quickly determine possible AI use.

Not all writers see this as a good thing. “There is such distaste and anger at the AI detection software,” says Jane Friedman, an author and publishing expert. “There’s this feeling like they are just as evil, if not more evil, than the AI companies themselves.” Outside of publishing and higher education, Pangram isn’t a household name, but I suspect it’s about to be; the demand to distinguish LLM churn from human writing grows with each passing day. The question to ask now is: How much can the company be trusted?

Max Spero, Pangram’s 30-year-old cofounder and CEO, dials into our Google Meet from his phone, takeout box in one hand and skyscrapers in the background. He’s wearing a beige T-shirt and has short dark hair, a boyish expression, and a wide smile. He says he’s rushing home with lunch and will call back. Ten minutes later, Spero reappears inside his Brooklyn apartment. He’s been on hiring calls all morning, he says. In July, Pangram raised $9 million and announced the launch of its newest model, Pangram 4. The company’s website lists six new job openings, which would increase headcount by 25 percent.

I ask Spero about growing up in California, a softball question that makes him visibly uncomfortable. Discussing the nuances of Pangram’s tech comes more naturally to him than answering personal queries—or speaking to the company’s involvement in literary scandals. Spero takes a bite of his meal and says he was raised in the Los Angeles suburb of La Crescenta. He loved programming and joined his school’s robotics team. As an undergrad at Stanford, he met Bradley Emi, his eventual Pangram cofounder. (My several emailed requests to interview Emi were ignored by the company’s comms team.) After school, Spero went to Google, where he worked on FLoC, a technology designed to replace third-party cookies by grouping Chrome users by interests. (Google killed off FLoC in 2022 after the product was met with privacy concerns.) Spero later worked for the autonomous car company Nuro, while Emi made his way through Tesla and AI biotech company Absci. After ChatGPT launched in 2022, the duo saw a business opportunity to confront a future filled with AI content. In 2023, they founded Checkfor.ai, then renamed the company Pangram a year later. By then, at least a dozen other companies were crowding the detection space, including Originality.ai, GPTZero, and Turnitin; Pangram performed well in some early, independent testing and emerged as a front-runner.

Tech.title: The 42 Best Deals From the REI Labor Day Sale
Tech.content:
Deals on Tents

Courtesy of REI

The REI Half Dome 2 is the best budget two-person backpacking tent. I’ve toted it on many backpacking trips and found it plenty sturdy, quick to set up, and capable of fitting two people along with their gear. It even comes with a footprint (which I never bother with, but it's nice to have it if you have to deal with pointy rocks).

The Big Agnes Copper Spur series is our top pick among freestanding ultralight tents. This is the bike-packing model, which features shorter pole segments that are easier to haul on a bike, but I really prefer it for the more subdued colors. The Copper Spur is a high-quality, well-designed tent that's lightweight, easy to set up, and roomy enough to be livable in the backcountry. The “awning” design (with trekking poles or sticks) is a nice extra.

Nemo's Dragonfly tents are roomy for the weight. There's a generous amount of mesh at the top, which provides some nice ventilation on warm summer nights and is perfect for falling asleep under the stars when the weather permits. The Osmo fabric is a blend of nylon and polyester that absorbs less water than pure nylon rainflies.

MSR's Groundhog stakes aren't cheap, but they're the best backpacking tent upgrade you can make. They're superstrong—I've never had one bend or pull out on me—and considering their strength, they're pretty lightweight. I suggest carrying a mix of stakes when backpacking—some of these, some carbon fiber pegs, and some shepherd hooks. That way, no matter the terrain, you've got something that'll work.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

REI's Base Camp tent is my favorite car camping tent. It's a traditional dome tent design, with two crossed poles and two side poles, that hold up very well in wind. The floor is high-quality 150-denier polyester, which so far has not shown any signs of abrasion, despite quite a few nights on rough ground out West. Inside, there are loads of storage pockets, and the double doors make great vents in warmer weather, with huge windows that ensure you catch any whiffs of breeze on hot nights.

The Marmot Halo is my favorite all-weather four-person family tent. The low-profile design stands up better to wind, while the steep sidewalls maximize interior space. It also has a nearly full-length rain fly, which helps make this a real haven in a storm. The name comes from the unusual pole design. There are two cross poles, like every square, domed tent, but the side poles connect halfway up the tent body instead of at the ground. The only downside is that you can't stand up in it. If you want more room, the six-person version, which, with a 76-inch peak height, may be tall enough for you to stand up in, is also on sale.

Deals on Hiking Boots and Shoes

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

My favorite barefoot sandals are 25 percent off right now. I always call these the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust, and I'd still bring Chacos if I were white-water rafting, but for everything else these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale.

The best all-around barefoot shoe, the Prios are your classic sneaker reimagined for barefoot shoe enthusiasts. When you were a kid, you had just one pair of shoes: The Prios are that pair. The toe box is wide enough for my toes to splay out nicely, and the heel cup is snug with no slipping. The ground feel is great too, enough feedback to feel barefoot, but you're not going to wince when you hit a sharp stone.

Courtesy of Altra

Altra's Lone Peak shoes have carried countless thru-hikers to the finish line. The Lone Peak first came on the scene in 2011 and quickly built a cult following. They're light (11.5 ounces) and very comfortable in our testing. The reinforced toe and heel offer excellent protection against rough, rocky trails, and while they're much more padded these days than early versions, they're still zero drop.

Keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

The La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky.

Camping Gear Deals

Courtesy of Kelty

This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is somewhat huge, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works well and has produced some great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example: It's comfortable (it does wobble a little side-to-side when you move) and less than half the price of competitors.

I've noticed that when people try to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter backpack, they struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which smashes anything soft down to about half the size of the same item in a regular stuff sack. This works well with sleeping bags and clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino wool.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

The Flash 22 is one of the best-value day packs on the market, especially on sale. It's surprisingly comfortable despite the lightweight straps and minimal padding. It carries loads up to 15 pounds without straining the shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. Note that this deal is only on the patterned colors.

WIRED staffers have North Face duffels that have been going strong for 25 years, earning a spot in our Buy It for Life guide. They're big ol' bags (this one is 62 liters), capable of swallowing gear like a whale, and unlike all the other identical cases on the luggage carousel, they’re always easy to spot. This version is made of phthalate-free, recycled PVC and recycled nylon that’s treated with a non-PFC water-repellent (DWR) finish.

Deals on Outdoor Clothing

Now is a great time to score some new base layers and mid layers ahead of the cooler months, or pick up one of our favorite rain jackets.

Photograph: Adrienne So

Arc'teryx's Beta AR rain jacket is one of the burliest rain jackets I've tested. The Beta AR uses 40D fabric for most of the face, with reinforced 80D patches in high-wear areas, all of it with a Gore-Tex Pro 3L membrane. It's been the only Gore-Tex jacket I've tested that hasn't wetted out yet, and the pit zips provide excellent ventilation. At 1 pound, 0.3 ounces, it's not the lightest jacket, but you'd be hard-pressed to find anything else this durable at this weight.

This is an REI Outlet deal because it's been discontinued, which is a shame (hopefully that just means new colors are coming next year). REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides, but if you prefer, the regular top (on sale for $30) is also on sale, as is the base layer bottom (on sale for $30).

Nothing says outdoors like a hatchet loop on your pants. Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers give you that and great ventilation. The Vidda Pro uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere and extras like ventilation zippers, reinforced knees (with openings for pads), and that sweet, sweet hatchet loop on the leg.

Sleeping Bag and Sleeping Pad Deals

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Our favorite backpacking sleeping bag, the Bishop Pass 15 offers the best warmth-to-weight ratio while packing down small and staying affordable. I have slept in this bag for more than two weeks, with nighttime temps ranging from 28 to 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and, yes, it was too warm in the heat, but on those warmer nights, I unzipped it and used it as a blanket. It isn't perfect, but it's a versatile bag.

REI's Magma line of down gear is some of the best value around. The Magma 15 sleeping bag has long been an affordable option that's perfect for shoulder-season trips when the temperature potentially swings lower than you expect (the comfort rating is 21). There are three lengths and three widths, which makes it easy to find a perfect fit for your body, and the 850-fill-power goose down (Bluesign-approved) packs down nicely and small. If you don't need the shoulder-season coverage, the Magma 30 is also on sale for $262 ($87 off), and it makes a great summer sleeping bag.

This down mummy bag has a spoon-shaped design for side sleepers and extra room in the elbows and knees so you can roll over onto your side without feeling like you're slipping into a straitjacket. It's built for temps down to 30 degrees Fahrenheit and has zippered gills you can open to avoid overheating when it's warmer.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

The best budget ultralight quilt, the Magma Trail is a great value for the money. The lower price does mean that this one is a bit heavier (it uses 850-fill-power down), though at 24 ounces for the long, wide version I have, it’s competitive on the scale. The straps for attaching it to your sleep pad aren’t as nice as what you’ll get with something like the Enlightened Equipment's Revelation Quilt, but it’s just as warm and does a respectable job of keeping out drafts. There's even a zippered foot box with a drawstring for cooler nights.

Nemo's Pulse quilt uses RDS-certified, gold-infused 1,000-fill-power ExpeDRY down, which does a good job of shedding moisture from tent condensation and reportedly dries faster than standard down, though I've never figured out a good way to test this. The Karo Step baffle stitching keeps down well distributed, and at 12 ounces for the regular, this one is pretty dang lightweight.

Courtesy of REI

This is our favorite sleeping bag for car camping. The REI Siesta is plenty warm and affordable. It's also not a mummy bag because you're not climbing Denali here. The rectangular cut makes for a much roomier, more comfortable sleeping experience. The 20-degree-Fahrenheit rating makes it warm enough for three seasons, and unlike most rectangular bags, the Siesta has a hood, which helps on those cold nights.

The Kindercamp makes a great car camping bag if you've got young children. Once your kids are about 4 feet tall, an adult sleeping bag works just fine. Prior to that, they'll benefit from a kids' sleeping bag like the Kindercamp, which is cut smaller so your little ones don't have to heat up a huge, adult-size sleeping bag to stay warm.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

There are other good sleeping pads out there, but nothing compares to the Therm-a-Rest NeoLoft for comfort. This pad reinvigorated my love of backpacking by ensuring that I get a great night's sleep. It's cushy and comfortable, especially if you're careful not to overinflate it. The R-4.8 insulation keeps you warm down to about freezing, though I've used it in colder conditions by pairing it with a closed-cell foam pad.

The Z-Lite Sol weighs next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), folds up compact enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and will completely change your backpacking experience for the better. I am too old and too soft to sleep on just this anymore, but I use it as a chair, padding for a nap on the rocks, a table, extra padding on cold nights, and more. It's possibly the most versatile piece of gear I own.

If you want to feel like you never left your bed at home, this is the camping pad to get. You really have no idea how comfortable tent camping can be until you sleep on a Megamat. The firm, 4-inch-thick pad is both soft and surprisingly firm thanks to the closed-cell foam inside, which relieves pressure and feels about as close to the mattress in your bedroom as you're going to get in the woods.

Camp Stove and Water Filter Deals

Nothing says camping like roasting marshmallows over open flames and burning beans on the camp stove. Check out our guides to the best backpacking stoves and best camping stoves for more picks.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe is our top pick for a backpacking stove. It wins the title thanks to its larger burner area, which allows the flame to spread out for faster boil times and better fuel efficiency, especially with larger pots. It also fared better in the wind than smaller burners. The genius of the deluxe model is the small curved lip around the burner, which helps keep wind from getting to the base of the flame. It's a small design element, and one that you certainly want. During long-term testing, I found it more effective at maintaining a simmer in the wind, should you want to do any actual cooking.

You can put together a lighter cooking setup, but Jetboil's Stash is the lightest all-in-one system out there, and it does boil water a bit faster than the rest. The heat diffuser design speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I could only match indoors in still air), but the real appeal is how this kit packs down into itself and how simple it is to use.

Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

While I prefer the larger burner head of the Deluxe model above, the MSR PocketRocket 2 is lighter at 2.6 ounces compared to the Deluxe's 2.9. It still has wide enough arms to support just about any one- or two-person pot. It's simple to use, even while wearing gloves, and it's efficient. At 947-foot elevation, it boiled 1 liter of water in 3 minutes, 47 seconds. You can even get it to simmer, though the flame radius is small, so fancier cooking isn't easy.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

MSR's WhisperLite series is probably the most popular backpacking stove ever made. They last forever (mine is over 30 years old and still works great), and this model, the Universal, can use just about any fuel you can imagine—white gas, kerosene, unleaded gasoline, and isobutane-propane canisters, to be precise. The only downside is that it can be fiddly compared to stoves like the Jetboil. But if you're headed out on a long trip, buying fuel as you go, this is the most flexible option out there.

This is by far the most compact two-burner stove I've tested. It's my pick for any situation where space is at a premium—whether that's canoeing or just because you have a small car. The burners are large, and with some practice, I could get a light, simmer-friendly flame. My main gripe is the windscreen, which is not the best. The Basecamp version, with fitted pots, is also on sale for $300 ($100 off).

Courtesy of Coleman

My favorite stove in Coleman's current lineup, the Coleman Cascade 3-in-1 features heavy-duty cast-iron grates and comes with a cast-iron griddle and grill. It'll comfortably fit a 12-inch pan and a 10-inch pan side by side, and it's significantly sturdier and more robust than other Coleman stoves, making it worth the extra money if you use it often. That said, the much cheaper stove below will get you by if you're only using it a few nights a year.

This stove is ubiquitous at campgrounds for a reason. It's well-built, sturdy on a table, and just works. It's not the most powerful stove, and it lacks frills like push-button ignition, but it's capable of holding a low flame, simmering soups, and cooking scrambled eggs without browning them. It's also incredibly durable.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

The MSR Gravity Autoflow filter is a must-have for backpacking with a group. To use this filter, scoop up 10 liters of water in the dirty water bag, attach the hose, connect your water bottle, and sit back and relax. The filter is good enough to keep you safe from all the usual protozoa and bacteria, and the flow rate is a solid 1.5 liters per minute when the filter is clean.

The MSR Guardian is our pick for trips with sketchy water sources because it filters down to 0.02 microns, which will even remove viruses. It is heavy at 22 ounces and may be overkill for trips in the US, but it's a great option for overseas adventures. I really like that it's designed to be self-cleaning, which makes field maintenance incredibly easy, and that it screws right onto a Nalgene bottle. Also, because it's a pump filter, it's very fast. You can crank out a couple of liters in hardly any time at all. The gravity-fed version is also on sale at Backcountry for $232 ($78 off).

Deals on Action Cameras and Gadgets

If you snap a selfie in the woods and Instagram isn't around to see it, did it happen? You'll never have to answer that question if you've got one of our favorite action cameras or 360 cameras with you.

Photograph: Scott Gilbertson

Insta360's X6 360 camera just launched—our review will be coming soon—but the X5 is still a great option, especially on sale. The twin 1/1.28-inch sensors capture 8K video, which means you can reframe your footage to fit rectangular video formats and still have nearly 4K clips sharp enough to mix with footage shot with your phone. The dynamic range is impressive, and the X5 also has great battery life.

If you're going to turn your action camera on yourself, consider the Ace Pro 2, our top pick for vlogging. It has a great lens and sensor co-engineered with Leica, is capable of recording 8K video at up to 30 frames per second (fps), and has some pretty darn nice color even in the default settings. My guess is that the Ace Pro 3 is coming pretty soon, but this is still a good deal.

Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

Tech.title: A Prop 65 Crash Course: What You Need to Know (2026)
Tech.content:
My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.

I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.

California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.

So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.

Courtesy of Stephen Osman/Getty Images

Proposition 65, Explained

In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.

It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.

“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.

The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.

And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.

Prop 65 Is Everywhere

Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.

The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.

FAQs

Are Booking.com Coupon Codes Available for Flights and Car Hire, or Just Hotels?

Genius is Booking.com's free loyalty tier. Once you've stayed a certain number of times, you unlock automatic discounts (typically 10% or more) on eligible properties, plus perks like free breakfast or room upgrades — no code needed, it applies automatically at checkout.

It depends on the property and offer terms. Genius discounts are usually baked into the displayed price, while promo codes are applied separately, so it's worth checking the final total before confirming.

Tech.title: Oura’s Menopause Impact Scale Expands Out of the App and Into Women’s Health Care
Tech.content:
Despite 1.3 million women entering menopause each year, this stage in a woman’s life remains stigmatized and understudied. But a rise in femtech centered on menopause could help change that.

In June, Apple announced that its Health app now supports cycle tracking for both menopause — when a woman’s menstrual period permanently stops, and she can no longer get pregnant — and perimenopause, the transition to menopause. One month earlier, Oura released its Menopause Impact Scale, a self-reported questionnaire in its app that establishes how menopause symptoms impact a woman’s quality of life.

On Wednesday, Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, announced in a press release that its MIS is expanding beyond the app and into women’s health care and tech. The first 10 partners include menopause-focused clinical care companies Alloy Health, Gennev, Wisp and Pomelo; women’s health care companies Maven, Tia and Xella; and hormone and biomarker tracking companies Oova, Mira and Hertility.

“By integrating the MIS into how our partners work with patients, we’re giving women a measurement that travels with them and gives every provider they see the same starting point,” said Dorothy Kilroy, Oura’s chief commercial officer, in the press release.

How the MIS works

Developed by Oura’s own science and clinical teams, the company explains on its website that the MIS differs from current menopause assessment tools, which were created decades ago and measure only symptom frequency and severity. Instead, the MIS has Oura app users reflect on 22 symptoms associated with perimenopause and postmenopause across seven domains: sleep maintenance, cognitive functions, body image, hot flashes, sexual function and vaginal symptoms, musculoskeletal pain and urinary tract symptoms.

Both the total and domain scores can be exported as a PDF, so users can share this information with a doctor. Oura

For each symptom, a user is asked about how much it has affected their quality of life over the past two weeks. They can select: none, a little, moderately, quite a bit or extremely.

A mean score is calculated for each of the seven domains, ranging from 0 to 4, and the sum of these scores yields a total impact score from 0 to 28: 0 to 7 means minimal impact, 7 to 14 means mild impact, 14 to 20 means moderate impact and 21 to 28 means high impact.

Once the first assessment is complete, a reminder is sent 30 days later for reassessment and to monitor symptom trends over time.

According to the press release, over 600,000 Oura members have taken the MIS, and 35% of the members who have completed it once complete it at least one additional time.

Note that just like the Oura Ring and the Oura app’s other features, this questionnaire is not for diagnosis or treatment of medical conditions. A doctor is still required for that.

When will the MIS partner integrations occur?

Starting Wednesday, Oura members can integrate their MIS results with Alloy Health, Oova, Xella, Pomelo and Wisp.

Although there’s no specific release date, Maven, Mira, Hertility, Gennev and Tia integrations will be available later this year.

How much does Oura cost?

To access the MIS, you need both an Oura Ring and an Oura subscription. The Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, and the membership is $6 per month, totaling $72 per year.

The transition to menopause typically lasts between seven and 14 years, adding up to an additional $504 to $1,008 if someone wants to use the MIS repeatedly and, most importantly, as intended to keep track of their symptom trends.

Oura and privacy

In its privacy policy, Oura states that it doesn’t sell or rent members’ personal information. Members control third-party integrations and can disconnect them at any time.

Following an Electronic Frontier Foundation report in July about how most smart fitness devices lack essential data protection, Oura committed to issuing transparency reports in the future.

However, you should always exercise caution before sharing your information — especially health data — with any company.

What this means for women’s health

As femtech expands and more companies create technology that brings women’s health to the forefront, the stigma surrounding topics such as menopause could decrease, expanding into doctors’ offices as medical professionals start to take women’s symptoms seriously.

At the same time, this also means more companies will attempt to capitalize on the trend or, as a 2022 New York Times article called it, the “menopause gold rush.” We’ve already seen devices costing hundreds of dollars that are marketed toward women experiencing menopause in the name of hot flash relief.

With the rise of menopause-focused femtech, there are both benefits and drawbacks. Hopefully, the former will outweigh the latter, making it easier for women to have conversations about what they’re experiencing in their bodies — especially where it may matter most: in doctors’ offices.

Tech.title: The Cheap Kitchen Tool I Bring to Every Rental House or Airbnb
Tech.content:
You don’t need chef training to be picky about the tools you use in the kitchen. That goes doubly for when you might be called to someone else’s kitchen, whether that’s a family holiday situation or a rental property. If you’re cooking for the group — by coercion or self-nomination — you have every right to want to use whatever tools and gadgets make you most confident about the outcome. Especially when feeding a crowd.

I’m known to travel with cooking supplies and have even taken my cake pans across the Atlantic. In my defense, I was A) making a multi-tiered birthday cake and B) making it for my future siblings-in-law, whom I was meeting for the first time. My then-boyfriend, now-husband, is a great cook, it must be said, but cake wasn’t a regular part of his repertoire, and I didn’t want to take my chances with whatever might have been lurking in the darkest corners of his kitchen cabinets.

I used to travel to summer beach rentals with all manner of basic tools: tongs, a whisk, a rubber spatula, you name it, plus a fleet of knives, a good bottle of olive oil and bagged-up samples of my entire spice rack.

After a couple of years, I realized that most beach rentals, at least on the East Coast, were pretty well-equipped, and I was happier not having to schlep my entire kitchen to feel empowered to make dinner. I might stash a chef’s knife, just in case, but more often than not, even that would stay tucked in my bag.

Kitchen gear at a rental house is always hit-or-miss. Connect Images/Getty

There is only one tool, however, whose utility is so singular that it can’t be substituted, that, in my experience, is the key between a good dinner and a great dinner (and dessert) and that, surprisingly, you can’t always reliably find in other people’s kitchens.

My Microplane, myself

The Microplane is an essential tool I can’t count on finding in the drawers of an Airbnb. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Yes, it’s a Microplane. If you’re now puzzling over how a handheld zester of all things is that important a tool, well, some of you have never enjoyed scraped-together key lime pie for breakfast at the beach, and it shows.

But seriously. There is no other tool that does what a Microplane does to the same degree. Using a paring knife to gingerly cut the rind off citrus fruits without taking the pith with you and then mincing that up? I’ve done it. Hard pass.

A box grater is not likely to do the trick. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t start with me about some cheap grocery store zester that manages to be both ergonomically overcomplicated and entirely ineffective. A box grater that you would typically use for cheese or carrots that has that one plane dedicated for zesting? Have you tried it lately? (Actually, has anyone ever? It just looks like a recipe for pulpy zest and bloody knuckles.)

Microplane Zester $18 on Amazon

Why the zester is an essential kitchen tool

Maybe your dubiousness isn’t so much the quality of the tool itself, but why any kind of zester is that critical? To which I challenge you: the next time you make salad dressing or pasta, enchiladas or pad thai, or anything at all that calls for citrus juice, add a hit of zest and see what that does to the outcome. Citrus zest adds several times the flavor, minus the sharp acidity. In a word, it adds vibrancy to whatever you’re doing, without the pucker. It’s a wow factor with the simplest execution. Not to mention: key lime pie for breakfast.

A hit of zest is like fairy dust for food. Pamela Vachon/CNET

And the economics are inarguable. Even in today’s economy, a lemon or lime can only set you back so far, but it contributes so much. And the Microplane itself? Is all of about $18.

Here I am waxing all poetic about citrus, but let’s also talk about two other cooking champions whose processing is made infinitely easier by a Microplane. Garlic and ginger — also cheap yet dynamic ingredients. A garlic press is a fine thing, but if yours is as difficult to clean after use as most I’ve owned have been, ditch it. The microplane can do that work for you, and basically rinses clean afterward.

A zester will inspire you to grate cheese over, well, everything. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Or if you’ve been buying pre-shredded Parm or another hard cheese, here’s another taste test challenge for you. It’s so quick to just grab a hunk and shave directly into or onto whatever you’re making or eating, with the added bonus of leaving out the additional starches that act as anti-clumping agents in the pre-shredded stuff. I could also make a point here about freshly grated nutmeg, but that would be extra. Suffice to say, I never make béchamel without it.

Microplanes of a different color

My go-to zester comes in more than a dozen colors.

If you’re convinced, I am partial to the Microplane brand here, whose handles are especially comfortable and which includes a protective sleeve for storage. Incidentally, you can also get a Microplane in over a dozen colors, and they are made in the US, if buying locally is a compelling argument.

If you’re already a Microplane evangelist and have made it this far, here’s an invitation to maybe upgrade yours. They don’t last forever, as the blades will dull over time. I recently switched out my 15-year-old model, and it has brought new life to my kitchen.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

For argument’s sake, I also checked out one of Amazon’s best-selling and least expensive models, the MasterChef version, which retails for only $10. It’s a little more generous in width, and its protective cover is admittedly a little easier to maneuver. Functionally, it works just like the Microplane, but is made in China for those keeping score.

Tech.title: How to Tell if That New Device Is a Flock Surveillance Camera
Tech.content:
US cities continue to fight about Flock Safety and the company’s AI cameras and license plate tracking technology. Some areas, including my own town, are canceling Flock contracts and even wrapping cameras in trash bags, while others are setting up new Flock cams — often without residents even knowing what’s going on.

The problem is that while there’s so much concern over Flock cameras and various abuses by law enforcement, people aren’t always great at spotting Flock cams in the real world. It leads to lots of mistaken fears about radar, traffic cameras, trail cams and other various, nontracking devices. That’s one reason I’m not a huge fan of crowdsource-dependent apps such as DeFlock, which can give conflicting information based on what people think is Flock.

That’s why I’m breaking down exactly what a Flock installation looks like — and how to tell whether you’re looking at one, a similar ALPR camera or something else entirely.

Look for the telltale Flock camera shape and logo

You can still identify most Flock cameras by their distinctive design. Allen J. Schaben/Contributor/Getty

Flock Safety’s brand has a very clear camera shape, so with a closer look, it’s typically easy to tell if it’s a Flock automatic license plate reader camera or something else.

Watch for the classic oval, hooded shape of the camera with a circular lens, a near-universal mark of Flock camera.

Notice this competitor brand Obvio has a distinctly different design than Flock, and may not offer the same surveillance services.

Not all license plate cameras are Flock, and that can matter for your privacy. Chip Somodevilla/Staff/Getty

Keep in mind, Flock offers a variety of additional camera features, including AI person detection and sound detection, like listening for gunshots, so not every model looks exactly the same. But this is still one of the first and simplest ways to detect a Flock brand camera. If you get very close, you can also small, shiny, stem-like Flock logo on the front of the cameras.

Some Flock cameras don’t have the slim hood, but the color, general design and logo still give them away. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

I have seen reports of other ALPR cameras hidden inside objects like fake plants, but this doesn’t appear to be Flock’s typical approach and is very rare so far.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

Look for Flock’s visible solar panel arrays

Flock’s solar panels often have a distinctive look. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

Next, look for Flock’s large, dark-colored solar panels, which are typically angled above the camera or close by on the same mount. Many ALPR cameras use solar panels so they can be installed nearly anywhere, but Flock’s have a unique design that’s more noticeable the longer you look at the cameras.

If you see what you think is a surveillance device without a solar panel, it probably isn’t one, or at least not one associated with Flock and its camera competitors like Axon or Obvio.

For example, red-light or speed cameras may be wired into traffic-light mounts, but they are used for traffic enforcement and don’t carry the same surveillance baggage as general ALPR cameras. While they automate certain aspects of traffic enforcement and take pictures of license plates, they don’t typically have the AI recognition, broad police search capabilities, or ways to recognize individual vehicles and people like Flock can (although they can still make communities uncomfortable).

Red light and traffic cameras aren’t Flock, and don’t have the same surveillance capabilities as Flock. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Contributor/Getty

Remember, Flock and ALPR solar panels are always larger and more public than the panels people use for their home security cameras. Fortunately, there are other ways to make sure.

Check what surveillance equipment local law enforcement has bought

Searching the Atlas of Surveillance by city or county can surface Flock Safety camera locations, contract details and any reported data-sharing agreements with federal agencies. EFF

I recommend confirming your community is using Flock cameras even if you think you’ve spotted one. One of the best ways is with the Atlas of Surveillance website, which uses dedicated research to collect the different surveillance technologies that cities, police and sheriff departments have bought and are using.

The Atlas of Surveillance tries to stay as current as possible, and you can search by town or county in just a few seconds. It links to reports or public records to confirm use if possible. I’ve used it frequently to trace Flock activity in certain areas, not only with cameras but with growing numbers of surveillance drones, too. It works with multiple types of devices and platforms that law enforcement uses, making it one of the most dependable ways to corroborate that your local government recently started using Flock cameras.

When I talked to senior research Beryl Lipton from the Electronic Frontier Foundation about using the website, she said, “People should start by searching for their town and county to see what technology is in play close to home. While folks may expect some larger cities to use some of these devices, I think people will be surprised to see how common they’ve become in mid-sized and rural areas too.”

Lipton also recommended using a similar tool, the Street-Level Surveillance hub, which is more focused on the complex ways today’s agencies use surveillance technology. With both tools together, you should have a good idea what your community is facing.

Check who owns the property and what contracts they may have

Private companies like Home Depot can use Flock too, which makes it confusing when cameras are posted around parking lots. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

Flock doesn’t just contract with cities or police departments. That means that while a city government may have canceled Flock Safety cameras, local businesses can use them on their private property, which can cause a lot of confusion among worried people.

If it doesn’t appear your local government is using Flock cameras, try to find out who owns the property with a camera on it, and if they contract with Flock. Home Depot and Lowe’s, for example, are very open about using ALPR cameras, including Flock’s, in their parking lots, and sometimes share that data with police.

Local businesses and neighborhood entities like HOAs can also contract with Flock, but you can often ask them directly if they have AI surveillance cameras and why.

Ask your city council

Asking your city government and showing up to meetings is a great way to find out what’s going on with Flock. The Washington Post/Contributor/Getty

Going to your city council, especially in person, can also be helpful (even Darth Vader thinks so). You can find out about present or future connections with Flock and make your opinion heard. You may also discover that, as I’ve seen before, cities have canceled their Flock contracts and no longer use the cameras, but they still stay up because no one is sure how to legally remove them.

I’ve also seen city councils unsure what Flock cameras are or how police use them, essentially signing off on police and sheriff budgets without knowing what they’re paying for, which is a sign that auditing and accountability practices are lacking. Or, I’ve noticed some cities announce new camera or surveillance programs but carefully avoid using the word “Flock” even though they are contracting with Flock Safety.

Asking direct questions to public servants can help handle issues like these. Look for council meetings where the public is welcome, and try writing or calling your city council to ask about their plans for Flock, if any.

File a public records request

Check if your city or state supports public records requests. You may be able to use a government website to formally request access to information about ALPR cameras, installations and contract documents.

Depending on the public records portal, you may have to be very specific about the kind of information you want, and which government body has it — the police department vs. the city, for example. My other steps are a good start to the research you need if you want to access public records like this.

While not every camera is from Flock, knowing which are — and which have ALPR or person detection capabilities — is a key step in avoiding confusion and protecting your privacy.

Tech.title: How to Watch Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ Event Next Week
Tech.content:
Apple

Apple is holding its next event, which the company is calling “Surprise and shine,” next week on Sept. 9. Historically, Apple has used its September event to announce new hardware, particularly the newest models of iPhones. That means we only have a few days left to see if Apple will release the rumored foldable iPhone.

You can catch the Apple event on Apple’s website, Apple TV, the Apple Developer app and the company’s YouTube channel on Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. ET, 6 p.m. BST). We expect to hear from Apple’s incoming CEO, John Ternus, for the first time in his role after he takes up the mantle on Sept. 1.

Here’s what Apple could announce at the event.

A foldable iPhone

Whether Apple calls it the iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra or the iPhone Flip, the company could show off a foldable iPhone at its September event. Leaks and supply chain reports suggest the foldable iPhone will be a squat, book-style foldable, similar to the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8.

This is a mock-up of what a possible iPhone Fold might look like, according to CNET designer Jeffrey Hazelwood. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Those same leaks also suggest the price of the iPhone foldable could be between $2,000 and $2,500, which could price many people out. According to a CNET survey, US adults are only willing to spend an average of $781 on a foldable iPhone, which is less than the price of the base model iPhone 17 ($799).

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, said that foldable phones remain a niche interest among most shoppers, but that Apple is likely to price the device to reflect its expensive manufacturing costs.

New iPhone 18 Pro models

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

According to Bloomberg, Apple could unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at its September event, too. Those iPhones could also see a price hike, with prices starting at $1,200, up from the iPhone 17 Pro‘s starting price of $1,100.

You might notice that entry-level iPhone 18 models are missing from that lineup. That’s because Bloomberg suspects Apple will split the iPhone launch this year. That means we could see the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September before Apple rolls out the iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and potentially a refreshed iPhone Air in the spring.

New Apple Watches

The (from left to right) Apple Watch Ultra 3, Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch SE 3. Apple could show new Apple Watches at its event in September. Carly Marsh/CNET

Apple is also reportedly preparing to announce an Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its September event. According to Bloomberg, the new watches could include faster chips and new health and fitness features. However, the new watches likely won’t receive a design change.

There’s no solid information about how much these watches will cost. However, Apple has raised a lot of hardware prices this year, so while the starting price of the Apple Watch 11 is $399, the Apple Watch 12 could cost more at launch.

The AirPods 5

The AirPods 4 (pictured) are a few years old now, so Apple could show AirPods 5 at the company’s September event. Apple/CNET

Bloomberg also reports that Apple could debut the AirPods 5 at the September event, releasing an updated version of the company’s entry-level headphones. Apple released the AirPods 4 almost two years ago, in 2024. Apple isn’t expected to show the rumored camera-equipped AirPods at the September event. We could see those later this year, or in 2027.

The AirPods 4 had a starting price of $129 at launch, but given Apple’s other price increases, the AirPods 5 could also see a higher starting price.

Apple did not immediately respond to CNET’s request to comment.

For more Apple news, here’s what to know about the new M6 Mac Mini and when you might be able to preorder an iPhone 18.

Tech.title: Acer Recommits to Repairability With New Vero 16 Laptop
Tech.content:
Acer is a brand closely associated with budget workhorse machines — the company largely manufactures laptops for entry-level gamers, students and office workers. It’s an admirable (and tough) niche to fill at a time when RAMageddon is inflating hardware component prices and even sub-$700 laptops feel like a dying breed.

Maybe that’s why the company is continuing to throw its weight behind the right-to-repair movement with the fourth-generation Vero 16 revealed at IFA 2026. If you’re going to be shelling out more cash for a so-called “budget laptop,” it makes sense that you’d want it to stand the test of time. The repairable and upgradable Vero 16 is one way for the company to adapt to changing market conditions.

While that more modular Vero design is one of the laptops Acer is positioning front-and-center at the show, its other clamshells certainly aren’t being ignored: Two new lightweight Swift laptops are making their debut at IFA 2026.

The latest Vero 16 doesn’t look quite as distinguishable as its predecessor. Whether that’s a good thing is up to you. Acer/CNET

Vero 16

When Acer revitalized its Vero laptop line last year, sustainability was the name of the game. The 2025 version of the Vero 16 had a chassis composed primarily of recycled post-consumer plastic waste and oyster shells. It was a gritty, textured clamshell shot through with gray-blue specks — a spectacle piece, to be sure. And while vague commitments to sustainability and repairability are great, there wasn’t anything especially interesting going on aside from the computer’s oceanic aesthetic.

The next-generation Vero 16 brings the sustainability theme to one of its natural conclusions, and the company ended up with a more interesting computer in the process. The 2026 Vero 16 is an even more repairable laptop, allowing you to swap out or upgrade parts. That could cut back on some waste — and additional expenses for you, the laptop owner.

Parts of the chassis (including the bottom cover, hinge and I/O port covers) are removable, granting Vero 16 owners access to the laptop internals for quick repairs. You’ll be able to swap out a bad battery or SSD on your own, and the device is designed to support processor upgrades for the next two generations. You still might need to bring the computer into a repair shop for more serious maintenance, but there’s a lot here that you can service completely on your own.

While Acer isn’t the only computer manufacturer hopping on the repairability trend, the Vero 16 feels like it fills a niche for folks who might not feel technically savvy enough to benefit from, say, one of Framework’s fully modular computers. This laptop even has a visual repair guide engraved on the chassis to help owners feel more confident about completing simple swapouts. Hey, who knows, maybe that’s what it’ll take for your dad to phone you for computer help a little less frequently?

Every fourth-generation Vero 16 configuration has an OLED panel, with 2.8K (2,880×1,800-pixel) and 2K (1,920×1,200-pixel) resolution options available. The 1,920×1,200-pixel panel will support an optional touchscreen. This clamshell will house up to an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H processor with integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, up to 32GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of storage.

The diminutive Swift Blade is a durable 14-inch laptop. Acer/CNET

Swift Blade 14

Acer’s Swift laptops might not be quite as funky-looking as the Vero 16, but the two new additions to the company’s more premium lineup are some of the sleekest laptops ever from Acer.

The Swift Blade is the more compact entry. This 14-inch laptop weighs just 1.76 pounds and is half an inch thick, making it appreciably lighter than the Swift Edge 14 AI. The Swift Blade 14 can be configured with up to a 2.8K OLED panel, an Intel Core 7 350 Wildcat Lake processor, 12GB of LPDDR5 RAM and 1TB of storage.

With Acer laptops, you’re usually making build quality compromises, as many of the company’s computers have plastic chassis. That’s not the case with the Swift Blade 14, which will be built from a magnesium-aluminum alloy and carbon fiber. These lightweight metallic build materials are crucial for a thin laptop to withstand accidental stress, so I think the Swift Blade could carve out a meaningful place in the brand’s lineup, depending on its price.

The Swift Air 16 is a refresh of one of Acer’s more premium lightweight clamshells. Acer/CNET

Swift Air 16

Unlike the Swift Blade 16, the Swift Air isn’t an entirely new entry into Acer’s sleek laptop lineup. In fact, this 16-inch laptop refresh is rather beefy compared to the rest of the Swift lineup, weighing in at 3.3 pounds. Perhaps that can be attributed to the all-aluminum build, since Acer ditched its magnesium alloy for this particular clamshell.

Like its predecessor, the Swift Air 16 features an up to 2.8K display with OLED and IPS options — certain IPS panels will offer touchscreen support. This laptop houses up to Intel Core 7 350 silicon, 16GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of system storage.

Acer has neither confirmed when its new laptops will be available for purchase nor the prices for the Vero 16, Swift Blade 14 and Swift Air 16. Stay tuned for that information in the coming days.

Tech.title: Acer Shows Off a Transformer-ish Concept for a Windows Gaming Handheld
Tech.content:
Project DualPlay Mini Acer/CNET

While we tend to think of Windows gaming handhelds as primarily gaming devices, they really have more in common with ultralight laptops: They run Windows, have a built-in screen and perform like them thanks to mobile processors with integrated graphics. And though some people have always used them as a primary computer, today’s high prices for both handhelds and traditional computers make handhelds seem like an even more attractive general-purpose option for gamers.

But if you want to play a game with a keyboard and mouse, much less nongaming uses, you frequently experience the cumbersome process of connecting to the input devices or being restricted to wherever you’ve got a dock set up.

Project DualPlay Mini Acer

Acer’s Project DualPlay Mini concept takes a Transformers-like approach to making a handheld more suitable for general computing and KBM gaming: It’s a clamshell laptop design with the speakers on either side of the display, but the 8-inch screen flips up, and the grips are on the back of the speakers, so it turns into a traditional handheld when closed.

You’d still have to connect a mouse, but the built-in keyboard remedies the most awkward design issue. As with any of these devices, you can connect to an external monitor as well as other peripherals as well.

The closest I’ve seen to a multipurpose design in a Windows gaming handheld is Lenovo’s Legion Go series (not the Legion Go Fold, though). But “close” in this case just comes down to a built-in kickstand that makes it a little easier to use on a desktop.

Predator Atlas 7

There aren’t any specs for it — it’s not a real product, at least at the moment — but Acer says it will use the same Intel G3 chips as in its Predator Atlas 8, announced at Computex 2026 in May and slated to ship later this month for an as-yet-unannounced price. The company has followed that with another launch this week for the Predator Atlas 7, a slightly smaller, lighter — and presumably cheaper — 7-inch model. It’s expected to ship around October or later in 2026.

Tech.title: Dell Doubles Down on Cheap Student Laptops With Lower-End Dell 14S Configs
Tech.content:
Dell seemingly isn’t content with taking on Apple’s MacBook Neo with just the XPS 13 for student dollars and attention. On Wednesday the company brought in budget laptop reinforcements with new lower-end, more colorful versions of its mainstream Dell 14S laptop. Dell is playing coy and won’t reveal pricing until we get closer to seeing these new laptops later this fall, which is understandable given the volatility around the ongoing component shortages.

While we await pricing details, here’s what we do know about these new machines. They’ll come in four fun Neo-esque colors, offer Intel Wildcat Lake processors and start with just 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.

New Dell 14S models: Colorful and affordable

The Dell 14S isn’t new. Dell released the 14S series along with its larger 16S sibling back in May. These mainstream laptops are based on Intel Panther Lake processors and were priced north of $1,000. Currently, the cheapest Panther Lake Dell 14S model costs $1,350 (and that’s after a $50 discount).

The new Dell 14S models feature Wildcat Lake processors, which are less powerful, more efficient versions of Panther Lake. You’ll have a choice of either a Core 5 320 or Core 7 350, each of which is a six-core processor made up of two performance cores and four efficient cores. The popular Panther Lake chip, the Core Ultra 7 355, that Dell offers on the inaugural 14S is an eight-core chip with four performance and four efficiency cores. Wildcat Lake processors run at 15 watts with a turbo power limit of 35 watts, while Panther Lake operates at 25 watts with a max turbo power of 55 watts.

So while you are giving up two performance cores in dropping down to Wildcat Lake, you are getting greater efficiency, which should result in longer battery life and quieter operation. Dell says you can expect all-day battery life from the relatively modest three-cell, 61-watt-hour battery.

The Dell 14S offers four color options, including a bold green.

Along with a choice between Core 5 and Core 7 Wildcat Lake processors, the Dell 14S offers a pair of 14-inch display options. Both are IPS panels, but one has a 2K resolution (1,920 by 1200 pixels), 60Hz refresh rate and 300-nit brightness rating, while the other has a finer 2.8K resolution (2,880 by 1,800 pixels), smoother 120Hz refresh rate and brighter 450-nit rating.

Like the XPS 13, the Dell 14S comes with 8GB or 16GB of RAM. Unless you plan to use your laptop for the lightest, most basic of tasks, you are probably better off spending more for 16GB of RAM. I tested both 8GB and 16GB versions of the XPS 13 and concluded that the 16GB model is worth Dell’s steep $200 upcharge for most people. Unlike the XPS 13, the Dell 14S starts off with an undersized 256GB SSD. That’ll fill up fast. Dell offers 512GB and 1TB storage upgrades.

The Dell 14S has a larger display than the 13.4-inch XPS 13 and weighs a bit more because of it. It weighs 2.5 pounds, and the trim XPS 13 is just 2.2 pounds. The 13-inch MacBook Neo is the heaviest of the three at 2.7 pounds. All three laptops offer all-metal designs, which is not a given among the budget class where all-plastic or partially plastic constructions aren’t uncommon.

The Dell 14S has a better port selection than the XPS 13. It has the same pair of 10Gbps USB-C ports as the XPS 13 but also adds an HDMI port and headphone jack.

The Dell 14S in dusty rose looks strikingly similar to the blush color Apple offers for its MacBook Neo.

I really liked the XPS 13, but one of my complaints was targeting it toward students and then not offering any of the fun colors that Apple does with the Neo. With the Dell 14S, you get four color options that rival the cheerful hues Apple offers for the Neo. There’s dusty rose (a soft pink), washed denim (a light blue), velvet green (a bold green and my favorite of the bunch, based on Dell’s photos) and linen (a beige-y gold).

How low can Dell 14S pricing go?

It’s difficult to form too firm an opinion of the Dell 14S before we get pricing for it, but it will face steep competition from Apple’s MacBook Neo and Dell’s own XPS 13 when it’s released later this fall.

With their premium designs and high-resolution displays, both the Neo and XPS 13 are excellent budget options at their discounted student prices starting at $600. The upgraded Neo with more storage and Touch ID at $700 and the upgraded XPS 13 with more memory at $800 are also great buys with their student discounts.

The Dell 14S will need to limbo below those low bars to add a competitive third option for the school set.

Editors’ note: Matt Elliott’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Lenovo. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: This Robot Vacuum Aims to Compete With the Suction Power of a Stick Vacuum
Tech.content:
Robot vacuums are a great way to do some general cleaning, but most lack the power of a dedicated vacuum cleaner because you can’t pack enough suction into a small design. iRobot may have an interesting solution for that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which it describes as the “most powerful robot ever” because it uses a proprietary vacuum seal technology that concentrates suction power on the floor.

“With the Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot, we not only increased overall suction power, but also changed how that suction gets applied to the carpet,” Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said in a statement. “With SealForce, we’re able to seal the chassis against the carpet fibers, so the airflow, which has the greatest impact on pickup performance, has somewhere to go instead of escaping around the edges. More suction helps, but the seal is what takes it to a level beyond what’s previously been possible.”

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA Berlin 2026, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. I’m excited to see the Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot in person on Wednesday. I’ll report back with my impressions later.

iRobot

In a video call with me prior to IFA Berlin 2026, Pope described the technology as being similar to pressing down harder on the carpet when you’re vacuuming with a regular vacuum, to increase the seal and focus the suction on a particular spot. In the case of the Max 875, rather than pressing down, the robot vacuum’s chassis lowers a “skirt” that forms a tight seal against carpet fibers.



Once the seal is established, it can use 35,000 pascals of suction to clean the floor, which iRobot describes as “tornado-like airflow.” The company also says that it has three times deeper carpet cleaning and the best pickup performance to date among its models. Essentially, rather than just boosting suction power, the robot vac is making its suction more targeted and efficient on the surfaces it cleans. It’s a good idea if it works as promised. In our testing, we’ve generally found that cordless vacuums have better suction than robot vacuums, but this type of tech could help robots catch up.

There’s also some other interesting cleaning technology under the hood. To handle dried-on stains on hard floors, the Max 875 Combo continuously sprays heated mist as it mops, loosening and softening older stains so the mop roller can remove them. Pope told me that the new roller mop is also the industry’s largest, has 300 rotations per minute and 18 newtons of downward pressure. The company claims that all this gives the robot vacuum twice the stain removal, 3.75 times deeper scrubbing and 1.2 times wider coverage per pass.

iRobot

Available on other robot vacuums, the 875 Combo has an AI-powered carpet-detection feature that automatically raises the mop when it detects carpet and lowers a protective shield to prevent dripping. It also comes with the other high-end features we’ve come to expect from flagship robot vacuums, including antitangle and hair-cutting main brushes, side brushes, lidar navigation and AI object recognition for more than 300 household objects.

The 875 Combo also has a docking station that washes the mop with water heated to 176 degree Fahrenheit and dries it with air heated to 131 F; it also auto refills cleaning fluid and self-empties into a debris bag that should last up to 90 days.

iRobot

The Roomba Max 875 Combo will cost $1,199 and launch alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. The 678 Combo falls more into a midrange price segment, but it has plenty going for it. It comes with its own unique feature that iRobot calls SprayForce AI.

It uses 40,000 pascals of high-pressure water (not heated) to break up dried messes and improve mopping efficiency by 40%. The mop rollers come with 15 newtons of downward pressure and 30,000 pascals of suction for vacuuming, as well as the SealForce tech. Other capabilities are pretty similar, including automatic mop lifting (without the protector), antitangle and hair-cutting brushes, edge cleaning, lidar navigation and AI obstacle avoidance as well as a self-emptying and self-cleaning docking station.

Both the $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot and AutoWash Dock and the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot and AutoWash dock models are available now at iRobot.com.

Editor ’s note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
